* fix(trusty-installer,trusty-mpm): the supervisor LaunchAgent runs Interactive, not Background, and tm doctor flags a stale ProcessType (Refs #8415)

launchd passes a job's ProcessType to every child. The supervisor plist
declared Background, so each tmux server it resumed, and every tm session
inside it, ran at Darwin priority 4 on efficiency cores.

- plist_bootstrap: template declares ProcessType Interactive.
- install: a failed supervisor plist write or reload now fails the install
  instead of printing a non-fatal warning; the downgrade refusal stays info.
- tm doctor: new launchd_process_type row fails on Background and warns on
  any other value short of Interactive for com.trusty.mpm and its supervisor.
- deploy/supervisor template declares Interactive.

* feat(trusty-mpm): tm doctor reports a running tmux server held at background priority (Refs #8415)

A tmux server keeps the scheduling class it started with, so fixing the
plist does not lift a server that is already clamped. The new tmux_priority
row reads the server PID from `tmux display-message -p '#{pid}'` and its
priority from `ps -o pri= -p <pid>` through an injectable runner:
- below 20 fails, naming the PID, the priority and the restart remedy;
- 20 or above, or no server, is Ok;
- any spawn error, non-zero exit or unparsable answer is Unknown.

fix(trusty-mpm): the configured tmux.alternate_screen decides claude's renderer on every managed and CLI launch path (Refs #8405) (#8446)

* fix(trusty-mpm): config tmux.alternate_screen reaches the daemon-spawned claude, whatever the tmux server inherited (Refs #8405)

The managed launch decided CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ALTERNATE_SCREEN from the
pane environment only. A pane inherits the tmux server's global
environment, a snapshot of whichever process started the server, so the
daemon's own value never reached it and config alternate_screen: true
was ignored: an inherited =1, or no value (default 1), kept claude on
the classic renderer.

- core::alt_screen: configured_env() turns alternate_screen: true into an
  explicit =0 assignment; configured_alternate_screen_at() reads it from
  the named state root; apply_default_when_unset() no longer overwrites
  an assignment the command already carries.
- runtime: ManagedLaunch carries alternate_screen into the spec's env_set
  for spawn, resume and attach. ClaudeCodeAdapter reads the config before
  any side effect and fails the launch on an unreadable config instead
  of falling back to the default.

* fix(trusty-mpm): config tmux.alternate_screen decides the renderer in both directions, on the CLI launch lines too (Refs #8405)

fcfd38e71 fixed only the daemon launch spec and only the `true` direction.
The `tm launch`, `tm connect`, `tm session start` and client `/connect`
lines still carried `${CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ALTERNATE_SCREEN-1}`, so the tmux
server's inherited value decided, and with `false` an inherited `=0` put
claude on the fullscreen renderer.

- core::alt_screen: configured_env(false) now assigns `=1` explicitly;
  configured_shell_assignments(bool) renders it for shell lines (the mouse
  default keeps its yielding operand); configured_alternate_screen() reads
  the operator's state home. managed_shell_assignments() had no caller left
  and is removed.
- core::model_inject: build_claude_command(_with), build_inplace_session_command,
  build_client_session_command and build_agent_command take the resolved
  alternate_screen flag.
- tm launch / tm connect / tm session start / DaemonClient launch_session and
  connect_session read the config first and fail the launch on an unreadable
  config instead of launching on the default.

fix(trusty-mpm): tm-epic manual procedure's phases-block recipe is portable and guarded (#8449)

## Outcome

`crates/trusty-mpm/src/assets/skills/tm-epic/references/manual-procedure.md`
step 6 used `awk -v tbl="$(cat phases-table.md)"`, which on macOS's stock BSD
`awk` throws `newline in string` and emits empty stdout. `gh issue edit
--body-file` accepts the empty file without error, silently wiping the
epic's body. That happened for real while filing #8445 and was recovered
only from a saved copy.

Fixed by moving both the body and the replacement table through file
handles into a `perl` whole-file substitution, so no multi-line value passes
through a shell scalar. Two guards added: capture `body.orig` before any
edit, and refuse to push a regenerated body that is empty or has lost either
marker.

Refs #8376

## Changes

- `crates/trusty-mpm/src/assets/skills/tm-epic/references/manual-procedure.md`
  — step 6's recipe rewritten to use `perl` file-handle substitution instead
  of an `awk -v` shell-scalar interpolation; added `body.orig` capture and a
  non-empty/both-markers guard before pushing the regenerated body.
- `crates/trusty-mpm/changelog.d/8376-manual-procedure-portability.md` — new
  changelog fragment.

Out of scope: the templates' content, the skill body itself, and any Rust.

## Risk

Normal. This is a bundled documentation asset that every epic-filing
dispatch reads, not executed code — but the bug it fixes destroys an epic's
body silently, with no error signal, so leaving it unfixed is the higher
risk.

## Tests

- `cargo fmt --check` — clean on `trusty-mpm`
- `cargo check -p trusty-mpm` — clean
- `cargo clippy -p trusty-mpm --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo test -p trusty-mpm --no-fail-fast` — 7865 passed, 1 failed (baseline,
  see below)
- `bash scripts/check_sld.sh` — 0/0
- `bash scripts/check_test_pointers.sh` — 0 dangling
- `bash scripts/check_line_cap.sh` — 0 violations
- `bash scripts/check_changelog_fragment.sh --staged` — OK

Plus live verification: the old recipe was reproduced failing with
`newline in string` and 0 bytes of output against a three-marker fixture.
The new recipe run against the same fixture changed only the rows between
`phases:start` and `phases:end` — every byte outside the markers identical.

## Baseline

issue #8410 —
`core::builder_capacity::tests::live_readings_are_plausible_on_this_host`,
host-dependent, not branch-caused.

## Gates not run

fix(trusty-mpm): worktree removal admits a tree only when its content has landed, a merged PR carries its HEAD, or its own PR merged — every other case refuses (Refs #7889) (#8440)

* wip(#7889): checkpoint before PM restart

Landed-content admission for both worktree-reclaim ladders (Refs #7889).

Shared predicate `core::worktree_landed_content`: refresh `origin` under a
caller-chosen bound, resolve the landing base (origin/HEAD, else
origin/main, else origin/master), then `git merge-tree --write-tree <base>
HEAD` + `git diff --name-only <base> <tree>`. Empty residue grants and names
the base commit; a residual path refuses and names it; every failure arm is
`Unavailable`, which never grants. `merge_residue` is also what
`merge_into_base_is_a_noop` now calls, so the merged-PR residue check and the
admission cannot drift apart.

Guard: `landing_evidence` distinguishes "GitHub answered, no merged PR" from
"the lookup did not answer"; only the first reaches
`landed_content_admission`. Sweep: gate 5's `NoPr` arm consults the same
predicate through an injected probe, behind gate 6's unsaved-work check; the
doctor's read-only survey never offers it and keeps the pre-#7889 refusal.

State at checkpoint: `cargo check -p trusty-mpm --all-targets` reported three
compile errors in existing test files, all fixed in this commit but not yet
re-verified. No gate has a green verdict line yet.

* fix(trusty-mpm): --user alias for --account, and registry-first gh identity for daemon gh spawns

`tm <url> --user bob-duetto` was refused two ways. clap knew only
`--account`, and in the bare form it stops applying global flags once it
starts collecting the external subcommand's argv, so a trailing flag
arrived as raw tokens and died on "takes no further arguments".

`--user` is now a visible clap alias of the same global arg — one arg, one
field, so every parse position and the existing `is_name_segment`
validation carry over — and `split_trailing_account` lifts either spelling
back out of the external form's tokens.

The second half is the identity the daemon then fails to use. `tm --user`
persists the account onto the project's REGISTRY record, while
`worktree_reclaim_gh::resolve_daemon_gh_env` resolved only the static
`TrustyToolsConfig` `projects:` list, which no operator-facing pinning path
writes. A repository only the pinned account can see was therefore probed
as the machine's global account. The new `core::gh_account_registry` reads
`projects.json` synchronously — no file lock, per `ProjectStore`'s reader
contract — and `resolve_daemon_gh_env` consults it before the static
config, returning the same `GhEnv` shape the session-spawn path injects.

It fails CLOSED. An unreadable registry, an unparsable matching record, and
a pin with no usable credential all return `Err`, which the four gate
closures propagate into the existing `BranchPrState::LookupFailed { reason }`
naming the pinned account. Only "no pin recorded" falls through. An
account pinned without a `config_dir` fails closed for #5851's reason:
`gh auth token -u <account>` does not discriminate on a keyring-backed
host, so minting from it would be the wrong-user probe this prevents.

fix(trusty-mcp,trusty-memory): the stdio bridge recovers inside a live MCP session (#8351) (#8359)

* fix(trusty-mcp,trusty-memory): the stdio bridge recovers inside a live MCP session

The trusty-memory MCP stdio bridge could not recover once its daemon was
unreachable, because two of its failure modes were permanent for the life of
the client session. `run_stdio_bridge` returned `Err` when the daemon could not
be brought up, which exits before stdin is ever read; and every method,
`initialize` included, was forwarded, so a daemon down for the handshake window
made the client mark the server failed. An MCP client re-spawns neither. Ten
seconds of daemon downtime during a `cargo install` ended memory for a session.

trusty-mcp gains three additive seams on the shared forwarder:

- `with_local_handler` answers chosen methods in the bridge process.
- `with_socket_resolver` re-resolves the daemon socket per request, so a bridge
  that resolved a stale path heals on the next call. A resolver failure is an
  error carrying the request's id, never a fallback to the configured path.
- `UdsBridgeConfig::with_bridge_version` names the consumer's build in
  transport-error text, so the next such report is attributable to a binary.

trusty-memory wires all three: the guard's failure is reported on stderr rather
than returned, `initialize` and `tools/list` are answered from
`commands::serve_stdio_local` and the socket is re-resolved per request. The
drift guard is that there is no second table — the local answers come from
`trusty_mcp::initialize_response` and `crate::tools::tool_definitions_with`,
the same calls `transport::rpc::dispatch` makes.

#1152's no-spawn contract is unchanged: nothing here starts a daemon. Its other
half — that an unreachable daemon makes the bridge exit — is deliberately
replaced, and `stdio_bridge_exits_when_no_daemon` is renamed to
`stdio_bridge_exits_on_stdin_eof_and_never_orphans_a_daemon` with the reason at
the change site.

trusty-analyze is left unchanged: it uses the forwarder as a per-call RPC
client and already answers `initialize` in its own dispatcher, so it never had
this failure mode. Every change here is additive.

A `[dev-dependencies]` edge from one workspace crate to another welds their
compile graphs together for every `cargo test -p <crate>` and every
`cargo clippy -p <crate> --all-targets`, while a production `cargo build` pays

each crate's normal-edge closure over workspace members, and fails on any
dev/build edge reaching outside it. An optional normal dependency counts as
normal, so a dev edge that re-declares a crate the normal tree already names —
to turn a test-only feature on — is not flagged; resolver v2 adds no crate for
it.

`.dev-dep-edge-allowlist.tsv` is a ratchet: a row must name an issue, and a row
whose edge no longer exists fails too. It carries one row, trusty-code-gui ->
trusty-code, with the blocker stated.

The fixture suite proves the gate can fail: a test-only edge, that edge
allowlisted, a stale row, a reason with no issue reference, a transitively
normal dep, a build-dependency edge, and a vacuous scan. It runs in CI
immediately before the gate, mirroring the line-cap job's selftest-then-gate

fix(trusty-code-tui): cancel shows "cancelling…" and holds input until the daemon confirms the stop (#8307)

## Outcome
Ctrl-C on a running turn now waits for the daemon's actual answer before
reopening input, instead of assuming the cancel succeeded.

## Changes
- Cancel enters a `cancelling` state: scrollback prints `cancelling…`, the
  composer shows `[cancelling...]`. `accepts_submit()` (`!busy && !cancelling
  && no pending permission`) keeps input closed until `ReplEvent::CancelSettled`
  arrives. Text typed meanwhile is queued in the composer the same way PR #8300
  queues it for a busy turn, so nothing is dispatched and no `-32003` can come
  back.
- `CancelReply::{Stopped, StillCancelling, Failed}` drive the settle: `Stopped`
  prints `cancelled` and reopens input; `StillCancelling` (daemon `-32010`)
  prints a plain sentence, keeps input closed, and a second Ctrl-C asks again;
  `Failed` leaves the cancelling state, never prints `cancelled`, and keeps the
  turn presumed live. No raw JSON-RPC code is ever rendered.
- `TuiEngine::cancel_session_reply` is additive with a default implementation,
  so every existing implementor compiles unchanged. The only implementor
  outside test doubles is `CodeEngine`; `trusty-agents` does not implement
  this trait.
- Known limitation, unchanged by this PR: the daemon's permission gate does
  not watch the cancel flag, so Ctrl-C at an open permission prompt yields the
  `StillCancelling` sentence. Esc still does not cancel in the TUI; only
  Ctrl-C and busy-Up do.
- Pre-existing, not touched here: three `current_task.lock().unwrap()` calls
  in `crates/trusty-code-tui/src/run/mod.rs`.

fix(trusty-common): host sampler refreshes disk metrics every 15 s, not every 1 s sample (#8272)

* fix(trusty-common): refresh disk metrics on a 15 s cadence, not every 1 s host sample

trusty-console idled at a continuous ~5% CPU. A 30 s `sample` of the live
process put essentially the whole cost in `self.disks.refresh(true)` inside
`HostSampler::sample`: on macOS `sysinfo` walks every mounted volume through
`CFURLCopyResourcePropertiesForKeys` and the CacheDelete free-space path, with
os_log calls per volume — hundreds of samples under
`sysinfo::unix::apple::disk::with_autorelease`, against 1 for
`refresh_cpu_usage` and ~13 for `networks.refresh`.

CPU, memory and network keep the owner's 1 s cadence for the per-second
graphs. Disks now refresh on the first sample and thereafter once
`DISK_SAMPLE_INTERVAL_SECS` (15 s) has elapsed, serving the cached
`DiskMetrics` unchanged in between. `HostSampler::with_thresholds_and_disk_interval`
injects the cadence; trusty-console exposes it as `serve --disk-sample-interval`,
mirroring `--host-sample-interval`.

* feat(trusty-agents): inbound dispatch generalizes over channels, #7609 slice 4 (Refs #7609)

One selector decides which channel wakes an assistant for an inbound event,
and it answers exactly one of three sources: the assistant's own channel, a
global channel naming it in `route_to`, or its legacy absorbed `[[listeners]]`
binding. Precedence is (1) then (2) then (3), so a backfilled `route_to` and
the binding it was derived from never both fire for one message.

Every provider runs through the same path, so Slack and Telegram gain global
routing on Gmail's terms. A per-assistant binding that overlays an
account-wide global channel is now storable and stored, which closes the open
item slices 1-3 left; the startup sweep backfills `route_to` for each such
pair through `toml_edit`, preserving comments and key order.

Fail-open arms are logged rather than absorbed: an unreadable assistant
roster, a `route_to` naming an assistant this host does not have, and a

fix(trusty-mpm): bound the reclaim and hygiene sweeps so the daemon keeps answering /health (Refs #7965) (#7978)

## Outcome

The automatic post-merge worktree reclaim sweep and the in-project hygiene sweep no longer stall the daemon. Incident 2026-09-14: `tm ls` and `tm session new` timed out, `GET /health` did not answer within the CLI's 500 ms probe (`core/discovery.rs`), and `pm_guard`'s builder-slot claim denied every builder dispatch. Cause: both sweeps are serial subprocess loops on the blocking pool with no ceiling per child; a sample caught them parked in `small_probe_read` on a child's stdout that never reached EOF, so their hold on host IO was permanent. `/health`'s own synchronous catalog walk (filed separately as #7968) then missed the probe under that load.

Refs #7965

## Changes

New `core/bounded_proc.rs` (kill-on-timeout lifted from the `gh` probe's #6867 implementation; `worktree_reclaim_gh::run_with_timeout` is now an adapter over it, failure taxonomy unchanged); `GIT_TIMEOUT` 60 s per hygiene git command, `PASS_BUDGET` 180 s per hygiene pass, `FETCH_MIN_INTERVAL` 6 h read from `.git/FETCH_HEAD` mtime (fails open toward fetching), `BASE_PAUSE` 200 ms, `TMUX_PROBE_TIMEOUT` 3 s, `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0`; one permit serializes the two sweeps (`services/sweep_status.rs`, `PassGuard` releases on panic); the tmux liveness probe moved off the caller's thread; `tm doctor` gains a background-sweeps row (enabled state, last pass duration, warns at `SLOW_PASS` 60 s); the env kill switches `TRUSTY_MPM_WORKTREE_RECLAIM` and `TRUSTY_MPM_INPROJECT_HYGIENE` are unchanged.

`reclaim_with_probes` previously did `(probes.in_use_now)().unwrap_or_default()`, so a liveness probe that could not answer turned into an empty `LiveClaims` — every candidate then read as unclaimed on the DELETE path. An unanswerable probe now demotes the pass to `ReclaimMode::Report` (survey and list, delete nothing). Every timeout arm refuses rather than reading a candidate as clean/merged/unclaimed, and a killed child's partial output is discarded. Destructive-path invariants #2919/#5661/#6927/#7232/#5856 are untouched.

One `Channel`/`ChannelScope` model replaces the split listener/binding config
surface, with a one-shot migration that writes it into the user's config
without touching the legacy tables. Consumers keep reading the old fields
unchanged; dispatch is deferred to slice 4.

## Changes

Added `crates/trusty-agents/src/channels/{model,resolve,migrate}.rs` holding
the unified `Channel`/`ChannelScope` model. `GlobalConfig` and `AgentConfig`
gain a `channels` field with a `listeners()` derived view over the legacy
`[[listeners]]` tables; the legacy tables keep parsing for one release and now
emit a deprecation warning.

A one-shot migration runs on load: it writes `[[channels]]` into
`~/.trusty-agents/config.toml` via `state_writer::atomic_update` and leaves
`[[listeners]]` untouched. A detached startup sweep separately writes absorbed
per-assistant bindings into `agent.channels.json`, but only when the existing
loader accepts them.

`Binding` gains `event_types` (omitted from serialization when empty) and
`From`/`Into` conversions with `Channel`. `union_channels_by_id` merges
channel lists for `extends`. `resolve_channels` picks per-assistant over
global on a provider+target match; it has no production caller yet.

Every existing consumer of the old listener/binding fields reads through the
derived `listeners()` view, so runtime behavior is unchanged by this PR.
Dispatch onto the new model is slice 4. One known gap from that boundary: a
migrated Gmail listener has no destination, so izzie's binding stays in
`agent.toml` and is absorbed only in memory — slice 4 decides whether to
synthesize a target or relax validation.

Owner rulings applied: 2026-09-12 "same behavior, events and messages";
2026-09-14 global routing option (A), `route_to` (field added now, dispatch
in slice 4).

## Risk

High — this touches persisted user config
(`~/.trusty-agents/config.toml`, `agent.channels.json`). Mitigated by the
migration being additive-only (legacy tables are never modified or removed)
and by a fail-closed parse path: a malformed `[[listeners]]` or `[[channels]]`
table returns `ChannelMigrationError::Parse` naming the offending key and
writes nothing. `GlobalConfig::load`'s pre-existing parse fallback was not
widened by this change.

feat(trusty-memory): MCP results fold to a byte ceiling with a truncation notice and a full escape (Refs #7493) (#7925)

* feat(trusty-memory): MCP results fold to a byte ceiling with a truncation notice and a full escape (Refs #7493)

The seven result-returning MCP tools now fold their serialized response to
48 KiB, enforced once in `dispatch_tool` rather than per handler. Whole
entries are dropped from the tail — never one cut mid-object — and the
response carries `truncated`, `returned`, `withheld`, and a one-sentence
`truncation_notice` naming the knobs that fetch the rest. A recall's L0
identity and L1 essential drawers are protected by layer, not by position,
so the fold drops L2 hits first.

`max_bytes` overrides the ceiling up to 512 KiB with the clamp reported in
the response; `full: true` disables it. A non-integer `max_bytes` or a
non-boolean `full` is an invalid-argument error, not a silent coercion. A
response whose smallest foldable form still exceeds the ceiling ships
anyway, under a notice that says so rather than one claiming it fits. A
measurement that cannot be taken is an error, never an unmeasured body.

Mirrors the trusty-search twin's design (#7493) without importing from it;
consolidation into trusty-common is a follow-up.

* feat(trusty-search): MCP results fold to a byte ceiling with a truncation notice and a full escape (Refs #7493)

One conceptual `search` spilled 77k characters into a session's context.
Diverting an oversized result to a worker model costs about 20k prompt
tokens per round trip, so the owner ruling (2026-09-14) folds it
server-side instead, the shape `session_context_catchup` already uses.

The eight result-returning MCP tools now measure their serialized
response and, over a 48 KiB ceiling, drop WHOLE hits from the tail until
it fits. `meta` reports `truncated`, `returned`, `withheld`, and a
one-sentence `truncation_notice` naming the arguments that fetch the
rest. `max_bytes` overrides the ceiling up to a hard 512 KiB, above which
it is clamped and the clamp reported; `full: true` disables it.

A single hit larger than the ceiling is returned alone rather than as an

* feat(trusty-search): compact field mode for MCP search hits and path_prefix on list_chunks (Refs #7676, #7677)

A hit envelope was 48-72% metadata: `content` repeated `compact_snippet`
verbatim for a small chunk, and ten more fields rode along that an identifier
lookup never reads. `search`, `search_lexical`, and `search_all` now take
`compact: bool` (default false, so no existing caller's shape moves). A
compact hit keeps `path`, `start_line`, `end_line`, `compact_snippet`,
`score`, and `match_reason` — plus `index_id` on the fan-out, the only way to
tell which project a hit came from. The rest are absent, not null. Measured:
7222 bytes -> 2652 bytes for a 10-hit `search`, 63% saved.

The transform lives on the MCP surface, not in the daemon. `SearchQuery.compact`
already defaults to true over HTTP, so making field-dropping follow that flag
would change the shape every HTTP integrator reads today, and the crate's
CLAUDE.md documents that surface as an integrator contract. The MCP layer
instead pins `compact: true` in the daemon body — guaranteeing the snippet that
replaces `content` — and trims the response it returns. No parallel hit type.

`list_chunks` takes `path_prefix`, matched at a path-segment boundary through
the same `path_match::matches_file` predicate `search`'s `path_prefix` uses, so
`foo` does not match a sibling `foobar/`. The filter runs before paging, so
`total` and `next_cursor` describe the scoped set and a one-directory cursor
walk terminates. The durable redb seek is skipped when a prefix is set: it
returns `limit` unfiltered rows, which would produce short pages beside a
whole-corpus `total`.

feat(trusty-mpm): load project MCP entries that match already-registered servers without a trust command (Refs #7672) (#7692)

* feat(trusty-mpm): load project MCP entries that match already-registered servers without a trust command (Refs #7672)

`project_trust::is_project_trusted` because both ship with the clone. That is
right about arbitrary content and wrong about the ordinary case: nearly every
real entry names a server the operator installed themselves, so the warning
fired on projects asking for nothing new.

Owner ruling 2026-09-12 — TRUST BY CONTENT. An untrusted project's entries are
now classified rather than discarded. KNOWN means the executable spec already
exists outside the repository: a trusty-* framework builtin, or an entry in the
operator's own `tm mcp add` registry. KNOWN entries load exactly as they would
for a trusted project; UNKNOWN entries are ignored as before.

`core::mcp_content_trust` owns the comparison. It normalizes both sides to an
executable spec — resolved command path (or an identical unresolved spelling),
args, env keys and values for stdio; transport, URL and headers for remote —
and fails closed on every doubt: a malformed entry, an unmodelled key, a
non-string arg or env value, a resolved/unresolved command split, an unreadable
registry. A matching name is never sufficient, and a reserved builtin name
matches only evidence under that same name, so a spoof cannot borrow another
registered server's content to shadow a framework name.

The `session-scoped MCP config degraded` warning now fires only when an UNKNOWN
entry exists and names it, instead of reporting the whole file as ignored; an
all-known project logs one `debug!` line. `tm doctor`'s session_scope check
reports the KNOWN/UNKNOWN split. `tm project trust` is unchanged.

`[session] plugins` stays fully gated — a plugin carries skills, commands and
hooks rather than one executable spec, so it has no content-equivalence rule.

* fix(trusty-mpm): mcp share grants bind to the server's content digest; share refuses unregistered names; remove unshares (Refs #7672)

The PR #7692 re-review found the share store's lifecycle disconnected from the
registry's: `tm mcp share` recorded a grant for a name with no registered
server, `tm mcp remove` never dropped one, and a grant attached to a NAME — so
share-then-remove-then-re-add under the same name made an unrelated, unshared
server matchable by content, contradicting the module invariant.

The grant is now given to CONTENT. `McpShareStore` records, per name, the
sha256 of the registry entry's normalized executable spec, computed by the one
`mcp_content_trust::normalize` both sides already share. `KnownServers::classify`
treats an entry as shared only while its current digest equals the recorded one;
a mismatch is `UnsharedMatch { stale: true }`, which does not load and whose
warning says the share is stale and names the `tm mcp share` that renews it. A
digest that is not the shape `spec_digest` emits is dropped at load, so a
hand-edited sidecar fails closed.

The CLI closes the same gap from the other side: `tm mcp share` refuses a name
with no registered server (and one whose entry will not normalize) rather than
warning and writing a grant that matches nothing; `tm mcp remove` drops the
grant with the server, best-effort so a broken store never blocks the removal;
and `tm mcp add` over an existing name drops the grant the replaced entry
carried unless `--share-with-projects` re-records it. The three lifecycle cores
take both roots as arguments, so they are tested without a `$HOME` write, which
this binary's `env_isolation_tests` ratchet bans.

* feat(trusty-mpm): auto-memory is a fallback only — off when trusty-memory is reachable, import-auto-memory migrates the index into the palace (Refs #7685)

Owner ruling 2026-09-12: trusty-memory is the memory, and Claude Code's own
auto memory is the FALLBACK that carries a session while trusty-memory is
down. The branch turned auto memory off unconditionally, which would leave a
session with no memory at all whenever the daemon was unreachable.

Conditional writes. `core::memory_reachable` is the one answer to "is
trusty-memory available": one `memory.health` call on the derived socket,
1.5 s, and a JSON-RPC error counts as reachable because only a running daemon
produces one. `prepare_session_inner` resolves it once and writes
`autoMemoryEnabled: false` only when it is true, logging one INFO line naming
the fallback when it is not; `RuntimeAdapter::spawn`/`spawn_resume` resolve it
the same way and hand it to `env_bin_prefix`, which now emits
`CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1` only on that branch. The string builders
stay pure functions of their arguments — the caller resolves, exactly as it
already does for `gh_env` and `session_mcp_env`. Both branches are tested with
an injected boolean: `prepare_session_with_memory_reachable` for the settings
half, `spawn_command`/`resume_command`/`env_bin_prefix` directly for the env
half.

Migration. `tm memory import-auto-memory [--project <dir>]` reads
`<claude-config>/projects/<slug>/memory/`, stores each fact through the same
`memory_remember` call `tm memory import` uses — tagged
`migrated-from-auto-memory`, `name:<name>`, `type:<type>` — moves the file into
`memory.archived-<YYYYMMDD>/` beside the memory directory, and archives and
empties `MEMORY.md` only once every fact has landed. Nothing is deleted, a
failed store leaves its file and the index exactly as they were, and a second
run finds nothing.

Doctor. The `auto_memory` row is tri-state: Fail when trusty-memory is healthy
and auto memory is on or the index still holds facts, Warn when trusty-memory
is down and the fallback is carrying the project, Ok when auto memory is off
and the index is empty. `--fix` still writes only the settings key and names
the migration rather than running it.

The `session_scope` check reported the DECISION — "plugins NOT loaded:

at launch, so a session paused before that write existed, or resumed across the
upgrade that added it, runs against a settings file that never took it. Nothing
compared the decision against the file, and nothing re-applied it.

now the one composition all three consumers read: `write_enabled_plugins` is

merely that nothing is scoped out.

the #7423 output-style precedent. Both writes go through the launch path's own
functions — `write_enabled_plugins_with_trust` and
`session_mcp_scope::provision_at` — never a second implementation. The
`.trusty-mpm/` directory is the guard: no marker, no write and no step. It is
idempotent (a current file takes no write and keeps its mtime), it preserves
every other settings key, a failed write is FAILED rather than applied, and a
successful one is verified back off disk before it is reported.

* fix(trusty-search): coalesce deferred rescans so a batch of undecidable admissions costs one pass (Refs #7396)

disarms the gate as it takes a `Rescan` off its channel, so a defer raised

fix(trusty-console): rebuild the saver's WKWebView after three failed loads, and stop retries cancelling themselves (#7614)

The saver showed the bundled offline preview for three days while the console
answered /ui/screensaver in under a millisecond. Two causes, both here.

A reload lands in the same WebContent process, so a page macOS has parked at
running-suspended-NotVisible comes back hidden and #7112's recovery reloads it
again. After three consecutive failures to get a live page on screen — a failed
or timed-out load, or a visibility recovery — the view now tears down its
WKWebView and builds a fresh one, which is a fresh WebContent and network
process. The decision is made on the failure COUNT and never on what the page
reports about its own visibility: a page reporting itself hidden inside a saver
the host is animating is not evidence of occlusion. Only a probe answering
`visible` clears the count; didFinish does not, because every reload in that
three-day loop finished. Rate-limited to one a minute, widening to one per ten
minutes once the console has been down past fastRetryWindow.

The retry delay was a flat 5 s against a 6 s load deadline, so every retry
issued a load over an attempt WebKit had not finished with; WebKit reported the
supersession as NSURLErrorCancelled (-999), enterOffline read the view's own
cancellation as a fresh failure and armed another 5 s retry. 139 of those in two
hours of the owner's log. fastRetryInterval is now derived from loadDeadline
rather than chosen, and the view cancels any attempt it abandons and recognises
the cancellation that comes back — so a -999 it counts can only have come from
outside.

PaintHarness gains two modes against the never-answering listener: `recreate`
asserts the WKWebView instance is replaced after three failures and that the
replacement opens its own connection, `one-failure` asserts one failure replaces
nothing. All nine modes pass on the rebuilt bundle.

* fix(trusty-mpm): the savings-ledger repair carries a live producer's append, and derives the marker directory from the producer

Five code-critic findings on 80537bdaa, closed here.

The ledger has a LIVE producer — a Claude hook appends on session start — and
`plan` read the file while `apply` renamed over it. A row that arrived in
between sat on the old inode, and the rename stranded it while the command
printed success. The plan now records the byte offset it consumed, and the last
thing `apply` writes into the temp file is everything past that offset, carried
across verbatim and reported as `carried N row(s)`. That narrows the loss window
to the rename itself, which no lock these producers take could close; a carried
row is unclassified, and the next run classifies it. A ledger SHORTER than the
plan read is not the file the plan describes, so it is refused rather than
rewritten from a stale plan.

`MARKER_DIR` was a second spelling of `savings_sidecar::NO_FOLD_WARNED_DIR`. A
rename on either side would have left `--markers` moving nothing, counting
nothing, and exiting 0. It now aliases that constant, and a test pins
`marker_dir(root)` to the parent of the path the producer actually writes.

The temp-file create/write/sync arm had no test. A ledger holding one genuine
row plus a blank line is not clean yet quarantines nothing, so `apply` reaches
the temp file having written no sidecar; run against a `usage/` at mode 0555 it
must error, leave the ledger byte-identical, and leave no `.repair-*.tmp`. The
test probes writability first and skips where the mode is not enforced.

`repair_savings_ledger_dry_run_writes_nothing` passed `markers = true` with no

feat(trusty-agents): key the native memory-tool palace per assistant (Refs #7443) (#7575)

* feat(trusty-agents): key the native memory-tool palace per assistant (Refs #7443)

The native memory tools — `store_memory`, `retrieve_memory`,
`list_memory_keys` and `memory_recall` — address `Segment::AgentMemory`, and
both palace-backed stores derived a palace id from that segment alone. Every
caller therefore resolved to ONE `trusty-agents-mem` palace, so two assistants
served by one process would have read and written each other's memories the
moment a backend was wired in. #7428 fenced the gap rather than closing it;
this closes it.

`memory::scope::MemoryScope` is the assistant component of the key, and
`memory::scope::palace_id` is the one place either store formats a palace id —
`trusty_backed` and `trusty_client` each carried their own copy of that format
string, kept in step by a doc comment pointing at the other.
`MemoryScope::for_assistant` resolves the scope through #7428's own
`resolve_palace_plan`, so the identity is the palace that assistant already
reads and writes, not a new config knob. A palace id that would escape a data
root when joined onto it is refused at construction.

`TrustyBackedMemoryStore::new_for_assistant` and
`TrustyMemoryClient::new_for_assistant` key their palaces by that scope. The
file-backed store also roots its durable payload sidecar under the scope: `get`
reads the sidecar, not the palace, so scoping only the palace id would have left
two assistants sharing one `payloads.db` and handed either of them the other's
value after a reopen. `open_memory_store_for_assistant` scopes the redb data dir
for the same reason — the two backends isolate on different things, and the
guarantee has to hold under both.

`tools::native_memory::open_assistant_memory_backend` is the only way
production code obtains a backend for these tools, and an assistant that
resolves to no palace gets an error, never the shared palace. The degradation
that would have been silent is the one that writes another assistant's drawer.

Unscoped stores keep their pre-existing palace ids and data roots, so the
single-tenant seeders and CLI paths read the palaces they already wrote.

fix(trusty-agents-common): native test compression keeps failure diagnostics and every suite summary (Refs #7544) (#7546)

filter_test_runner was an allowlist: a line survived only by containing
FAILED/error/warning or starting `---- ` / `failures:`, and only the LAST
`test result:` line was kept. That dropped the panic location, the
left:/right: assertion values and every multiline context line, and let a
passing suite's summary replace a failing suite's — a failed-then-passing run
compressed to output ending `test result: ok`.

It is now a blocklist. Passing and ignored per-test lines go, as does cargo's
indented build-progress chatter (Compiling/Finished/Updating/Downloading/
Downloaded/Fresh/Locking); `Running` stays because it names the suite each
summary belongs to, and a column-0 line is a test's own stdout and is never
dropped. Every other line is emitted in its original position, so every suite
summary survives in order beside the diagnostics that explain it and an
unrecognised harness's output is kept rather than discarded. Runs of blank
lines collapse to one. A green run still compresses to its running/Running
lines and summaries.

Six regression tests drive the fixtures through the native fallback entry
point with `no_rtk`, so the route is deterministic; four of them fail against
the previous function.

* fix(trusty-agents): seed a new assistant's config.toml inside the MCP override lock (Refs #7454)

`write_at` called `AssistantHome::ensure()` before taking the `config.toml`

truncates the file back to the bare `id = "…"` stub, silently discarding the

`AssistantHome::ensure` is split: `ensure_without_config` creates the five
directories and `instructions.md`, and `ensure` then seeds `config.toml` on top
of it, so every existing caller behaves exactly as before. `write_at` calls
only `ensure_without_config` outside the lock — `create_dir_all` is genuinely
idempotent — and decides `config.toml`'s absence inside `atomic_update`,
starting an absent document from `AssistantHome::seed_config_body` rather than
an empty string. That reuses the one seed source instead of copying the stub,
and mirrors `migrate_if_absent`'s decide-absence-inside-the-lock pattern.

The doc comment that claimed `ensure` was "additive and idempotent, so it is
safe outside the lock" is replaced by the mechanism: the claim was false for the

* feat(trusty-agents): gworkspace (Gmail) two-way channel binding (Refs #7427)

Gmail reached an assistant only down the listener path: the agent config named
a listener it followed, and nothing in it named a correspondent. A channel
binding addresses the other way round, so a gworkspace binding is a Gmail
DM-equivalent.

A binding target is `from:alice@example.com` (globs included, matched with the
listener's own sender globs) or `label:INBOX`. Inbound reuses the existing
Gmail history-poll listener: `poll_once` offers each stored event to the
bindings first, and a message a binding addresses dispatches through that
binding rather than the generic `[[listeners]]` wake. `wake_path` makes that
exclusive — one message takes one path, never both — and a message no binding
addresses is untouched and reaches the listener wake exactly as before.

Outbound is `trusty-gworkspace`'s own `compose_email` behind a `GmailSend`
trait, which exists because `compose_email` takes a concrete `BaseClient` and
writes `GMAIL_API_BASE` into its own URLs — there is no endpoint to point a
mock server at. A turn woken by an inbound message replies in its thread (the
wake metadata carries the Gmail message id, and `compose_email`'s reply action
fetches the thread and headers itself); any other turn opens a fresh message to
the bound address. A `label:` binding can answer but has no address of its own,
which is `ChannelError::Destination`, a 400.

`receive_slack` becomes `receive_inbound(provider, …)` and `receive_selection`
asks the adapter whether a target addresses the event, through a new
`ChannelAdapter::addresses` whose default is the equality Slack and Telegram
already used.

A gworkspace binding names no `credential_ref`: Gmail authenticates with the
per-account OAuth token in gworkspace's own `TokenStorage`, and the credential
registry has no key for it — its one Google entry, `google-oauth`, is the OAuth
client secret that refreshes those tokens, not a credential an email is sent
as. `credential_providers()` is therefore empty and `Binding::validate` refuses
any reference, which is DOC-63 §7.1b's separate-grant rule in force: an OKG
source's read-scoped Google credential cannot be named as a channel send
credential. Routing the gworkspace account through the credential authority is
deferred; sends use the default gworkspace account until it lands.

* fix(trusty-agents): one wake dispatch per Gmail poll cycle across both inbound paths (Refs #7427)

The Gmail listener caps itself at one wake dispatch per `poll_once` call
(#3820). The channel-binding path arrived beside it with no cap: every claimed
message spawned `run_pm_task_with_persona` of its own, so five emails from one
bound correspondent between two polls bought five model dispatches.

The cap is now one `DispatchBudget` the poll cycle owns and hands to both paths
in turn. A binding that dispatches spends it, so the `[[listeners]]` wake that
follows sees it spent; a binding the budget refuses still reports the message as
claimed, so the listener wake does not pick up what a binding owns. Slack and
Telegram pass `DispatchBudget::PerEvent` and are unchanged — one update in, one
turn per bound assistant out.

A refused message is not silently dropped. It is appended to the event store,
published on the event bus, and counted on its binding by
`channels::status::record_rate_limited`, which warns with the assistant, the
binding and the message id and publishes a `rate_limited` counter in the channel
view. It does NOT come back next cycle: the dedup set holds its id and the
cursor advances past it, so its store semantics are "stored and visible, no
assistant turn" — the same semantics a listener-path event rate-limited by the
#3820 cap already had.

`compose_args` also refused to open a fresh message on a glob sender target. A
`from:*@example.com` binding is valid — `parse_target` accepts it and the
inbound path matches it against every sender at that domain — but it names a set
of correspondents, not one address, so a non-reply send composed a literal
`*@example.com` recipient. That is now `ChannelError::Destination`, a 400,
alongside the `label:` arm. An exact address still sends and replies in-thread
are unaffected on both.

`agent_channels.rs` reached 509 SLOC with the budget in it, so the
provider-neutral inbound path moved to `agent_channels/inbound.rs`: the parent
keeps the configuration surface (load, validate, save, send), the child holds
selection and dispatch.

* fix(trusty-mcp): config file saved 0600; Debug redacts env and header values (Refs #7452)

A stdio server's `env` and a remote server's `headers` routinely hold API keys
and bearer tokens. Two paths were handing them out.

  `0666 & !umask` — `0644` on a default umask, so every local account could
  read the config the rename put in place. It now opens the temporary file
  with mode `0600` under `#[cfg(unix)]` and sets the mode again afterwards, so

  carries over, so the config is never briefly readable at its real path.
  Windows has no mode bits and no trusty-* daemon runs there, so it keeps the
  plain write.

  value and every header verbatim into logs, panic messages and error
  reports. `Debug` is now hand-written and renders those maps with their key
  names intact and each value as `<redacted>`. `command`, `args` and `url`
  still print in full — they identify the server and none is a credential.
  `McpServerConfig`'s derived `Debug` inherits the redaction through its
  `transport` field.

* fix(trusty-agents): attachments re-confine manifest paths, serialize same-name writes, hide paths from 5xx, widen fences, remove orphans (Refs #7370)

Five findings from the review of the attachments slice.

1. The manifest is a plain JSON file in the user's own home tree, so its
contents were never this crate's word — yet `hydrate` joined `stored_name`
straight onto the session directory. `Path::join` REPLACES the base when handed
an absolute component, so a row saying `/etc/hosts` resolved to `/etc/hosts`
and the download route read it. `hydrate` now applies the same
`single_segment` guard the upload applies, refusing the row rather than
repairing it, and `read` re-checks the canonical result against the canonical
session directory before opening anything — which also catches a symlink that a
name check cannot see.

2. Choosing the file name and writing the bytes happened outside the manifest
lock. Two concurrent uploads of the same name both chose the unsuffixed name,
one overwrote the other, and the loser recorded a digest and size for bytes
that were no longer on disk. `Manifest::lock` now hands the caller a guard, so
reserve, write and append are one critical section.

3. `refuse` returned the error's own message for every variant, and `Io`,
`Manifest` and `MissingFile` all carry an absolute path from the operator's
home. A caller who can only address attachments by id was being handed the
on-disk layout. Server errors now go through `internal`, which logs the detail
and answers a fixed sentence; only client errors keep their verbatim message.

4. Attachment text was spliced into a fixed three-backtick fence, so a Markdown
file or code listing containing its own fence ended the block early and the
rest of the file reached the model as prose. The fence is now one backtick
longer than the longest run inside the content.

5. The bytes were written before the row was recorded, so a failed append left
a file no row referred to — unreachable, and permanent. The file is now removed
when the append fails, and only when that call created it.

Every one of the eight new tests fails against the code it fixes. The
`stored_name` proof is literal: without the guard the refusal assertion reports
`stored_path: "/etc/hosts"`, and without the `refuse` change the 5xx body
carries the tempdir's absolute manifest path.

* fix(trusty-agents): memory PUT refuses another assistant's palace; ensure_palace never overwrites (Refs #7428)

Three findings from the security review and the live API smoke.

`PUT /api/assistants/{id}/memory` guarded only the caller's OWN binding, so an
assistant binding no palace could `PUT {"palace":"cto"}` and take one that
belongs to someone else. `own_palace` resolved it as `PalaceSource::Config`,
`own_is_bound()` answered false, and the chat path then treated that palace as
a derived one of its own — recalling from it, persisting its turns into it, and
issuing a create against it. `write_at` now walks `discover_instances`, resolves
each OTHER instance through the same `own_palace` rule, and answers 422 naming
the assistant that already owns the name. A free name is still settable, so this
is a collision check rather than a ban.

`ensure_palace` asked for nothing and created unconditionally. trusty-memory's
`handle_palace_create` does not refuse an existing name: it builds a fresh
`Palace` with `created_at: Utc::now()` and hands it to `create_palace`, which
rewrites `palace.json` — the same metadata-destroying create #4911 guards
against in `memory::trusty_backed`. It now asks `memory.palace_get` first and
creates only on a not-found, following `trusty-installer`'s
`ensure::project_setup::create_palace`, including its rule that only a not-found
falls through: any other error is the daemon reporting a problem, and creating
on top of it would turn a reportable failure into an overwrite.

`POST /api/agents` wrote `role = "assistant"` and no `extends`, while
`roster::is_instance` accepts a config only when it IS the base or declares
`extends = "assistant"` — and the handler's own `name` insert removes the first
condition. Every agent created through the UI was therefore invisible to every
instance enumeration, so `GET /api/assistants/{id}/memory` answered 404 until
someone hand-edited the manifest. It now writes `extends = "assistant"` for an
assistant-role agent.

Fan-out recalls now run concurrently (`futures::future::join_all`) instead of
serially. The own palace is still awaited first and alone, since it gates the
turn; results are collected in config order regardless of completion order.

`force: true` stays on the create, against the review's suggestion to drop it.
It bypasses the daemon's project-slug name enforcement
(`project_root::validate_palace_name`), which a palace named after an assistant
instance can never satisfy — spec-001 Phase 1 licenses exactly this per-tenant
use, and removing it would make derived-palace creation fail outright. It
bypasses no existence check, because the daemon has none; the `palace_get` probe
is the whole protection.

The derived palace id stays the bare instance id per product spec §5.1 —
`izzie` and `cto` are already palace names on the daemon. Multi-tenant
namespacing is a follow-up, noted in the doc comment as `// See #7425`.

* fix(scripts): tolerate only grep's no-match exit in the heading pipelines (Refs #7359)

The previous commit put `|| true` at the END of the `new_headings` pipeline,
matching what `base_headings` already did. Under `pipefail` that also swallows a
`git diff` or `sed` failure: the result is empty, the `[[ -z ]]` guard reads
that as "no new headings", and the gate goes green on tool trouble. That is the
opposite of the stance the same script takes 20 lines below, where an unexpected
nonzero from check-changelog-assembled.sh is reported as a hard finding rather
than swallowed.

Both pipelines now guard grep alone — `| { grep -E '...' || true; } |` — so
grep's no-match is the one nonzero exit treated as "nothing to check here", and
a git or sed failure fails the gate.

`git show` in the `base_headings` pipeline keeps its own guard, because a path
absent at the merge base is expected rather than an error: that is a crate whose
CHANGELOG.md this PR ADDS, and it correctly means "no prior headings". Removing
that guard would break every new-crate PR. Both `sed` calls and `sort -u` are
now unguarded.

Verified against the committed state: plain run on this branch exits 0; a
synthetic deletion of crates/tc-services/CHANGELOG.md exits 0 with the OK line;
a hand-written '## [99.0.0]' section leaving fragments stranded still exits 1
with the full STRANDED-FRAGMENTS block; a newly-added crate CHANGELOG.md (the
git-show-absent case) still resolves; and an isolated pipeline check confirms a

quoted absolute path containing spaces was cut at its spaces and the name
read as a fragment of the path. That misread the command in both
directions: `"/Applications/My Tools/sed" -i x f` resolved to `My` and
slipped the shell-edit deny, while `"/opt/make tools/echo" hi` resolved to

gets the same answer its space-free spelling gets. Quoting the lexer
cannot decode — an unbalanced quote, an interior quote, a `$` or a
backtick — keeps the answer it had before.

extend — it classifies `git` by subcommand and only `apply` denies — so
every read-only spelling the issue reports already passes both bands. A
regression table pins that, and the issue's literal command joins

the Claude Code harness rather than from here (#6982).

reported byte counts and a compression path but never the wrapped command's
own status — `bytes_before=0` read the same whether the command found nothing,
failed, or had its stdout redirected away. The `tm hook` PreToolUse rewrite now
wraps the command in a brace group whose trailing `printf` reports `$?`, and

caller's output. The line carries `exit=N`, `exit=unknown` for an unwrapped
`tm compress < file`.

#7377: the rtk_binary path returned whatever the subprocess printed, and rtk
can exit zero having printed nothing — an 824-byte `git diff --stat` came back
as 0 bytes, reported as a successful 100% reduction. #6986's backstop covers
the native filter chain only; the rtk subprocess never reaches it. The raw text
now passes through with one warning naming the tool, the input size and the

* fix(trusty-mpm): compress rewrite skips commands a brace group cannot wrap and proves the wrapped shape in a real shell (Refs #7384)

Critic round on adffd1ecc. The brace group #7384 introduced puts the command,
the exit-status `printf` and the closing `}` on one physical line, and two
command shapes break that. Neither is composition, so
`has_unsafe_pipe_composition` let both through.

An unquoted `#` — `cargo test # explain` — comments out the group's own
`printf` and its closing brace, so the group never closes. Reproduced in all
three shells against the exact rewritten string: sh and bash abort with
`syntax error: unexpected end of file`, zsh with `parse error near '\n'`. The
command never runs at all.

A trailing unescaped `\` escapes the template's `;`, so `printf`, its format
string and `"$?"` become arguments to the command instead. Reproduced in all
three shells: `grep` reports four missing files, still prints its match, and
the sentinel is lost. No error, silently wrong output, status gone.

`cannot_be_brace_wrapped` rejects both, conservatively — any `#`, quoted or
not, since telling a comment from `grep -c '#include' f` needs a shell parser
and under-rewriting is the safe side. Such a command takes the documented
no-op and goes uncompressed.

The new `every_rewrite_this_module_emits_runs_correctly_in_a_real_shell`
EXECUTES what the module emits under sh, bash and zsh rather than asserting its
shape, which is how round 1 shipped a string every shell rejects while its
assertions matched.

The sentinel was not moved onto its own line: with every `#` rejected no
comment can reach the `printf`, a newline would not help the backslash case
(it escapes the newline instead), and whether Claude Code's `updatedInput`
tolerates a multi-line command cannot be verified from this worktree.

* feat(trusty-mpm): tm session disk reports disk usage per session (Refs #7313)

Slice 1 taught `disk_survey` to attribute every managed worktree to the session
that created it and to roll the rows up by session, but nothing in the shell
could ask for it — an operator wanting to know which session is holding the
bytes had the console Disk view or nothing.

`tm session disk` is that view. With no argument it lists one row per session of
the current project, bytes descending, with a total; with a session id or
friendly name it breaks that one session down — build-directory bytes against
the rest — and lists every worktree it owns across EVERY project, because a
session's worktrees are not confined to one repository. `--json` emits the same
structure; the table goes to stdout and diagnostics to stderr.

It runs no survey of its own. One `disk_survey` call with `group_by: "session"`
over the daemon's loopback `POST /rpc`, so the walk, the classification, the
attribution and the ordering all stay slice 1's — the CLI and the console cannot
disagree about which session is first. There is no HTTP route for the survey
(DOC-73 §16.4 makes the tool the only way in) and adding one would be a second
surface over one implementation.

An id no worktree is attributed to exits non-zero with the reason on stderr and
nothing on stdout. Reporting zero bytes for a typo is indistinguishable from a
session that genuinely holds nothing, and the operator acts on the wrong one.

Three supporting changes, each removing a duplicate rather than adding one:

- `human_bytes` moves from `daemon/doctor_worktree_disk.rs` to
  `disk::human_bytes`. The `tm` binary is a separate crate from the library and

* fix(trusty-mpm): tm pr cleanup fetches the base ref before the merge test and re-probes the tree before removing it (Refs #7275)

Round 4 of `tm pr cleanup`, on top of the landed-detection round the critic
approved. Both additions can only make cleanup refuse in more cases.

The merge test compares a branch against `origin/<base>` as the local ref
store holds it, and the run's only fetch was step 5 — after the worktree
step. The first cleanup following a merge therefore diffed against a base
predating that merge, found the branch's content missing, and refused a tree
that had genuinely landed; only the next sweep, a fetch later, saw it. One
`git fetch origin <base>` now runs on first use and is shared across the run,
so a sweep over five worktrees still pays one round trip. A fetch that fails
refuses rather than comparing against the stale ref.

The unsaved-work probe is taken again immediately before `git worktree
remove`. The first probe and the removal are separated by the merged-pull-
request lookup, the merge-tree comparison, the claim read and the claim
tombstone; ending a claim is record-only, so the agent that held it could
write a file or make a commit in that window and the removal would run on a
reading taken before all of it. The re-read covers the uncommitted-file
count, the unpushed-commit count and `HEAD`, and names which of the three
moved. A `git rev-parse HEAD` that cannot be run refuses too.

`**/target-*/` replaces `**/target-worktree/` in .gitignore. Dispatch briefs
name the build directory `target-<issue>` as often as `target-worktree`, and
an unignored one is untracked content that makes the whole worktree read
dirty — the one thing cleanup refuses on.

feat(trusty-mpm): script post-merge cleanup as tm pr cleanup <n> and the supervisor sweep (Refs #7275) (#7295)

* feat(trusty-mpm): script post-merge cleanup as `tm pr cleanup <n>` (Refs #7275)

The delivery chain ended at the squash merge, and everything the merge made
obsolete — the remote head branch, the worktrees holding it, the local branches
pointing at it, and the session records claiming those directories — was
reclaimed by hand or not at all. Owner ruling 2026-09-09: "let's script post
merge cleanup, it should be deterministic unless it errors. It should be run as
the final step after merge confirmation."

`tm pr cleanup <n>` is that executor. Five steps, one line of output each,
exiting 0 only when all five succeeded:

  pr             confirm `gh pr view <n>` reports MERGED
  remote-branch  delete origin/<head> when the remote still lists it
  worktree       end any session claim, then remove each tree holding the head
  local-branch   delete the head branch, its round-N siblings, and each
                 `worktree-agent-*` at the merged head commit
  prune          `git worktree prune`, then `git fetch --prune origin`

A worktree holding uncommitted or unpushed work is the one refusal — cleanup
never passes `--force`. `--dry-run` runs every read and issues no mutating
command.

Three triggers share one engine in `core::pr_cleanup`, so they cannot disagree
about what cleanup means: this command, `tm pr merge`'s final step after the
merge it performs, and a supervisor sweep every five minutes over the pull
requests `tm pr open` recorded (`TRUSTY_MPM_PR_CLEANUP_INTERVAL`, `0` disables).
The registry stamp makes the sweep idempotent — a cleaned PR is never asked
about again.

A merged PR makes its worktree's session claim obsolete, so cleanup ends that
claim and proceeds; the merge is the determiner, not the claim. Ending it is
record-only, through `SessionManager::decommission_record_only` in the daemon
and `?record_only=true` from the CLI, so cleanup never kills a process it does
not own.

Round-N siblings are the other half. A review round lands on `<branch>-r2` and
`version-control` pushes it onto the PR's head name, so the PR merges under
`<branch>` while `<branch>-r2` and its tree survive with no merged pull request
carrying their name — eight such trees were refused on 2026-09-09. Cleanup scopes
to this PR's own branches by their round-stripped stem, and proves the merge
carried a sibling before deleting it: `git merge-tree --write-tree origin/<base>
<tip>` then `git diff --name-only`. Not `git cherry` — every merge here is a
squash, so its per-commit patch-id comparison reports `+` for content that IS on
the base (observed on #7258). A non-empty diff refuses and names the residue.

The ADR-0057 `git worktree remove` guard consults the same fact. Its
unpushed-commits check ran `@{upstream}..HEAD`, and `gh pr merge --delete-branch`
leaves that tracking ref stale, so it refused five clean, merged trees — the exact
cleanup this ruling requires. Both that arm and the merged-PR arm now fall back
to the merge-into-base test, so a stale upstream and a sibling with no PR of its
own are reclaimable, while genuinely unpushed work still denies and says how to
see it.

asked whether merging HEAD into the base would change anything and GRANTED on

round-stripped sibling — the relation `core::pr_cleanup::plan::is_pr_branch`

resolves, or a round sibling whose own name no pull request ever carried. A

Everything downstream of an engagement already existed — `distribute` packages
one, `package` signs a return with one's key, `verify` checks it — and nothing
created one. The auditor hand-edited a template: paste the OpenRouter key,
decide the window in prose, and produce an ed25519 seed with some other program
and paste that too. Each of those steps is silently skippable, and the run that
skips the signing key exits 0 with an unsigned package.

`engagement::create` is that hand-editing as one verb. It writes
`engagement.toml` at mode 0600 carrying the key, the window and a freshly
generated seed, plus the retained public half in `retained.pub` — the file
`verify --public-key` reads, and the one that never travels with the package.
It reaches no network: the key is the operator's, conveyed out of band, the
keypair comes from the OS, and the tool pins come from the template rather than
a release lookup. `config::with_engagement_identity` is the second half of the
existing substitution rather than a third writer of a plaintext credential, so
the previous engagement's board credentials, signing key and client labels are
dropped and reported by name.

Two fail-open shapes are closed. A directory already holding an engagement is
refused rather than overwritten, because replacing the signing key orphans the
public half the auditor retained; `force` is how an operator says they meant
it. A mint that cannot write the retained public key removes the config it just
wrote, so a failure never looks like an engagement on the next `ls`.

The config gains `[audit] window_weeks`, defaulting to 52 so a config written
before it existed still loads and still means one year. A declared `0` is
refused at parse time — a zero-week engagement sweeps no history and would

mismatch until `trusty-audit verify --public-key` rejects a genuine package
weeks later.

`workdir::stage_pair` publishes the pair as one unit. Every fallible write —
the content, the 0600 mode, the exclusive open that refuses a pre-planted
symlink (#5868) — happens into temporaries beside the two targets, so a failure
there has touched nothing. `StagedPair::commit` then publishes by rename only,
moving the private half out of the way first and renaming it into place last,
so at every point an observer can look, a private key on disk is accompanied by
its own public half; the states between the renames are missing files, never
disagreeing ones. A commit that fails partway puts the previous pair back. This
orders and bounds the damage of a hard kill rather than making the pair a
transaction: a kill between the renames can leave only the public half, with
the previous pair recoverable under its `.bak` name.

The existence check and the writes now run under the engagement config's
exclusive lock, `trusty_common::file_lock::with_exclusive_lock` — the same
sidecar `registry::register` takes over the same file — so two `create` calls
aimed at one directory can no longer both pass the check and one clobber the
other. The pre-lock probe stays as the cheap early refusal; the check that
decides is the one under the lock.

put it there, and a parked directory could not be cleaned up afterwards. That

fix(trusty-mpm): decide the commit stats footer by git's commit source (#7279)

## Outcome

Fixes the bundled `prepare-commit-msg` hook to decide the commit-stats trailer
treatment by git's own commit-source argument, instead of applying the same
treatment to every commit regardless of source.

Refs [#7249](https://github.com/bobmatnyc/trusty-tools/issues/7249)

## Changes

The hook ignored git's second argument (the commit source), so every commit got
the same trailer treatment. A merge or squash commit was stamped with the
committing session's token counts, and a cherry-pick kept the *original*
commit's trailer block — `already_stamped()` read the inherited trailers as this
session's own work and left the stale figures in place.

The hook now reads the source and passes it to `tm commit-trailers
--commit-source`, which applies four rules:

- `merge`, `squash`: write nothing — the message is assembled from other commits.
- `commit` (cherry-pick, revert, `--amend`, `-c`/`-C`): strip the inherited
  block, then stamp this session's figures. With no current session the strip
  still runs and nothing replaces it — no block is correct where another
  session's block is not. This is the one source that runs the stamper outside
  a Claude Code session.
- `message` (`-m`/`-F`), `template`, and the empty source of an editor commit:
  stamp as before.

`strip_trailers()` removes a block only when the message's last content
paragraph is entirely this footer's five keys — the exact shape
`append_trailers()` writes — so a `Model:` line inside someone's prose is out of
scope. `already_stamped()` stays the idempotency guard within one source, so the
block never doubles.

Out of scope: the trailer content or format itself — only when it is applied,
and stale-trailer handling on non-`message` sources, changed.

## Risk / blast radius

Confined to `trusty-mpm`'s bundled hook and its `commit-trailers` command path
— `crates/trusty-mpm/src/assets/hooks/prepare-commit-msg`,

* fix(trusty-mpm): bound the commit-time transcript read (Refs #7074)

`tm commit-trailers` streamed the entire session transcript on every
`git commit`, with no size cap and no timeout, and git blocks on the
`prepare-commit-msg` hook that calls it. A day-long session's transcript
reaches hundreds of megabytes, so every commit after that point slowed
for the rest of the session.

Two bounds, both present:

- A byte cap. `fold_transcript` reads at most the last 8 MiB
  (`TRANSCRIPT_TAIL_BYTES`), seeking to `len - cap` and discarding the
  partial line at that offset so every line it parses is whole.
- A wall-clock budget in the hook. The stamper runs in the background
  under a 2-second budget (`TM_COMMIT_STATS_TIMEOUT`) and is killed if it
  outruns it; the commit then proceeds with its trailers omitted.

What the footer claims when the cap cuts: the tail window, labelled.
`session_record.rs` stores only the transcript's PATH — there are no
running per-session totals that would let a tail read stand for the whole
session — so narrowing the claim is the only honest option. A truncated
fold sets `TranscriptUsage::truncated`, which `gather_stats` turns into
`Tokens-Window: last 8 MiB of a larger transcript`. It is a separate
trailer rather than a suffix on the numbers, so `Tokens-In` and
`Tokens-Out` stay plain integers for anything parsing them back, and it
is emitted only when there is a count to scope.

The message file is now written through a temp-file rename. The budget
can kill the stamper mid-write, and a half-written `COMMIT_EDITMSG` would
cost the operator their commit message; the rename leaves either the
original or the stamped text.

Hook marker bumped v1 -> v2 so the installer replaces an installed v1.

* fix(trusty-audit): kill a clone that crosses the disk budget mid-fetch (Refs #5669)

`--budget-gb` was checked only between repositories, so 19 GiB spent against a
20 GiB ceiling still admitted a 100 GB monorepo and finished at 119 GiB. This
runs unattended on a client's own machine during an engagement, with nobody
watching to intervene, so a start gate that cannot interrupt is not a budget.

`clone::watchdog` now spawns both acquisition children — `gh repo clone` and the
local `git clone` — and measures the staged tree every 500ms while one runs.
Once `spent + staged` crosses the ceiling the child is signalled: `SIGTERM`
first, so `git` and `gh` remove their own temporary pack files, then `SIGKILL`
after a five-second grace. The child is reaped either way. `finish_one` removes
the partial tree by the same path a failed clone takes, so nothing survives
under staging or reaches `Area::Repos`. Overshoot is bounded by the sampling
interval, not zero.

Neither child gets a second `Command::new`: the `gh` one is still built by
`clone_command` and configured by `trusty_common`'s `GhCommand::to_std_command`,
the `git` one still by `local_repo::clone_argv` hardened through
`crate::git::spawn` (#6079).

The outcome lands on its own `CloneState::BudgetExceeded` rather than on
`Failed` or the start gate's `Skipped`, and renders as `OVER BUDGET — stopped
mid-clone at <size> against a <size> ceiling`. A recipient reading `FAILED`
would go looking for a wrong name or a revoked credential; there is no fault
here, and the gap line says to raise `--budget-gb` or drop the repository.

- A sample that cannot be taken kills the child and reports the attempt, rather

* fix(trusty-audit): kill the clone's process group, not just its child (Refs #5669)

bytes. After the parent died an orphan kept fetching into, and recreated, the
staged directory `finish_one` had already removed. The child now leads its own
process group and both signals go to the group.

  that could not be removed left its bytes on disk while the report said zero.
  The surviving bytes are now measured, counted against the budget, and named in
  a gap line of their own.
- A tree whose own ROOT could not be opened measured zero for a checkout of any
  size. `measure_tree` is now the one measurement all three call sites use — the
  watchdog's sample, the freshly promoted checkout, and a checkout reused from an
  earlier run — and it separates an unopenable root (a failure that propagates)
  from an unreadable entry below it (a floor). It also opens the root once, so
  the guard-then-walk race in `sample` is gone.
- `terminate` read `Ok(Err(_))` from `timeout(grace, child.wait())` as an exit

* fix(trusty-audit): forward Ctrl-C to the detached clone group (Refs #5669)

`process_group(0)` is what lets one signal reach a whole clone tree, and it is
also what takes that tree out of the terminal's foreground group. The crate
installed no signal handling, so a raw Ctrl-C killed `taudit` on SIGINT's
default disposition — no destructors, `kill_on_drop` never reached — while
`ssh` and `git-index-pack` kept fetching into the client's disk with the
watchdog dead.

Each detached group is now recorded while it runs, and a task the binary spawns
forwards SIGINT to every one of them, kills whatever is still running 250ms
later, then re-raises SIGINT under the default disposition so a shell or CI
runner sees the run as interrupted rather than as finished. The kill names the
group directly rather than probing with `getpgid`: the first signal kills the
leader, which is then reaped, after which `getpgid` can no longer recognise the
group and the follow-up SIGKILL would land on nothing.

Second finding: `discard_at` folded a root-level measurement failure into
`(0, false)`, so a tree that could be neither removed nor measured was reported
as "at least 0 bytes are still on disk" — a figure that reads as measured for a
tree that may hold gigabytes. That case now names the measurement failure and
says the size is unknown, and its bytes stay out of the budget ledger with
`bytes_complete` cleared, which marks every later budget decision in the run a
floor.

`bridge/map` is the daemon's whole REST route set, one path per JSON-RPC method,
so PR 2c is a deletion rather than a migration. `POST /rpc` is deliberately
absent: a row for it would forward an arbitrary method by name, which is the
reviewability the table exists for. `bridge/routes` keeps the guard stack the
daemon's listener carried — the same-origin CORS and write guard outside,
`require_bearer` inside — and the ticket half of bearer auth, because
`EventSource` cannot send a header.

Two things are copies, both pinned against the originals by tests that fail if
either drifts, and both deleted at the far end by PR 2c: the JSON-RPC-to-HTTP
status table, and the Markdown transcript renderer. The renderer has no RPC twin
— the daemon's REST handler made two calls and formatted the result — so it came
across with the layer it lives in rather than dropping the download button.

`stream_response` writes the response head before reading anything, which is a
deliberate divergence from trusty-console's bridge. Peeking the first frame there
turns an open-time refusal into an HTTP status; here it withholds the head on a
healthy stream, because `workstream.events` is a pure live tail with no replay
and a quiet workstream sends nothing at all. Measured against a real `tcode
serve`: curl received zero bytes and no status line. A short peek window is not
the fix — `FramedStream::next_frame` is not cancel-safe, so a peek that timed out
mid-frame would drop that event silently. The refusal instead arrives as
`sse_tail`'s terminal error event, which is what an `EventSource` could act on
either way.

divides the two byte counts it is handed, and both the freshly built binary

whole chain the issue names: a compression that takes the native path, elides
lines, and reports a reduction equal to the byte delta and strictly above zero.

fix(trusty-console): memory graph "load everything" no longer freezes the tab (#7138)

* fix(trusty-console): memory graph "load everything" no longer freezes the tab

The view ran its force simulation on `setInterval(tick, 16)` and reassigned the
reactive `nodes` array at the end of every tick, so all 200 steps of a full
re-layout each repainted the whole SVG. On the live trusty-tools palace
"load everything" draws 1,242 nodes and 5,000 edges — 7,484 SVG elements —
repainted 200 times, and the tab stayed unresponsive for over twelve minutes.

The steps were never the cost. One step over that payload measures 3.15 ms,
0.63 s for all 200. One repaint of that DOM measures 180 ms in Chrome, so the
paints alone were 36 s before Svelte's own per-tick re-derivation of the edge
and degree maps on top.

Three changes:

- The simulation moved into a Web Worker (`graph/layoutWorker.js`) driven by
  `graph/layoutRunner.js`, which commits at most ONE position snapshot per
  animation frame and coalesces anything that arrives in between. The main
  thread now only writes coordinates the worker already computed.
- Coordinates moved out of the reactive `nodes` array into a plain
  `Float64Array` plus a `posVersion` counter, so a committed frame no longer
  invalidates `links` (a 5,000-triple scan) or `shownDegree` (a 5,000-link scan).
- Above 400 edges the edges collapse from one `<line>` each into a single
  `<path>`: 43 ms per commit instead of 180 ms, and 2,488 SVG elements instead
  of 7,484. Below the threshold the per-line renderer keeps its arrow markers.

`stepBudgetFor` clips the settling passes on an oversized graph so runtime stays
bounded as the palace grows, and the view says when it did. A progress bar with
a working cancel button runs alongside, and `defaultScheduleFrame` falls back to
a timer while the tab is hidden so a backgrounded layout still finishes instead
of stalling on a `requestAnimationFrame` that never fires.

Full load also rendered nothing at all once it stopped freezing. It derives its
node list from triple endpoints, so each id arrives once per incident edge —
10,000 entries for 1,242 distinct nodes — and `mergeSubgraph` tested membership
against a snapshot taken before the merge loop rather than the set the loop was
filling. Every repeat got through and the keyed `{#each}` threw
`each_key_duplicate`. First paint of the full graph is now 440 ms.

fix(trusty-memory): recall-all releases the palaces it opened only to serve the query (#7130)

The three recall-all entry points — `MemoryService::recall_all`, the
`memory_recall_all` MCP tool, and the chat dispatcher's `execute_recall_all` —
each walked the whole estate into one `Vec<Arc<PalaceHandle>>` via
`open_palaces_blocking` and held every handle for the duration of the query.
Peak residency therefore scaled with the palace count: on a 94-palace estate
that hydrates 94 drawer tables, HNSW graphs, KG adjacencies and redb page
caches at once, roughly 13x the on-disk bytes. When the local `Vec` dropped,
the 64-slot LRU was left holding its most recent victims — a multi-GB floor
that persisted until `idle_evict` ran. `DEFAULT_MAX_OPEN_PALACES` bounded the
cache, never the peak and never the residue.

All three now share `service::recall_stream::recall_streamed`, which walks the
palace list in `RECALL_PALACE_BATCH` (8) chunks: open the batch on the blocking
pool, hand it to the caller's search, release it, move on. Peak residency
tracks the batch width instead of the palace count, and the daemon's
open-handle count after a recall-all matches its count before one. Every palace
is still opened and still searched — a cache-only answer would silently drop
most of the corpus (#4637) — so the only thing that changed is when.

Palaces the registry already held when the query arrived are snapshotted first
and never released, so an operator's working set survives a recall-all
untouched. Release goes through `PalaceRegistry::release_if_unreferenced`
(#7106), which pops only when the cache holds the sole reference, so a
concurrent recall, remember, or dream cycle holding the same `Arc` is never
disturbed. Release runs before a failing search's error propagates, so an
erroring batch cannot leak the handles it was handed. Per-batch results are
merged by drawer id, re-sorted and truncated to `top_k`; the global top-k is
unchanged, because it is always a subset of the union of the per-batch top-ks.

The `palaces_list` half of #7125's acceptance (defaulting `counts` to false for
pollers) is not in this change.
