fix(trusty-common): bound every ONNX embed batch at the embedder; dream dedup chunks match (#7126)

`FastEmbedder::embed_batch` handed fastembed its whole cache-miss list with
`None`, taking fastembed's own default of 256 inputs at up to 512 tokens. One
attention tensor at that batch is `256 x 12 heads x 512^2 x 4 B` ~= 9.7 GB
before hidden states, QKV projections and the FFN, and ORT keeps roughly three
of them live per layer — which is how one dream cycle took the trusty-memory
daemon to 21.3 GB RSS. The peak was set by the batch, not by the corpus, so a
141-drawer palace spiked as hard as a 365-drawer one.

Every caller now runs through `embed_in_bounded_batches`, which slices the
cache-miss list at `TRUSTY_EMBED_ONNX_BATCH` (default 16) and passes the
ceiling to fastembed as an explicit `Some(batch_size)`. Chunking here rather
than relying on fastembed's own `batch_size` matters because
`TextEmbedding::transform` collects every internal batch's raw ORT output
before exporting any of it, so its chunking bounds the attention tensor but
still accumulates one hidden-state tensor per chunk across the call. Passing
the ceiling rather than the slice length keeps it `>= texts.len()`, which is
what stops a dynamically-quantised model (`TRUSTY_EMBEDDER_MODEL=int8`) from
rejecting a batched call.

`DREAM_EMBED_CHUNK` drops 256 -> 16 to match. The dedup pass checks its
`max_cycle_ms` budget between chunks, so a chunk larger than one inference
would hide several ONNX runs inside one uninterruptible step.

Output order, count, the cache-hit path and whole-call failure on a mid-batch
error are unchanged and covered by `batching_tests.rs`; six of its twelve tests
fail when the chunking body is reverted to a single unbounded call.

fix(trusty-memory): dream scheduler caps concurrent cycles, staggers first ticks, chunks embeds (#7124)

* fix(trusty-memory): dream scheduler caps concurrent cycles, staggers phases, chunks embeds

PR #7115 bounded the daemon's steady state, but live verification still showed
a 43 GB transient at launch+300 s and an 8 GB one 300 s later. The peak is one
cycle's working set times how many cycles run together, and nothing bounded
either factor: `spawn_dream_scheduler` spawned one loop per resident palace,
every loop slept the same `idle_secs` from the same startup instant, and each
cycle handed its palace's whole corpus to a single `embed_batch` queued behind
one ONNX mutex. 61 `dream_stats.json` mtimes landed inside one 31-second window.

Four mechanisms:

1. A process-wide semaphore, sized by `TRUSTY_DREAM_MAX_CONCURRENT` (default 2),
   that every cycle acquires before it runs — the idle loops and the on-demand
   `palace_dream` / `dream_consolidate_room` tools alike. The permit releases on
   drop, so no error or early-return arm can leak one.
2. A deterministic first-tick stagger: palace k of n waits `idle_secs * k / n`
   past its first interval, and the plain interval thereafter, so the offset
   persists for the process's life and a restart reproduces the schedule.
3. Chunked embedding — 256 drawers per `embed_batch` call, with the
   `max_cycle_ms` budget checked BETWEEN chunks rather than after one
   whole-corpus call that could overrun it by minutes.
4. One drawer-table clone per cycle instead of four. Content-prune and prune
   collect victim ids under the read lock; the closet refresh builds from the
   read guard. No lock is held across an await.

`cycle.rs` was at 459 of its 500-SLOC cap, so the inference-backed half moved to
`dream/semantic.rs` to make room. `Dreamer::start` is deleted: nothing called it,
and it was a second spawn path with neither the stagger nor the cap.

Five regression tests, each proven red against the pre-fix hunks: the ten-palace
peak-concurrency test (peak 10 before, <= 2 after), a cycle blocking when every
permit is held, the loop honouring its stagger, and the two dedup chunking tests
([600] before, [256, 256, 88] and [256] after).

fix(trusty-memory): test-spawned daemons exit when their spawner dies, including on SIGKILL (#7108)

* fix(trusty-memory): make a test-spawned daemon exit with its spawner

A `serve --foreground` daemon spawned by a test outlived the test whenever
the test process was killed outright. `DaemonGuard` reaps in `Drop`, and a
SIGKILL runs no destructor, so a `cargo test` timeout or a torn-down agent
process tree left the daemon running against a temp data dir that was already
gone. A census on 2026-09-08 counted 102 such orphans holding 12.6 GB.

The mechanism has to live inside the daemon. `trusty_common::parent_death`
stamps `TRUSTY_EXIT_WITH_PARENT` on the spawner's `Command`, and the daemon
arms a watchdog thread from that variable at the top of the foreground path.
The watchdog polls `getppid()` and a `kill(pid, 0)` liveness probe every
250 ms and exits when the stamped parent is gone. Nothing arms unless the
variable is set, so launchd and hand-run daemons are untouched.

The reparent prong is armed only when the stamped pid is the direct parent.
A stdio bridge auto-starts a DETACHED daemon that outlives the bridge by
design; that grandchild inherits the stamp and watches the stamped pid's
liveness only, which is what makes it die with the test rather than seconds
after it starts. Six orphans per full suite run came through exactly that
path.

`trusty-agents` had a private copy of the same watchdog for its `--api`
sidecar. It now calls the shared implementation, so one cross-crate
capability has one implementation.

`orphan_reap_7085` spawns the daemon through the real helper from a child
process, SIGKILLs that child, and asserts the daemon's pid disappears. It
fails on the pre-fix daemon after 20s and passes in under 3s after.

* fix(trusty-memory): parent-death watchdog survives pid reuse, scrubs the stamp from detached children, exits gracefully

Four gaps the code-critic found in acf481a5b.

A pid is not an identity. For a detached grandchild there is no reparent
signal, so `kill(pid, 0)` alone was the whole liveness check — and a pid the
OS recycles onto an unrelated process would have read as "parent still alive"
forever, which is the permanent orphan this work exists to prevent.
`ParentIdentity` now pairs the pid with the parent's process start time, read
at arm time and compared on every tick. macOS reads it through
`proc_pidinfo(PROC_PIDTASKALLINFO)`, Linux from `/proc/<pid>/stat` field 22;
a platform that can report neither degrades to the liveness probe rather than
to a false "gone".

`spawn_detached` no longer inherits the stamp. It scrubs
`TRUSTY_EXIT_WITH_PARENT` by default, so a stray value in some operator's

* fix(memory-ui): batch the activity feed so it stops starving the main thread

The feed wrote reactive state once per SSE frame and handed a 500-row keyed
{#each} to Svelte on each write. Measured on a scratch console against the live
daemon at 200 events/s: one 46,420 ms main-thread task, 97% of a 69 s window
blocked, and 1 of ~69 one-per-second /health polls completed. That is why the
SPA reported `timed out after 35s: /api/v1/palaces` and flipped Health offline
while curl answered the same endpoints in 19 ms and 1.5 ms.

Two costs, separated by measurement. Collapsing the feed — same ingest, no
{#each} — cut the worst task to 9,114 ms, so the per-frame state write and the
render were each responsible for part of it. Batching alone (one write per
250 ms window) still peaked at 8,273 ms with 21 tasks over 200 ms, because a
single flush could hand the keyed list up to 500 new keys. Bounding the rows
per flush is what removes the rest.

- `feed-buffer.js`: a Svelte-free batcher (injected timer, so the cap and the
  write count are assertable) plus the two list reducers. One reactive write per
  250 ms window, at most MAX_PER_FLUSH rows each, MAX_EVENTS retained.
- A flush that drops frames prepends a `lag` row saying how many, rather than
  losing them silently — the shape the daemon's own slow-consumer frame uses.
- History paging is capped too. It appended without one, so scrolling grew the
  list one 50-row page at a time against a 49,551-row archive.
- The stream drops while `document.hidden`. EventSource delivery is not
  throttled in a background tab, but the SPA's own /health poll is, so a hidden
  feed won a race it should never have entered.
- `describe()` gains a `hook_fired` case. It had none, so the type that
  dominates the stream (421 of the last 500 rows) fell to the default branch and
  paid a `JSON.stringify` per row per render — and rendered as raw JSON on
  screen. The default branch no longer stringifies either, so the next event
  type the daemon adds cannot reintroduce the cost.
- Health waits for two consecutive failed polls before reporting `unreachable`,
  in both the topbar's shared state and the Health view's own poller. One
  starved poll is not evidence about the daemon.

/health polls at 22 ms median, 31/31 palace rosters at 79 ms median and 610 ms

200 ms budget is honoured rather than overshot by 256 `read_dir` calls.

installed as the cached root total — caching it would serve an arbitrary
fraction of the tree for a whole `max_age` window, to a later reader that

`InferenceAdapter::supports_structured_output` advertised a capability no
request could express, so a caller needing schema-valid JSON had to render its

`ChatRequest` gains `response_schema: Option<StructuredOutput>`, held in a
neutral shape and rendered per dialect by the adapter:

- OpenAI-compatible family (openrouter, fireworks, openai, together,
  atlascloud, and the local wrapper) — `response_format: {type: json_schema,
  json_schema: {name, strict, schema}}`, translated once in
  `OpenAiCompatAdapter::wire_body` so both the buffered and streaming paths
  agree.
- Anthropic-direct — `output_config.format`, which carries the schema alone.
- Bedrock — the Converse API has no equivalent parameter, so its registry
  `structured_output` flips true -> false.

A schema sent to a provider whose registry capability is false is
`InferenceError::UnsupportedCapability{provider, capability}`, raised before any

An agent file on disk carried no marker saying which of three writers produced
it — the framework's own deploy, tm-agent-manager composing one on request, or a
human hand-writing one through Claude Code's /agents. The never-clobber-what-we-
did-not-write rule needs that distinction, and Origin::is_framework_owned cannot
supply it: it answers only from the ownership ledger, so every file with no
ledger entry reads identically. Owner ruling, 2026-08-03, verbatim: "We use
frontmatter to track this."

The new agents::provenance module owns the three values the issue title names —
framework-owned, tm-agent-manager-built, user-authored — the parse, and the
absence rule. #4698's design note fixes that rule: "ABSENCE of the field is
itself the signal for 'not ours, never touch.'" So an absent field resolves to
user-authored, never to a framework-owned default, and an unrecognised value is
rejected with a typed error rather than degraded to that default — degrading
would read a typo'd framework-owned as user-authored and freeze a framework file
permanently, which is #4408's unrecoverable shape.

Provenance is a property of the WRITE, not of the source: the same source tree
composed by the framework and by tm-agent-manager yields two files with
different authors. So the writer supplies it. compose_agent_with_provenance
stamps the composed output, and the deployer calls it with framework-owned for
every file it writes — which also means a new bundled asset has no per-file
declaration to forget.

Precedence, where both records exist: the manifest wins, in both directions, and
a disagreement is warned with the file named. The ledger is the record the
deployer wrote under a lock and checksummed; the frontmatter is the copy anyone
with an editor can change. An untracked file is exempt from the check entirely —
a declaration cannot stand in for a ledger entry, which would manufacture the
user-owned quarantine exemption out of a field anybody can type (tier_audit's
invariant 2).

than of the composition, so an adopted file matches its own row and the next
deploy upgrades it into the stamped form.

fix(trusty-common): size accepted UDS sockets explicitly — Linux does not inherit the listener's buffers (#6896, red main #6511) (#6942)

* fix(trusty-common): size the accepted end of a UDS connection, which Linux does not inherit

`Rust tests (pre-publish gate)` has been red on `main` since #6907. On the
ubuntu runner `an_accepted_socket_inherits_the_listeners_sizing` read
`send: 212992, recv: 1048576` off the accepted socket against
`send: 425984, recv: 2097152` off its listener.

That is not a doubling or clamp artefact in the test: the accepted socket
carries the host's `net.core.wmem_default` / `rmem_default`, untouched. Only
macOS copies a listener's `SO_SNDBUF` / `SO_RCVBUF` onto the sockets `accept`
returns, in `sonewconn`. Linux AF_UNIX builds the server-side socket from
scratch in `unix_stream_connect`, so #6896's listener-only sizing left every
server-side socket on Linux at the platform default — paying, on one end of
every connection, the round trips that issue exists to remove. Verified on a
6.x kernel: listener 2097152/2097152, accepted 212992/212992, and 2097152 again
once the accepted socket is set itself.

`uds::accept_sized` accepts and then sizes, through the forgiving entry point
so a liveness probe that has already closed stays a probe. The two serving
accept sites in `uds::server` call it in place of `listener.accept()`; the
shutdown drain, which accepts only to close, does not.

The test now compares the two GRANTED figures against each other and never
against `SOCKET_BUFFER_BYTES` — Linux answers 2 MiB to a 1 MiB request, and
425984 where `wmem_max` is 212992, so only two sockets sized the same way on
the same host are comparable. Removing the sizing puts it back at
`212992/212992` against `2097152/2097152`, which is the same failure.

* fix(trusty-search): M005 re-reads through the extractor, keeping office docs (#6910)

M005 re-read every file with `read_to_string`. That fails on the zip and
binary containers `core::extract` handles, so a `.docx`, `.pdf` or spreadsheet
contributed no chunks to the re-chunk, and the orphan sweep then dropped every
vector it had. matsuoka-com fell from 64,517 chunks to 3,526 on its first query
after the 0.54.0 upgrade.

`rechunk_all` now reads through `core::extract::read_content`, the same seam
`service::reindex::batch` and `service::watch_loop` read through, so M005
extracts a file exactly as the pass that first indexed it did.

A file that still cannot be extracted keeps its vectors. Removal is the one
step of the pass that cannot be undone without re-embedding, so it now needs
affirmative evidence the file is gone from disk: `partition_orphans` holds back
every old id whose file is in the unreadable set, and an existence probe that
errors counts as "still there".

* fix(trusty-search): M005 holds back a file that extracts to nothing, and reads its batch concurrently (#6910)

Three code-critic findings on the previous commit.

CRITICAL — extraction can succeed and still yield nothing usable.
`extract::pdf` returns `Ok(Extracted { text: "", warning: Some(..) })` for a
scanned or image-only PDF, and `chunk_text` emits no chunk for empty content,
so the file landed in neither `remap` nor `unreadable` and every id it had was
classified an orphan. That is the issue's own failure mode reached by a branch
the first commit did not close. `rechunk_all` now holds back any file that is
still on disk and produced no chunks, whatever the extractor returned.

HIGH — a batch cost the sum of its files, not the slowest.
`EXTRACT_TIMEOUT` is 30s per file and `BATCH_SIZE` is 64, so a pathological
batch held the pass for up to ~32 minutes before the next cancel checkpoint,
while `DELETE_QUIESCE_TIMEOUT` (service/server/search.rs:247) gives a delete
30 seconds. Reads now go through `futures::future::join_all`, the shape
`service::reindex::batch::prepare_batch_payload` already uses.

MEDIUM — the `Err` arm of `file_is_gone` had no test. It has one now, driven
by a path whose parent is a regular file so the underlying stat fails ENOTDIR:
deterministic, and independent of the uid the suite runs as.

fix(trusty-search): chunk ids carry the end line; M005 re-chunks the corpus under the index permit (#6902)

* fix(trusty-search): chunk ids carry the end line (Refs #6581)

A named chunk id was `{file}::{type}::{name}::{start}` and omitted the end
line, so two declarations sharing a name and a start line shared a primary
key. A minified bundle is one physical line, so `assets/index.js` collapsed
2,299 declarations onto 225 ids and #6571's dedupe dropped the other 2,070 —
those symbols were absent from search entirely.

Owner ruling 2026-09-05 (comment 5546058592), applied verbatim:

1. The id carries the end line: `{file}::{type}::{name}::{start}::{end}`. Two
   declarations with an IDENTICAL span still build one base id, so the second
   and later occurrences take a deterministic `::dup::{n}` suffix instead of
   being dropped. Positional ids for unnamed chunks are byte-identical.
2. M005 (schema version 4 -> 5) clears the corpus and re-chunks it from source.
   It re-embeds nothing: the text is unchanged, so the stored vector is handed
   to the new id by re-pointing the HNSW key sidecar. `TRUSTY_MAX_CHUNKS`
   applies exactly as it does on a fresh index.
3. `is_chunk_id_suffix` accepts both named shapes until an index's own M005
   marker is set, then only the new one. The policy is per index.
4. The re-embed budget is zero, proved by an embedder that fails the run if it
   is called at all.

* fix(trusty-search): M005 is crash-recoverable and never advances the schema over missing chunks (Refs #6581)

Fail-Open Check. M005's idempotency guard decided "is a pass outstanding" by
looking for a pre-#6581 named id in the corpus — but Step 3 clears that corpus
before rebuilding it. Any interruption between the clear and the final flush
therefore left no legacy id to find, the guard read that as "already migrated",
`apply` returned Ok, and `run_migrations` stamped schema_version = 5 over a
partial index — or, when the crash landed before the first batch committed, an
entirely empty one. Silent, permanent loss reported as a successful migration,
and unrecoverable because a v5 index never runs M005 again. The guard's answer
was decoupled from whether Steps 3-6 ever finished, so it failed open by
construction rather than by accident.

The fix is a durable recovery plan, not a completion boolean. `files`,
`vector_by_text` and `old_ids` are all derived from the pre-clear chunks, so a
bare marker would leave a resumed pass unable to say which files to re-chunk or
which stored vector belongs to which text. `m005/plan.rs` persists all three
into the corpus `_meta` table under `m005_plan` BEFORE the clear and removes
them only as Step 7, after every other step has succeeded. Its presence — never
the corpus contents — is what says a pass is outstanding. `_meta` survives
`clear_corpus_for_rechunk`, which empties the chunk, entity and KG tables, and
redb commits the blob atomically, so the marker can never be half-written. Any
failure leaves it in place, returns Err, and pins the version at 4.

Rejected the alternative of re-chunking alongside the old keys and swapping
atomically: the up-front clear exists so `TRUSTY_MAX_CHUNKS` behaves as it does
on a fresh index (`commit_parsed_batch`'s cap pre-filter decides by
`corpus.contains_key`, so ingesting new keys onto a populated corpus
double-counts and drops the tail). Removing it means making the commit path
migration-aware, and the owner ruling left the chunk cap unchanged.

A query landing inside the re-chunk window used to be answered `200` with an
empty result set: the migration runs under the SHARED teardown lock, which
blocks a delete and not a search, and every corpus read succeeds while the
corpus is merely incomplete. `IndexMigrationInProgress` now refuses it, rendered
as `503 index_migration_in_progress` / `retryable: true` — the same reporting
contract `CorpusReadUnavailable` uses for a corpus that cannot be read at all,
and deliberately not that type, which is about a FAILED read and is cleared by
any successful one. `MigrationWindow` is RAII because Steps 4 and 5 propagate
with `?`; a manually paired clear would be skipped on failure and leave the
index refusing every query for the process's lifetime.

Also corrects `set_chunk_ids_migrated`'s doc, which named `run_migrations` as
its only caller when `M005ChunkIdEndLine::apply` calls it first.

* fix(trusty-search): M005 excludes reindex for its rechunk span and the fan-out reports a migrating index (Refs #6581)

Round 2's crash-safety fix left a second way to lose the same data, this time
to a concurrent writer rather than a crash. M005 was dispatched holding only
the SHARED side of the teardown lock, which blocks a DELETE and nothing else,
so an incremental reindex on the same index ran beside it. The reindex's
`copy_all_from` is #839's fix for exactly this class of loss: it snapshots the
LIVE corpus so hash-skipped, unchanged files survive the staged-corpus swap. A
snapshot opened while M005 held the corpus cleared copies nothing; the reindex
then commits only the files it saw as changed, and `commit_staged_corpus_swap`
renames that staging file over the live one. Every unchanged file's chunks are
gone, with no error and no log distinguishable from a clean reindex. M001-M004
were in-place rewrites and never held the corpus open in a cleared state, so
this window is one M005's own design opened.

`run_migrations_exclusive` closes it by taking the SAME per-index permit
`reindex::runner` already holds for a reindex's whole run — including the
snapshot and the swap — so the two can never overlap. Nothing in the reindex
path changes. The alternative the review offered, checking `is_migrating()`
before snapshotting, is TOCTOU: M005 can start between the check and the
snapshot, and a check is not exclusion.

Lock ORDER is what makes this safe rather than a deadlock. `reindex::runner`
and `reindex::defer_embed_queue` both take permit-then-teardown-read;
`spawn_index_migrations` took only the teardown read. Acquiring the permit
inside `apply`, under that guard, would have inverted the order, and with a
DELETE pending on the teardown write side — its only writer, and tokio's
RwLock is write-preferring — M005 would hold a read guard waiting for the
permit while the reindex held the permit waiting for a read guard. So the
acquisition sits in a new wrapper, permit first, matching both existing writer
paths.

Two narrower reopenings of the same reporting failure, closed with it:

- The `IndexMigrationInProgress` 503 reached only the single-index HTTP path.
  The multi-index fan-out dropped a migrating index through its generic error
  arm with NO counter incremented at all, so the caller saw a complete-looking
  sweep. It now reports `migration_in_progress_indexes_skipped`, alongside the
  `corpus_read_failed_indexes_skipped` precedent #5917 set for the identical
  problem.
- An unreadable recovery-plan blob degraded to "no plan" and fell through to
  the corpus-contents check — over the very corpus that pass had emptied,
  reproducing round 1's fail-open through corruption of round 2's own marker.
  It now fails closed: the version stays at 4 and the log names the remedy.

fix(trusty-mpm): gh poll timeout kills the process group, serializes per root, and backs off after repeated timeouts (Refs #6867) (#6886)

## Outcome

Refs #6867: `gh` calls made by `tm doctor`, `tm session prune-worktrees`, and
the hook-time probe can time out without killing the child's process group,
leaving orphaned `gh` subprocesses behind, and repeated timeouts against the
same root retry immediately instead of backing off.

## What changed
- A poll timeout now kills the whole process group the spawned `gh` sits in,
  not just its direct pid, so a `gh` subprocess (and anything it forked) does
  not survive the timeout.
- `gh` polls are serialized per root — concurrent callers against the same
  root queue instead of racing duplicate `gh` invocations.
- Repeated timeouts against the same root trigger a backoff before the next
  attempt, instead of retrying at the same cadence.
- Out of scope: the ~10 s poll cadence originally reported is not produced by
  a daemon timer in this code path; see the open question below.

## Risk / blast radius
Rung 3 — localized to `trusty-mpm` (`trusty-common` unchanged), with a
`code-critic` review round completed because this touches process lifecycle.

- `cargo clippy -p trusty-mpm --all-targets -- -D warnings` — 0
- `cargo test -p trusty-mpm --no-fail-fast -j 4` — 54 targets, 10498 passed,
  3 failed, 19 ignored; 16 new tests for this change pass

* fix(trusty-console): the saver never shows a black frame, and its tile shows the dashboard (Refs #6838 #6839)

The saver already drew a fallback in every non-live state. What it lacked was
anything that forced a repaint: `loadConsole()` set no `timeoutInterval`, so a
console that had bound its port mid-restart but could not yet answer held the
request for `URLRequest`'s 60 s default, and the class never overrode
`animateOneFrame()`, so every repaint depended on one of three navigation
callbacks firing. A first paint the full-screen host dropped stayed dropped.

#6838:
- `loadConsole()` sets a 5 s `timeoutInterval`, and a 6 s watchdog timer enters
  the offline state when WebKit reports neither success nor failure. The grace
  second lets WebKit's own error win the ordinary race so the log keeps the real
  NSError.
- `animateOneFrame()` invalidates the view once per second while the live page
  is off screen; `startAnimation()` invalidates once on the way in, so the first
  composited frame is already the fallback.
- The 15 s repeating retry becomes a one-shot rescheduled per attempt: 5 s for
  the first three minutes of an outage, 30 s after. `offlineSince` is set by the
  first failure of a run and cleared on `didFinish`, so a console that comes
  back is picked up without restarting the saver and a second outage gets fast
  retries again.

#6839:
- `Resources/ConsolePreview.png` is a 1920x1080 render of the services frame,
  generated by `scripts/render-console-saver-preview.sh` from the live
  `/ui/screensaver` page using the Chromium `website/`'s Playwright install
  already caches. `scripts/build-console-saver.sh` copies it into
  `Contents/Resources/` and refuses to build a bundle without it.
- The gallery tile draws it at full opacity; the offline fallback draws it at
  35% under a `TRUSTY CONSOLE · OFFLINE` banner, so a photograph of old numbers
  cannot read as live ones. A missing asset falls back to the old wordmark.

`PaintHarness.swift` is the new test: it reads the view's rendered bitmap through
`cacheDisplay` in three modes — a closed port, a listener that accepts and never
answers, and `isPreview: true` — asserting the frame is non-black and carries
drawn content within one second, and that the slow-daemon case produces at least
three connection attempts in 34 s rather than one 60 s hang.

Rung 6 (UI surface). No `crates/*/src/**` Rust changed.

feat(trusty-search): default TRUSTY_VECTOR_QUANT=f16 for new indexes, plus a one-shot backfill (Refs #6822) (#6843)

New indexes are built at f16 instead of f32: half the vector bytes in RAM and
on disk, with recall@10 measured at 1.00 — the same as f32 — on the
ooc_quick_wins fixture's query set. `TRUSTY_VECTOR_QUANT=f32` keeps full
precision; `i8` stays opt-in. An empty value now means "unset" and resolves to
the default rather than to f32.

Existing indexes are untouched. usearch writes the scalar kind into the
snapshot header and both `load` and `view` rebuild the metric and casts from
it, so opening an f32 index under the f16 default reads it as f32 and rewrites
no bytes.

The default reaches an index at creation time only, and `reindex --force` does
not change that — the store object is built once at warm-boot and a reindex
upserts into it, so a forced reindex re-embeds at the old precision. (The
memory-tuning table claimed otherwise; that claim is corrected here.) The
conversion is therefore its own command: `trusty-search quantize` and
`POST /indexes/:id/quantize` re-encode an index's vector arena in place,
carrying the chunk_id -> key map over unchanged.

Why not a `reindex --quant` flag (#402): a reindex resolves a root and walks a
tree, which is the machinery that hijacked another index's corpus and pruned
it. `quantize` accepts no root, performs no walk and never re-registers a
handle — it is addressed by index id through `state.registry.get` alone. It
also refuses while a reindex is running (the same `ReindexStatus::Running`
check `shutdown_flush` uses, #1717 / #3970), and its single durable write goes
through `UsearchStore::save`, keeping that function's #1711
empty-over-populated and #1717 shrink guards.

`GET /indexes/:id/status` gained `semantic_coverage.vector_quant`, read from
the live index rather than the env var — the only reading that is true for an
index built before the flip.

`main.rs` sits on a frozen line-cap budget, so the new subcommand's flags and
`cleanup`'s move into `clap::Args` structs beside their handlers. The CLI
surface is unchanged.

fix(trusty-agents): reprovision keeps a bundled file the operator hand-edited (#6831)

Every `cargo install` changes the bundle stamp, and the refresh that followed
rewrote any bundled file whose bytes differed from the shipped template. An
operator's edit and an older binary's deploy are indistinguishable from bytes
alone, so the pass archived the edit to a `.stale.<digest>.bak` nobody was told
to look for and wrote the template over it. That fired four times in one week
and reverted a model routing decision, a `[tools]` block, the `scopes` line that
reaches gworkspace, and whole persona sections — silently, because an agent
whose memory grants vanish does not error, it just behaves as though it has no
memory.

`.bundled-provenance` in the deployed directory now records the digest of what
this module last wrote at each bundled path. That is what separates the two
cases:

- Content matching the recorded digest is this module's, so a shipped template
  change still reaches an older install exactly as #3556 intended.
- Content that does not match is the operator's. The automatic pass leaves it
  untouched, counts it in `ReprovisionReport::preserved`, and names it in a
  `warn` plus a stderr line at startup and in `tagent agents deploy` output.
- `tagent agents repair` still overwrites everything, archiving the current
  content first, and the messages name that command.

`reprovision_embedded_locked`'s `refresh_stale: bool` becomes a `RefreshPolicy`
enum, because the pass now has three behaviors rather than two. `provenance` is
read once per pass and written back inside the same lock, only when the pass
changed it, so the matching-stamp fast path stays a true no-op.

Reading the manifest fails CLOSED: a missing file, an unreadable one, or a line
that will not parse yields no entry, and a path with no entry is the operator's.
So a machine with no manifest — every install in the field — protects its edits
from the first pass onward, and gets its pristine files vouched by that same
pass. The worst case of a corrupt manifest is a template update that waits for
`tagent agents repair`, never a lost edit.

Three existing tests hand-wrote divergent content and expected the automatic
path to refresh it. Two now record that content as deployed, which is what an
older binary would have done; the third drives the force path, since its subject
is the refreshed file's journey through the resolver rather than which entry
point refreshed it.

fix(trusty-mpm): the picker's first menu is sorted like every later one (Refs #6753) (#6829)

`run_tty_picker` applied the scope's filter and sort at the BOTTOM of its loop
only, so its FIRST menu printed the daemon's ascending-slot order. The attached
session — usually the highest slot — came last; bare Enter targets position 0,
so it aimed at the oldest session (usually stopped, firing `ConfirmRestart`)
while the hint read "resume most recent"; and the whole list reordered under the
operator after the first action. `tm ls`'s connector sorted before its first
render and the bare-`tm` path did not.

The order is no longer a call-site responsibility. `prepare_menu` derives the
whole render state — the list order, the launch-new number, the stale-slot

fix(workspace): internal dependency version requirements must accept their crate (#6818)

The root `[workspace.dependencies]` table carries both a `path` and a `version`
for each internal crate. In-tree the path wins, so cargo never evaluates the
requirement and no workspace build, check, or test can see it drift. The
requirement is only consulted when the crate resolves from crates.io — at
publish time, and by any external consumer.

Two rows had drifted out of range:

- `trusty-console` required `^0.9.0` while the crate is `0.11.0` (#6776)
- `tga` required `^6.0.1` while the crate is `7.1.0`

For a `0.y.z` crate the minor is the breaking component, so `^0.9.0` excludes
`0.11.0` outright; `^6.0.1` likewise excludes `7.1.0`. Both now track the
crate's current minor (`0.11`, `7.1`), matching how the trusty-common,
trusty-review, and trusty-installer rows are already written.

`scripts/check_workspace_dep_versions.sh` closes the class: it reads every
internal row, resolves the member crate from the row's `path` (not its key — the
`tga` row points at `crates/trusty-git-analytics`), and asserts the crate's
version satisfies the requirement under Cargo's caret rules. It fails closed on
an unreadable member manifest, an unmodelled requirement operator, and a
vacuous scan (#4618).

It runs as a step of `version-parity.yml`'s `pr-version-bump` job — a required
context that runs unconditionally on every PR, needs no toolchain, and asks the
adjacent publish-safety question. Its selftest runs immediately before it, so
the gate's green is never unproven.

* feat(trusty-audit): opt-in OSV.dev lookup over the scanned dependency inventory

version} and matched none of them against an advisory database. The
cargo-audit leg answers only for a Rust lock file, so every npm, PyPI, Go
and Maven dependency in an engagement reached the report unmatched — listed
in the Dependency Inventory beside a Security Posture section that
disclaimed having checked it.

Adds one opt-in leg. It reads the inventory trusty-review already measured
from investigation.json rather than re-parsing lock files, maps each row's
ecosystem onto an OSV name, and asks POST /v1/querybatch in chunks of 1000.
Results reach the bundle three ways: osv.json per repository, findings rows
the report renders under "Known vulnerabilities (OSV)", and a severity count
table in index.md that says "not run (opt-in)" when the collector is off.

Off unless [collectors] osv = true, because it is the one leg that tells a
third party the recipient's dependency names. [osv] offline = true — or
TRUSTY_AUDIT_OSV_OFFLINE — answers from the state/osv-cache/ TTL cache alone
and opens no socket. A 429 or 5xx is retried with exponential backoff, and a
per-repository time cap stops one slow endpoint from costing the sweep.

Fail-open and never silent: an unpinned package, an unmapped ecosystem, the
row cap the renderer applies to the inventory, a batch that went unanswered,
and a repository with no coverage at all are each named in the gap list and
in osv.json's errors, so an empty scan can never read as a clean one.

* fix(trusty-audit): bound, pace and account for every OSV request

Six defects the review found in the #6780 lookup, all in how the batch
endpoint is talked to.

`http_client()` builds a client with no timeout and the cap was only checked
BEFORE a batch started, so a server that accepted the connection and never
answered parked `.send()` past every cap and blocked the sweep. Every request
now carries an explicit timeout of the repository's remaining budget, the
bound `validate.rs` already applies for the same reason.

`Response::text()` read an unbounded body from an endpoint named in
configuration. It is now accumulated against an 8 MiB ceiling — refused up
front on a declared Content-Length, then chunk by chunk — and over-cap is one
batch's error line, never a crash.

`TRUSTY_AUDIT_OSV_OFFLINE=false` turned offline ON, because any non-empty
value read as true. Only the truthy spellings count now, mirroring
trusty-review's `flag_is_truthy`.

A response with fewer results than the batch had queries lost its tail to
`zip` with no cache write and no error line, and the clean-scan gap fires
only when nothing matched — so a partial answer read as a complete one. The
shortfall is now counted and named. The `parse` doc claimed `zip` pads; it
truncates.

A 429 carrying `Retry-After` is now paced by it (delta-seconds or HTTP-date,
bounded by the remaining budget) rather than by a 250ms backoff the server
has already said it will refuse.

`write_render` returned None for the OSV roll-up while the package index read
it off disk, so one bundle stated "not run (opt-in)" in one index and its
advisories in another. A re-render now reads the source package's own
`osv.json` files — beside each manifest it rendered, not in the fresh output
directory the collector never touched.

* fix(tga): advance the credential chain instead of re-offering source 1 (Refs #6782)

Linking libssh2 exposed the next defect: with the SSH transport actually
running, the credential callback looped. `Cred::ssh_key_from_agent`
succeeds against an `ssh-agent` holding no identities, and the callback
answered from the top of the chain every time libgit2 re-entered it after
a rejection, so `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` was never reached. A live fetch of
`git@github.com:octocat/Hello-World.git` spent 120 s re-offering the
empty agent and then reported `class=Ssh (23); code=Auth (-16)`.

The chain is now an ordered list walked by a cursor the callback carries:
each source is offered at most once, in the documented order, and a
source that cannot apply is skipped without consuming a turn. The same
live fetch now returns Success in 0.74 s and writes origin/master.

own name rather than dropped, and a manifest that will not read contributes

* fix(trusty-audit): resolve a 409 index registration instead of dropping the evidence tier (Refs #6783)

A `409 Conflict` from `POST /indexes` cost a repository its whole search-derived
evidence tier: `ensure_indexed` reported the refusal, `ground` turned it into a
gap, and the run shipped a report with no findings, no complexity distribution,
no health factors and no symbol-verified finding — over a clean exit and an
unqualified coverage line. A client sweep hit it on all 59 repositories, because
#6149 changed the id derivation and every row an older release had written under
the checkout basename now collides with the hashed id.

trusty-audit now reads the daemon's registry over `search.indexes.list`, decides,
acts and retries the create once. The id registered at this checkout is reused;
a row holding the id at another root, or this tree under an obsolete id, is
deregistered and the create retried. Deregistration never destroys the corpus
(`delete_data` stays absent) and carries `expected_root_path`, so a row that
moved between the read and the write is refused rather than deleted on stale
information. Re-creating under the derived id rather than adopting the
registered one keeps the cross-process id contract that trusty-review's renderer
and tga's sweep both depend on.

When the collision cannot be cleared, and on every other arm that loses the
index, the gap now leads with one phrase — `evidence tier degraded: search index
unavailable (<error>)` — and names the trusty-analyze pass that did not run with
it, so a skipped analyze pass is the same headline rather than a separate silent
gap. The run's `index.md` counts those units and qualifies its coverage line,
`N of M repositories audited WITHOUT search evidence`, so an M-of-M run can no
longer read as complete.

No trusty-search change: `search.indexes.list` and `search.index.delete` are
already registered socket methods.

undocumented background-job layout, which is the load-bearing half — archiving

* fix(tga): re-classify stored commits when the detector version changes (Refs #6748)

`tga collect` classified a commit once, at walk time, and persisted the
verdict. Nothing re-read a stored row when the marker set changed, so a
commit ingested before a detector fix kept the old verdict forever. The
discriminator on the affected corpus was ingest date, not message content:
~700 commits carrying a literal AI trailer sit at `is_ai_assisted = 0`
because they were walked before #1334 landed, while byte-identical messages
walked afterwards are correct. The downstream warehouse cannot repair them —
`fact_commits` has no message column, so the text exists only in `tga.db`.

Migration v28 adds `commits.ai_detector_version` with a DEFAULT of 0. Every
row in an existing database therefore sorts as older than the shipped
generation (`ai_markers::DETECTOR_VERSION`, now 1) and is re-classified once.
`collect::reclassify` runs at the head of every `tga collect`, scanning only
rows below the current generation and stamping each one it reads, so a
settled corpus costs one indexed lookup and no detection.

The pass works in 1000-row batches, one transaction each. An interrupted run
leaves every completed batch stamped and the remainder still selectable, so
the next collect finishes it rather than restarting. A row's verdict columns
and its generation are written by the same statement, so neither can be
stored without the other.

The count reaches the operator as one line on the pipeline's warning channel

was stale. Nothing goes to stdout. `tga backfill ai-detection-commits` now
stamps the current generation across the slice it scanned, so a hand-run
repair is not redone by the automatic pass.

* fix(tga): pin the reclassify scan to a composite index (Refs #6748)

The previous commit claimed a settled corpus costs one indexed lookup. It did
not. `ORDER BY id` over a single-column index leaves the planner two options
that ANALYZE cannot separate: `sqlite_stat1` records `20000 20000` for the
index, one distinct value across the whole column, so an index search and a
rowid scan look equally expensive. Which one it picks varies by SQLite build.
The critic's environment reported `SCAN commits` — a full read of every commit
message on every collect. This checkout reported the index plus
`USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY` — a sort of the whole stale set. Both are the
same defect: the cost tracked table size, not stale-row count.

The index is now composite, `(ai_detector_version, id)`, and the scan orders by
those two columns in that order, so the range walk is already sorted and no
temp b-tree is built. The query pins the index with `INDEXED BY`, which turns a
planner that will not use it into a prepare-time error instead of a silent
regression to a full scan.

`the_scan_uses_the_index_on_a_populated_database` builds 20 000 rows, runs
ANALYZE, asserts the `20000 20000` statistic is present so the plan is being
read under the conditions that caused the problem, and explains the shipped
query string itself: it must search the index, with no `SCAN commits` and no
`TEMP B-TREE`. Against the previous shape it fails on the temp b-tree.

Migration 28 drops the index before creating it, so a checkout that already
recorded migration 28 with the single-column index picks up the composite one.
The migration is unpublished, so no released database is affected.

Also records that `DETECTOR_VERSION` is hand-maintained: nothing ties it to the
marker table, so a marker-set change that forgets to bump it silently skips
re-classification.

fix(trusty-mpm): pause appends the session log in one write (Refs #6732) (#6757)

`sessions-log.jsonl` is append-only, but `catchup::session_log::append_entry`
emitted each line as two `write(2)` calls: `writeln!` on a `File` formats
piecewise, so the JSON payload and its trailing newline went out separately.
`O_APPEND` makes an individual write atomically seek-to-end-and-write; it
guarantees nothing about a PAIR of them. Two concurrent pauses could therefore
land as `<lineA><lineB>\n\n` — one unparseable line plus one blank — and
`read_log` skips the malformed line, so that record is gone. What survives then
reads as a destructive rewrite of the log rather than an append.

The newline is now built into the buffer, so one line is one `write_all`, which
`O_APPEND` does serialize against every other appender on a local filesystem.

Two regression tests, both in `crates/trusty-common/src/catchup/session_log.rs`:

- `concurrent_appends_never_lose_a_line` runs 8 threads x 128 appends. Before
  the change it corrupts 439 of 1024 lines; after, none.
- `append_leaves_other_sessions_bytes_untouched` pins the ticket's other
  closure condition — a pause by A leaves B's and C's bytes byte-identical and
  appends exactly A's own line.

The fix lands in `trusty-common` because that is the only writer of the file;
`tm session pause` and the `session_context_pause` MCP tool both route through
it. No public API changed.

The owner's home-page ruling is a bar per second per card. The host window was
sampled every 5 s, and nothing in the console measured another process at all.

Host cadence: `HOST_SAMPLE_INTERVAL_SECS` is 1 and `HOST_HISTORY_CAPACITY` is
600, so the window covers the same ten minutes at six times the resolution. The
CLI default and the `sample_interval_secs` the history payload advertises both
read the constant, so the graph's x-axis follows.

Per-service samples: every registered service gets `{ id, status, cpu_pct }`
each tick, into a bounded 600-point ring per service, out on the SSE stream as a
new `services` event, and into the `history` snapshot under `service_samples`.
`HistorySnapshot.schema_version` goes to 2. `GET /api/console/services` entries
carry the newest `cpu_pct`, read from those same rings so the list and the
newest bar cannot disagree.

`cpu_pct` is `null`, never `0.0`, when nothing was measured: an idle bar and an
unmeasurable one must look different on the card.

A service's process comes from the discovery artifact it already publishes —
trusty-mpm's `daemon.lock` `pid` line, and the Unix-socket peer pid for
trusty-search and trusty-memory. trusty-agents serves TCP loopback, which
carries no pid, and trusty-analyze and trusty-review are on-demand members with
no resident process; those three report `null`. A failed lookup backs off 15 s
rather than retrying every second.

trusty-common gains the two capabilities the console must not reimplement:
`sys_metrics::ProcessCpuSampler` (one `sysinfo::System`, refreshed over the
tracked pids only — never the process table) and `uds::peer_pid`.

Fail-open throughout: an unresolvable pid, a process that exits between two
samples, or a lookup task that panics yields `None` for that one service and
leaves the tick running. A vanished pid is dropped so a recycled pid cannot be
read as the old service.

Measured cost: 179 µs per tick for refresh plus read across six pids.

* fix(trusty-console): size the history broadcast for 1 Hz and keep the sampler alive across a panicking tick (Refs #6642)

Two defects the 1 Hz cadence introduced, from the code-critic round on #6642.

`EVENT_BUFFER` was 128, chosen when a tick emitted one event every 5 s — 640 s
of slack. A tick now emits two events every second (`record_sample` plus
`record_service_samples`), so the slack was 64 s: a browser tab backgrounded for
barely over a minute came back to a `lagged` frame and a hole in its graph. It
is now `HOST_HISTORY_CAPACITY * 2`, which is two events per tick across the
whole 10-minute window and moves with the cadence rather than being a second
number that can drift from it. A subscriber further behind than that has missed
more than the rings retain, so the channel could not have caught it up anyway.

The sampler loop is one bare `tokio::spawn`, so a panic anywhere in a tick ended
the task: the window froze, every open SSE stream stayed connected emitting
nothing, and no log line said why — indistinguishable from a quiet machine. Each
half of a tick now runs under `catch_unwind`, logs the panic payload at `error!`
naming which half raised it, and lets the next tick run. Guarding per HALF and
not per tick is what keeps the host graph drawing when the service half fails;
the service series shows a gap for that tick, which the UI already reads as no
measurement rather than as 0.0. `start` keeps the loop's `JoinHandle` and logs
at `error!` if the task ever ends, which after the guard requires cancellation.

Both new tests fail against the old code: the buffer test reports "told it
lagged by 272" under `EVENT_BUFFER = 128`, and both panic tests propagate their
panic without the `catch_unwind`.

fix(trusty-audit): a trusty-search update notice is no longer the index-failure reason (#6721)

`trusty-search`'s main.rs prints an update-availability notice on stderr ahead of
every human-facing subcommand, `index` and `index add` included, whenever
crates.io has a newer version. Both of this crate's refusal messages quoted the
first non-empty stderr line, so on a machine one release behind the notice
became "the reason" and the real diagnostic was discarded.

A delivered client audit masked 60 of 61 repositories this way. Because
`grounding` short-circuits the evidence-grounding and complexity-ranking pass on
an indexing failure, all 60 reports rendered "not assessed" with nothing recorded
anywhere to diagnose.

`search_stderr::reason` now skips blank lines and update-availability notices and

The dashboard rendered its semantic lane badge from `stages.semantic.status`
alone. That status reports on the last embedding pass, not on what the vector
store holds, so the two come apart: `tm-trusty-tools-19` (58,415 chunks) and
`tm-trusty-tools-21` (58,167 chunks) report `semantic: "ready"`, advertise
`vector` in `search_capabilities`, and answer every vector query with nothing,
while their `hnsw.usearch` files sit at 112 bytes against ~98 MB for healthy
same-size siblings. A status-only badge paints both green.

The lane badge now reads the three signals together — the stage, the capability
the daemon advertises off it, and `semantic_coverage.vectors_present` against
the chunk count. An index with chunks that advertises `vector` and holds zero
vectors renders `Empty` in red under a `Degraded` verdict that names the lane at
fault. The semantic lane also shows cumulative coverage beside the existing
per-boot `embedded/total`, which counts only this boot's pass and reads `0` on a
healthy index whose snapshot was already current (#4787).

`skip_vector`, `lexical_only`, a `skipped` semantic stage and the daemon's own
`no_vector_store` are left alone — none is at fault for holding no vectors — and
a lane still embedding has not yet been granted the `vector` capability the flag
requires, so it is not flagged for being unfinished.

The Health page additionally names the indexes with a failed lane from the
`indexes_stage_failed_ids` array #6694 added to `GET /health`. That list is
`IndexStages::any_failed()`, which cannot see the zero-vector case above, so the
card says so rather than reading as an all-clear it cannot give.

bundles are rebuilt and re-stamped against the same source digest.

endpoint or one `/indexes/{id}/status` call per row — and that endpoint walks
each index's directory for `disk_bytes`, which on a 41-index daemon is a cost

feat(trusty-search): /health names the failing indexes, not just their count (Refs #6688) (#6694)

`GET /health` carried failing-index counters only, so a consumer reading
`indexes_stage_failed: 1` on a 41-index daemon could not tell which index
failed and had to poll `GET /indexes/:id/status` for every registration to
find it. That blocked per-index remediation and made trusty-review degrade
every review because one unrelated index on the host had failed lanes (#6686).

A new top-level `indexes_stage_failed_ids` array names them. The ids come from
the same `IndexStages::any_failed()` predicate, on the same `handle.stages`
read, in the same registry scan that already produces `indexes_stage_failed` —
there is no second pass and the two cannot disagree, including under the
fail-open arm where a contended `stages` lock skips a handle from both. The
list is sorted because the registry is a `DashMap` and iterates arbitrarily.

`any_failed()` and not `corpus_open_failed`: a corpus-open failure marks every
lane `Failed`, so those indexes are already named by their lanes. Folding the
flag in would name indexes no counter on this response counts.

The field is additive and optional (`skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none"`)
and sits on `HealthResponse`, which is `pub(super)` and therefore not public
API — `cargo-semver-checks` cannot see it, and no existing counter moves,
renames, or changes type. `WarmBootSummary` is `pub` and not

fix(trusty-review): the context gate decides from the index under review, and an unknown index skips instead of returning zero results (#6692)

The required-context gate read the host-wide `/health` counters, which count
registry handles and discard index ids. One failed index anywhere on the host
therefore degraded every review on it, including a review whose own index was
healthy, and stamped a NOT AUTHORITATIVE banner on the result. The banner reason
was counter arithmetic: it subtracted `indexes_corpus_failed` from
`indexes_stage_failed` and announced that the remainder "return LEXICAL results
only" — false for the index that produced the report, whose lexical lane had
also failed and whose `search_capabilities` was `[]`.

The gate now probes `GET /indexes/{id}/status` for the index the review queries.
`/health` keeps one job: is the daemon reachable and serving
(`HealthResponse::reachability_state`, which reads no warm-boot counter). A
healthy target index proceeds whatever else on the host is broken; a degraded
one still labels the review, with a reason naming that index and the lanes that
actually failed.

Landing that alone would make a clean host proceed while the 404 below stayed
swallowed, so both ship here.

`gather_context` collapsed every search error into `Vec::new()`, so
`404 unknown index` was indistinguishable from a query that matched nothing: a
review whose configured index did not exist ran with no code context and
published an authoritative verdict. The 404 now propagates as `UnknownIndexError`
and the runner skips without a verdict, naming the index; a query that fails
against an index that exists stays fail-open. The gate catches the same case one
step earlier, and no `require_search` opt-out relaxes it — that opt-out degrades
a daemon outage, not a missing index. `SubprocessAnalyzeClient::has_analysis`
reads its `index_id` argument instead of discarding it, so the analyze side can
catch it too.

The resolver's prefix-only matching is untouched, per the issue's scope note.

The drain wrote every project on a host under one prefix keyed by whoever ran

Owner and project come from the git `origin` of each source's root — git walks
up, so a log directory inside a checkout resolves to that checkout. A source
whose root is no checkout sets `owner:`/`project:` itself, or falls back to the
new section-level pair. A source that resolves none of the three is a hard
config error naming the source and its root; there is no placeholder key.
Sources group by destination AND project, so one bucket holding three projects
runs three passes, each with its own manifest.

`enabled: false` on a source opts one project out. It runs no pass and uploads
nothing, and `tm doctor` lists it as `disabled` beside the destination it would
have used, so an opt-out reads differently from a project that fell out of the
config. `log_drain.github_id` and `log_drain.session_id` are gone with the key
segments they filled, along with the `gh api user` probe and the persisted
per-install session id.

Objects already uploaded under the old layout stay where they are: the manifest
is keyed by destination and key, so the new prefix starts with an empty
manifest, re-uploads the current files once, and dedupes from then on.

is now the only one — verbatim owner and repo (no slugification), the host

feat(trusty-memory): kg.redb copy-then-swap compaction as a dream-cycle phase; palace stats and compact CLI (Refs #6652) (#6670)

* feat(trusty-memory): kg.redb prune-and-compact as a dream-cycle phase (Refs #6652)

A palace's kg.redb only ever grows. redb returns freed pages to its own
free list, never to the filesystem, so retracting a fact, forgetting a
drawer or dropping a table reclaims nothing on disk. The one step in the
dream cycle whose stated job was bounding that growth — `kg.checkpoint()`
— has been a documented no-op since the SQLite era.

Measured first, on the live `trusty-tools` palace (read-only):

    file_bytes            341946368
    reclaimable_estimate  321979228 (94%)
    triples active=33677 history=23808 stale(>90d)=0
    dead index triples_by_predicate: 33677 rows, 2844604 live bytes

Every table's live bytes sum to about 23 MB. The other 94% is redb slack.
The history rows are 41% of TRIPLES but none is older than 90 days, so the
age-gated prune frees nothing on this palace today — the rewrite is what
recovers the space.

What ships:

- `trusty-memory palace stats <name>` — read-only per-table measurement
  (rows, stored/metadata/fragmented bytes, active-vs-history split,
  superseded drawers, reclaimable estimate). Opens the file O_RDONLY, or a
  snapshot when the daemon holds it, so it runs against production.
- Copy-then-swap compaction, never `Database::compact` (which needs
  `&mut Database` and zero live read transactions — a serving daemon has
  neither). `prepare` streams every live row into `kg.redb.compacting`
  with no lock held; `commit` re-checks a per-table fingerprint, renames,
  and installs the already-open replacement handle. The palace write mutex
  is held across `commit` alone.
- `KgDbState.db` becomes `RwLock<Arc<Database>>` so that install is one
  pointer store shared by every clone of the store. Without it the
  daemon's own handle would keep serving the unlinked pre-compaction
  inode with no error to signal it.
- History rows closed longer ago than `dream.prune_history_after_days`
  (default 90, floor 7) are skipped by the copy rather than deleted in
  place — an in-place delete would grow the file before the rewrite shrank
  it. An export taken before a run is the retention story.
- `TRIPLES_BY_PREDICATE` maintenance is removed and the table dropped by a
  fail-open at-open migration. No reader consumed it anywhere in the
  workspace; every assert and retract was maintaining an index nothing
  queried.
- Config: `dream.compact`, `dream.prune_history_after_days`,
  `dream.compact_min_bytes`, `dream.compact_keep_backup`.
- `palace_dream` gains `compact` and `dry_run`; `palace_compact` is
  unchanged but now says outright that it is vector-index-only.
- `trusty-memory doctor` reports the largest kg.redb: warn at 100 MB,
  fail at 500 MB.

Fail-closed branches, each with a test: an unknown table aborts rather
than dropping it; a failed or short backup aborts before the copy starts;
a fingerprint change between the copy and the swap aborts the rename; a
crash before the rename leaves the original untouched; a crash after the
rename leaves the correct file, which a reopen picks up; a stale
`.compacting` is removed rather than reused.

* fix(trusty-memory): the compaction swap excludes every kg.redb writer (Refs #6652)

Addresses the code-critic BLOCK on effb8c343. Three findings, all confirmed
before fixing.

CRITICAL — the swap was fail-open. `handle.write_mutex` does not gate every
writer: `KgWriter`'s actor commits on a `spawn_blocking` thread holding only
`Arc<KgStoreRedb>`, and a grep for `write_mutex` under `store/` returns
nothing. So `KnowledgeGraph::assert`/`retract` — and `kg_assert`,
`kg_retract_triple`, `share::supersede`, every direct KG mutator behind them —
could commit between the swap's fingerprint re-check and its `rename`. The
write went to the inode the rename then unlinked, and the caller was told it
succeeded.

Reproduced first, with the new test against the unfixed code:

    a_kg_writer_commit_inside_the_swap_window_is_never_dropped ... FAILED
    assertion `left == right` failed: a KgWriter commit inside the swap
    window was silently dropped (swap result: Ok(544768))

The fix puts the exclusion where every writer already passes: `KgDbState`
gains a `swap_lock: RwLock<()>`, and `begin_write_guarded` takes it for
reading before reading the live handle, so a writer that blocked on an
in-flight swap resumes against the NEW file. The eleven `self.db()
.begin_write()` sites now go through it, and the guard is bundled with the
transaction so it cannot be dropped early. `swap_database_exclusively` takes
it for writing across the re-check, the rename, and the install together —
there is no longer a window between them. Acquisition is bounded at 5s: a
palace whose writers stay busy skips the cycle rather than stalling
`remember` behind the palace mutex (#6366). The swap runs on a blocking
thread, since `swap_lock` waits for in-flight redb transactions to drain.

Lock order is always palace write mutex, then `swap_lock`. `swap_lock` is
per-store rather than per-handle, which is also the scope the file actually
has — one `KgStoreRedb` serves every `PalaceHandle` over a canonical path.

HIGH — `drop_dead_predicate_index_fail_open` is deleted. It ran
unconditionally at every Writer open, and `delete_table` walks every page of
the table, so the first restart after this landed would have paid a
full-table page walk inline on the daemon's startup path for the 342 MB
palace — the #6366 symptom. It was also redundant: `DROPPED_TABLES` already
excludes the table from the copy and `stats.rs` already counts its bytes
toward the compaction gate. The maintenance removal stays; the table is now
reclaimed only by the gated, backed-up, off-path rewrite.

MEDIUM — after the handle install, `sync_parent_dir` and `file_len` no longer
propagate `Err`. Both ran past the point of no return, so a failure there
made a completed swap return `Err`, the dreamer log "the live file is
unchanged" (false), and the reclaimed-bytes stat read zero. Both now warn and
report best-effort.

`version-control` re-derives four mechanical judgments on every PR it opens —
is the seven-field body contract satisfied, is the attribution footer exact,
were the shipped `--assignee @me --label trusty-mpm --label ws/<session>`
defaults attached, does this diff owe a changelog fragment. All four are
written down as prose in `tm-workflow.md` and enforced only by the agent
remembering them. The merge-queue procedure has the same shape: a fixed
stop-condition table over three `gh` reads, where skipping one under time
pressure is the recorded failure mode.

`tm pr open` runs the four checks before spawning `gh`. A failure names itself,
exits 2, and `gh` is never called. `--issue N` emits `Refs #N`; `Closes #N`
requires `--closes`, and a body smuggling an unrequested `Closes` is rejected.
`--dry-run` prints the assembled argv.

`tm pr queue-check` prints one `MERGEABLE` / `BLOCKED: <reason>` line per open
PR, reporting the FIRST stop condition among draft, hold label,
`CHANGES_REQUESTED`, an unresolved `code-critic` BLOCK, and a required context
missing or not `SUCCESS`. Required contexts are read live from branch
protection, never hand-copied. Exit 1 when any PR is blocked; `--json` emits
the same verdicts as an array.

Every `gh` call routes through `trusty_common::gh::GhCommand`, this
workspace's single `gh` entry point (#5475), behind a `GhRunner` trait so the
whole decision table is tested against canned JSON with no network.

`scripts/required-checks.sh` prints the live required contexts and refuses an
empty list, and `scripts/is-branch-caused.sh` turns the Baseline-Failure
Protocol into `PRE-EXISTING` / `BRANCH-CAUSED` / `INCONCLUSIVE` with exit
0/1/2, reproducing the gate in a throwaway worktree at the base ref without

method refuses with `-32602`.

One of the five was live: `tctl`'s `probe_socket` dials `memory.health`, which

and rejected in #6555: there are two decode sites, and neither reaches
trusty-memory's ~75 fallback methods, so the wire contract would hold at one and
not the other. Binding `memory.health` to `NoParams` was also rejected — it
genuinely takes `probe` and `deep`.

trusty-memory's contract suite gains the arm that catches this class. Every
existing arm hands the daemon `json!({})` by hand, so none of them builds the
frame `tctl` sends; the new one calls the real `probe_daemon_http` against the
real router, binding on the DERIVED socket path because `tctl` takes no socket
argument. It fails on the pre-fix commit with the `-32602` verbatim.

fix(trusty-console): stop the screensaver's body rule clipping every console tab (Refs #6658) (#6662)

No console page scrolled. `Screensaver.svelte` carried
`:global(body) { margin: 0; overflow: hidden; }`, and Vite emits one CSS
bundle for the whole SPA, so that rule shipped on every tab whether the
screensaver mounted or not. It sat later in the bundle than `App.svelte`'s
`body` rule at equal specificity, so it won, and anything taller than the
viewport was unreachable.

Remove the rule rather than scope it. `.saver` is already
`position: fixed; inset: 0; overflow: hidden`, so the screensaver clips
itself and takes no space in flow; `App.svelte`'s `body` rule already
supplies the `margin: 0` this one duplicated, plus a `min-height: 100vh`
that leaves the screensaver route exactly one viewport tall with nothing
to scroll behind it.

`src/bodyOverflow.test.js` fails on the pre-fix bundle and source, and
checks both: no unscoped `body` selector in `dist/assets/*.css` clips
overflow, and no component style clips a bare `:global(body)`.
`body:has(.saver)` stays available for a route that genuinely must clip.

The bundle under `ui/dist/` is rebuilt and re-stamped, so
`check-ui-bundle-freshness.sh` still passes.

feat(trusty-console): bounded machine-metric history with SSE stream (Refs #6641) (#6653)

* feat(trusty-console): bounded metric history and a per-service transition log, streamed over SSE

Refs #6641
See #6516

trusty-common gains `host_metrics::history::MetricRing`, a fixed-capacity FIFO
whose `push` is the single write path — so a sample the console takes and one a
service pushes (#6284) enter the buffer identically. `HOST_HISTORY_CAPACITY`
(120) and `HOST_SAMPLE_INTERVAL_SECS` (5) pin the owner's 10-minute window.

trusty-console holds that ring plus a transition log that records only the
moments a service's derived state changed, never a row per poll. A report that
goes stale past a 60 s grace reads `down`, because the metrics poller retains
the previous report when a poll fails — a cached entry is not liveness.

`GET /api/console/machine-status/history` returns the window and the log as
JSON, answering 200 with empty arrays before the first sample.
`GET /api/console/machine-status/stream` opens with one `history` event, then
sends `sample` and `transition` events; a subscriber that outruns the broadcast
buffer gets a `lagged` event naming the dropped count instead of a silent gap.
History is in-memory only and resets on restart, by owner ruling.

One loop in `machine_history::sampler` now writes both the point-in-time host
cache and the ring, replacing `host_status::start`, so the two cannot disagree
about the newest sample. It runs on its own 5 s cadence
(`serve --host-sample-interval`), independent of the 15 s `--poll-interval`.

The five per-service metrics handlers moved to `routes::metrics`; the new routes
put `server/mod.rs` four lines over the 500-SLOC cap.

* test(trusty-console): prove subscribe hands a mid-run subscriber every sample exactly once

Refs #6641
See #6516

The exactly-once guarantee of `MachineHistory::subscribe` against
`record_sample` rested on lock-scope proof alone: moving `events.subscribe()`
out of the read guard — what `let snapshot = self.snapshot().await;` does —
broke nothing any test could see, while a sample recorded in the gap reached
neither the snapshot nor the receiver.

A writer task now records 20 000 sequence-tagged samples while the main task
subscribes in a tight loop, and every mid-run subscription must resume live one
past the last sequence its snapshot held. Resuming later means a sample fell in
the gap; resuming at the same sequence means it was delivered twice.

Two shape choices earn their comments, both measured against the broken
version: an 8-slot ring keeps each snapshot near-free so tens of thousands of
subscriptions fit in the run (a full-size ring caught the break once in ten
runs, the small ring at 20 000 samples catches it ten times in ten), and one
subscriber beats three, which only starve the writer of a core.

Also states two inherited choices in the transition-log docs, so #6642 does not
have to rediscover them: a service's first observation is seeded silently, so a
late-starting daemon gets no `up` entry; and a report with no
`collected_at_unix` is never judged stale.

fix(trusty-installer): stack doctor probes trusty-memory over its UDS health method (Refs #6630) (#6640)

trusty-memory has been probed over the UDS transport since #6286, but the
JSON-RPC frame this crate's probe_socket built carried no params field at
all. RpcRouter::typed decodes an absent params as Value::Null, and
memory.health binds HealthQuery -- a plain derived Deserialize that refuses
null however many of its fields carry #[serde(default)] (that attribute
governs a missing key inside an object, not a null standing in for the
object). Every probe therefore answered with a coded invalid_params
RpcError, which health_string() renders down, so a live, healthy
trusty-memory read down in stack doctor / status / stack health / the
install verify tail.

analyze.health and search.health bind NoParams, whose hand-written
Deserialize accepts anything including null, so only trusty-memory was
affected -- the same asymmetry trusty-console's detect::memory::probe_health
already documents at its own #6356 fix for the identical mismatch.

probe_socket now sends an explicit "params": {} on every UDS health
dial, matching what trusty-console sends and what trusty-memory's own
uds_tests.rs exercises (daemon.ok(METHOD_HEALTH, json!({}))). {} is a no-op
for NoParams-bound methods (IgnoredAny accepts an empty object same as
null) and is what lets HealthQuery decode via its per-field defaults.

fix(launchd): restart waits for the unload before bootstrapping; memory bridge never spawns onto a launchd-owned socket (Refs #6618, Refs #6619) (#6626)

* fix(trusty-installer): tctl restart waits for launchd to finish the bootout

`launchctl bootout` returns when the unload is ACCEPTED, not when the job is
gone. `launchd_control`'s Restart arm called `bootout()` then `bootstrap()` back
to back, so the bootstrap reached launchd with the label still registered and was
refused: `booted out successfully; bootstrap failed: launchctl bootstrap gui/502
…/com.trusty.memory.plist failed: Bootstrap failed: 5: Input/output error`. A
plain retry seconds later succeeded, which is what identifies it as a race.

trusty-common gains `launchd_restart`: `await_unload` polls a label out of
launchd, and `restart_sequence` orders the bounce around that wait — quiesce,
boot out, wait, bootstrap, and one retry after a SECOND wait, because a retry
that skips the wait re-runs the losing race. Effects are injected, so the
ordering is asserted rather than described.

The quiesce is #6590's `guard_short_grace`, not a copy of it: the restart's
bootout is bounded by the same loaded `ExitTimeOut` that `service install`
already guards, so the method is now crate-visible and both callers share it.

`tctl restart` routes through `LaunchdConfig::restart_gracefully` and reports the
wait it paid; a restart that still fails names the label, both waits, and
launchd's own reason. The #4470 port gate still runs before the bootout.

`bootstrap_sites_tests` counts one bootstrap site in `lifecycle.rs` instead of
two, and its reason records that Restart's bootstrap now lives in trusty-common
where this scan cannot see it.

* fix(trusty-memory): no unsupervised spawn onto a launchd-owned socket

`ensure_daemon_running`'s single-flight `flock` (#5267/#6286) coordinates stdio
bridges with each other and cannot see launchd. During a `com.trusty.memory`
bootout/bootstrap window the production socket is transiently unserved, so a
bridge read "nothing is running" as licence to spawn — starting an unsupervised
daemon without the plist's FASTEMBED_CACHE_DIR/FASTEMBED_CACHE_PATH on the very
path launchd's instance wanted. launchd's process then found the socket held and
exited 0 ("another instance is already running"), reporting success while a
misconfigured orphan owned the socket.

trusty-common gains `launchd_claim`. `launchctl print` alone cannot answer who
owns the socket: in the window that loses the race the unit is booted out and
launchd reports nothing, so the INSTALLED PLIST counts as registration too. That
is the whole fix, and `socket_owner_defers_while_the_unit_is_booted_out` pins it.
`launchd::plist_path_for_label` and `launchd::label_is_loaded` are the label-only
readers behind it; the `LaunchdConfig` methods now delegate, so there is one
spelling of the plist path and one `launchctl print`.

Caller side: the guard waits for the unit, bounded by the termination grace, and
errors naming the label instead of spawning. Callee side: a startup refuses the
production socket when a unit is registered and launchd positively reports it
does not run this process — which holds for a daemon started by anything, not
only by the fixed bridge. `Unknown` supervision PERMITS: both signals read
launchd, so refusing on an unanswerable one would trade an orphan for an outage
on every host with an unreadable `launchctl`.

Both guards apply only to the canonical production socket. `is_production_socket`
is the single predicate, and a `TRUSTY_DATA_DIR_OVERRIDE` sandbox is never it —
the plist sets no override, so a process that has one is by construction not the
unit launchd runs.

trusty-analyze's `commands::daemon_guard::ensure_daemon_running` has the same
shape and is left unchanged: this fix is scoped to the crate that lost the race.

`wait_for_spawn` replaces `wait_for_socket`: it asks the socket first on every
iteration, then `try_wait`, so a dead child is answered within one poll

process's stderr unchanged, so the operator's log stream is unaffected. A
DETACHED child keeps `Stdio::inherit()`: it outlives its spawner, and a pipe
whose read end left with that process turns the child's next log write into

* fix(trusty-common): serve_until_idle drains in-flight connections on shutdown

Refs #6601

The shutdown arm returned the instant the signal resolved, unlike the idle arm
which reaches zero connections through drain_backlog. Every accepted connection
holds an Arc<RpcRouter> clone — in trusty-analyze that reaches a redb Database —
so the caller's socket unlink ran on top of handles still in use. The unlink is
what tells a client to spawn a successor, and the successor then died on
"Database already open. Cannot acquire lock." (#6595).

drain_shutdown waits for the in-flight count to reach zero, bounded by the new
RpcServeOptions::shutdown_drain (defaulting to shutdown::termination_grace, the
process's own SIGTERM-to-SIGKILL window). Connections are counted whether or
not an idle policy is configured, via IdleTracker::counting_only, so every
service behind this loop gets the guarantee. A client that dials during the
drain is accepted and closed at once — an immediate NoResponse rather than a
wait in the backlog ending in a reset.

trusty-analyze's caller-side Arc::strong_count poll from the #6595 fix is gone:
it was this wait done one layer too high, where only that service benefited,
and its 1 s SHUTDOWN_FLUSH_TIMEOUT could not cover an analyze.review handler
that runs for minutes. release_stores is a plain drop again.

`shutdown::CLEANUP_RESERVE` was documented as bounding trusty-memory's BM25 exit

and flushes every resident palace with no deadline, so a slow flush spent the

test(trusty-analyze): racing-servers test waits for the loser's exit instead of a wall-clock deadline (#6617)

`two_racing_server_processes_leave_exactly_one` counted surviving children
when a 30s timer expired and asserted the count was 1. Under load the loser
can still be alive at that instant without ever having bound, so the count
measured how loaded the host was rather than whether
`bind_singleton_hardened` held. #6467 fixed the SIGKILL-vs-probe ordering and
never touched this.

The completion condition is now the event: the loop ends when a child exits.
The winner holds a 120s idle window and the guard stays at 30s, so the first
child to exit is always the one whose bind was refused. The 30s is a hang
guard — its expiry no longer decides the verdict.

The verdict comes from two facts that hold at every instant. The socket file's
(device, inode) must be unchanged: a second server cannot reuse an occupied
path, so taking one over means unlinking it and creating a fresh one. And when
the loser did exit, its status must be a failure — a refused bind leaves
`main` as exit 1, so a success would mean that child had served.

Reproduced on the pre-fix test at 12-way parallelism under 96 spinners: 1
failure in 48 runs, `left: 2, right: 1` after 30.84s, with only one child ever
printing its serving line. Post-fix: 48/48 and 10/10 under the same load, the
whole on_demand target 3/3, and `cargo test -p trusty-analyze --no-fail-fast`
556 passed / 0 failed / 1 ignored across 8 targets. Forcing the guard to
expire immediately still passes; rebinding the socket mid-test still fails.

precisely while the drain test is inside its 20 s entry guard.

* fix(tga): collect skips the full history walk when the extract db is current

The fully-unbounded collect path — no `since_date`, no `--weeks` — has no
`collection_runs` week bookkeeping, so it re-walked the entire history on every
invocation. trusty-audit retries a failed repository by re-running all nine
sweep stages, so any render-stage failure paid a full re-collect; the issue
measured that against a 594 MB extract database.

Schema v25 adds `repo_walk_state`: one row per repository recording the head
SHA and ref name the last completed walk reached, plus a digest over every
branch and remote-tracking ref. On the next collect an unchanged repository is
skipped with a log line; an advanced head hides the recorded commit so only the
new commits are walked; a recorded commit that is no longer reachable —
force-push or rewrite — falls back to a full walk naming that as the reason.
`--force`, the existing re-collect lever, restores the unconditional walk.

The digest covers all refs, not HEAD alone, because the default revwalk seeds
from every branch and remote-tracking ref: a side branch that moved under a
stationary HEAD carries commits a HEAD-only comparison would drop. The state is
written incomplete before the walk and complete after it succeeds, so the
Ctrl-C-and-rerun flow re-walks in full rather than skipping on partial data.

A database predating v25 gains an empty table, which reads as never walked.

`CollectionStats` gains `repos_skipped`, the only observable separating a
skipped walk from a full re-walk that inserts nothing.
