* fix(tga): the walk skip reads the walk's scope, and an aborted walk is not complete

Two ways the #6073 skip could drop history permanently.

`--branch`, `--head-only`, a per-repo `branch:` override and `skip_merges` all
narrow what a walk records, and none of them appeared in `repo_walk_state`.
A `--branch main` run therefore recorded a tip digested over every ref —
including the side branches it never walked — and the next unscoped run read
that tip as current and skipped. The side-branch commits were then absent for
good. `repo_walk_state` gains `walk_scope`, derived from the collector rather
than the pipeline's flags so it cannot drift from what the revwalk seeds, and a
run whose scope differs from the recorded one walks in full.

The revwalk loop used to `break` on a yielded error and still return
`Ok(written)`, so a corrupt or unreadable object left a partial traversal
recorded as `walk_complete = 1` and every later run skipped on it. The walk now
commits the rows it wrote and returns `CollectError::WalkAborted`, which the
pipeline reports as a stage failure and never records as a completed walk.

* fix(trusty-analyze): wait for the last connection before the shutdown unlink

Refs #6595

Critic follow-up on the #6595 fix. Releasing the router before the unlink is
right for the idle exit, where `IdleGuard` guarantees no connection is open,
but `serve_until_idle` returns `Shutdown` the instant the signal future
resolves with no such check. A SIGTERM mid-request therefore left a connection
task holding a router clone — and with it the `FactStore`'s `Arc<Database>` —
so the unlink ran on top of a lock still held, which is the #6595 failure moved
to the shutdown path.

`Arc::into_inner` could not simply be retried: it consumes the `Arc` on its
`None` arm, so a failed attempt has already dropped the reference. The wait
polls `Arc::strong_count` instead, which is sound here because the count only
falls once the accept loop has returned.

`release_stores` now waits out SHUTDOWN_FLUSH_TIMEOUT — the budget whose own
doc scopes it to "the accept loop returning and the socket unlink" — before
warning. A handler with no read budget, `analyze.review` being the case, can
still outlast it; that path warns and names the consequence rather than
passing silently.

The new test forces the `None` arm deterministically: a peer that is accepted
but never completes its request frame parks the connection task in a read, and
an answered request on a second connection proves the accept queue got past it.
It fails on the previous commit with `Database already open. Cannot acquire
lock.`

Also records why the idle-exit test keeps `#[serial]` — a sibling's `set_var`
would race its child spawn's read of the environment under single-process

fix(trusty-common): verify the ACTIVE launchd grace before bootout (Refs #6590) (#6593)

launchd applies the ExitTimeOut of the job it has LOADED, and re-reads the
plist file only at `bootstrap`. `install_and_activate` writes the corrected
plist and then calls `bootstrap`, which boots the old job out FIRST — so the
60 s window #4393 added to `render_plist` never governed the termination that
races the snapshot flush. On a host whose loaded unit predated #4393 that
window was launchd's 5 s default, so the daemon was SIGKILLed mid-write and
KeepAlive respawned the old binary as an orphan holding :7878.

The new `launchd_grace` module reads the window launchd will really grant --
the loaded job's `exit timeout` first, falling back to the installed plist,
where an absent key resolves to the 5 s default rather than to "unknown". When
it is shorter than `shutdown::TERMINATION_GRACE_SECS`, the daemon is sent
SIGTERM directly, which launchd does not bound, and waited for; the bootout
then unloads an already-exited job. An unreadable unit changes nothing.

`trusty-search start`'s "already running" refusal now names the remedy
(`kill -TERM <pid>`), the flush window to allow, and who restarts the daemon.

fix(trusty-common): stream log bodies and record oversize skips once (Refs #6547) (#6588)

The drain read each log file whole — plaintext, decoded, filtered, scrubbed,
gzipped, five live copies — which is the only reason its 64 MiB ceiling
existed. On the first live run that ceiling left 29 of 86 daily-rotated daemon
logs, up to 176 MB each, permanently undrainable, and the drain re-decided the
same ~40 files every 15 minutes: 1,276 identical "skipping oversize file" WARNs
in 48 hours.

The new `log_drain::pipeline` module streams: 1 MiB reads split on the last
line terminator, with the level filter's disposition and a scrub window carried
across each boundary. The scrub window holds back the last
`longest needle - 1` bytes of every chunk, which is what makes chunking safe
for a secret that straddles a boundary — the hazard #6534 refused to chunk
over. `DEFAULT_MAX_FILE_BYTES` moves 64 MiB to 4 GiB; a second bound,
`max_wire_bytes` (64 MiB), caps the COMPRESSED body, which is the one buffer
that still scales with the file because `LogDestination::put` takes an
in-memory `Bytes`.

A file that trips either bound has the decision written to the manifest as a
`SkipRecord`, so it is made once per (file, size, mtime). A later pass over an
unchanged file counts it in silence; a size or mtime change re-evaluates; and
any file the pass can read has its record dropped, so raising a bound takes
effect on the next pass. The `log_drain` doctor row reports
`N over the size ceiling (M newly recorded)`.

fix(trusty-search): refuse basename fallback in index id derivation (Refs #6550) (#6573)

`resolve_project_root` returns the start path when nothing above it is a git
repository, and `derive_index_id` then takes its basename. A registration
handed `$HOME` therefore produced index `masa` — a well-formed id naming the
operator, which a later reindex repointed at an unrelated repository. The
derivation cannot detect that itself: a basename looks equally plausible for a
real project root and for a directory that names no project.

Both derivation sites now refuse instead of guessing, through one shared
predicate:

- `trusty_common::refuse_unindexable_root` (and its pure `*_against` form)
  refuses the home directory and the filesystem root, comparing by
  `identifies_same_path` so a symlinked or case-variant `$HOME` still matches.
- `ensure_project_indexed_reporting` and the incremental `index_files_inner`
  path log at error and return no id, so no caller can pin one. New
  `IndexRegistration::RefusedUnindexableRoot` reports the outcome.
- trusty-search's `detect_project` returns `ProjectRootRefused`, which names
  the refused root and points at `--index <id>`. `detect_project` and
  `index_resolve::resolve_index` are fallible as a result; the five CLI
  handlers propagate it.

The refusal is checked against the RESOLVED root, so a `$HOME` that is itself
a git repository is refused through the marker arm too.

fix(trusty-search): bound the FSEvents-overflow rescan; drop degenerate chunks before embedding (Refs #6570, Refs #6571) (#6582)

#6570 — the overflow fallback re-parsed and re-committed the whole corpus
every time. 22 passes in 48h, each logging files_reindexed=17284
chunks_indexed=183348 on a tree where nothing had changed. Excluding
directories from the watch is not available (notify's recursive FSEvents
stream takes no exclusion set) and neither is a bigger buffer (the overflow
is the kernel's, not a userspace queue notify exposes); an mtime watermark
is unsound and the module already documents why. So the pass keeps
full-tree coverage and drops the work instead: every walked file is still
read and fingerprinted with the same SHA-256 the reindex pipeline uses, and
a file whose content matches what the index holds skips the tree-sitter
parse, the embed, and the redb commit. The cache is warmed from the durable
corpus when this process has not populated it, so the first overflow after
a restart is cheap too. `.trusty-search/` — the daemon's own colocated
storage, which sits inside the watched root and is rewritten by every
commit — joins SKIP_DIRS, which is what the watcher's per-event filter
reads and which never consults .gitignore. The reconcile log line gains
files_unchanged.

#6571 — not a NaN or zero vector. The add error was "Duplicate keys not
allowed in high-level wrappers": make_chunk_id omits the end line, so a
minified one-line bundle's many `function e(...)` declarations all produced
the id `…/index.js::Function::e::1`. upsert_batch resolved one usearch key
for every occurrence, added the first, failed the rest, and then let the
failure rollback delete the id-to-key mapping the successful add had
installed — a vector in the graph with nothing pointing at it, and a file
that never became searchable. chunk_ast now drops a chunk whose id an
earlier chunk in the same file claimed, so the duplicates are never
embedded; upsert_batch collapses duplicate ids at the boundary that owns
the one-vector-per-id contract. The warning reports the error the add
returned instead of asserting a cause it did not observe.

fix(trusty-common): log_drain local manifest cache is keyed by destination — switching buckets re-uploads (Refs #6548) (#6562)

The cache lived at `<state_dir>/log-drain/<github_id>/<session_id>/` and
described no particular destination. Repointing one session from bucket A to a
brand-new bucket B loaded A's record, and because B had no remote manifest of
its own to override it, every file A already held hit the size+mtime fast path
and was classified SkipUnchanged. 86 files never reached B; sources with no
prior entry uploaded normally. That record was then saved to B, so B's
remote-authoritative manifest lists objects B never received.

The cache path now carries `DestinationUri::cache_namespace()` — scheme,
bucket-or-path and key prefix, hashed to one path segment. `?region=` is
excluded: it changes which endpoint serves a bucket, never its contents, so
adding one must not orphan a valid cache. `LogDestination` gained a
`cache_namespace` method so the identity comes from the destination rather
than from a caller who could name a different one. The remote manifest key is
unchanged; it already lives under the destination.

Taint recovery is detection plus a documented manual repair. A run whose
manifest came from the destination heads ONE sampled entry and warns when that
object is absent, counted in `DrainReport::manifest_spot_check_missing`. A
per-file head would put ~150 extra round trips on every steady-state pass,
forever, to guard against a defect that can no longer occur. Nothing is
re-uploaded automatically: an object a bucket lifecycle rule legitimately
expired would otherwise re-upload the whole session every run. The repair —
delete the manifest object — is in docs/reference/log-drain.md.

Scrub-before-upload and skip-not-chunk are untouched.

fix(trusty-agents): embedder gate init survives 429 and cache-lock races (Refs #812) (#6567)

Gate 4 of the pre-publish workflow burned two release trains on 2026-09-01, on
the same test, with two different errors: `http status: 429` from the
HuggingFace hub, and `Lock acquisition failed: .../blobs/<sha>.lock` from
hf-hub's per-blob lock. Both came from the same cause.

`FastEmbedder::default_cache_dir` hard-coded `~/.cache/trusty-agents/models`.
The gate pre-seeds the model into `FASTEMBED_CACHE_DIR`
(`/home/runner/.cache/fastembed`), and no env var could reach the hard-coded
path — so the pre-seed served trusty-common's and trusty-memory's selected
tests and never trusty-agents'. Its three tests re-fetched the ~23MB model from
HuggingFace on every gate run, and nextest gives each test its own PROCESS, so
three of them fetched it at once: one run hit the rate limiter, the next lost
the blob-lock race.

Three changes:

- `FastEmbedder` resolves its cache through
  `trusty_common::embedder::resolve_fastembed_cache_dir`, the existing shared
  resolver, rather than its own hard-coded path. hf-hub 0.5's `get()` reads the
  local snapshot without touching the network when the file is present, so the
  pre-seed now spares all eleven selected tests any request at all. It also
  stops the two caches holding the same model twice (87MB + 110MB locally).
- Init retries a transient fetch failure — 429, `Lock acquisition failed`, 5xx,
  timeouts — five times with exponential backoff and pid-keyed jitter, so
  concurrent processes do not re-collide on the next attempt. A terminal error
  (missing file, 404, corrupt model) still fails on the first attempt. This is
  one helper behind `FastEmbedder::new`, so every consumer gets it: the code
  indexer, the REPL, the recall tool, a user's first start, and the gate.
- Gate 4 sets `NEXTEST_TEST_THREADS: "1"`. Every test it selects loads an ONNX
  model; running them concurrently is what put eleven processes on one lock and
  one rate limiter. Serialising costs under a minute on a 60-minute job and
  removes the race instead of narrowing it.

Ten unit tests cover the retry helper with injected failures — no test added
here touches the network. `retry_recovers_after_transient_failures` fails the
first two attempts with the verbatim lock error from the job log and asserts
the third succeeds.

* fix(trusty-mpm): orphan_gc reads pane rows correctly again; tm doctor reports pty headroom (Refs #6529)

tmux sets its CLIENT_UTF8 flag purely from LC_ALL / LC_CTYPE / LANG. Without
that flag the server pushes every printed line through utf8_sanitize(), which
replaces each byte below 0x20 with `_`. A launchd-started daemon inherits no
locale variables at all, so the TABs separating the columns of

PaneInfo.session_name held the whole joined row, pane_current_command came back
empty, and classify_session's idleness gate could never fire. 456 orphaned
`tm-*` sessions survived every 60-second sweep for five days and took the host

Phase 1+2 of the log-drain epic: the drain core only. No scheduler, no
config plumbing, no consumers, and no GitHub-identity resolution.

  `object_store`-backed implementation covering `s3://` and `file://`.
  `get` is present because the manifest's "remote copy is authoritative"
  rule needs the remote document's content, not just its existence.
- `DestinationUri`: hand-rolled closed-scheme parser. `gs://` and `az://`
  are recognised and refused so the message names what IS supported.

  caller supplies `DrainTarget`; an empty component is refused with
  `MissingIdentity` before anything touches disk or network.
- Manifest: size+mtime fast path, SHA-256 tiebreak. Identical bytes are
  never re-uploaded just because mtime moved; the entry is refreshed so
  the next run takes the fast path.
- Collector: level filter (continuation lines inherit; a non-tracing file
  passes through verbatim), `scrub_secrets`, then gzip — fixed order, so
  no body reaches a destination having skipped the scrub. Oversize files
  are skipped, never chunked: the scrub needs a whole body to catch a
  secret straddling a boundary.
- S3 credentials reuse the AWS default provider chain already used by the
  Bedrock adapters, bridged into `object_store`'s `CredentialProvider`.
  No bucket or region is hardcoded.

compiled out from under the collector, and is added to the `core`

Critic round on fbe4bd891, three findings.

the request path with a raw `starts_with`. That is component-wise but purely
lexical, and the two sides routinely reach the daemon through different

claimant spelled the other way was missed and adoption proceeded against a tree

residual and what closing it would need are stated at the function.

fix(trusty-code): authenticate the loopback HTTP/SSE surface; /health discloses nothing unauthenticated (#6491)

* fix: require a credential on every trusty-code HTTP route, and stop /health disclosing pid and binding

`tcode serve --http` bound loopback and merged its ~30 routes and two SSE
streams with no caller check. A loopback bind limits remote reach; it
establishes no identity among local callers, and a page in the operator's
browser reaches 127.0.0.1 from inside that browser. Any local process could
read sessions and transcripts and drive the mutation, task, filesystem, and
catalog routes.

trusty-common gains the two halves this needs, behind a new `daemon-token`
feature: `daemon_token` (the 0600 credential file, minted on the server side,
read best-effort on the client side, compared in constant time) and
`server::bearer_auth` (the router-wide `require_bearer` guard, applied to the
fully-merged router so a route added later cannot slip past it). It sits beside
`origin_guard`, which deliberately passes every request that sends no `Origin`
and so was never authentication.

`run_http` establishes the credential before it binds and refuses to serve if it
cannot. `GET /health` stays public — trusty-console's gateway polls it holding
nothing — but answers an anonymous caller `{"status":"ok"}` alone; the full
payload, including the pid and the bound project's root path, now requires the
credential, which is what keeps `tcode tui`'s auto-attach binding check working.
Browser `EventSource` cannot send a header, so `POST /auth/sse-ticket` exchanges
the credential for a single-use ticket that expires in 30 seconds, rather than
writing the durable token into every access log.

Consumers updated: the TUI engine's RPC, SSE, and health-probe paths;
`TcodeConnector`; and trusty-code-gui, whose Tauri shell reads the token
(`get_daemon_token`) and whose webview installs one credential-attaching `fetch`
at bootstrap so a call site added later is authenticated by default. The
credential is withheld from any non-loopback target, so pointing
`TCODE_DAEMON_URL` at a remote host cannot make a client disclose it.

This is hardening, not the end state: a 0600 file is an OS-user and
browser-origin boundary, not isolation from an untrusted process running as the
same uid. The UDS transport fronted by trusty-console (ADR-0032, the 2026-08-19
ruling on #5439) is what closes that, and #5439 stays open for it.

🤖🤖🤖 Generated with trusty-mpm — https://github.com/bobmatnyc/trusty-tools

* fix: parse the loopback gate as a URL, not an Origin header, and narrow the SSE ticket

The credential-exfiltration gate #5439 introduced could be walked past. Both
clients gated on `server::origin_guard::origin_is_loopback`, which parses an
`Origin` HEADER: it splits the authority at the FIRST `:`, while WHATWG URL
parsing splits userinfo at the LAST `@`. So it read
`http://127.0.0.1:7882@attacker.example` as host `127.0.0.1` and answered
"loopback", while the HTTP client dialling that URL reached `attacker.example`.
Setting `TCODE_DAEMON_URL` (or the GUI's `TRUSTY_CODE_URL`) to that string sent
the durable token off-machine on the next request. The withholding tests used
plain hostnames, which parse correctly, so they stayed green over the hole.

`daemon_token::url_targets_loopback` replaces it — WHATWG parsing, any userinfo
rejected outright, unparseable is not loopback. `daemon_token::credential_for`
now owns the whole resolution (gate, override, file read) that each consuming
crate had spelled for itself; two copies of a security gate is one copy that
will not get the next fix, which is exactly how this bug reached both.

Four further findings from the same review:

- `credentials_match("", "")` was `true`, so a daemon holding an empty token
  would have authenticated a bare `Authorization: Bearer `. It now refuses an
  expected value below `MIN_TOKEN_LEN`, and `DaemonAuth::new` refuses to
  construct around one at all — a visible startup failure rather than a daemon
  that `401`s every real client.
- The token file was truncated in place, so a concurrent reader saw an empty
  file and two daemons starting together overwrote each other's mint. It is
  written tmp-then-renamed at `0600`, the discipline the far less sensitive
  `http_addr` file already gets.
- An SSE ticket was redeemable on any path and method, so one read from a trace
  log within 30s bought an arbitrary authenticated request, `POST /rpc`
  included. It is now bound at issue time to one path and `GET`, and mintable
  only for the two SSE streams.
- The webview matched the daemon by URL prefix — `http://127.0.0.1:7882` is a
  prefix of `http://127.0.0.1:7882.attacker.example`, the class #3280 already
  fixed once. It compares parsed origins. Its SSE subscription also re-mints on
  a drop: single use is what breaks `EventSource`'s own reconnect, which
  re-sends the spent ticket, takes a `401`, and would have died permanently and
  silently.

Test isolation: each spawned e2e daemon now gets its own
`TRUSTY_DATA_DIR_OVERRIDE`, so a test run no longer rewrites the operator's live
credential and concurrent test daemons no longer race for it.

* fix(trusty-mpm): refuse a binary reinstall from a source behind origin/main (Refs #4462)

`tm` is one global binary on PATH, shared by every managed session on the
machine, and `tm reinstall --binary` rebuilds it from whatever `--path` source
cargo's ledger recorded. Installing from a worktree that predates a fix
regressed that fix for every session at once, silently: the binary's own
version number does not move when its source is merely stale, so no probe said
anything. Publishing already has this guard (check-publish-ready.sh, "publish
only from merged main"); local installs had none.

refuses and names `TRUSTY_MPM_ALLOW_STALE_INSTALL=1`, mirroring the
ALLOW_UNMERGED_PUBLISH convention — installing from a feature branch is a
legitimate dev-loop action, so the guard makes it deliberate rather than
impossible. It refuses on positive evidence only: a source that is not a git
repository, has no origin/main, or has no usable git warns and installs.

`core::install_freshness` splits the git probe from the decision, so the
refuse, override and unknown branches are covered without running an install.

* feat(trusty-mpm): per-client durable inbox replaces the shared bus ring (Refs #6462)

Every subscriber of one bus instance shared a single 64-slot broadcast ring, so
#4271's fix could only stay truthful by refusing the publish: one client that
stopped reading made every publish to that instance answer 503, healthy
co-subscribers included, unboundedly.

Each subscription now owns a bounded inbox (DOC-60 §7). A stalled client falls
behind alone — publishes are accepted, co-subscribers keep receiving, and the
stalled inbox displaces its own oldest unread envelope. Every displacement
writes an `inbox_eviction` record to the §9 stream naming the message, the
instance and the subscription that lost it, and the reader gets a `lagged` frame
at the point of loss, so nothing recorded `delivered` is lost without a record.

`BusError::SubscriberLagged` and its 503 / CODE_UNAVAILABLE answer retire with
the wedge. A dropped subscription detaches itself, so a disconnected client
costs the instance nothing and no daemon-side timer is needed.

fix(trusty-mpm): mark a peer-bus envelope delivered only when it is (Refs #4271) (#6461)

* fix(trusty-mpm): mark a peer-bus envelope delivered only when it is (Refs #4271)

`broadcast::Sender::send` answers `Ok` for a receiver that is attached but
behind, so publishing into a full 64-deep instance channel overwrote an unread
envelope while the DOC-60 §9 durable log recorded `delivery_state: "delivered"`
for the one that displaced it. The sender got `202 Accepted`, the log said
delivered, and the recipient never saw the message or learned it was gone.
`routes.rs` compounded it: the SSE stream mapped `Lagged(n)` to `None`, so the
subscriber that lost the frames was not told either.

`PeerBus::publish` now asks `LiveInstance::saturated_backlog` before sending.
When the recipient's channel already holds `INSTANCE_CHANNEL_CAPACITY`
envelopes its slowest subscriber has not read, the new message is refused with
`BusError::SubscriberLagged` (503 / `CODE_UNAVAILABLE`) and recorded `dropped`.
Refusing the newest rather than silently discarding the oldest makes the
invariant hold: what the log calls delivered is exactly what the subscriber
receives. The SSE stream emits an `event: lagged` frame carrying the missed
count and the durable log's path, so a subscriber that races past the publish
check can still recover the envelopes it missed.

* fix(trusty-mpm): close the bus publish check/send race and surface its 503 (Refs #4271)

Review findings on the #4271 fix.

`saturated_backlog()` measured the channel and `tx.send()` filled it under two
separate acquisitions of the broadcast tail lock, so the measurement was stale
by the time the send ran: two publishers that both saw `capacity - 1` both sent
and the second evicted an unread envelope both records called Delivered. That
is the original fail-open narrowed to a window rather than closed.
`LiveInstance::deliver` now holds a per-instance gate across the measurement and
the send, and every clone of a `LiveInstance` shares it, so publishers that
resolved the instance separately still serialize.

`AuditLogger::try_log` wrote the record and its newline as two unbuffered
writes, so concurrent publishes interleaved into a line no reader could parse.
Both now go out in one `write_all` — the stream that answers "sent, or never
read?" has to survive the concurrency this change makes ordinary.

Also: `publish_message`'s status enumeration gained the 503 and its retry and
availability semantics; an HTTP end-to-end test pins that the route actually
answers it; and `SubscriberLagged` drops the `backlog` field, which could only
ever equal the ring's depth.

The availability consequence is documented rather than bounded: one stalled
subscriber makes its instance refuse every publish, and it clears when that
receiver drops or the instance is deregistered. A daemon-side timer has no
mechanism here — `broadcast` offers no per-receiver eviction, and dropping the
channel would discard envelopes already recorded Delivered, re-creating #4271 by
another route. The per-subscriber buffer that would bound it is DOC-60 §7's
durable inbox, deferred to the owner.

Under forced structured output the reviewer's response text IS the JSON

Consumers read that field as the human-readable review: the GitHub comment
builder splices it in as the prose summary, and a downstream app that passes
a non-empty daemon body through unchanged posts it as the whole comment.
#4999's audit of 22 dry-run reviews found 19 posting

map-reduce, which builds its body from the synthesis summary instead.

`render_review_body` now converts a structured payload into the narrative the
model wrote and leaves every other body untouched. It renders no verdict and
no grade: the pipeline settles both after this point, so a copy rendered here
could only disagree. A payload with no narrative renders a marker rather than
the JSON, keeping "the model wrote no prose" distinguishable from "the
renderer did not run".

* fix(trusty-review): drop a citation past the file's last diffed line (Refs #4999)

Citation integrity verified quoted content only, so a cross-file
misattribution that quoted nothing substantial survived with its severity
intact — the shape behind 5 of the 19 fabricated-or-partial findings in
#4999's audit, every one of which also misattributed another file's content.
The cited line is the only checkable claim there, and it is checkable without
an LLM.

`DiffContentIndex` now records the highest line each file's hunks reach, over
both sides of every `@@` header and over Stage-B-dropped hunks as well, so
counting can only widen a span and reduce false drops. A finding whose own
line, or whose `[code: ...]` locator line, is past that maximum is dropped. A
file with no parsable header fails open. Locators are collected whether or not
the bracket also quotes an excerpt, which is what lets an excerpt-free
citation be checked at all.

A write acquires the per-palace write mutex and then runs embed → vector

after. A slow commit therefore held the mutex for as long as it took, and

can never trip it). On expiry the pipeline future is dropped, which releases

A reindex progress stream opened against a running reindex could lose an

buffer under the `events` lock and broadcast after releasing it, while a
stream opened by snapshotting that buffer under the same lock and
subscribing after releasing it. An event appended after the snapshot and
broadcast before the subscribe reached neither path; one appended before the

replay buffer, the status, and the subscription under that same lock. The two
critical sections are then ordered, so every event lands on exactly one path.

The SSE route and the socket method each had their own copy of the two-step
open; both now call the one method, so they cannot drift apart again. Neither
route's frame sequence changes for a client that was not hitting the race.

`no_event_is_lost_or_duplicated_when_a_stream_opens_against_live_pushes` is

holding the array — made the whole response fail to deserialize. The
verdict-keyword scan then salvaged the verdict, discarded the evidence, and
printed APPROVE with `Findings: none`, byte-for-byte indistinguishable from a

  returns UNKNOWN with `is_fail_safe = true`, and the runner copies the reason

  lost findings rather than a bare `Findings: none`.

fail against the pre-fix parser, with `parse_double_encoded_findings_are_recovered`

* fix(trusty-console): bound the stream open, release the reader on disconnect

Three code-critic findings on PR #6392.

- Opening a stream is bounded at 60 s. `send_framed_stream_request_capped`
  applies its one timeout to the dial, the request write, AND each frame read,
  and that figure is `STREAM_FRAME_TIMEOUT`'s day so a stalled reindex is not
  cut off. A listener whose backlog is full accepts and then reads nothing, so
  the browser waited a day for a response head. `open_stream` and
  `stream_response` now take an `open_timeout` and wrap the open — the helper
  call and the first `next_frame` — leaving the long per-frame budget in force
  once the head is written. Abandoning that first read is safe: the stream is
  dropped with it.
- The SSE reader task selects on `Sender::closed()` beside `next_frame`, the
  shape `trusty_search::service::rpc::streams` uses on the producer side. A
  browser leaving a quiet status stream used to go unnoticed until the next
  frame, holding the socket and the daemon's producer open for that long.
- `routes::BODY_LIMIT` was a second 64 MiB literal for the figure
  `search_uds::MAX_FRAME_BYTES` already holds; it is gone, and the invariant is
  restated as a FLOOR — this client's budget must be at least the listener's,
  since smaller breaks a response the daemon already produced while larger has
  no failure mode.

The critic's remedy for that third finding was a dev-dependency on
trusty-search so the two constants could be compared directly. Deliberately not
taken: it would build tantivy, tree-sitter and ORT into `cargo test -p
trusty-console`. `the_frame_budget_is_at_least_the_listeners` reads the
`pub const MAX_FRAME_BYTES` declaration out of
`crates/trusty-search/src/service/socket.rs` source text instead and asserts the
direction, failing closed when the declaration moves.

fix(trusty-console): send params on the memory.health probe so a live UDS daemon reads as running (Refs #6356) (#6359)

The probe built its `memory.health` frame with no `params` field.
`RpcRouter::typed` decodes an absent `params` as `Value::Null`, and
trusty-memory binds `HealthQuery` — a derived `Deserialize` that refuses
null however many of its fields default. Every dial came back `-32602`
("params do not decode: invalid type: null, expected struct HealthQuery"),
`probe_health` read any error as no-answer, and the dashboard rendered a
live daemon as "Available — Binary found but daemon is not running".

The request now sends `params: {}`, which takes every `HealthQuery`
default — the cheap health path, not the embedder round-trip `probe`/`deep`
would ask for. The sibling analyze and review daemons bind `NoParams`,
whose hand-written `Deserialize` accepts null, which is why only this
connector was affected and why their frames are left alone.

`probe_health` also stops collapsing "answered with an error" into "did not
answer": a daemon that answers is running, so that case now reports the
row model's existing `Degraded` state carrying the daemon's own error,
instead of repeating a "not running" line the operator has already
disproved. It is not fail-open — an error answer still never reads as
`Running` and never carries a version.

fix(trusty-audit): GitHub collection is bounded under secondary rate limits (Refs #6084) (#6303)

The two paths in #6084 both live in tga, which trusty-audit drives as a child
process: PR-review collection under `github.fetch_prs`, and the per-`#N` issue
lookup under `github.fetch_on_reference` (default true).

Neither bounded anything across requests. Each retried on a fixed 1s/2s/4s
ladder that never read `Retry-After`, then moved on to the next item, which
retried the same way — so a secondary rate limit made every remaining item pay
four more rejected requests. On this repository that was 2625 pull requests and
3681 references, and the run sat in the loop for 45+ minutes.

Both paths now route through one `FetchBudget` shared for the whole run:

- `Retry-After`, or an `x-ratelimit-reset` when a drained
  `x-ratelimit-remaining` marks a primary limit, drives the wait. A plain 403
  with no rate-limit evidence is still returned immediately rather than retried.
- Each wait is clamped to 60s and charged against a 120s per-run allowance.
- Exhausting the allowance latches a breaker: every later call returns
  `CollectError::Throttled` without sending a request.
- Paginated walks stop at 100 pages; reference lookups stop at 500 per batch.

Nothing that stops early is presented as complete. Page caps append to the
budget's truncation ledger, which reaches the run through
`PrProvider::fetch_notices` as a `CollectionFault`; a rate-limited reviewer pass
records a stage failure so it reaches the exit code; and the reference path
returns `IssueBatch::stopped_early` naming what went unclassified.

A rate-limited reference is no longer cached as a resolved "no signal".
`fetch_issue` now separates "GitHub answered, there is nothing here" (`Ok(None)`,
cacheable) from "GitHub refused" (`Err`, not cacheable), and `warm_generic` only
caches keys it actually got an answer for — which fixes the same fail-open for
JIRA, Linear, Shortcut, Confluence, and Datadog.

fix(trusty-search): swap resolution restores a truthful hnsw_path/is_view on the live store (Refs #6299) (#6301)

A reindex could leave an index unable to accept any vector write for the life
of the daemon. Each checkpoint saved to the reindex staging file and recorded
it as the store's snapshot source; an idle or memory-pressure demotion then
re-viewed the store from that file; `commit_staged_hnsw_swap` /
`abort_staged_hnsw_swap` renamed or deleted it without telling the store. Every
later write then failed `usearch failed to promote view -> mutable load: No
such file or directory`, permanently, because a failed promote never clears
`is_view`. Three production indexes wedged this way (cto today, two more in
July).

Two changes, one for each half of the guarantee:

- The wedge is now impossible at its only producer. Both swap resolutions call
  `VectorStore::resolve_staged_snapshot` once the on-disk side has settled, and
  only when it succeeded: a commit re-points the store at the live path (same
  bytes, new name), an abort restores it from the live snapshot through the
  existing #4707 adoption path, which re-validates that snapshot against every
  ordinary load guard. A store that recorded some other path is left alone.

- Any residual wedge is now self-healing. When `promote_view_to_mutable` cannot
  re-read the recorded snapshot, it rebuilds the graph from the mapping it
  still holds — a mapping outlives the unlink or rename of its file — instead
  of failing this and every future write. No vector is lost doing it.

Regression coverage, all four failing against the pre-fix code with the exact
production error string: `write_after_commit_swap_succeeds_when_store_was_
demoted_to_staging_view`, `write_after_abort_swap_succeeds_when_store_was_
demoted_to_staging_view`, `write_after_abort_swap_rebuilds_when_no_live_
snapshot_exists`, and `test_promote_rebuilds_from_view_when_snapshot_vanished`.

fix(tga): config structs redact credentials in every Serialize path (Refs #5775) (#6302)

Six credential fields were written verbatim by a derived `Serialize`:
`LinearConfig.api_key`, `GithubConfig.token`, `JiraConfig.token`,
`BitbucketConfig.app_password` and `.token`, `AzureDevOpsConfig.pat`, and
`ClassificationConfig.openrouter_api_key`. #5770 fixed the `Debug` half of the
same leak; a `Serialize` leak reaches a file, a manifest, or a response body
rather than a log.

Each struct now has a hand-written `Serialize` in
`core::config::credential_serialize` that writes every non-credential field
unchanged and writes the credential as the fixed `<redacted>` marker, through
the same constant and the same two mask helpers the `Debug` impls use. `Config`
and `PmConfig` embed these sections and still derive `Serialize`, so they
inherit the redaction.

Every impl destructures `Self` exhaustively with no `..`, so a field added to
any of these structs fails to compile until this file names it, and a field
named but not written trips `unused_variables` under `-D warnings`. A secret
newtype would be stronger for a struct that does not exist yet, but all three
wrappers in this workspace refuse `Serialize` on purpose (DOC-45 `C-8.3`), so a
config field of that type would strip `Serialize` from `Config` rather than
redact it — and a fourth wrapper would change six public field types and every
authentication call site in `collect::`.

The round-trip break is deliberate (#5775 closure condition 1): a serialized
config read back carries the literal `<redacted>`. Nothing writes a config out
today, and the marker authenticates with no provider, so a future reload fails
at authentication rather than silently as the wrong identity.

The tests live outside the crate and use only the public API, so they compile
unchanged against the pre-fix source — all seven fail there, six on "the whole
credential reached serialized output".

feat(trusty-common): multi-frame streaming responses over UDS (Refs #6286) (#6296)

`uds::server` answered exactly one frame per connection, so a daemon migrating
off HTTP under ADR-0032 had to buffer a token stream into a single response or
keep its HTTP endpoint. #6287 deferred the multi-frame extension "until a daemon
has a real cross-crate SSE consumer"; trusty-memory's `POST /api/v1/chat`, which
streams LLM tokens off a `ReceiverStream`, is that consumer, and the owner ruled
to build the extension rather than degrade chat.

Wire contract. A request gains ONE optional field, `"stream": true`. Absent means
false, and false is the protocol byte for byte as it stood — one request frame,
one response frame. So an old client against a new server, and a new client
calling a method that does not stream, behave exactly as before. A request that
asks for a stream, against a method registered with `RpcRouter::typed_stream`,
gets a sequence of newline-terminated frames on the same connection, each
carrying a `"stream"` discriminant a plain response never has: zero or more
`"stream":"item"` frames, then EXACTLY ONE terminal frame — `"stream":"end"` or
`"stream":"error"`.

A stream terminates on a frame, never on EOF. `write_stream` has no path that
returns without a terminal frame: a producer that fails mid-stream, one that
fails to open, and an item over `max_frame_bytes` all become terminal error
frames. The client reports EOF-without-a-terminal-frame as `NoResponse` rather
than returning what it received — a truncated token stream read as a complete
answer is the Fail-Open branch this shape exists to close, and
`stream_reports_a_truncated_stream_rather_than_an_empty_success` fails if that
guard is removed.

Both protocol mismatches fail immediately, in the shape the caller reads. A
request without the flag against a streaming method gets one ordinary response
frame carrying `CODE_STREAM_REQUIRED`. A streaming request against anything that
does not stream gets one terminal error frame carrying `CODE_STREAM_UNSUPPORTED`,
naming the methods this listener does stream. Neither hangs.

Producer shape is the shape chat already has: `typed_stream`'s handler returns a
`tokio::sync::mpsc::Receiver`, which `ReceiverStream::new` also takes. Client
side, `send_framed_stream_request` returns a `FramedStream` that yields items
through `next_frame()` or adapts into a `futures_util::Stream`, with the same
`_capped` budget option. `max_frame_bytes` applies per frame in both directions;
`read_timeout` does NOT apply between streamed frames — the gap between two
frames is the model's production latency, and a budget there would kill a working
answer.

`RpcRequest` is deliberately untouched. Its fields are all public and it is not
`#[non_exhaustive]`, so a new field would have made an additive feature a 0.x
break; the flag is read through a private probe struct, and only on a router that
registers at least one streaming method. The new `UdsRpcError` variants are
APPENDED, not inserted: placing them ahead of `Timeout` shifted its implicit
discriminant 7 -> 9, which `check_semver.sh` reported as a major break.

feat(trusty-common): RpcRouter fallback seam for generic dispatchers (Refs #6286) (#6295)

`RpcRouter::dispatch` answered every unregistered method with
`method_not_found`, so a daemon that already owns a transport-agnostic
`(method, params)` dispatcher could only mount on the UDS server by
re-registering each of its methods by name. trusty-memory has ~75 of them, and
a second copy of that table is the silent-drift risk the common-entry-point
rule exists to prevent.

`RpcFallback` is a catch-all taking the method NAME as well as the params, and
`RpcRouter::fallback` mounts one. It is consulted only after the `BTreeMap`
lookup misses, so a registered method still wins and a service can override one
method of its own dispatcher by registering it. An error the fallback returns
becomes the response's error half verbatim, so a refusal is a coded JSON-RPC
frame rather than a dropped connection.

Additive: a router that sets no fallback behaves exactly as before, and every
existing test passes untouched. The `jsonrpc` version check is unchanged —
normalisation is the bridge's job in a later slice.

changed. `check_semver.sh --crate trusty-common` reports 196 pass / 58 skip,

* fix(trusty-analyze): start resolves the one socket it probes and spawns for

`handle_start(socket: &Path)` probed the socket it was handed, spawned a child
with a bare `serve` — which derives its own path from the data directory — and
then printed the path it had probed. For any argument but the derived default
that is a split brain: probe one socket, serve another, report the first.

Only one call site exists and it passes `service::socket_path()`, so nothing
misbehaves today. The signature was the defect: it promised a socket parameter
the body did not honour, and `Cmd::Start` has no `--socket` flag to make the
promise good.

Dropping the parameter is the cheaper correct fix than forwarding it. The
child must derive its path or consumers cannot find it, so there is exactly
one right value — and resolving it inside the function is what makes the
probe, the spawn and the message read the same one. `handle_stop`,
`handle_status` and `handle_doctor` keep their parameter: they only observe a
socket, never start one, so taking a path is correct for them.

The argv moves into a pure `serve_args()` so the no-`--socket` contract is
assertable without spawning anything — the pattern tga's
`audit::analyze::serve_args` already uses.

  fallback is deleted: two port moves out of date, and trusty-mpm's daemon port
  since #2566, so a running `tm` reported trusty-review as Running.
- trusty-installer's probe gains `uds_socket_for` and `classify_rpc_response`.
  The envelope rule is unchanged — a health body is a health body whatever
  carried it — but a JSON-RPC error frame gets its own `ProbeOutcome::RpcError`,
  since a socket has no status code. Like `HttpError` it renders `down` and is

serve site says so. They are browser-CSRF machinery with no meaning on a socket;
the boundary is the 0700 directory, the 0600 socket, and `ensure_peer_is_self`

this daemon with `KeepAlive::Always` and a 10s throttle, so a SIGKILLed
predecessor leaves its socket file behind; `bind_hardened` refuses an occupied
path and the successor would crash-loop with no visible cause. The singleton
bind probes first and takes over only a socket the kernel proves nobody serves.

The frame budget is raised to 32 MiB on the serve side. The response is bounded
by the reviewer model's output, but `local_diff_text` is caller-supplied and
`truncate_diff` only cuts it AFTER the frame is read, so a large monorepo diff
can pass 8 MiB.

`trusty-review port` becomes `trusty-review socket`: it prints the path and
whether anything answers, and still exits non-zero when nothing does.

`trusty-review` leaves the port-assignments table and both sibling

feat(trusty-common): generic framed-JSON-RPC UDS server loop (#6280)

* feat(trusty-common): a generic framed JSON-RPC server for the uds module

`uds::rpc` dials, writes one frame and reads one back; nothing owned the
other end generically. The only server-side accept loop was
`webhook_relay::serve`, which serves exactly one method and conditions its
answer on a durable write, so a service migrating its transport under
ADR-0032 had to hand-roll a fourth accept loop.

`uds::server` is that loop as a shared entry point. A caller registers method
names against handlers over its own request and response types; `RpcServer::run`
binds through `bind_hardened`, runs `ensure_peer_is_self` on every accepted
connection before reading a byte, dispatches each connection in its own task,
and unlinks the socket on shutdown. An unknown method answers a JSON-RPC
method-not-found frame rather than dropping the connection.

Neither `bind_hardened` nor tokio's `UnixListener` unlinks the socket path, so
the cleanup is explicit and runs before the listener is dropped — reversing
that order lets this process delete a successor's fresh socket.

`webhook_relay` is unchanged.

* fix(trusty-common): surface a panicking uds rpc handler, and pin the frame-budget boundary

Review findings on PR #6280.

The per-connection `tokio::spawn` dropped its JoinHandle, and tokio drops a
panicking task's payload along with the handle. A handler that panicked left
the client with a dropped connection and the server with no log line at all.
The connection now runs in an inner task whose handle is awaited, so a
`JoinError::is_panic` becomes one `tracing::error!` naming the failure. Costs
one task per connection; buys the only record that the panic happened.

`max_frame_bytes` counts the terminating newline, so the usable payload is one
byte less. That is not an off-by-one to correct: `uds::rpc`'s `read_one_frame`
reads with the same `take(max_frame_bytes)` and the same comparison, and moving
the line on one end alone would produce a frame the client sends happily and the
server refuses. The doc now states the boundary exactly, and a test pins it from
both sides.

Test readiness now probes with `uds::probe::socket_is_serving` rather than
checking that the socket file exists — `bind_hardened` creates the file before
`serve_until` reaches its first accept, so the existence check could hand a test

feat(trusty-mpm): tm wait polls a condition instead of sleeping (Refs #5843) (#6235)

* feat(trusty-mpm): tm wait polls a condition instead of sleeping (Refs #5843)

An agent has no guard-compliant way to wait for a long-running background
operation. Foreground `sleep` is rejected by the guards, and the harness
auto-backgrounds a foreground call near ~120s — so an agent facing a cold build
measured at 1h04m ends its turn and loses the work.

No sleep length fixes this, because no single call may run that long. `tm wait`
polls a CONDITION in bounded slices instead: one invocation returns before the
ceiling, and the agent re-issues the identical command until the wait reaches a
terminal state.

The verb surface is the exit code plus one `tm-wait …` line on stdout:

  exit 0  status=met      terminal — the condition holds
  exit 75 status=pending  NOT terminal — re-run the identical command
  exit 1  status=timeout  terminal — the hard --timeout budget is exhausted
  exit 2  status=error    usage error, or a probe that failed 4 times running

75 is EX_TEMPFAIL, so "not done yet" can never be read as success or as the
hard timeout. The --timeout budget SPANS re-runs — it is recorded in a state
file keyed by the condition — so re-issuing the command does not reset the
agent's own deadline. The pending line carries `remaining=` and the exact
`rerun=` command.

Three verbs:

- `--for run` — a PID, or a file-backed job handle holding one. Met when the
  process is gone.
- `--for file` — a sentinel's existence, or a literal substring it must carry.
  The substring case is what makes `<cmd> > gate.txt; echo EXIT=$? >> gate.txt`
  work: the file exists long before the command finishes.
- `--for check` — a PR's checks settling, through one-shot `gh pr view` reads
  routed via `trusty_common::gh::GhCommand`. Never `gh pr checks --watch`, which
  streams a whole CI run into context. A check settles only on its own terminal
  fields; `bucket` is not deserialised at all, and an empty rollup counts as
  UNSETTLED unless --allow-empty-checks is passed, because GitHub reports zero
  check runs for a window after a push.

Poll spacing is floored per verb (1s local, 10s GitHub) so a wait cannot become
a blind-poll storm, and --slice is clamped to 5..=500 so one invocation can
never reach for the whole harness ceiling.

pm_guard classifies by verb and denies nothing here, so `tm wait` passes today.
`evaluate_bash_command_never_denies_tm_wait` is the defence that keeps it
passing: a future deny rule keyed on binary name would silently take the one
sanctioned in-turn wait away from every agent.

fix(trusty-common): scan exactly to 1024 points and scale ef above it (Refs #5179) (#6226)

`HnswStore::search` was exact only up to 256 live drawers and traversed the
graph with `ef_search` pinned at 64 above that, so recall decayed as a palace
grew with no signal. Measured on this repo's own palace embeddings, 17.4% of
queries lost a true top-10 neighbour at 512 drawers and 24.5% at 1024.

Three changes:

- `EXHAUSTIVE_SCAN_MAX_POINTS` 256 -> 1024. Recall@10 misses go to zero over
  the whole raised range; the scan costs ~450us per query at 1024. No palace
  migrates: no graph is persisted, and `open_with_mode` rebuilds from the raw
  `VECTORS` rows on every open.
- `ef_search` scales with the live-drawer count, `max(64, 2k, live/4)`, with
  the live-scaled term capped at 1024 — a measured latency ceiling of roughly
  3ms per query, not a cost equivalence with the scan.
- The graph arm no longer truncates its candidate list before filtering
  tombstones. Deleted drawers could spend the caller's `k` result slots, so a
  palace whose nearest neighbours had been deleted returned nothing while live
  neighbours sat in the index. Tombstones are now filtered before the pool is
  judged deep enough, and the pool widens until `k` live drawers survive.

Recall above 1024 drawers is improved, not closed: 23.3% -> 17.7% of queries at
2048, 20.2% -> 15.6% at 2879.

fix(trusty-common): GitHub search qualifiers cannot be injected by a filter value (Refs #6216) (#6221)

* fix(trusty-common): GitHub search qualifiers cannot be injected by a filter value (Refs #6216)

`search_issues` built the GitHub issue-search `q` string by interpolating
caller-supplied values raw. GitHub separates issue-search qualifiers by
WHITESPACE, so an `assignee` or free-text `query` containing a space added a
second live qualifier — `is:`, `archived:`, or a `repo:` that widened the
search past the configured repository.

The JQL sibling (#6198) does not port. GitHub documents backslash escaping
only for CODE search, and that page states the syntax for non-code content
such as issues "is not the same", so there is no escape for a `"` inside a
quoted issue-search value. Emitting `\"` would look like a fix while relying
on a sequence GitHub never promised to honour.

Each field is handled per its own grammar position instead:

- free-text `query` becomes ONE quoted phrase, so an embedded `is:archived`
  stays a search term rather than a live qualifier;
- `assignee` is allowlist-validated against the GitHub username grammar
  (plus the `*` and `@me` sentinels) because that qualifier takes a bare
  value that never legitimately contains whitespace;
- each `label` keeps its documented `label:"..."` quoting, now checked for
  the characters that would close it.

A value carrying a `"` or a control character is refused with a specific
error rather than escaped. A backslash is left alone — with no escape
processing in this grammar it is an ordinary literal, and rejecting it would
break legitimate label names.

Construction moves into a pure `build_search_query` in `types.rs`, mirroring
the Jira fix's `build_list_jql`, so the defense is testable without an HTTP
round-trip. `urlencode`'s doc no longer claims to prevent search injection:
GitHub percent-decodes `q` before parsing qualifiers, so `%20` is a live
separator again by the time the search parser sees it.

fix(trusty-common): compact_orphans liveness re-check is O(candidates), not O(live) (Refs #6195) (#6206)

Code-critic follow-up to #6204. Two findings.

HIGH — the delete-txn liveness re-check scanned all of VECTOR_KEYS, so the
write-lock hold grew from O(orphans) to O(live_count+orphans), blocking
concurrent upsert/memory_remember for a full live-table scan on large
palaces — the exact concurrency scenario #6195 names. Fix: capture each
delete candidate's uuid in an UNLOCKED read txn, then re-confirm liveness

serialises the delete txn against every upsert, so a candidate live at the
lookup instant is skipped; a candidate with no captured uuid cannot have
become mapped since (allocate_vector_id refuses any id already in VECTORS,
and upsert never remaps an existing uuid), so it is a true orphan.

with a #[cfg(test)] two-party rendezvous (compact_race_barrier) that
compact_orphans waits on twice right after its live snapshot. The test now
drives a real atomic store.upsert into the exact (live-snapshot, orphan-scan)

fix(trusty-common): compact_orphans deletes a concurrently-upserted vector row (TOCTOU) (Refs #6195) (#6204)

* fix(trusty-common): compact_orphans re-checks liveness inside the delete txn (Refs #6195)

compact_orphans classed orphan candidates from read-txn snapshots taken
before its delete transaction. An upsert committing after the live
snapshot but before the delete left its brand-new VECTORS row in the
orphan scan while its VECTOR_KEYS mapping was live, so the row was
deleted as a false orphan. On the next open the drawer never entered the
HNSW graph and vector search could never return it — silent data loss.

Fix (approach b): keep the O(N) VECTORS scan in a read txn, but re-read
VECTOR_KEYS inside the delete write transaction and skip any candidate
that is live there. redb serialises the write txn against every upsert,
so a row live at the moment of deletion is never deleted. The write lock
is never held over the O(N) scan, only over the small VECTOR_KEYS
re-read. The #5005 id-reuse/high_water fix is untouched — not deleting a
now-live row only strengthens VECTOR_KEYS/VECTORS consistency.

Adds a deterministic regression test that reproduces the interleaving via
a held redb write txn as a hard rendezvous; it fails on the pre-fix
commit at the survival assertion.

The symbol graph keyed nodes by bare `function_name` with first-write-wins and
resolved every callee against one global bare-name map. Two consequences, both
measured on the 85k-chunk dogfood index: a name defined in several files got one
node and the rest were dropped, and any call to a common name became an edge to
whichever crate registered first. A probe over 15 entry points found 99 callee
edges, 12% same-file and 74% pointing into an unrelated crate.

Node identity is now `<file>::<symbol>`, so every definition gets a node. A
callee becomes an edge only with grounds — the caller's own file, then its
directory, then its package, then a name unique in the whole corpus — and an
ambiguous name produces no edge at all. Cross-file resolution requires a
matching file extension and a callable target, so a Rust call no longer binds to
a `.ts` method or a module.

Entry anchoring accepts `<path>::<symbol>`, which used to 404, and a bare name
matching several definitions now names the alternatives instead of silently
picking one.

Pre-fix proof on a 4-definition fixture: node_count 3 (one `write` dropped) and
`callees_of("upsert")` returning a cross-crate `write`. Post-fix: 4 nodes, no
edge.

fix(trusty-search): a search over an unreadable corpus is an error, not an empty result set (Refs #5917) (#6119)

* fix: a search over an unreadable corpus is an error, not an empty result set

The in-memory chunk map and BM25 corpus are a CACHE of the durable redb
corpus. Idle eviction empties them; the rehydrate that would refill them read
the same corpus and reported its failure only to the log; and
`fetch_chunks_for_ids` did the same before falling back to those now-empty
maps. A search against an index holding 85,269 chunks therefore returned
`results: []` at HTTP 200 with `bm25_lane_degraded: true` — a flag that means
"still warming up", which is the one thing this state is not. The workaround
was to delete and recreate the index.

#4087's guard covers a corpus that fails to OPEN. This one opens, is
populated, and then goes bad — redb's "Previous I/O error occurred" state,
which fails every later read for the process's lifetime — so that guard passes
and every reader absorbed the failure on its own.

A failed durable read is now recorded on the index (`CorpusReadFault`, an
`Arc`-shared cell the detached rehydrate task can reach) and consumed at the
tail of `search_with_drops`, which refuses rather than publishing the empty
lanes that failure produced. `fetch_chunks_for_ids` propagates its own read
failure instead of downgrading to the in-memory map. The record clears on any
successful durable read, so a transient failure cannot wedge an index into
refusing every query.

The HTTP layer answers `503 index_corpus_unavailable` naming the index and the
fault, where it previously answered `500 internal search error` with the cause
discarded. The two producers of that error code now carry one field set: the
open-failure body gained `retryable` beside `transient`, and the read-failure
body gained `failure_kind: "read_failed"` and `transient` beside `retryable` —
the contract says `retryable` is never absent, and a relay cannot paper over
two bodies disagreeing about which field carries the split.

`spawn_disclaim::timeout::disclaimed_stdout_with_timeout` adds the one spawn
shape the module lacked: it spawns through the existing

so a kill cannot race a reap onto a recycled pid. The probe now uses a 5-second
deadline and, on timeout, fails safe to "no native output-style support"

fix(trusty-review): per-endpoint analyze fetch budgets, and one failing endpoint no longer discards the rest (#6042)

The `--analyze` adapter used a single 15 s timeout for every trusty-analyze
request. The diagnostics endpoint runs project-scoped clippy under the daemon's
own 180 s cooperative deadline, so the client gave up on a request the daemon
went on to answer: measured live, diagnostics returned 200 at 142 s with
`tools_run: ["clippy"]` while the client had already timed out at 15 s.

Two changes:

Each endpoint now carries its own budget beside its path, so cost and timeout
cannot drift apart. Diagnostics derives its budget from trusty-analyze's own
ladder — `TRUSTY_DIAGNOSTICS_DEADLINE_SECS` (default 180 s) plus the 90 s of
handler grace, router margin, and client margin that ladder stacks above it.
The client therefore outlives the daemon's outermost responding rung at every
configured deadline, which is the invariant #6034 established server-side: the
daemon's structured answer, including the 504 body it sends when its own
deadline is hit, always reaches the caller. The cheap endpoints keep 15 s.

The per-repo fetch is no longer all-or-nothing. Complexity, diagnostics, and
refactor suggestions are fetched independently; whatever answered is kept and
rendered, and each endpoint that did not answer is named under Gaps & Caveats
along with why it dropped out. A fetch where no endpoint answered still falls
back to the repository scan rather than rendering empty metrics as a clean pass.

#6040's transport retry is unchanged — timeouts stay excluded from it, which
remains correct now that a timeout is its own error variant.

The endpoint vocabulary moved to a new `report::analyze_endpoints` module,
which keeps `analyze_adapter.rs` under the 500-SLOC cap.

* fix(trusty-analyze): bound the diagnostics endpoint and run clippy once per project

`GET /indexes/{id}/diagnostics` ran unbounded: the handler awaited one
`spawn_blocking` that looped every unique file and spawned one subprocess per
file-scoped tool, with no per-request deadline. On the 4097-file trusty-tools
index that ran past ten minutes and every client abandoned the connection at
the transport layer — zero bytes, no status line.

The dispatch now takes a wall-clock deadline and checks it between subprocess
spawns, so it stops mid-corpus and returns the work already done. The response
carries `timed_out` plus a `cutoff` object naming the files never reached and
the tools never invoked, so a truncated list cannot read as a clean corpus.
The budget defaults to 180 s (`TRUSTY_DIAGNOSTICS_DEADLINE_SECS`); past that
plus a 30 s grace the handler answers 504 with a JSON body. `service/routes.rs`
layers a 300 s `tower_http::timeout::TimeoutLayer` as a last-resort net, applied
before `/sse` is merged in so the event stream is not cut off.

Same code path, second defect: `ClippyTool::run` invoked `cargo clippy` in a
manifest-less scratch dir, so it errored "could not find Cargo.toml" on every
file and returned `Ok(vec![])` — structurally useless, and the endpoint's main
cost driver at ~0.155 s per file. `ClippyTool` is now project-scoped like the
existing Roslyn tool: `run_project` groups files by their enclosing cargo root
(the workspace root when one exists, so a 21-crate workspace is one build), runs
`cargo clippy --workspace` there under the build-class timeout, parses that
output once, and keeps the diagnostics belonging to the requested files.

* fix(trusty-analyze): derive the whole request-timeout ladder from one deadline

Critic follow-up on #6018. The deadline fix bounded the innermost timeout and
left the outer three as independent hardcoded constants, which reintroduced the
original body-less-timeout symptom from two directions.

The router's blanket TimeoutLayer was a fixed 300 s while the handler's budget
is deadline + 30 s grace. That ordering held only at the default deadline:
raising TRUSTY_DIAGNOSTICS_DEADLINE_SECS past 270 s pushed the handler beyond
the layer, so the layer's empty-bodied 504 beat the handler's structured JSON —
on the exact remediation path the handler's own error message recommends.

The MCP client was worse: a flat 150 s request timeout, below the 180 s default
deadline, so `run_diagnostics` over a large index wrote its answer into a socket
the MCP caller had already abandoned. Default configuration, no tuning needed to
hit it.

Both now derive from `core::deadlines`, a single module owning the ladder:
deadline -> handler budget -> router timeout -> MCP client timeout, each rung
computed from the one inside it. `core` rather than `service` because `service`
is behind the `http-server` feature and `mcp` is not. A floor keeps the client
timeout above the 120 s OpenRouter ceiling `deep_analysis` needs no matter how
low the deadline is set.

Third defect, same class: the deadline gated only whether `run_project` STARTED.
Inside, each `cargo clippy` (and each of Roslyn's two `dotnet` spawns, per
project) ran under a flat `build_tool_timeout()` — 300 s default, independently
tunable. Since `spawn_blocking` cannot be cancelled, one cold project or several
in series kept building for multiples of that after the client had its 504, and
a client retry stacked another build behind it on the same toolchain lock.
`StaticTool::run_project` now takes the deadline; both project-scoped tools cap
each spawn at min(remaining budget, build_tool_timeout()) and recheck between
project roots, so the existing kill-on-timeout path terminates the child when
the request ends. The default impl checks the deadline between files.

fix(trusty-mpm): a nested bare repo no longer reads CLEAN to the reclaim guard (#6033)

The guard decided "is this directory a repository root" by matching an entry
named literally `.git`. A bare repository has none — `git clone --bare` lays
down `HEAD`, `objects/`, `refs/`, `config`, `hooks/` and `info/` at its own
root — so the gitignored-subtree walk descended past it, found nothing, and a
candidate holding the only copy of a commit reported `dirty_files = 0` and was
deleted. `git status` on the candidate is empty because the path is gitignored,
and `git worktree list` does not mention a different repository, so every other
question answered clean too.

A root is now recognised by that entry OR by the `HEAD` + `objects/` + `refs/`
triple, and the hit is routed through the same `object_store_dies_with`
discriminator as any other nested repository — so a bare repo whose store
survives the candidate is still not counted as dirt. Stopping at the root also
stops the walk spending its 50k-entry scan budget inside `objects/`, which is
what let a loose-object bare repo fail-safe to DIRTY by accident while a packed
one read clean.

Two smaller gaps from the same issue close with it. A short list of gitignored
names that are unrecoverable if deleted — `.env*`, `*.bak`, `*.orig` — now
counts as unsaved work, found by the walk that was already visiting every entry,
so it costs no extra I/O. Anything under a disposable build directory stays
excused. Measured read-only across 27 live worktree leaves: 1 becomes newly
dirty, naming a real pre-edit `settings.json.bak` — not the 30-of-31 flag rate
that made "count every ignored entry" unusable. And a tracked file deleted from
`.trusty-mpm/` is counted again: pass 1 skips those status lines on the promise
that pass 2 owns them, and pass 2 returned 0 without running git whenever the
directory was absent, which is exactly what deleting the last file under it
produces.

`nested_repo_roots` documented itself as answering the nested-repository
question "EXACTLY, not heuristically" while the residual-risk list omitted bare
repositories entirely. Both now state what the walk actually covers and what it
does not.

Every new arm keeps the module's fail-safe direction: a bare-repository probe
that cannot answer, like every other error here, resolves to DIRTY.

fix(trusty-common): a closed unhealthy_signal disables its select branch instead of spinning (#6025)

`watch::Receiver::changed()` resolves `Ready(Err(_))` on every poll once the
last sender drops, and an immediately-ready future never yields. The
`unhealthy_signal` arm in `supervision_loop` logged and `continue`d on that
`Err`, so it re-armed the same ready future and won the `select!` again
instantly — 88,897 loop passes in 300ms, measured, for the remaining lifetime
of the child. It is the hazard #3023 fixed for `shutdown_rx`, on the branch
beside it.

The branch is now gated on `unhealthy_signal.has_changed().is_ok()`, so a
closed channel is excluded from the `select!` before its future is polled and
supervision continues through `child.wait()` and `shutdown_rx`. The state is
recomputed each iteration rather than latched like `shutdown_closed`:
`shutdown_rx`'s sender lives for the whole supervision, but `unhealthy_signal`
is replaced by the new client's receiver after every respawn, and a latched
flag would leave the replacement sidecar's health unwatched — a sidecar that
wedges without exiting is invisible to `child.wait()`, so it would never be
restarted.

Two regression tests, plus `#[serial]` on the `shutdown_tests` tokio tests so
the shared `SUPERVISION_LOOP_ITERATIONS` counter is not raced by a concurrent
supervision loop (follow-up recorded on #3026 from the #3023 delta review).

fix(trusty-mpm): an out-of-order SubagentStop resolves once its agent_id lands (#6020)

`PostToolUse` is installed `async: true` and `SubagentStop` synchronously, so
each is its own `tm hook` process and their arrival order at the daemon is a
race. `on_subagent_stop` resolves only by `agent_id`, and only `on_launched`
teaches one — so a stop that won that race matched nothing, was discarded, and
nothing re-checked. The delegation stayed `Running` for the full six-hour
staleness window as a phantom in-flight agent, corrupting the "what is in
flight" answer /tm-session-pause depends on.

A stop that cannot be resolved is now held in a bounded, TTL'd ledger keyed by
the exact `(session, agent_id)` it quoted, and `on_launched` applies it the
moment that id is taught. The two arrival orders converge on one record.

Nothing guesses. The key is the same one in-order resolution uses, so the
deferred path terminalizes precisely the record the in-order path would have,
or nothing at all — no "most recent Running" fallback in either direction.

Fail-closed on every error arm:

- A stop whose `agent_id` names an already-terminal delegation is a
  redelivery, not an ordering failure, and records nothing.
- `on_launched` peeks rather than takes; the entry is spent only after the
  terminalization it authorises has actually landed.
- Both bounds — 256 entries, 15-minute TTL, aged by the existing 60 s sweep —
  drop entries by leaving the delegation live for the staleness sweep, exactly
  as before this existed. Nothing here can close a delegation no stop named.

`classify_dispatch`'s KNOWN LIMITATION is NOT closed by this and its note is
corrected to say why: a response that never teaches a usable `agentId` has no
key for a stop to be held against, in any order.

Closes #4142

fix: a read-only here-document no longer spends the PM file-change budget (#6019)

Closes #5356

The pm_guard redirection check treated any unquoted `>` as a file write, and
its quote scan knows only `'` and `"`. A `>` inside a here-document body — a
`len(k) > 3` comparison in a `python3 <<'PY'` script, an `->` arrow in
`cat <<EOF` prose — therefore read as a redirect, so a pure read was
classified as a shell file edit. That classification is budget-eligible: three
such reads were allowed silently while consuming the per-turn budget, and the
fourth was denied as "PM file-change budget 3/3 used this turn" with zero
files changed.

`pm_guard_bash::heredoc` now marks here-document body bytes so the redirection
scan skips them. Only the body is data: a redirect on the operator line
(`python3 <<'PY' > out.rs`) or after the terminator is still a file write and
still consumes the budget. The scan claims nothing when it cannot parse with
confidence — unbalanced quotes, or a `<<` with no terminator line, which is
also what an arithmetic `$((1 << 3))` looks like — so an unparseable command
keeps the pre-fix over-deny.

* fix(trusty-audit): refuse packaging when the GitHub credential changed between sweep and package

Second-round code-critic finding on 4682677e1: the CRITICAL 3/4 fix made
packaging re-resolve `gh auth token` fresh, but scanning outbound files with
a NEWLY re-resolved token can never catch an OLDER token a child echoed into
a file when the operator's active `gh` account differs between sweep time
and package time (a real scenario on this machine). The critic proved it: a
file containing account A's token, packaged with account B's token
resolved, packaged successfully.

Fix: a truncated, non-reversible SHA-256 fingerprint of the sweep's resolved
credential (GithubAccess::fingerprint, 8 bytes / 16 hex chars — enough to
detect a different token, never meant to guard as a secondary secret) is now
persisted in the run checkpoint (RunProgress::github_credential, via the new
GithubCredentialRecord::{NoToken,Fingerprint} enum). At packaging time,
github_issues::verify_unchanged compares the freshly-resolved credential's
fingerprint against the persisted one before from_checkpoint trusts it as
the outbound scan's needle:

- Matching fingerprint, or "no token" on both sides -> proceeds.
- Mismatched fingerprint, or a token now where the sweep had one but package
  time has none -> Err(AuditError::GithubCredentialChanged), fail closed,
  package refused.
- No github_credential recorded at all (checkpoint predates this field) ->
  proceeds, but the returned package's `excluded` names the uncertainty
  rather than silently assuming agreement. Refusing every pre-existing
  engagement's checkpoint outright was disproportionate to a narrowly-scoped
  verification that mostly does not apply to a repo-only engagement.

chain::assemble re-verifies too rather than threading one value through from
collect -- consistent with session::package's re-resolution, and both share
the one verify_unchanged code path.

assemble() itself is intentionally unchanged and still does not verify the
credential -- from_checkpoint is the enforced entry point both real callers
go through; assemble's docs now say so explicitly.

packaging_refuses_when_the_active_github_credential_has_changed exercises
the critic's exact proof through the real from_checkpoint path (a file
carrying account A's token, packaged with account B's token resolved).
Verified red by calling package::assemble directly (the mechanism unchanged
by this fix, and all that existed at 4682677e1) with the same mismatched
setup: it still succeeds, proving assemble alone never closed this gap --
only from_checkpoint's new verify_unchanged call does.
packaging_proceeds_when_the_github_credential_matches and

fix(trusty-agents): bound the shared LLM HTTP client, and fail the test whose timeout fired (#5966)

`HTTP_CLIENT` was `reqwest::Client::new()` — no connect timeout, no read
timeout, no total timeout. Against a live-but-unresponsive listener the request
never returned, so any LLM call could block an agent turn indefinitely. On the
machine that filed #5943 that listener was a half-open local `ollama`: `lsof -i
:11434` showed it LISTENing while `curl -m 3` timed out, and `curl -w` put the
connect at 0.26ms with `starttransfer` never reached — the stall is entirely in
the read, which is why a connect timeout alone would not have caught it.

The client now carries a 10s `connect_timeout` and a 300s `read_timeout`, and no
total `timeout`. `read_timeout` resets after every successful read, so a
response that keeps delivering bytes runs as long as it needs; a blanket
`timeout()` would cap the whole exchange and break a long completion. The POSTs
here are non-streaming, so their gap between "request sent" and "first byte
back" is one silent interval and the read budget doubles as their generation
ceiling — 300s against a crate default `max_tokens` of 2048, which is tens of
seconds from a cloud provider and three to four minutes from the slowest local
CPU ollama model.

A timeout is no longer retried. `with_llm_retry` makes four attempts, so a
retryable timeout spent the budget four times over — twenty minutes against a
wedged endpoint rather than five — and an endpoint that produced no byte for the
whole budget does not produce one on the retry. Connection-refused and DNS
failures stay retryable: they fail in milliseconds and do recover.

`persona_python_plugin_is_registered_by_the_dispatch_path` wrapped the turn in
`tokio::time::timeout(120s, ...)`, discarded the result, and asserted on captured
logs either way — so it reported success from a run that had timed out, taking
exactly 120.01s to do it. Expiry is now a failure. `OLLAMA_HOST` and
`OPENROUTER_BASE_URL` are pinned at a reserved dead port so the module doc's
"absent Ollama" and "no external network call" hold by construction rather than
by whatever the developer happens to be running.

`engagement.toml` gains a `[[targets]]` array and becomes what an
engagement's target set IS. `<work-dir>/state/audit-targets.toml` stays,
as a working copy rebuilt from the config on every write and read only
when the config declares no set at all.

`registry::engagement_targets` is the one read and owns the precedence.
`register` / `deregister` write the config under the same cross-process
lock the registry took, publish it at mode 0600 through
`workdir::write_private_atomically`, and mirror the result into the
working copy second — so a config write that fails leaves both files
untouched.

An engagement whose config declares nothing adopts the working copy, so
an upgrade keeps every target registered before this change. `targets =
[]` is a declaration of zero and does not adopt. `add` and `remove` now
refuse in a directory with no engagement config rather than writing a
file nothing treats as authoritative.

fix(trusty-agents): bound self-project exe walk-up at the build root (#5962)

`detect_self_project`'s strategy 2 climbed from `current_exe().parent()` to
the filesystem root looking for `.trusty-agents/agents/pm.toml`. That climb
reads the executable's real location and consults no environment, so it sailed
past the checkout the binary was built from and matched the developer's real
`~/.trusty-agents/agents/pm.toml` — the user-level config tier, which is not a
project.

Two consequences. Shipped, as #4826: an installed `~/.cargo/bin/tagent`
resolved `$HOME` as the project and the Slack gateway answered users against
the wrong corpus. #4826 only made an explicit `TAGENT_PROJECT_DIR` hint outrank
the climb; with no hint it still escaped. Latent, and the subject of this fix:
a run with `$HOME` pinned to a tempdir got the real home back, so
`tests/plain_cli_repl.rs` wrote `.trusty-agents/state/build.json` into the
developer's actual home while its own doc comment claimed the run was
sandboxed.

`self_project_from_exe` now requires a `target/` ancestor and returns that
directory's parent when it carries the marker. `cargo run`, a `cargo test`
binary under `target/debug/deps/` and a release binary invoked from an
unrelated cwd all still resolve their checkout — in each of those the checkout
IS the `target` parent, which is the case the strategy was written for. An
executable with no `target` ancestor has no knowable build checkout, so
inference declines and detection falls through to the cwd strategy.

The cwd strategy is unchanged: it can still resolve `$HOME` when cwd sits under
a home carrying the marker, but a test controls cwd, so it is not an isolation
escape.
