* feat(trusty-audit): a launch with no engagement.toml creates one before it asks what to audit

A bare `trusty-audit` in a directory with no `engagement.toml` registered
targets, printed `Tools: 0/4 installed`, named `trusty-audit install`, and
stopped — never asking for the OpenRouter key. Three gates hit the same missing
file and none of them named it.

The launch now sets the engagement up first, in the order the owner ruled: ask
for the key, write `engagement.toml` at mode 0600 with an exact version pinned
per tool, preflight all four pinned tools, install them, and ask what the audit
covers LAST. A directory that already holds a config skips all of it.

The pins come from the latest published stable release of each tool, resolved
once and written into the file; every run after the first reads the file, so
`latest` never reaches a second run. A compiled-in default set was the
alternative and was rejected: nothing in this workspace bumps such a constant,
so an old client would pin old tools forever behind a config that reads as a
deliberate choice.

The preflight is a new capability inside `trusty_installer::download::pinned`,
not a second resolver in this crate. `preflight_pinned_set` runs checks 1 and 2
of the install pipeline — a Tier-1 target check and a release-list lookup — and
`stage_one` now calls the same `resolve_pin`, so the dry run and the install
that follows it cannot disagree.

A write that fails stops the launch with `AuditError::EngagementNotCreated`,
naming the file and stating that the key was not saved. Nothing advances past a
failed credential write.

fix(trusty-mpm): run the health probe's blocking client on its own thread (#5968)

`RealHttpProber::get_health` built a `reqwest::blocking` client directly on the
caller's thread. `tm`'s `main` is `#[tokio::main]`, so every `tm services`
subcommand that probes health constructed reqwest's internal runtime inside the
async runtime and panicked with "Cannot drop a runtime in a context where
blocking is not allowed" before printing anything.

Release builds only looked healthy: the guard that raises that panic is
`#[cfg(debug_assertions)]` inside reqwest, so it compiles away. The call still
parked the thread it ran on from inside `poll`, for up to HEALTH_PROBE_TIMEOUT
per service. Spawning a dedicated OS thread and joining it keeps the nested
runtime off the async worker entirely, matching
`trusty_common::search_index::best_effort_create_index`.

The `HttpProber` trait stays synchronous, so no call site and no public API
changes. `init` and `restart` were never affected — they do not probe.

* fix(trusty-mpm): identify the daemon by its port and its own lock record (#1731, #5951)

Both defects are the same failure: nothing in the crate could authoritatively
say which process is the daemon, so three hand-rolled lock-file parsers and a
first-match `pgrep` each answered differently. `core::daemon_identity` is now
the one place that answers it, and `core::discovery`, `daemon::lock`, the `tm`
welcome panel, `tm stop` and the service discoverer all route through it.

#1731 — the lock file was never present, despite the daemon writing it since
the issue first closed. The writer shipped; the deleter was the problem.
`daemon::lock`'s unit test called `write_lock` then `remove_lock` against the
real `~/.trusty-mpm/daemon.lock` to prove they do not panic, so every
`cargo test -p trusty-mpm` run overwrote a live daemon's record with the test
process's PID and then removed it. Observed live during this work: the file
held `pid = 48689` at 03:51, a sibling worktree ran the suite, and by 03:58 it
was gone with daemon 48689 still answering `/health`. Removal is now
ownership-checked in the daemon's shutdown handler and in `tm stop`, so neither
an unrelated process nor an outgoing daemon can delete a successor's record,
and that test is hermetic.

The record also carries `product = "trusty-mpm"` and readers reject anything
without it. `daemon.lock` is not a unique filename — Claude Code writes one at

rewrite of the dispatch's arguments that `tm` cannot confirm the harness

corrupts another session's branch.

daemon still grants and warns on stderr; a running daemon that does not answer
denies, with a message that names the failure and points at explicit isolation,
which needs no rewrite and never reaches this question.

`claim_shared_tree_on` is the one place the reply-to-verdict mapping lives, so
the two call sites cannot drift; only the warning that fires on an answer
differs. `live_shared_tree_writers` keeps its fail-open contract unchanged — it

that digest. Importing the same export twice is a no-op, a superset adds only
what is new, two machines' overlapping exports converge, and a merge keeps

feat(trusty-search): resolve merge-base deltas against the working tree, not HEAD (ADR-0050) (#5815)

* feat(trusty-search): resolve merge-base deltas against the working tree, not HEAD

ADR-0050 indexes a worktree as the delta against its merge-base. The only
merge-base helper in the crate, `core::git::resolve_branch_files`, ran
`git diff --name-only <base>..HEAD` — a comparison of two COMMITS. On a
four-change fixture it reported 1 of the 4 real differences: it missed the
uncommitted edit, the untracked file, and the deletion. A live agent worktree
is mostly uncommitted work, so a delta computed that way would omit most of
what the worktree contains.

`resolve_merge_base_delta` replaces it as the one entry point. It diffs the
merge-base against the WORKING TREE, adds untracked files via
`ls-files --others --exclude-standard`, and returns changed and deleted paths
separately — a deletion means "drop the base facet's chunks", which is not
expressible in the single list the old helper returned. `-z` throughout keeps
paths with spaces or non-ASCII bytes verbatim instead of arriving quoted.

A failed untracked-file step returns None rather than a partial delta. A
partial delta reads as a complete answer while silently omitting files that
exist in the tree, and the caller cannot tell the two apart.

`resolve_branch_files` now delegates, so the #122 branch boost also covers the
file a developer is editing before they commit it.

fix(trusty-agents): bound runtime shutdown so a wedged background task cannot block exit (#5939)

The seven `plain_cli_repl` integration tests failed with `tagent did not exit
within 120s`. The REPL was fine: it read `/quit`, printed `Bye.`, and `run()`
returned. The process then never exited.

`main` was `#[tokio::main]`, which drops the runtime at the end of `main`, and
that drop calls `BlockingPool::shutdown` with no ceiling. Startup fires a
background code-index file watcher whose construction calls the synchronous
`FastEmbedder::new`, which reaches the embedding-model cache through
`fastembed` -> `hf_hub` -> `std::fs::read_to_string`. Running it inline pinned a
runtime worker inside that `open` syscall, so the pool never drained and the
drop waited forever. `sample` on a hung child showed exactly that: the main
thread parked in `BlockingPool::shutdown`, the worker stopped in `__open`.

Two changes:

- Both launchers call the new `trusty_agents::run_to_completion`, which owns the
  runtime and tears it down with `shutdown_timeout(5s)`, warning when that grace
  is consumed. Healthy runs pay nothing.
- `build_file_watcher` constructs its `CodeStore` and `FastEmbedder` on the
  blocking pool instead of on an async worker.

`wedged_model_cache_cannot_block_process_exit` reproduces the wedge without a
wedged filesystem: a FIFO stands in for the cached repo ref that `hf_hub` reads,
and the test holds its write end open so the child's read never completes. That
also proves the child reached the cache, so a fastembed layout change fails the
test loudly rather than leaving it exercising nothing. Against the pre-fix
commit it fails on the 120s timeout.

fix(trusty-memory): never drop a bm25 index whose eviction flush failed (#5892)

* fix(trusty-memory): never drop a bm25 index whose eviction flush failed

Both eviction sites in `Bm25Lane` removed the index from the LRU first and
only then flushed it. `LruCache::push` and `pop_lru` hand back an owned
victim, which drops at the end of the arm, so a failed flush logged one
`warn!` line and took the palace's unflushed documents with it. The doc on
`enforce_text_budget` claimed the opposite — "flushing each first, so
eviction can never lose a write" — and the doc was right about the intent.

Eviction now routes through `evict_coldest_flushed`, which walks residents
coldest-first, flushes each in place with `peek_mut` (no LRU reordering),
and removes an index only once its snapshot is on disk. A palace that
cannot be persisted stays resident and the next-coldest is evicted instead,
so one unwritable palace does not disable enforcement.

When nothing can be flushed the two callers differ, deliberately:

- the budget sweep stays OVER BUDGET and retries on the next tick. Under
  memory pressure that is the trade: the overshoot is bounded by the
  retained text of the palaces that cannot be written, it is logged every
  tick, and it clears itself the moment the snapshot becomes writable. A
  dropped write is silent and permanent.
- a cold load FAILS rather than buying its slot with another palace's
  writes. The caller loses one operation, which is recoverable.

Closes #5887

* fix(trusty-memory): stop the bm25 eviction sweep re-flushing what it cannot flush

* fix(trusty-common): main_worktree_root declines a root it cannot reconcile

`main_worktree_root` took `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` and returned that
path's parent unchecked. The parent is the main working tree only when the
common dir is `<root>/.git`. Inside a submodule — or any repo created with
`--separate-git-dir` — the common dir is `<outer>/.git/modules/<name>`, so it
returned `<outer>/.git/modules`: git internals, named confidently, that no
checkout sits under.

A second `git rev-parse --show-toplevel --git-common-dir` run under the derived
path now has to agree on both before it is returned. Reconciliation goes through
the shared common dir rather than a prefix test against `start`, because a linked
worktree provisioned outside the main checkout is a legitimate answer no prefix
test would accept. An answer that cannot be reconciled produces `None`, so every
consumer falls back rather than trusting a wrong path.

Downstream, trusty-memory's prompt-context project-scope filter was handed that
internals path as its session root. Every drawer with a `creator:cwd` tag failed
containment, canonicalised successfully (the directory exists), failed again, and
was dropped; untagged drawers survived, so recall degraded rather than emptying.

both plus the resolved session root at debug — including the disabled-filter case,

Outcomes do not arrive in queued-turn order: `enqueue` reports a
queue-full failure synchronously while accepted turns finish later in the

erased the degradation signal the feature exists to surface. The bound

says its counters under-report, and the observer warns instead of

fix(trusty-mpm): stop the merged-PR reclaim deleting a live agent's worktree (#5853)

`tm session prune-worktrees --merged-prs --force` deleted the worktrees of
three live dispatched agents on 2026-08-15/16, twice while they held unpushed
commits.

`worktree_reclaim::classify` never read the ownership sentinel. Its liveness
gate reads `SessionRecord.workspace_path`, and a dispatched agent has no
session record; its ownership gate asked only whether a sentinel FILE exists,
never whose claim it carries. Since #4311 agent worktrees carry a sentinel, so
a tree owned by a working agent on a merged branch passed every gate.
`prune_orphaned_worktrees` and `worktree_reconcile::classify` both apply the
`SentinelOwner::Agent` check; this third path never got it.

`classify` gains gate 4 and `recheck_before_delete` re-applies it adjacent to
the deletion (#4118's precedent). An agent-owned worktree is reclaimed only
when the delegation registry positively reports that agent's delegation ended.
A registry holding no record of the agent refuses: the delegation map is
rebuilt empty at every daemon boot, so its silence is undeterminable rather
than absent (ADR-0045). A sentinel inside `.claude/worktrees/` that is empty,
malformed or unreadable refuses for the same reason. Session-owned
`.worktrees/<name>` reclamation is unchanged.

The liveness definition is the delegation half of
`agent_worktree_reap::paths_in_use` — every non-terminal delegation in every
session — resolved per agent id by the new `delegation_state_for_agent`, so
the two destructive paths read the registry once between them.

* fix(trusty-audit): give the child-log scrubber one contiguous search space (#5869)

A code-critic round reproduced two ways a credential escaped the filter this
PR added. Both are the same defect: the scrubber never saw the whole needle,
because the implementation cut the stream into pieces and searched each piece
alone.

The pump scrubbed only `pending[..cut]`, so a needle whose start lay in
`[cut - len + 1, cut - 1]` was split by the cut, matched neither half, and both
halves went to disk verbatim. The reproduction wrote a log byte-identical in
length to its input — not one byte redacted anywhere. It now scrubs the whole
buffer and takes the cut from the scrubbed result.

`scrub_mixed` split at every invalid UTF-8 byte and scrubbed each run alone. A
needle cannot CONTAIN an invalid byte, which is what the old doc argued, but
nothing stops a child injecting one INTO it: a key cut after its 20th character
by one stray byte reached the log as two recoverable fragments. `scrub` now
searches the valid runs concatenated and splices each match back by byte
offset, so invalid bytes outside a match still reach the log unchanged.

The hold-back that survives covers only a needle that has not finished
arriving, and counts TEXT bytes so injected garbage is retained with the
characters it interrupts — a raw-byte hold-back sliced nine characters off a
prefix padded with 20 junk bytes.

remove a value the redactor would have left alone.

* fix(trusty-audit): stop the hold-back's raw cap from writing out a partly-arrived key (#5869)

`Scrubber::cut_for` walked TEXT bytes to place the flush cut, then clamped the
result in RAW bytes. The two units disagree whenever invalid padding sits inside
the arrived prefix: with ~4KB of non-UTF-8 near the flush boundary the raw clamp
moved the cut past the walk's own boundary and wrote the prefix to the log in the
clear. The remainder arrived in a later segment without its start, matched
nothing, and both halves landed. `.min(bytes.len() / 2)` was a second clamp of the
same shape, and the "fewer text bytes than the hold-back wants" branch was a
third.

The cap is now honoured by lifting the invalid padding OUT of the hold and
writing it, never by moving the cut. Invalid bytes are not credential characters,
so writing them leaks nothing. The carried tail is at most MAX_HELD_BACK bytes in
every encoding, so the pump's buffer bound stays SEGMENT_LIMIT + MAX_HELD_BACK
and neither stall vector — an absurd needle, or garbage padding — reopens. The
one cost: in that case the padding reaches the log ahead of the text it
interrupted rather than being removed with it.

empty set as proof every candidate is dead: two unowned records sharing one
literal `workspace_path`, zero of them live, picks a survivor by recency and

includes the host-state gate refusing tmux access on a reassigned `$HOME`, not
only a missing binary. No error handling at the call site could have caught the
second: there was no error.

#3823 `ensure_server_up` guard, then propagates `list_sessions()` rather than
defaulting it, and lives next to the probe it protects. Every way of failing to
observe tmux now reaches `dedup_stale_duplicates` as `Err`, which logs and
skips the pass — returning `Ok(vec![])` so `reconcile_on_boot` still runs its
deploy-validate and auto-resume tail. `NoopTmuxDriver::list_sessions` reports
`TmuxUnavailable` instead of zero sessions; `reconcile_on_boot` and
`session_exists` already degrade explicitly on `Err`, so their behavior is
unchanged.

it. Auto-reviving would resurrect the #2777 case it cannot be told apart from —

* fix(trusty-audit): the atomic writer refuses a pre-planted temporary (#5868)

`write_temp` opened its temporary with `create(true).truncate(true)` — no
`O_EXCL`, no `O_NOFOLLOW` — and the temporary's name is guessable: the pid is
visible in `ps` and `DefaultHasher` is fixed-seed over a fresh process's
near-deterministic main `ThreadId`. A local attacker who pre-planted a symlink
at that name had the open follow it. The first-run credential prompt wrote the
plaintext OpenRouter key into the attacker's file, and `rename` then published
the symlink itself as `engagement.toml`.

Mode 0600 did not prevent it. `OpenOptions::mode` constrains a file at
CREATION, and an open that follows a symlink to an existing file creates
nothing.

`create_new(true)` is the fix rather than an unpredictable name from
`tempfile::NamedTempFile`: it closes the hole at the syscall that has it, and
it makes guessing the name worthless rather than merely harder — the attacker
who wins the name now gets an error, never a redirect. It also keeps
`tempfile` a dev-dependency. The residual cost is that a determined local
attacker can make the write fail by re-planting; that is a visible error, not
a silent leak.

Both writers are one function, so `write_atomically` is fixed with
`write_private_atomically`. A temporary left by a writer that crashed holding
this tag is still recovered — unlink and re-create ONCE, exclusively, so a
racing re-plant loses rather than being followed.

The doc claim this falsifies said the credential was never observable at a
wider mode "not even for the instant between two syscalls". That was not an
instant but an open window, and the exposure was the file's location rather
than its mode. The rewritten doc names each guarantee and the mechanism that
buys it.

fix(trusty-agents): name stale backups by content so reprovision stops destroying repeat local edits (#5848)

The backup was written only when `<file>.stale.bak` did not already exist.
The first reprovision archived a hand-edit; every reprovision after that
overwrote the file and skipped the backup because one was already sitting
there. A second edit-then-reprovision cycle lost the work with no error, no
warning, and no recoverable copy.

The backup path now carries the SHA-256 digest of the bytes being archived:
`<file>.stale.<digest>.bak`. Two different contents can never target the same
path, so no pass can clobber another's backup — the property the fixed name
was protecting — and every divergence stays recoverable.

What bounds the set: one file per distinct content ever overwritten at that
path. An unchanged file is never overwritten and never archived, and
re-archiving identical bytes resolves to the path already there, so repeated
`tagent agents repair` runs add nothing. The set grows only with real
divergences, never with the number of reprovisions.

Each archive now logs a WARN naming the file and its backup, so a refresh that
discarded local content is distinguishable from one that refreshed a pristine
file. Existing `.stale.bak` files are left alone; both agent listers already
skip `*.bak`, so the new names never surface as bogus agents.

`repeated_divergence_is_recoverable_across_reprovisions` fails against the
pre-fix code with `backed_up: left 0, right 1`.

ADR-0048 decision 1 grants every dispatched writer its own worktree when the
session stands in a main checkout, and the decision is mechanical — the guard

repo has neither and pays only the costs: agent edits land in
.claude/worktrees/agent-<id>/ and never reach the checkout, a second agent has to
copy them across, and the trees and branches pile up needing reclamation.

replaces isolation — edit in place, commit on the branch the checkout already
has, push — appended to the prompt through the same updatedInput rewrite the
grant uses.

runs and which ADR-0044 decision 6 narrowed to the daemon-unreachable
provisioning fallback. Neither key reaches the other's decision, and
agent_worktree reads no registry layer at all. The exemption covers the worktree
grant only: the ADR-0044 main-checkout write boundary is unchanged, and the

* fix(trusty-search): refuse a re-registration that names a different tree

Registration was asymmetric. A second id claiming a registered tree was
rejected and hardened three times (#2336, #2519, #3993), but the same id
over a DIFFERENT tree was accepted: create_index_handler canonicalized the
supplied root_path and then compared only the id, answering
200 {created: false, reason: "already exists"} while the previously
registered tree went on serving every query.

best_effort_create_index read only resp.status(), so that answer was
indistinguishable from a real create. The caller pinned the id and reported
success, and a session opening in one checkout had every search answered
from another — no error, no warning.

An index identifies one directory tree, so a request naming a tree the
daemon does not hold under that id has not been satisfied:

- create_index_handler compares the requested root against the registered
  one and returns 409 naming both. Live handles and cold-parked entries are
  checked with the same rule, per #3993's reasoning for the mirror guard.
- The already-exists response now carries root_path, so a client can verify
  which tree it joined instead of inferring it from a 2xx.
- best_effort_create_index reads that field and withholds confirmation on a
  mismatch. A daemon that omits it leaves the verdict unchanged.

The (dev, ino) comparison moves to trusty_common::index_id::identifies_same_path
and both guards route through it. canonicalize preserves the case it was
given rather than normalising it, so on APFS two spellings of one directory
compare unequal as strings; a second copy of that rule is how the two guards
would drift. Filesystem-only, so a non-git tree compares like a checkout.

A genuine re-registration of the same tree stays idempotent, including a
differently-cased spelling of one inode.

checkouts .../bob-duetto/api and .../bobmatnyc/api both derive `api`. That
second registration is now refused rather than silently bound to the first

fix(trusty-mpm): reap an agent's worktree when its session ends, not only on SubagentStop (#5846)

* fix(trusty-mpm): reap an agent's worktree when its session ends, not only on SubagentStop

`spawn_on_stop` was the only caller of `reap_worktree`, so the reap had one
trigger and one attempt per agent. Every exit route that delivers no
`SubagentStop` — the harness session exiting or restarting under an in-flight
agent, an interrupt, a `tm hook` POST that loses its 2 s budget — reached it
never, and `prune_orphaned_worktrees` skips a `SentinelOwner::Agent` tree by
design, so nothing else could reclaim it. The worktree leaked permanently and
nothing recorded that it had.

Measured in this machine's daemon log: 54 distinct agent worktrees registered,
30 reaped, 24 never reaped. 17 of those 24 carry no reap decision line of any
kind; the other 7 were refused once as holding unsaved work and never retried.

`spawn_on_session_end` is the second trigger. A subagent runs inside its parent
Claude Code session's process and cannot outlive it, so a `SessionEnd` is proof
every agent that session dispatched has exited — the same signal #4337 already
treats as unambiguous. It resolves the store from the payload's `cwd` exactly as
`rebuild_from_disk` does and runs the UNCHANGED gate stack against every tree
whose sentinel names that session as parent. No gate is weakened: a tree holding
unsaved work, one a live process stands in, or one another session's agent owns
is still kept.

A refusal now logs at `warn!` rather than `info!`, and each session end reports
how many trees it reclaimed and how many it kept, so a tree the gates decline to
clear is visible instead of silent.

feat(trusty-audit): register audit targets additively, validating access first (#5822) (#5834)

* feat(trusty-audit): register audit targets additively, validating access first (#5822)

`taudit add repo <owner>/<name>` and `taudit add board <jira|linear>:<KEY>`
record what an engagement audits, and each add proves the target can be READ
before it is persisted — with the credential the sweep will later use. A target
that cannot be reached is refused at registration, not discovered as a gap an
hour into an unattended run.

Registration is additive: a second `add` never rewrites what is already
registered, and re-adding one is a no-op that does not re-validate, so a
network blip cannot fail an entry that already passed. `taudit targets` lists
the registry and `taudit remove <target>` drops one entry.

Validation reuses what exists rather than adding a client. GitHub goes through
`discover::credential_probe` and `trusty_common::gh::GhCommand`; the HTTP client
still comes from `trusty_installer::download::http_client`, with the timeout
applied per request. JIRA and Linear follow tga's collector conventions — Basic
auth with email plus API token against `/rest/api/3/project/<KEY>`, and a bare
`Authorization` header with no `Bearer` prefix against Linear's GraphQL
endpoint.

The client's own board credentials arrive in the engagement config under a new
`[boards]` table as `SecretKey` values, so they cannot be serialized into an

* fix(trusty-audit): serialise the target registry's read-modify-write (#5822)

Session::add_target and Session::remove_target each ran Registry::load →
mutate → Registry::save with nothing making that sequence indivisible. Two
concurrent `taudit add` runs against one working directory loaded the same
snapshot and each saved their own; the later save discarded the earlier one's
target while both reported success. workdir::write_atomically does not close
that — it makes one write untearable, not a load-mutate-save atomic.

the workspace's one implementation of it, extracted after trusty-search's
indexes.toml lost updates the same way (#5344). Validation stays OUTSIDE the
lock: it reaches the network under a 30-second ceiling, so holding the lock
across it would stall every other add in the working directory. The locked
section re-reads the file, so the append is decided against the current
snapshot. Session runs it via spawn_blocking, as file_lock's own contract
requires of an async caller.

2), so the path is not knowable at dispatch time. The agent supplies it
instead: every hook payload a subagent emits carries `agent_id` beside the
`cwd` that hook process is standing in, and for an isolated agent that cwd is
the harness worktree. The daemon already receives and discards those events.
No worktree is created, none is relocated, and no hook is installed.

`SubagentStop` then reaps the tree behind six gates, every one refusing toward
keeping the directory: already gone, not a `.claude/worktrees/<name>` leaf,
still held by a live session or an unfinished sibling delegation, claimed by
no git registry, holding unsaved work, or a `git worktree remove --force` that
did not succeed. The unsaved-work gate is #4091's own implementation rather
than a second copy, and no argument reaches its force-discard policy. Removal
is git-mediated with no `remove_dir_all` fallback and the branch is never
deleted. A `Stale` delegation is not reaped — that status means tracking lost
the agent, not that it exited.

The ADR is deferred: the next number is reserved by an unmerged branch.

ADR-0048 decision 4 denied `git commit` there on the verb, with no
conditions. Together they let a doc be written where it could never be
landed. The owner ruled that documents can be written AND committed
there.

The gate now reads the staged set rather than the verb. Documents and

edit-tool write boundary cannot disagree about a file.

live-writer check: a commit moves the shared HEAD exactly as far as a pull
does, and which branch it lands on has never depended on the file
extension.

Every other arm keeps the pre-existing deny — an unreadable index, an
empty index, and `-a`/`--amend`/`--include`/`--only`/a pathspec, each of
which commits content the index does not hold. Flag recognition is an
allowlist, so this classifier can only turn a deny into an allow.

`git add` is untouched: it writes the index and moves no ref.

DOC-66 §0.5 said read-only-ness "should not be enforced" for the tm
checkout, contradicting a shipped and enforced decision. ADR-0049
decision 7 scopes it: the checkout is source-restricted, neither read-only
nor freely writable. ADR-0030 stays Proposed and otherwise untouched.

* fix(trusty-mpm): gate tmux and host-process discovery behind a real-environment check (closes #5784)

A daemon started under a throwaway $HOME still reached the real tmux
server. tmux is keyed to the OS user, not to $HOME, so a scratch
daemon's startup auto-discovery listed the operator's live panes,
adopted them, and — because an adopted record carries the real
project's working directory — refreshed .claude/skills/ inside real
project checkouts, one of them in a different repository.

core::host_state_gate compares $HOME against the home the OS password
database records for this uid. The passwd entry is the signal that
works: the process can reassign $HOME but not its own passwd entry,
and it names the same OS user the tmux server is keyed to. Comparing
the resolved data dir against "the default" cannot work, because a
scratch daemon uses the DEFAULT formula ($HOME/.trusty-mpm) — only the
$HOME it resolves against changed.

TmuxDriver::discover consults it. That is the crate's only constructor
for a tmux-backed driver and the field is private, so holding a
TmuxDriver is proof the gate passed — startup discovery, the reap
loop, orphan-GC, the idle reaper, the session services, the
claude-config restarter, and the session manager's RealTmuxDriver are
all covered by the one check. discovery::discover_all repeats it to
cover the ps/lsof scan, which touches no tmux but adopts the same real
sessions.

The gate fails closed, inverted from this crate's usual direction: an
environment it cannot classify is refused too. A wrong skip costs a
test daemon that adopts nothing; a wrong proceed writes into live
project directories. Every refusal logs its reason at warn!, and the
daemon's startup line now reports a gated environment as gated instead
of as "tmux not found".

TRUSTY_MPM_ALLOW_HOST_STATE=1 lifts it.

Review of PR #5787 found the gate was the worst of both worlds: it broke
`tm supervisor` in a container while leaving the actual mutation path
open. `tm launch` and `tm connect` create and kill sessions on the real
uid-keyed tmux server through `create_managed_session(None, …)` and

letting the retried apply-and-verify cycle emit a dozen refusals for one
`tm launch`. `TmuxDriver::discover` keeps its own gate so a gated daemon
fails fast with a diagnosable message instead of N refused subprocesses;
its doc no longer claims coverage it does not provide.

Four sites swallowed the refusal. `tmux_service` mapped it to
`SessionNotFound` — a 404 reading "that session does not exist" to an
operator whose real problem is a reassigned $HOME — and the reap and
orphan-GC loops fell through a bare `if let` / `continue` silently, every
60 s, forever. All four now carry the reason. `POST /sessions/discover`
gained a `skipped` field so a refused scan is distinguishable from one
that found nothing.

The boot inproject-hygiene sweep is gated: `repos_root()` is only
$HOME-scoped when nothing overrode it, and a scratch daemon launched from
the operator's shell inherits TRUSTY_MPM_REPOS_ROOT /
TRUSTY_MPM_WORKSPACE_ROOT. The comment above it claimed that sweep does a
"safety-gated hard-reset"; it runs `git merge --ff-only` and never
`git reset --hard`.

On non-unix the gate now allows rather than blocking: it returned
`effective_home()`, and Windows normally leaves $HOME unset, so
`classify` hit its `(None, _)` arm and refused every tmux path on a
platform with no tmux to refuse.

test cannot flip the gate mid-spawn.

* feat(trusty-mpm): grant dispatched writers a worktree and enforce the main-checkout write boundary

ADR-0044 decided the main checkout is read-only apart from documents and
configuration, and that the rule is enforced mechanically for the PM and every
agent it dispatches. Only the destructive-git half was built, and no path gave
a dispatched writer anywhere else to write — so agents wrote to the shared
checkout because it was the only tree they had. Three sessions in one checkout
produced a commit on another workstream's branch, with no error at any step.

Both gaps close together; either alone is half an invariant.

Part A — a dispatched agent that may write is granted its own worktree when the
session is standing in a main checkout. The guard emits
hookSpecificOutput.updatedInput carrying the dispatch's own input with
isolation: "worktree" added, so the harness provisions and reclaims the tree.
Trusty-mpm creates nothing, per ADR-0044 decision 4. An agent this binary
cannot classify is treated as a writer here — the opposite of #4480's fail-open
direction, because in a main checkout a false allow corrupts another session's
branch while a false grant costs one worktree.

Part B — in a main checkout, an edit tool targeting a source file and
git commit are denied for the PM and every dispatched agent. Documents,
configuration, and everything in a worktree stay writable. Each denial names
the remedy.

Part C — live_shared_tree_writers no longer filters on the asking session. The
hazard is a shared git HEAD, which belongs to the directory; the session filter
is what made the guard blind to the reported shape. The launch-on-main
collision record drops to info!: with writers isolated and the boundary
enforced, sharing a read-only checkout is expected.

session's own worktree and its Consequences admitted nothing checked it:
pm_guard_bash's git-verb classification stopped at `reset --hard`, `clean -fdx`
and `checkout -- <pathspec>`.

`main_checkout::main_checkout_head_move` classifies the three verbs and returns
the verb plus the directory; `pm_guard` then asks the daemon's directory-keyed
`live_shared_tree_writers` — decision 7's query, reached from a Bash call for
the first time — who else is writing there, and denies only when both answers
are positive. The query claims nothing: the route re-derives eligibility from
the payload and `Bash` is not a dispatch tool, so its record closure never runs.

The rule sits in the Bash block ahead of Guards 1 and 4 for the reason decision
4 gives: the restriction binds dispatched agents, and both automatic markers
return ALLOW for exactly that population. The operator escape hatches still lift
it.

Why the verb alone is safe here, given #5356: none of the three has a form that
leaves HEAD alone, so no argument analysis is needed. `checkout <branch>` and
`switch <branch>` stay uncovered because their argument is genuinely ambiguous
between a ref and a pathspec — the ADR now says so rather than lumping all five
together. `--abort`/`--continue`/`--skip`/`--quit`/`--edit-todo`/
`--show-current-patch` are exempt: they resolve an operation that already
started, and refusing them would park a shared checkout mid-rebase with no
remedy reachable from there.

Ordinary work cannot be denied: a pull in a worktree, a pull in a checkout
nobody else is writing in, `git fetch`, and an unreachable or unusable daemon
answer all ALLOW.

The grant rewrote a dispatch into an isolated one, but the daemon's
`matcher: "*"` tracker recorded the ORIGINAL payload, so every writer the
grant had just moved out stayed recorded as writing unisolated in the shared
checkout. Decision 10 reads exactly those records, so `git pull` there was
denied on a phantom for the six hours of RUNNING_STALE_AFTER_SECS — the
release flow's own fast-forward step.

Posting the rewritten input to the existing shared-tree route cannot fix it:
that route re-derives eligibility with `shares_the_callers_tree`, which an
isolated input makes false, so its record closure never runs. Nor can
`observe` — it returns early on a `tool_use_id` that already exists, so it
corrects nothing whenever the tracker won the race, and the two hooks fire on
one event. So the daemon gains a `granted-worktree` route whose record is a
genuine UPSERT: it overwrites `isolation` on an existing record, and both
arrival orders converge on one isolated record.

That same call answers who holds the checkout, so the #4480 verdict is
computed BEFORE the grant instead of being skipped by it. Skipping assumed
the harness applies `hookSpecificOutput.updatedInput` for `Agent`, which this
binary cannot verify; if it does not, a second unisolated writer that used to
be denied was admitted.

Also: `Explore` and `Plan` are classified read-only, since a granted worktree
is cut from a commit and hid the session's uncommitted work from the agents
asked to read it; the HEAD-move query keys by the checkout root as well as the
command's directory; the in-progress carve-out matches positionally; the deny
attributes its claim to the daemon's records; and the head-move integration
tests capture the request body instead of trusting a canned one.

Round-two review, seven findings.

sequentially on one thread, so deleting the mutex left the suite green. A

fix(tga): stop seven config credentials printing via Debug (#5776)

`LinearConfig`, `GithubConfig`, `JiraConfig`, `BitbucketConfig`,
`AzureDevOpsConfig`, `ClassificationConfig` and `ClassificationEngineConfig`
derived `Debug` over a plaintext credential — `api_key`, `token`,
`app_password` (Bitbucket carries two: Basic and Bearer), `pat`, and
`openrouter_api_key`. Any `{:?}` of one printed the live secret: a `tracing`
field, an `anyhow` context, a `dbg!`, a panic message.

None of these is reachable from a live call site today. Nothing in the crate
debug-formats a `Config` or any of its sections; the only production `{:?}`
over a config value is `region = ?cfg.region` in the Bedrock arm of
`classify/tiers/llm.rs`, a single non-secret field. The OpenRouter key sits
closest to the edge: `TuiState` derives `Debug` and holds a whole `Config`, so
one `{:?}` in the TUI — the module where a developer reaches for one — would
have printed it. The exposure lived in the types, so the fix is by
construction rather than by auditing call sites.

All seven now have a hand-written `Debug` in `core::config::credential_debug`.
Every non-credential field renders unchanged, because the non-secret fields are
the reason anyone formats a config; the credential is replaced with a fixed
`<redacted>` marker. `ClassificationEngineConfig` lives in `classify` and its
impl is here anyway: it holds a clone of `ClassificationConfig`'s key, and
splitting the two would put half the answer in another file.

Every impl destructures `Self` exhaustively with no `..` rest pattern. Reading
fields by name would let a later field vanish from the output with no compiler
error — for a credential that is worse than the bug being fixed here, since it
hides the next occurrence instead of surfacing it. Adding a field now fails
compilation with E0027 at the impl site, which forces a decision about whether
it is a secret.

The mask is unconditional and carries nothing from the value — no prefix, no
length. None of these fields is format-validated: they are plain `String` /
`Option<String>` filled from YAML or an env var, so a fingerprint that echoes a
fixed-length head, such as `trusty_common::credentials::redact_secret`, would
disclose four characters of real entropy for any credential whose shape is not
the provider's documented one. Same reasoning settled on #5733.

An unset `Option` still renders as `None`. Presence is not a secret, and "is a
credential configured at all" is the first question anyone debug-formats a
config to answer.

Every assertion was run against code that lacked the fix. The derived `Debug`
printed `api_key: Some("9f3Kq7Zt2Wm4Bx8Lv6Nc1Rd5Ph0Sj")`,
`pat: "9f3Kq7Zt2Wm4Bx8Lv6Nc1Rd5Ph0Sj"` and
`openrouter_api_key: Some("9f3Kq7Zt2Wm4Bx8Lv6Nc1Rd5Ph0Sj")`. A head-echoing
mask was then substituted for the fixed marker, printing `"9f3K…<redacted>"`,
and all seven tests failed on the leading-fragment assertion — every masked
field routes through one helper, so the mutation reaches the non-`Option` `pat`
too.

`Serialize` is a separate and unfixed question: all seven structs still derive
it. No workspace call site serializes them, so nothing reaches disk or a
response body; the derive is reported rather than changed here.

Closes #5770

fix(ci): link trusty-memory's Linux legs natively and let the audit block a partial release (#5767)

trusty-memory's Linux x86_64/aarch64 release builds have failed at link on
every tag since 9ee1b57e (#2051) switched those legs to `cargo zigbuild` —
five tag pushes over 40 days, most recently trusty-memory-v0.23.0 (run
31883156657).

Root cause: the config table asserted "No ORT bundling (no ONNX in the
released binary)" for this crate. That is false. trusty-memory depends on
trusty-common with the `memory-core` feature, and `memory-core` implies
`embedder-bundled-ort` -> `fastembed/ort-download-binaries-native-tls`,
which links a prebuilt ONNX Runtime archive built against GNU libstdc++.
zig cc ships LLVM libc++, so `ld.lld` fails on hundreds of undefined
`std::__cxx11::...` symbols referenced from `libort_sys-*.rlib`
(onnx-ml.pb.cc, unsqueeze.cc). This is the same limitation #2051 already
documented and worked around for trusty-search and trusty-analyze; it
simply missed that trusty-memory has it too.

Separate the conflated flag. `al2023_variant` answered two unrelated
questions at once: "does this crate need native GNU-ABI linking?" and
"does this crate also want an AL2023-container asset?". trusty-memory
needs the first but not the second — it exposes no `load-dynamic` feature
path, so an AL2023 build would fail. A new `native_linux_link` key answers
the linking question on its own; `al2023_variant` keeps the container-asset
question. The toolchain choice now keys off `native_linux_link`, while the
aarch64 FEATURE substitution stays keyed off `al2023_variant`, since that
substitution exists only because trusty-search's bundled-ort has no aarch64
archive to use.

Make the completeness audit actually gate the release. `release-completeness-audit`
has computed `missing_required` and exited 1 since f6f54774, but was not a
dependency of `release`, so it sat red while the release published green —
trusty-memory-v0.23.0 shipped one macOS asset that way. Adding
`needs.release-completeness-audit.result == 'success'` to the release job's
`if:` would have re-created the #3540 bug, because a false `if:` SKIPS the
job and a skipped release is silent. Instead the audit is a `needs`
dependency whose verdict is enforced by a STEP that fails loudly before any
upload. A failing build leg still lets the release job run (#3540 preserved);
a missing REQUIRED asset now stops the publish. This matters because the repo
has Immutable Releases enabled, so an incomplete release can never be
repaired in place.

Verified by generating the real matrix from the real config+matrix steps for
all 9 binary crates before and after: the only delta is trusty-memory's two
Linux legs moving from linux-zigbuild to standard. trusty-search's five legs
and every other crate are byte-identical.

fix: unbreak Gate 1 — the link gate that examined nothing, and the 20 links it missed (#5759)

* fix(scripts): stop check_rustdoc_links.sh passing over a scan that examined nothing

Run locally the gate reported

    SUMMARY  25 crate(s) documented, 0 broken link(s), baseline 0, 0 examined

and exited 0 on a tree carrying 20 broken links that CI counted on the same
commit. Two independent defects stacked to produce that.

The vacuous-scan guard fired only on `parsed_messages == 0 AND cargo_rc != 0`.
It asked whether cargo had COMPLAINED, not whether rustdoc had RUN. A warm
target dir makes `cargo doc` a no-op — cargo re-emits every `compiler-artifact`
with `"fresh": true` and invokes rustdoc for none of them — so a cached run
exits 0 with an empty diagnostic stream, satisfies neither half of the guard,
and prints a pass over nothing examined. That is the #5620 shape a third time.

The crate count was measuring the wrong artifact. Every workspace member is
COMPILED as well as documented, and the rlib artifacts outnumber the rustdoc
ones, so "25 crate(s) documented" came out of a run where rustdoc executed for
three. Measured here: 38 doc units, 35 served from cache.

The diagnostic count cannot carry the check, because a genuinely clean tree has
zero diagnostics too. The evidence is now the artifact: a `compiler-artifact`
whose filenames point into `target/doc/**/index.html` with `fresh: false` means
rustdoc actually ran for that crate. Zero of those FAILS whatever cargo's exit
status was, and a crate served from cache FAILS by name rather than being
counted as clean. The run also deletes the `doc-*` fingerprints up front, which
invalidates the rustdoc units and nothing else, so a warm tree produces real
evidence instead of a refusal; dependency compilation stays cached and CI needs
it too, since rust-cache restores a warm target dir there.

`--update-baseline` now refuses to write from a vacuous run. #5744 drove this
baseline to zero from a macOS measurement that had already gone vacuous, and a
bad baseline outlives the run that wrote it.

The gate also names every broken link it finds. Reporting a per-crate count and
nothing else is why #5753's links had to be recovered by reading raw CI logs.

check_rustdoc_links_selftest.sh drives all six fail-closed branches through the
`--json` entry point with synthetic streams, so it needs no doc build. The
load-bearing case is cached-no-op at cargo exit 0: the old script exits 0 on
that fixture, the new one exits 3.

Documented alongside it: `cargo doc` resolves default features only, so a
module behind a non-default feature is never examined. trusty-common's `docgen`
is the worked example — enabled only from `[dev-dependencies]`, which
`cargo doc` does not resolve, so two bare links lived there until
check_contracts.sh surfaced them.

fix(scripts): CHECK 8's run table loses an empty field to tab collapsing (#5760)

CHECK 8's internal run table was tab-separated, and tab is IFS whitespace — so
`read` collapses a run of tabs into one delimiter and an empty field disappears.
A queued or in-progress run is the only row with an empty `conclusion`, so its
html_url shifted left into $concl and $url came back empty.

Measured on run 31878535281, dispatched against this commit's parent:

    in_progress/https://github.com/.../runs/31878535281      (was)
    in_progress/<none>  https://github.com/.../runs/31878535281   (now)

The verdict was already right — a shifted url never equals "success", so an
in-progress run still failed the green test and still landed on the red-gate
arm. What was wrong is the diagnostic an operator reads to decide what to do
next, and a latent hazard: any future field whose emptiness is meaningful would
shift a neighbouring value into it silently.

Switches the table delimiter to `|`, which is not IFS whitespace and therefore
preserves empty fields. No field can contain one — targets are hex or a keyword,
statuses and conclusions are a fixed vocabulary, and a GitHub run URL has no
pipe in it.

The in-progress fixture is the only case with an empty conclusion, so it is the
one that catches a delimiter regression; it now asserts the url lands in its own
field. 39 assertions pass.

fix(scripts): CHECK 8 must credit a run to the commit it gated, not head_sha (#5758)

CHECK 8 asked the Actions API for `Pre-publish gate` runs whose `head_sha` is
the commit about to be published. Since #5741 added the `sha` dispatch input,
`head_sha` is no longer the commit a run examined: it is the dispatched ref's
tip at dispatch time, and the whole point of the input is to gate something
older. So the query was wrong in both directions at once — it counted runs that
examined a different commit, and it could not see the run that examined this
one.

Live on this repo, run 31864924233: conclusion `success`, `head_sha`
eb40680a (the tga 2.20.0 version bump), commit actually checked out and gated
0c44ff94. The old query at eb40680a returned that run among 2 green and printed
`[PASS]`. A release commit was one command away from being cleared by a gate
that never opened it — the same class as CHECK 6 and the mis-tagged tga-v2.17.0.

CHECK 8 now enumerates recent runs and asks each one which commit IT reports
gating, via the `::notice title=Pre-publish gate target::` annotation the
resolve-sha job emits. Only runs that name HEAD count. pre-publish.yml emits
that notice on its no-sha arm too, so every run is attributable rather than
only the sha-pinned ones.

Fails closed, with the states kept distinct: a run attributed to HEAD that is
red or still running is [FAIL] "red gate"; no run attributed to HEAD is [FAIL]
"never ran"; a run whose resolve-sha succeeded but whose target cannot be read
is neither answer, so it routes to the reason-taking PREFLIGHT_GATE_UNVERIFIED
arm. A run whose resolve-sha did not succeed gated nothing and is ignored
outright rather than counted either way. The override still cannot suppress a
red gate or manufacture a run that never happened.

The remedy text now prints `-f sha=$(git rev-parse HEAD)`, so the dispatch pins
the run to the commit being released instead of whatever the ref tip becomes.

The decision half is split into gate_decide() and covered by
scripts/preflight-check8-selftest.sh — 38 assertions over captured API output,
including the verbatim run-31864924233 attribution. Mutating the shipped
comparison back to the old behaviour turns 9 of them red. Wired into
tag-publish-parity.yml beside the CHECK 5 fixtures.

Also marks trusty-tui and trusty-kb `publish = false`. Neither has ever been on
crates.io and both are Slice 1 in-progress, so the permanent name is not worth
claiming. Both are used from PRODUCTION code by their dependents — trusty-tui by
trusty-code's src/cli/tui.rs and src/tui_client/, trusty-kb by trusty-agents'
src/tools/okg/ and src/stores/ — so [dev-dependencies] does not resolve the
publish constraint, and the manifests record what that costs rather than hiding
it. Neither dependent can publish today regardless: their `version = "0.1.0"`
requirements have nothing to resolve against.

extract_ticket_id reads a key from the commit subject only, so a branch
named feature/PROJ-123-thing and a PR body saying "Closes #N" reached
work_items through nothing at all.

A commit object carries no branch, and git branch --contains answers a
different question: under a squash-merge workflow it returns main for every
merged commit and the authoring branch for none — this repository has 2633
commits against 13 live remote branches. The branch survives in one place,
the pull request's head ref, and pull_requests.commit_shas already joins a
PR to the commits it produced. Migration v24 adds head_ref and
body_ticket_id there rather than a mostly-NULL column on commits. Both
columns are additive with defaults, and an existing v23 database keeps its
rows and reads the new columns as "no claim made".

correlate_commits now resolves a key through a stated precedence — the
commit's own text, then the branch name, then the PR body — declared as an
ordered constant rather than left to the order of an or_else chain. 323 of
this repository's merged commits have a subject key and a body key that
differ, and #5199's subject-position rule stays authoritative: neither new
source displaces a key the commit declares.

The rejection rules carry over unchanged, because re-admitting the noise
#5199 removed was the whole risk. A branch key is anchored at a segment
start and screened against the same ADR/DOC/RFC/SPEC list, so
fix/ADR-0029-followup yields nothing. No JIRA-shaped token is read from a
PR body at all: an unrestricted scan of this repository's 2433 bodies
returns 2501 matches across 423 distinct keys led by DOC-39, DOC-48 and
ADR-0024, and gating on an action keyword does not rescue it — Closes
<JIRA-key> appears 8 times and 6 are ADR-0038, ADR-0032, DOC-56, DOC-29,
RUSTSEC-2026 and a HIGH-1 severity label. A body must say closes/fixes/
resolves #N to be believed; a bare #N is rejected too, which keeps out 819
further bodies.

Measured through the real code path over 2376 merged pull requests:
from_pr_body 51, from_branch 0, no_ticket down from 363 to 312, and zero
JIRA-shaped keys harvested from either new source. The branch harvest finds
nothing here because this repository's branches are lowercase
(fix/5734-slug) — a property of its conventions, not of the extractor, and
CorrelationOutcome reports from_branch and from_pr_body unconditionally so
a source that finds nothing is distinguishable from one never consulted.

A provider that reports Some("") for a head ref made an empty claim and is
recorded as a skip_item fault; None means it never claimed to supply one

broken payload look exactly like a branch harvest of zero.

persisted. The concurrent PR-fetch drain moved to collect/pr_pipeline.rs,

fix(trusty-installer): probe trusty-mpm /health over HTTP instead of reporting unknown (#5748)

`probe_member_health` returned `ProbeOutcome::Unprobeable` for any member whose
`ManageStrategy` is `OwnVerb` — trusty-mpm alone — even though the daemon answers
`GET http://127.0.0.1:7880/health`, its `http_addr` discovery file is present, and
`probe_http::fixed_port_for` already maps `"trusty-mpm" => Some(7880)`.

Probeability is a property of the daemon's HTTP transport, not of its
lifecycle-management strategy. The two axes coincided while the probe was a
`<binary> health --json` subprocess and diverged when #4246 moved it to HTTP
`/health`; the match arm kept keying off the lifecycle enum. `OwnVerb` now takes
the same transport as `Launchd`; only `ManageStrategy::None` (a non-daemon) stays
`Unprobeable`.

`ManageStrategy` itself is untouched — it still governs `tctl start|stop|restart`
dispatch and `needs_kickstart`, which independently requires `Launchd`. That is
why this is a one-arm change and why mpm stays `OwnVerb` in `stable_set`: a
confirmed-down mpm now reaches `Refused` yet still cannot be handed to
`launchctl kickstart -k` against the nonexistent `com.trusty.mpm` label.

ACCEPTED POLICY CONSEQUENCE. mpm is `required: true`, and `down` — unlike
`unknown` — fails `VerifyTailReport::build` and degrades `status`'s exit code. A
user who has simply not started mpm now gets `tctl status` / `tctl stack health` /
`tctl stack doctor` -> `degraded`, exit 2, and `tctl install` -> NOT VERIFIED.
This is intended: mpm becomes consistent with its declared `required` flag rather
than exempt from it, exactly as a stopped trusty-search already behaves. No escape
hatch, env-var opt-out or `required: false` demotion was added. It also stops
`tctl up` issuing a redundant `start` against a daemon already known to be
serving.

Tests: `own_verb_member_is_unknown` is replaced by
`own_verb_member_is_probed_over_http` (the pin this issue removes, inverted rather
than deleted), plus `own_verb_member_refused_when_nothing_listens`,
`non_daemon_member_is_unprobeable`, and
`required_mpm_reporting_down_fails_verification`. The `OwnVerb` row of
`needs_kickstart_only_for_confirmed_down_launchd` is now load-bearing for a live
code path and says so. `stable_set::mpm_uses_own_verb` and
`manage_strategy_for_matches_the_stable_set` are unchanged and green — proof the
lifecycle axis was not touched.

Also corrects the doc comments and vmtest-harness sites that recorded the #4246
carve-out as a current invariant, and widens the harness oracle's `H_P` to accept
`down` for a non-launchd member pre-start (the same ordering artefact it already
accepts for a launchd member with no plist); a genuinely dead mpm still fails at

fix(docs): drive broken intra-doc links to zero and deny them at every crate root (#5744)

* fix(docs): drive broken intra-doc links to zero and deny them at every crate root

852 broken intra-doc links across 16 crates, measured with `--keep-going` (the
baseline recorded 873; 21 of those had already been fixed on main by the time
this branch started). docs.rs builds a release's documentation once from the
uploaded tarball, so each one was baked into that version permanently.

The dominant cause was one rustdoc behaviour, not 852 typos. When a module
carries BOTH an outer `///` doc on its `mod x;` declaration AND its own inner
`//!` doc, rustdoc concatenates the two and resolves EVERY link in the merged
doc against the PARENT module's scope. A bare `[`Foo`]` written inside the
module's own `//!` — correct in that module — comes out unresolved. 194 modules
were in that shape, accounting for 452 findings.

The repair keeps the prose exactly as written: Markdown reference definitions
(`//! [`Foo`]: crate::a::b::Foo`) are appended to the affected inner docs. An
absolute path in a definition resolves whichever scope rustdoc picked. The
alternative — deleting the duplicated outer block — would have removed 1741
lines of documentation on a redundancy claim that could not be verified per
module.

The remaining findings were resolved from each crate's real module tree:
- item renamed, moved, or reached through a private module -> link corrected to
  the path rustdoc actually documents
- item genuinely not publicly documented (private, `pub(crate)`, test-only, or
  in a binary's private tree) -> demoted to plain code formatting, since a link
  to an undocumented item renders as dead text on docs.rs
- `tests::` pointers from the Why/What/Test convention -> demoted the same way
  and for the same reason: `#[cfg(test)]` modules are never documented, so those
  links could never have resolved. Plain backticks is already the dominant form
  for this axis in the repo.
- brackets that were never links (`[global]`, `#[ignore]`, `[1]HEALTH`) ->
  escaped or backticked
- ambiguous module-or-function names -> disambiguated with `mod@`

`#![deny(rustdoc::broken_intra_doc_links)]` now sits on all 46 documented crate
roots, including `src/bin/tm/main.rs`, whose subdirectory layout hides it from a
`src/bin/*.rs` glob and which held 81 of the findings on its own. The ratchet
baseline drops from 873 to 0 rows.

- `cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --keep-going` with NO `RUSTDOCFLAGS`: exit 0,

refactor(trusty-memory): run BM25 in-process, delete trusty-bm25-daemon (closes #5329) (#5689)

* refactor(trusty-memory): run BM25 in-process, delete trusty-bm25-daemon (closes #5329)

BM25 ran as a per-palace subprocess reached over a UDS socket. The recorded
justification was an analogy to trusty-embedderd, where a subprocess amortises
an ONNX model load; an in-memory inverted index pays no such cost, and
trusty-search has always run the identical trusty_common::bm25::BM25Index
in-process alongside its own redb/usearch locks. The gate was never enabled in
any shipped configuration (#5186).

bm25_lane::Bm25Lane replaces the client and the supervisor: an LRU-bounded map
of bm25_index::PalaceBm25Index behind one mutex, plus a 100 ms tick that
coalesces snapshot flushes and enforces a retained-text budget. Snapshots are
read in place — the daemon's path and JSON format are unchanged — so an
operator who set TRUSTY_BM25_DAEMON=1 keeps their corpus with no migration
step, and a downgrade still reads what this writes.

Deleted: the trusty-bm25-daemon crate, trusty-memory's [[bin]] shim,
Bm25Supervisor, and trusty_common::bm25_client. The shared
uds::supervisor::UdsServiceSupervisor is untouched — trusty-console and
trusty-agents supervise trusty-review and trusty-analyze through it.

Cost: process-level fault isolation. A runaway BM25 index can no longer be
SIGKILLed independently of the recall path. The text budget bounds it.

`default = []` and 25+ modules sit behind opt-in features, so
`cargo test -p trusty-common` — the command CLAUDE.md prescribed as the
per-crate check — compiled none of them. It ran 328 of the crate's ~2062 tests
and exited 0, including with a `memory_core` file that did not compile at all;
PR #4899 reported a green gate on that basis before the correct code existed.

A new `build.rs` detects the build where Cargo activated no feature (`default`
discounted, since it is always present and empty here) and `lib.rs` turns it
into a `compile_error!` naming the command that covers what you changed. The
guard is `cfg(test)`-scoped, so `cargo build`, `cargo check` and all 20 consumer
crates are unaffected, and every narrow `--features <x>` run — including CI's
`clippy -p trusty-common --features codex-config` step — still builds. A second
guard fails the build if `build.rs` stops running, since an inert guard restores
the silent green.

Making `memory-core` a default feature was rejected: it implies
`embedder-bundled-ort`, so every consumer would compile and link ONNX Runtime,
and the mutually exclusive `embedder-load-dynamic` / `embedder-cuda` variants
the AL2023 and CUDA builds select would become unreachable without

covers only the always-compiled surface; the crate's doc pointers, CLAUDE.md and

the run to the commit already known green — main kept moving between
"CI settled" and "operator dispatches," restarting the 13-16 minute
gate against a newer, unverified tip.

Add an optional `sha` workflow_dispatch input. A new `resolve-sha` job
resolves it (or falls back to the ref's tip when omitted, unchanged
behaviour), verifies it is an ancestor of the dispatched ref via
`git merge-base --is-ancestor`, and reports the resolved commit via a
step summary and a `::notice::` annotation. Every downstream job
(ci-parity, rustdoc-links, audit, deny, ignored-tests, contracts)
checks out that resolved SHA instead of the ref's default tip, and
`summary` now also requires resolve-sha to have succeeded.

Fails closed: a malformed SHA, one absent from history, or one that
exists but is not an ancestor of the ref all produce a distinct
::error:: and a nonzero exit rather than a silent fallback to the tip.

fix(tga): read a ticket key from the commit subject, not from body prose (#5736)

The JIRA/Linear pattern `\b[A-Z][A-Z0-9]*-\d+\b` matches any hyphenated
uppercase token, and extract_ticket_id ran it over the whole message ahead
of the bare `#N` fallback. Every `ADR-0034`, `DOC-67`, `UTF-8`, `SHA-256`,
`RUSTSEC-2026` and `GCC-11` in a commit body therefore became that commit's
ticket key, overriding the GitHub issue its subject named. correlate_commits
then counted those in no_work_item — a reported coverage gap against a
ticket that exists on no board.

A JIRA/Linear key is now read from the subject line only: the first token
after an optional conventional-commit prefix and an optional `[`. The
documentation prefixes ADR, DOC, RFC and SPEC are rejected outright, and
anchoring at `^` also makes a tail segment of a longer identifier
(`SPEC-INSTALLER-01` -> `INSTALLER-01`) unreachable.

Measured over this repository's own 2633 commits: JIRA-shaped extractions
fall from 466 across 178 distinct keys to 21 across 17, with zero ADR / DOC
/ RFC / SPEC citations remaining, and 384 commits now resolve to the GitHub
issue they cite. The 21 survivors are this repo's own WI-/SM-/STUI- work
slices, written subject-leading.

The extractor still takes no configuration, so there is no project-key
allow-list that can be absent and no branch that returns nothing because a
repo was never configured.

is_ticketed is deliberately unchanged and still scans the whole message;
237 of this repo's commits are "ticketed" only via that pattern. Narrowing
an operator-facing quality metric last tuned by #445 is a separate call.

Two correlate.rs fixtures used mid-prose keys (`fixes PROJ-1 again`,
`sees PROJ-2`) and one ticket.rs test asserted a body-line `Relates to
SRE-999` extracts. All three encoded the defect; they are restated, not
weakened, and the behaviour each covers is unchanged.

perf(ci): cut cache-quota eviction and shorten the push-to-main critical path (#5730)

The Actions cache sits at 10.45 GB against a 10 GB limit and evicts
continuously. Measured consequence: 3 of 24 runs missed the cache and paid
+250s on the critical-path job, which is the entire p90 tail (4.02m -> 7.88m).
Six changes, none of which changes what CI verifies.

Cache quota:

- Add the main-only `save-if` guard that ci.yml already applies to every cache
  it owns to the four `Swatinem/rust-cache` steps that lacked it — sld-lint,
  version-parity, capabilities-drift and semver-checks. Measured at the time of
  writing, PR and worktree refs held 1.43 GB across exactly these four, none of
  it readable by any other PR.
- Guard the AL2023 cache the same way. It is the single largest entry at
  2.32 GB (22% of quota) and its workflow triggers on pull_request, so every PR
  touching trusty-search / trusty-embedderd / trusty-common could mint another
  unreadable copy. `actions/cache@v4` has no `save-if`, so this is spelled as a
  restore/save split with an `if:` on the save half.

Critical path:

- Move `cargo test --doc` out of test-shard (it ran on shard 1 only, ~68s) into
  its own `test-doc` job. A matrix finishes when its slowest leg finishes, so a
  cost carried by one leg was carried by the whole matrix. The `test` roll-up
  now gates on `test-doc` as well as on the matrix, so a failing doctest still
  turns "Rust tests (pre-publish gate)" red.
- Widen the shard matrix 4 -> 8. The per-shard build is ~496s and is not
  shardable; only the ~653s of test execution splits. Leg time goes from
  ~496+163 to ~496+82. The divisor is derived from `strategy.job-total`, so
  this is a one-line matrix change plus display names.
- Build the trusty-search smoke binary under a new `[profile.ci-smoke]`
  (release, minus thin LTO and opt-level 3) instead of `--release`. The job
  starts the daemon and asserts /health returns status=ok; that assertion is
  not sensitive to optimisation level.

Dead code:

- Delete the `.rcgu.o` sweep. Its own logging proved it reclaimed nothing on
  every run — run 31852921362 shard 1 printed `Before sweep: 45G` and
  `After sweep: 45G`, identical, in 0.16s. `CARGO_PROFILE_TEST_DEBUG=
  line-tables-only` already leaves nothing to sweep. Comments that credited it
  with remedying #3668 are corrected to name the settings that actually do.

Forget removed the drawer from redb and the vector store and never called
Bm25Client::delete, so the drawer's full text stayed in the palace's BM25
corpus — matching lexical queries, contributing to RRF fusion, and staying

dropped index request is repaired by the backfill, but the backfill only adds,
so nothing would re-attempt a dropped delete. When the lane is armed and its
daemon is unreachable, memory_forget now errors instead of reporting "deleted"
— a caller must be able to tell "deleted everywhere" from "deleted where we
could look". With the lane off nothing changes.

fix(trusty-agents): stop grading a rank-only RRF score A–F in search_code (#5622)

`chunk_to_hit_json` thresholded `CodeChunk::score` into an A–F letter and
shipped it to the agent LLM in every compact `search_code` hit. That score
is rank-only RRF: `search_hybrid` computes
`alpha/(60 + rank_vec) + beta/(60 + rank_bm)` and `classify_query` always
yields `alpha + beta == 1.0`, so its supremum is `1.0/61 = 0.01639` — below
the "B" cut at 0.018. The best possible hit in the corpus could only ever
grade "C". The same thresholds ran over the vector-only fallback, whose
score is a cosine in [0, 1], where a near-orthogonal 0.03 graded "A".

Drops the field and `grade_from_score`. `score` and `match_reason` are
unchanged, so a caller can still tell a fused hit from a vector one, and
array order carries the rank the RRF score encodes.

feat(trusty-audit): assemble and surface the unencrypted return package (refs #5499) (#5698)

* feat(trusty-audit): assemble and surface the unencrypted return package

`trusty-audit package` is the client's last step: it turns what a finished
sweep left across the working directory — each audited repository's report
directory under `out/`, its tga extract database under `extract/`, the verified
tool triple under `state/` — into one zip the recipient can attach to an email,
and prints its path.

The package is unencrypted and has no password. That is the same posture as the
readable engagement config: the recipient opens it and reads exactly what they
are about to send. Encrypting it would defend against nobody, since they hold
the plaintext either way.

Two refusals, both before a byte reaches the destination. A member carrying the
engagement OpenRouter key fails the whole assembly — `SecretKey` makes writing
the key into a file this crate GENERATES a compile error, but the members are
files other programs wrote and no type governs those, so every member's bytes
are scanned as they are copied. A symlink under `out/` or `extract/` fails it
too, because following one would read a file from outside the working directory
into an archive that leaves the recipient's network. The archive is built in a
sibling temporary file and renamed into place, so either refusal leaves no zip.

A sweep that audited nothing has no package. A partial sweep does, and it names
every repository it does not cover — in the returned value, the printed output,
`package.toml`, and a non-zero exit.

The boundary with #5481 is that this module signs nothing and hashes nothing.
Everything under `out/` is packaged verbatim, so #5481's signed manifest will
ride along with no change here; until it lands the generated README says the
package is unsigned rather than leaving the recipient to infer it.

`zip` and `walkdir` are new dependencies, both already in the workspace table.

* fix(trusty-audit): refuse a hardlinked package member, not only a symlink

Security review of #5698 found the symlink refusal does not stop a hardlink,
and the difference is a property of the filesystem rather than a gap in the
check. A hardlink is not a link TO anything — it is a second directory entry on
the same inode, equal in every way to the first. `is_symlink()` is false,
`is_file()` is true, and `canonicalize` returns the path it was given because
there is no other path to resolve to. Path containment cannot see it either:
the entry genuinely is inside the working directory, and so is its content,
which is also somewhere else. The link COUNT is the only thing that
distinguishes it, which is why `nlink() > 1` is the mechanism and not a
path-based check.

Both regression tests failed before this commit for the right reason — the
archive was produced and carried the outside file's 16 bytes as
`reports/00-acme-api/linked.key` and `extract/00-acme-api.db-wal`.

The false refusal this buys: a legitimate member that happens to carry more
than one link is refused even though its content is in scope. Nothing in this
crate's pipeline produces one, since a freshly created file has exactly one
link — `ordinary_audit_output_has_one_link_and_is_not_refused` asserts that for
the report, the manifest and the database. Reaching `nlink > 1` under `out/` or
`extract/` takes a deliberate `ln`, `cp -l`, or a hardlink-based backup tool
pointed into the working directory. For an archive built to be sent to someone
else, refusing is the right side to err on, and the remedy is to copy the file
instead of linking it.

`UnsafePackageEntry` gains a `kind` field rather than growing a second variant,
following `UnsafeArea`'s precedent — one refusal, two ways of detecting it.

Two smaller review points, both addressed:

- A failed `rename` left a COMPLETE archive at the `.part` path. Nothing landed
  at the destination either way, so it was tidiness — but a finished-looking
  zip beside the destination is exactly what a recipient might find and send,
  so it now cleans up like the fill-failure path.
- `WalkDir::follow_root_links` defaults to true, so a symlinked output root
  would have been followed even though nested symlinks are refused. Not
  reachable through this crate's own sweep, which creates that directory
  itself. Set to false explicitly rather than resting on the caller.

fix(trusty-audit): anchor a relative --work-dir to the caller's cwd (closes #5672) (#5692)

`run::spawn_tga` makes the work-dir root the child's working directory. Rust
resolves a relative program path against the CHILD's cwd, so `--work-dir w`
named `w/tools/tga` to a child already sitting in `w` and the spawn failed with
`os error 2`. The generated tga config, the output directory and the extract
database were wrong the same way, all for the same reason.

`WorkDir::resolve` now joins the chosen root onto the caller's cwd, which
returns an absolute choice unchanged. Every path handed to a child descends
from the root, so one anchor at the input boundary fixes all four. It joins
rather than calling `std::fs::canonicalize`: the root normally does not exist
yet — `WorkDir::create` makes it — and canonicalize fails on an absent path.

Nothing in the workspace cloned — #5215 records zero `Repository::clone`
production hits — so every entry in tga's `repositories[]` had to already be
a checkout a human made by hand. `trusty-audit clone <owner/name>...` is that
missing step.

credential `gh auth login` already resolved, through gh's git-credential
helper. Two facts make that the mechanism rather than one option: gh
configures the helper itself, so no token passes through this crate's hands
or its argv; and the workspace has no common entry point for spawning `git`,
so reaching for git directly would found a second process-spawning domain.
`gh` already has one — `trusty_common::gh::GhCommand` (#5475).

Fail-open guards, each with a test:

- A clone is built in a `.partial` sibling and renamed onto its destination
  only after gh exits zero, so "a directory under repos/ is a completed
  clone" is true by construction. A failed clone removes the partial and
  leaves nothing.
- A leftover partial from an interrupted run is discarded and refetched
  rather than resumed.
- `owner/name` is validated against an allowlist charset before it becomes a
  path, and the whole request is refused before any clone runs. This is what
  keeps `workdir`'s containment property intact.
- A `repos/` area that is a symlink is refused — the debt `workdir.rs:159`
  names for this issue.

Continue-on-failure per DOC-68 §14 Q2: one failure is a gap in the report and
the rest proceed; only every repository failing aborts. Disk use is shallow
by default, bounded at 20 GiB, and reported.

* fix(trusty-audit): close five review findings on clone acquisition (#5215)

A zero exit from `gh` was treated as proof of a usable checkout. A depth-1
fetch of a commitless repository exits zero leaving only `.git`, so the run
reported `Cloned`, counted it usable, and named no gap — an audit claiming
coverage of a repository nothing read. `verify_checkout` now runs before the
rename and demands a resolvable HEAD (loose ref, packed ref, or detached
SHA); a tree that fails becomes `CloneState::Empty` and a named gap, and
nothing is promoted.

Staging moved out of the repository namespace. `.` is a legal name character,
so the old `<dest>.partial` path was addressable by the legal repository
`acme/api.partial` — acquiring `acme/api` deleted its completed checkout and
then reported it `Cloned` at a path that no longer existed. Staging now lives
at `state/clone-staging/<owner>/<name>`, which no `repos/<owner>/<name>` can
address, so the collision is unrepresentable rather than unlikely.

The disk budget is a start gate, and now says so. It is checked between
repositories and nothing interrupts a clone in flight, so 19 GiB spent
against a 20 GiB budget still admits a 100 GB monorepo. Capping one clone
needs a watchdog that kills the child mid-fetch; that is not implemented, and
the doc comment, the CLI help, and the changelog no longer claim it is.

`--budget-gb` used a plain multiply that overflowed u64 above 2^34 — a panic
in debug, and in release a wrap to zero that skipped every repository and
ended in AllClonesFailed. Now saturating.

The symlink guard covered `repos/` only, and ran after `create`. A planted
`repos/acme -> /Users/victim/.ssh` was followed without complaint, and a
DANGLING `repos/` symlink had its target created by `create_dir_all` before
the guard ever ran, making UnsafeArea's "nothing was written" false. The
guard now runs first and covers the area, the owner directory, and the
destination.

Two judgment calls the review left open, both taken: a run with gaps exits 2
via `Outcome::exit_code` in the library, so `taudit clone … && taudit run`
does not chain into a sweep over an incomplete set; and `dir_size` reports
whether its walk completed, so an unreadable subtree renders as "at least X"
rather than a confident figure.

* refactor(trusty-common): one entry point for every gh invocation (#5475)

`gh` was spawned from 15 independent `Command::new("gh")` sites across four
crates, each re-deriving its own answer to the same four questions: what to do
when the binary is missing, when the user is not authenticated, when the exit
is non-zero, and where stderr goes. #5487 (repo discovery) and #5215 (clone)

`trusty_common::gh::GhCommand` (feature `gh-cli`) renders the argv, applies an

exit/stdout/stderr triple; a non-zero exit is returned, never raised, because
`gh pr checks` reports check state through its exit code.

`worktree_reclaim::gh_command` pass unchanged, and `gh_tools`' non-zero

* fix(trusty-common): correct the empty-token rationale and env call order (#5475)

Review findings on PR #5651.

The empty-output guard was justified by a mechanism that does not exist:
`gh auth token` exits 1, not 0, when no account is logged in (verified against
gh 2.89.0 under `env -i` with a throwaway HOME and GH_CONFIG_DIR, across all
four unauthenticated variants). The guard is still load-bearing, for a
different reason: `GH_TOKEN="   "` exits ZERO printing `"   \n"`, so a caller
checking only the exit status passes whitespace on as a credential. The
post-trim check is what catches that. Left as written, the doc would have told
the next implementer that exit status carries no signal for token reads.

`configure` applied all `env` calls and then all `env_remove` calls, so
`.env_remove("X").env("X", "v")` left X removed — the opposite of what the
chain reads as. One ordered `Vec<(OsString, Option<OsString>)>` now applies
both in call order. Not reachable from today's call sites; `worktree_reclaim`
already interleaves both in one chain, so the next migration would have hit it.

Also: deleted `stdout_blocking` and `gh_available_blocking` (no consumers —
the same objection `json()` survives by having one); restated `from_parts`'s
Why to its actual reason, that a downstream crate cannot struct-literal a
`#[non_exhaustive]` type in its tests; and named the argv-less builder
`GhCommand::bare()` so it stops reading as an oversight at the one call site
that wants a binary-and-environment carrier.
