* fix(trusty-mpm): ensure the tmux server is up before in-project name resolution (closes #3886)

On a host where tmux has never run, the socket directory exists but the
socket does not, so `tmux list-sessions` hard-errors. `tm`'s "launch new
session" died on it:

    Error: provisioning failed: name resolution failed for session <uuid>:
    tmux error: tmux error: protocol error: tmux list-sessions:
    error connecting to /private/tmp/tmux-501/default (No such file or directory)

The remedy already existed. #3823 added `TmuxDriver::ensure_server_up`
and made every caller responsible for invoking it before the first
`list-sessions` probe. `create_with_id` and `create_with_reserved_name`
honored that contract; the two in-project launch routes —
`spawn_managed_on_main` and `reserve_inproject_worktree` — did not. Both
call `SessionManager::resolve_session_name` directly, a bypass that is
itself deliberate (the name must be reserved before the worktree exists),
and neither added its own guard.

Rather than patch the two call sites, the guard moves INTO
`resolve_session_name`, adjacent to the `list-sessions` probe it
protects. A contract that two of four callers forgot is better expressed
as an invariant of the function that needs it than as an obligation on
everyone who calls it. `create_with_id`'s now-redundant call is dropped —
nothing between it and `resolve_session_name` touches tmux, so the
guarantee is unchanged and the call count stays at one.
`create_with_reserved_name` keeps its own guard: its first tmux call is
`dedupe_session_name`, which `resolve_session_name` never reaches.

The `list_sessions` stderr classifier is deliberately untouched. A
missing socket is a real condition `ensure_server_up` is meant to
RESOLVE, not something `list_sessions` should paper over as zero sessions.

Also fixes the doubled `tmux error:` prefix visible above.
`names_for_serial_allocation` and `dedupe_session_name` both did
`.map_err(|e| ManagedError::TmuxUnavailable(e.to_string()))` on a value
that is ALREADY a `ManagedError` — `ManagedTmuxDriver::list_sessions`
returns `Result<_, ManagedError>` — so `#[error("tmux error: {0}")]`
applied twice. Both now propagate with `?`.

`FakeTmuxDriver` grows two failure simulations: `cold_tmux_host`
reproduces #3886 exactly (`list_sessions` fails with the reported stderr
until `ensure_server_up` runs), and `list_sessions_should_fail` exercises
the un-doubled error rendering. Four of the five new tests fail against
this commit's parent.

fix(trusty-common): bound the concurrent indexing threads search_index spawns (#2798) (#5580)

* fix(trusty-common): bound the concurrent indexing threads search_index spawns

`index_files_best_effort` called `std::thread::spawn` once per write/edit tool
call with nothing capping how many threads could be alive at once. Against a
degraded but reachable trusty-search daemon a single file can occupy a thread
for ~6.2s (#2785's three attempts, each carrying a 2s client timeout), so a
burst of writes spawned threads faster than they drained.

Every batch now goes through one process-wide pool: 4 workers, a 64-slot
bounded queue. At saturation the batch is DROPPED — not blocked, not queued
without limit. Blocking would stall the agent task the fail-open contract
exists to protect; an unbounded queue would move unbounded growth from threads
to memory. The drop is observable: `BoundedDispatcher::rejected` counts it and
the caller logs at warn with the file count, project root, first path, and the
running process-wide drop total. A queued batch is not stale — each job reads
file content from disk when it runs.

A panicking job is caught so it cannot retire a worker; losing all four would
turn the bound into a permanent outage.

No public API change: `index_dispatch` is `pub(crate)` and
`index_files_best_effort`'s signature and non-blocking, fail-open contract are
unchanged.

* fix(trusty-search): stop the watcher orphaning chunks a capped write left behind (#100)

`index_file` raises its chunk-cap refusal AFTER committing whatever fit, so a
file that partly fits leaves chunks in the corpus and still returns `Err`.
`handle_modified` logged and returned without calling `indexed_files.record`,
so those chunks were untracked: a later delete found no `IndexedFiles` entry,
`handle_removed` returned early, and they stayed in the corpus, BM25 and HNSW
for the index's lifetime — with a later edit's stale-removal pass skipped the
same way, which also froze the file at its stale partial version because the
orphan kept occupying the index's last free slot.

The watcher now records the ids the corpus actually holds for the file, via a
new `CodeIndexer::chunk_ids_for_file`. Read from the corpus rather than from
the id set the file parsed into: when the two disagree, the corpus is what a
later removal has to act on, so this cannot leave a real chunk untracked. Error
paths that commit nothing return an empty set and record nothing. The two
removal paths in `files.rs` now share that scan instead of inlining it.

M001 discards `commit_parsed_batch`'s drop count. A chunk id embeds its chunk
type (`{file}::{chunk_type}::{name}::{start_line}`), and M001 visits only files
with zero `Constant` chunks, so every chunk it splits out is new to the corpus
and subject to the cap — nothing removes the wide `Code` chunk it came from
either. A legacy index near its cap could complete the migration having indexed
less than it claimed. The count is now summed and reported as a `warn!`, not an
error: failing would leave schema_version at 0 and re-run the whole pass at

fix(trusty-search): reconcile the watched tree when the OS drops filesystem events (#5582)

* fix(trusty-search): reconcile the watched tree when the OS drops events

When the kernel or user event queue overflows, `notify` reports the loss as
`Flag::Rescan` — "you missed some, re-scan". That signal never reached the
daemon. `notify-debouncer-mini`'s `DebouncedEvent` is `{path, kind}` and has no
field for the flag, so `add_event` destroys it: on macOS the one surviving path
names the DIRECTORY to rescan, which `handle_modified` discards at its
`is_dir()` guard; on Linux the event carries no path at all and the debouncer
records nothing. Nothing in the workspace read `need_rescan()`.

The result was silent data loss. The live index missed every change in the
dropped batch and a search over those files returned as though the edits had
never been made — indistinguishable from a correct answer.

Raw events are now tapped ahead of the debouncer by a `Watcher` wrapper, which
is the last point at which the flag still exists. A flagged event is tagged with
a sentinel path containing a NUL byte, so it survives the debouncer's path-keyed
map, inherits the 500ms coalescing, and cannot collide with any real file.

A rescan reconciles the full tree: `Flag::Rescan` means "assume any file may
have changed", so narrowing by mtime is rejected — `rsync --times`, `cp -p` and
`tar -x` all restore an old mtime and would miss exactly the writes this catches.
Every walked file is re-indexed in bounded batches, chunks for tracked files
absent from disk are dropped, and the symbol graph is rebuilt once.

Failures are not swallowed. A failed reconcile returns `RescanError`, is logged
at ERROR, and re-arms itself with backoff, so the loop never advances as though
the tree were back in sync. Files that could not be read are counted into
`RescanStats::files_unreadable` and reported at WARN rather than disappearing
into a debug line.

Verified against notify 6.1.1 / notify-debouncer-mini 0.4.1 in this workspace's
lockfile. `macos_kqueue` is off, so `RecommendedWatcher` is `FsEventWatcher`.

* fix(trusty-search): retry a rescan that skipped files, not just one that failed

A reconcile falls short two ways: it returns RescanError, or it returns Ok
having skipped files it could not read. The watch loop answered them
differently — the partial case cleared the consecutive-failure count and
scheduled nothing, so a transiently unreadable file was reindexed only if
some later event happened to touch it. That is the same silent staleness a
dropped Flag::Rescan produces, reached through this module's own error
handling instead of through the lost events, so it now gets the same answer.

rescan_follow_up is the single place that decides. Only a pass whose
RescanStats::is_complete() holds clears the counter; every other outcome
schedules a retry at the next backoff step. A permanently unreadable file
therefore re-walks the tree every RETRY_MAX forever, which is the cost this
module already accepts for a failed pass and for the same reason.

Extracting the decision is also what makes the re-arm testable. Only the
backoff arithmetic was covered before; rescan_partial_pass_schedules_a_retry_-
that_fires now drives a real reconcile over a tree with one unreadable file,
the real decision, the real scheduler, and the real channel, and asserts the
Rescan arrives. The unreadable file is invalid UTF-8 rather than chmod 000, so
the fixture does not depend on the test user not being root. Reaching through
spawn_watch_loop is not possible — its sender belongs to FileWatcher, so
injecting a Rescan needs the kernel overflow these tests cannot provoke.

* fix(trusty-search): refuse an over-budget index walk instead of truncating it

`create_index` accepted any `root_path`, and the only ceiling downstream was
`TRUSTY_MAX_CHUNKS`, which DROPS chunks past the cap and still emits
`complete`. Pointing an index at a 50 GB / 109k-file checkout therefore
produced a corpus missing the tail of the walk that reported success — and a
silently-partial index returns empty results a caller cannot tell from a
legitimate miss.

`service::index_budget::IndexBudget` checks the POST-FILTER walk (after
`.gitignore`, `SKIP_DIRS`, `extra_skip_dirs`, `exclude_globs`, `extensions`,
`path_filter`) against a file-count and total-byte ceiling in `run_reindex`,
before any staging corpus is opened, so a refusal leaves the existing index
byte-identical. The refusal marks the reindex `Failed`, emits a fatal SSE
frame, and sets `last_walk_error` — which `GET /indexes/:id/status` already
reports and `/health` already reads as degraded, so the truncation is visible
in the index's own state rather than only in a log line.

Defaults `TRUSTY_MAX_INDEX_FILES=50000` and `TRUSTY_MAX_INDEX_BYTES=2 GiB`;
either set to `0` disables that dimension. Behaviour change: a walk over
either ceiling now fails where it previously completed. The intended remedy is
to narrow the index (`exclude_globs`, `extra_skip_dirs`, `include_paths`,
`extensions` via `POST /indexes` or `PATCH /indexes/:id/config`) and the
refusal message names both that and the env override.

The `create_index` MCP tool also now forwards `exclude_globs`. `POST /indexes`
has accepted the field since the repo-config work, but the tool only ever sent
`id`, `root_path`, and `follow_links`, so an MCP caller had no way to narrow a
large tree at registration time.

* fix(ci): stop the stale-release guard from deleting what it cannot rebuild

#5571's "delete an asset-less release so softprops can recreate it"
strategy is destructive on this repo. Immutable Releases is enabled
repo-wide (every release object reports "immutable": true via the
API), and two GitHub-documented facts make delete-and-recreate
unrecoverable for any tag that was ever published:

  1. "Once you publish a release as immutable, its assets can't be
     added, modified, or deleted." (github.blog/changelog, 2025-10-28)
     — an asset-less immutable release cannot be repaired in place.
  2. "If you delete the immutable release, you can delete the tag,
     but you cannot reuse the same tag name." (GitHub Docs,
     code-security/concepts/supply-chain-security/immutable-releases)
     — deleting the release object to let softprops recreate it
     permanently forfeits the tag name.

Net effect: the guard turned a degraded (0-asset) release into no
release at all — exactly how trusty-installer-v0.5.0 reached its
current 404 state, reproduced empirically in the prior repair attempt
(fresh release object, all 6 assets uploaded, then
"tag_name was used by an immutable release" at finalize).

The guard now reads GitHub's own `.immutable` field off the release
object directly (the authoritative per-release signal) and never
deletes: a release with assets is left alone, a mutable asset-less
release is left for softprops's normal update path to fill in, and an
immutable asset-less release fails the job loudly, naming the only
real remedy (a new version) instead of destroying the release object.

See #5455, #5571.

fix(ci): clear a stale asset-less release before softprops runs (#5455) (#5571)

GitHub's Immutable Releases enforcement rejects any update to an
already-published release that touches target_commitish, and
softprops/action-gh-release@v2 submits it unconditionally on its
update-existing-release path (upstream: softprops/action-gh-release
issues #653, #641). Whenever a release object for a tag already
exists when this job runs, softprops's own GET finds it, tries to
reconcile fields via PATCH, and dies with "target_commitish cannot be
changed when release is immutable" before ever uploading assets.

This is exactly what happened to trusty-installer-v0.5.0: all three
build legs succeeded and produced valid tarballs, but the release was
left with zero assets because the publish step failed first (run
30961682562), breaking install.sh for every new user with a 404 on
the checksum download.

Add a step that deletes the release object (never the tag) when a
release already exists for the tag and currently has zero assets
attached, so softprops's normal create -> upload -> publish path runs
on a clean slate. A release that already carries real assets is left
untouched.

perf(trusty-search): wake the reindex RSS pollers on shutdown instead of waiting out their tick (#5047) (#5578)

* perf(trusty-search): wake the reindex RSS pollers on shutdown instead of waiting out their tick

`stop_pollers` cost 584-952ms on every reindex teardown, from two waits that
compounded. Both pollers tested their stop `AtomicBool` only at the top of their
loop, so a poller parked in `Interval::tick()` could not see the flag until the
tick expired (1s daemon, 500ms sidecar). `stop_pollers` then made it worse by not
signalling the sidecar poller until the daemon poller had already joined, so the
two waits ran back to back rather than together.

The pollers now park on `PollerStop::sleep_until_next_sample`, which selects over
the tick and a shutdown `Notify`, and `stop_pollers` signals both pollers before
awaiting either. The sampling cadence is unchanged — this is a wakeup, not a
shorter interval.

Nothing is skipped. The pollers already did no work between the flag being set
and their exit: they re-check the flag at the top of the loop and break before
sampling. `finish_reindex` takes its own synchronous post-teardown RSS sample for
both peaks, before and after. The flag remains the source of truth, so a lost
wakeup degrades to the old wait-out-the-tick behaviour rather than to a poller
that never exits.

Measured with `stop_pollers_returns_without_waiting_out_the_tick`, both pollers
running at production cadence:

  before: 1400, 1401, 1399, 1399, 1401 ms
  after:  969, 231, 542, 144, 161 us

Reverting either half of the fix takes that test back to 1401ms against its 250ms
ceiling, and fails three of the other four alongside it.

fix(trusty-search): surface an index frozen mid-walk with no reindex driving it (#5575)

* fix(trusty-search): surface an index frozen mid-walk with no reindex driving it

`reset_stages_for_reindex` flips `stages.lexical` to `InProgress` and the runner
stamps `last_walk_started_at`. If the reindex task then panics or is cancelled,
`ReindexTerminationGuard` marks the `ReindexProgress` `Failed` and emits an SSE
error but never touches the stage, so the handle claims `"walking"` for the rest
of the daemon's life. Nothing completes it, nothing retries it, and it reads —
on `/health`, on `/indexes/:id/status`, and to every caller of
`search_capabilities` — exactly like a genuine multi-minute reindex.

#4680's `index_is_stuck_unwalked` cannot see it: that predicate requires
`last_walk_started_at` to be `None`, and this walk stamped it.

`index_is_stuck_mid_walk` adds the liveness signal the stage surface lacks — the
index's own mutual-exclusion permit, which `run_reindex` acquires before it
flips the stage and holds until the task returns, so a panic or cancellation
releases it while leaving the stage frozen. `SearchAppState::reindex_progress`
could not serve as that signal: `reconcile::trigger_full_reindex` and
`components::spawn_component_catch_up` never insert into it, so a boot-reconcile
reindex is in flight with no entry there and every such index would have been
reported stuck.

Reported as `indexes_stuck_mid_walk` on `GET /health` (forcing
`status: "degraded"`) and `stuck_mid_walk` on `GET /indexes/:id/status`. The two
stuck predicates partition the `InProgress` lexical lane on `walk_started`, so
an index is counted by at most one.

Detection only. Nothing retries or rewrites the stage: a partial walk may have
committed chunks, and re-driving on a per-poll signal would loop against
whatever killed the first walk. An operator clears it with
`POST /indexes/:id/reindex`.

The pre-existing `health_does_not_flag_a_walked_index_as_stuck` fixture claimed
to represent an in-flight walk while holding no permit — it was an abandoned
walk. It now holds the permit, so it matches its own claim.

test(trusty-search): watcher tests wait on their condition, not on a fixed sleep (#5572)

The six filesystem-watcher tests slept 100-150ms for the OS watch to install,
saved once, then polled a 2-3s deadline. A save lost anywhere in that window is
never redelivered, so the race ends as a hang and a red test.

Losing it is real on macOS. When FSEvents overflows its kernel or user event
queue under heavy filesystem load, it reports the loss by setting
MustScanSubDirs on an event whose path is a DIRECTORY to rescan rather than the
file that changed. notify turns that into EventKind::Other carrying
Flag::Rescan plus that directory path (fsevent.rs callback_impl calls add_path
on every translated event, Rescan included); notify-debouncer-mini's
DebouncedEvent keeps only path and kind, so the flag is discarded; and
FileWatcher sees an ordinary Modified(<directory>), which handle_modified drops
at its is_dir() guard. The file's save is never learned.

Each test now re-applies its save once per debounce window and polls until the
condition holds, via the new service::watch_test_support. There are no fixed
sleeps and no deadline tuned against the 500ms debounce window. Negative
assertions get stronger, not weaker: cdk_out_file_is_not_indexed keeps feeding
the excluded path through a bounded window instead of writing it once and
sleeping 300ms.

The earlier candidate mechanism recorded on #4731 — a save landing before OS
watch registration finishes — does not apply: notify 6.1.1's FSEvents backend
does not return from watch() until after FSEventStreamStart. Zeroing the
startup sleeps left the cluster 25/25 green, which is what ruled it out.

Not reproduced on this host: 148 cluster runs (25 isolated, 48 under 24 CPU
spinners at concurrency 6, 72 under 96 spinners at concurrency 12) and 3
full --lib runs under load, all green. The hardening stands on the mechanism
above rather than on a red run.

`tm ls -a` / `--attached` keeps only the sessions a tmux client is
connected to right now, dropping the ones that are merely running.

"Attached" is tmux's own `#{session_attached}`, surfaced by the daemon as
the per-session `attached` flag that the picker and the sort grouping
already read. It is not the lifecycle `state` word: a session whose tmux
entity is live with nobody looking at it reports `active` with
`attached == false`, and `-a` excludes it. That exclusion is the feature —
without it `-a` would be a second spelling of the default listing.

`-a` forces the static table for the same reason `--all` does: a session
you already have a client on is the one target the picker's connect action
cannot do anything with. Matching nothing prints `no attached sessions`
and exits 0, so an empty result reads as an answer rather than a failure.
No effect on `--json` (raw daemon passthrough stays complete, matching
`--all` and the filter terms) or on `--projects`; `tm sessions ls` and
`tm f` pass `false` and are unchanged.

* fix(trusty-search): the teardown gate was defeatable by a named future; widen its scope rule

Round-4 review defeated the gate with idiomatic Rust:

    let fut = async move { idx.commit_parsed_batch(...).await };
    tokio::spawn(fut);

The write shares neither a line nor a brace with the spawn, and the async block
opens and closes on one line so its net brace delta is zero — the scope stack
never saw it. The gate attributed the write to the enclosing function's guard,
which is dropped the moment that function returns, and reported OK, exit 0. That

deferred body is a spawn call, an async block, or a closure — not just a spawn

opener on its own line is inside that body whether or not the brace balance ever
revealed it. The second is what catches the one-line case.

* fix(trusty-common): list_palaces no longer reports an unstattable registry as empty

`PalaceStore::list_palaces` guarded absence with `Path::exists`, which is
`fs::metadata(..).is_ok()` and coerces every stat failure to `false`. A
registry directory we were merely forbidden to stat therefore returned
`Ok(vec![])` without ever reaching `read_dir`, so the error propagation added
by #5488 and #5526 could not run and the destructive callers — `purge_palaces`,
`rebuild_palaces`, `merge_palaces` — reported a clean zero-palace run over data
they never read.

The guard now uses `try_exists`, which keeps "absent" (`Ok(false)`) distinct
from "cannot determine" (`Err`). A data root that does not exist yet, one whose
parent directories are missing, and a broken symlink all still yield an empty
list, so first run is unchanged.

The TCC premise behind #5488/#5526 is refuted, and this fix does not rest on
it. Measured on macOS 26.5.2 against real TCC-protected directories
(~/Library/Safari, ~/Library/Mail, /Library/Application Support/com.apple.TCC),
TCC permits `stat` — `metadata()` returns Ok and `exists()` returns true — and
denies only enumeration, with `read_dir` returning EPERM(1). Those paths are
mode 755 and owned by the running uid, so POSIX permits them and the denial is
TCC's. Under a TCC denial `read_dir` is always reached and the #5488/#5526
propagation fires as designed. The reachable trigger for this guard is instead
POSIX EACCES(13) from an unsearchable parent, which the new test reproduces
directly.

The new test strips a parent of the registry directory to mode 000 so the
failure lands on `stat` rather than `read_dir` — the arm the existing
regular-file/ENOTDIR harnesses cannot reach, since a regular file stats fine
and only fails once enumeration starts. It verifies the denial actually took
hold before asserting, so it cannot pass vacuously as root, and restores the
mode from a `Drop` guard so a panicking assertion cannot strand an undeletable
temp directory.

* fix(trusty-search): carry contributed graphs across the reindex corpus swap

A reindex opened a fresh staging corpus, seeded it with four tables, and
renamed it over the live file. `kg_contrib` was never among those four, so
every contributed graph was destroyed by the promotion while the run reported

indistinguishable from "nothing was ever contributed" — not an error path, so
no reporting layer could see it. ADR-0009 requires the opposite: contributed
data survives restart and reindex by construction.

`CorpusStore::copy_contrib_from` carries the overlay into staging before any
batch writes, and `begin_staged_corpus_swap` calls it on both the force and
incremental paths. `copy_all_from`'s doc comment claimed all KG tables are
rebuilt at the end of every reindex; it now distinguishes the derived tables

* fix(trusty-search): persist boot-integrity markers so an incomplete index is detectable

Both defects are the same shape: the daemon could not tell an index was
incompletely built, so it served partial results as if complete.

#4391 is the detection side. `indexed_head_sha` lived only in
`IndexHandle`, and both restore paths re-derived it from live git, so
`reconcile_git_path` compared current HEAD against current HEAD and
reported `up_to_date` for every git-backed index on every boot. Commits
landing while the daemon was down were structurally undetectable, and
`results_may_be_stale` stayed false. It is now a `PersistedIndex` field,
written wherever the in-memory stamp is written and read at restore. A
legacy entry with no stamp adopts live HEAD once and backfills it, so an
upgrade does not re-walk a whole fleet.

#4390 is the completeness side. A deferred-embed (C2) pass builds every
embedding in memory and commits once at the end, so a stop anywhere
inside it — crash, upgrade, or a clean `trusty-search stop` — persists
zero vectors, and nothing recorded that. `deferred_embed_pending` is set
before the pass is queued and cleared when it commits; restore re-arms
the catch-up for any index still carrying it, through the same
size-ordered queue so re-arms serialise behind the one background permit.

The two write directions are deliberately asymmetric: a lost SET costs
only the new detection, a lost CLEAR costs one idempotent gap-filling
pass. No write failure can produce a silently under-embedded index.

doc comment already claimed.

* docs(trusty-search): record the corruption redb reports as UpgradeRequired

The module docs claimed `UpgradeRequired` "says nothing is wrong with the
bytes". That is not quite true, and the exception is the one gap left in this
PR's classification split.

`TransactionHeader::from_bytes` (redb 4.1.0, `page_store/header.rs:323-335`)
reads the version byte and returns `UpgradeRequired(version)` for values 1 and 2
before it computes that slot's xxh3 checksum a few lines further down. The
version byte sits at offset 0 of each transaction slot, and the two slots are at
fixed absolute offsets 64 and 192. So a single-byte corruption landing on offset
64 or 192 that leaves the value 1 or 2 produces `UpgradeRequired`, not
`Corrupted` — the checksum that would have caught it is never reached, and that
case is silently recreated empty rather than quarantined.

`is_genuine_corpus_corruption` returns `false` there because that is what redb
reports; nothing at the `DatabaseError` level distinguishes the two. Closing it
would mean re-parsing the header and re-verifying redb's checksums independently
of `DatabaseError`, which is out of scope here. Documented rather than fixed.

with 400 naming the new format rather than a 404 that would read as
"already deleted". MemoryService::kg_retract_triple takes the object and
returns the closed count instead of bool, and rebuilds the prompt cache
on a hot predicate so a retracted Tier S fact stops being injected.

Ids are derived from the fields, never persisted or returned by any
endpoint, and the KG Explorer UI does not call this route — a caller
rebuilds an id by adding the object.

feat(trusty-audit): scaffold the auditor client — headless library + thin CLI (#5509)

* feat(trusty-audit): scaffold the auditor client — headless library + thin CLI

New workspace crate. The auditor client is handed to a client company to run
an audit on their own codebases; the owner's framing is that it is really an
installer runner. This is scaffold only: the crate exists, is wired into the
workspace, and carries the skeleton for dependency downloads and repo
selection. No audit run, no zip assembly, no signing, no GUI.

Two owner constraints shape the design, both permanent:

Headless first — a library with a thin CLI over it. The Tauri shell is a later
milestone and will be a view over this API.

Every feature must be CLI-testable, forever. That is enforced by the code
rather than by review: `session::Command` is the capability set,
`Session::execute` is the only way to run one, and `cli.rs` matches
exhaustively over `Command`, so a capability with no CLI invocation does not
compile. `main.rs` is a 20-line shim with no branch of its own.

A bare invocation enters the guided flow, which walks the pre-run steps in the
epic's order (repository selection, then tooling) rather than starting an
unattended sweep. Every capability also has its own subcommand.

The working directory is designed now rather than retrofitted: one root holding
tools/, repos/, extract/, state/, out/ and logs/. Nothing is written outside
it, which is what makes `rm -rf <root>` a complete uninstall — a tested
property, not a claim. It holds the recipient's cloned source, so the README
states what lands where. Three open questions are recorded, not resolved:
where the root should live, whether two runs may share one, and whether a
`clean` verb should exist.

The engagement config carries a spend-capped OpenRouter key; the deliverable
that comes back carries none. `config::SecretKey` implements `Deserialize` and
deliberately not `Serialize`, so writing the key into an output artifact is a
compile error; `Debug` and `Display` both redact.

`tools::install` is a seam, not an implementation — it returns an error citing
#5491 rather than falling back to anything. Downloading belongs to
trusty-installer, and a second implementation here would be a defect under
CLAUDE.md's common-entry-point rule.

The binary name `taudit` is a PLACEHOLDER; no CLAUDE.md alias row is added
because nobody has chosen a name yet.

docs(trusty-mpm): tm-workflow rule for keeping the main checkout fresh (#5533)

Worktrees branch off origin/main and stay current, but nothing refreshes the
main checkout, so it drifts. Measured this session: the checkout sat 61 commits
behind while origin/main moved. Every inspection read — git log, opening a file
to answer a question, checking whether a fix already landed — then silently
answers from old code.

The rule is git fetch + git pull --ff-only at session start and after a PR this
session merged lands. Fast-forward only cannot create a merge commit or rewrite
history, and fails loudly rather than resolving anything silently.

The failure branch is the part that makes it usable. When another session's
uncommitted work blocks the fast-forward, the rule is preserve rather than
discard: commit the orphaned work to a throwaway branch, switch back, then
fast-forward. That reaches the same clean tree as discarding, costs the same
number of steps, and cannot lose anything. git stash stays banned because the
stash is repo-level and shared across every worktree; git checkout --, restore,
reset --hard and clean stay banned because the main-checkout guard blocks them
and hunting for an unblocked equivalent is routing around a safety control.

Stated as inspection hygiene only — the main checkout stays read-only for work,
every edit still happens in a worktree, and git pull is already on the PM's
allowlist so this needs no new authority.

* feat(tga,trusty-review): make the audit report's inference required

`tga audit` invoked `trusty-review report --manifest <m> --analyze --out
<dir>` and never passed `--synthesize`, so `model.synthesis` was `None` on
every audit that has ever run and every audit report to date was fully
deterministic. This wires inference in and removes the fallbacks that let a
run ship without it.

tga passes `--synthesize`, and trusty-review makes synthesis unconditional —
both, because tga resolves trusty-review from PATH rather than a Cargo edge,
so the installed copy may predate this change and the flag is the only thing
that turns inference on there.

Every fail-closed site is now a hard error: provider failure, timeout,
unparseable and still-truncated responses, a wholly guardrail-rejected
response, and a provider that will not build. `Synthesizer::synthesize`
returns `Result<Synthesis, SynthesisError>`, and `SynthesisStatus` is gone so
the type cannot represent a failed pass. `Reporter::write` refuses a model
carrying no synthesis.

A missing credential fails before stage 1 of the sweep rather than after it —
DOC-67 gives the run one non-interactive shot, and an unset key was knowable
up front. A provider failure mid-run still leaves `manifest.toml` intact and
names the exact command to re-run just the render.

#5374's deterministic §2 composition is kept: the numeric guardrail can still
reject the written summary on its own, and that is when §2 would otherwise go
empty again.

Closes #5454

* fix(tga): stop treating the renderer's exit 0 as proof of a synthesis pass

`ReviewRun::success` is `output.status.success()` and nothing more, so the
`if !run.success` check in `render_report` never fired for the one arm that
matters: a pre-0.15 `trusty-review` accepts `--synthesize`, degrades to
`Synthesis::unavailable(reason)` on any provider failure, writes the
deterministic-only report anyway, and exits 0. tga reported a fully successful
audit while delivering the exact narrative-free report #5454 exists to abolish.
tga resolves the renderer from PATH, not a Cargo edge, so a new tga beside an
old renderer is an ordinary pairing rather than an exotic one.

Two guards, at the two moments that matter.

`require_review_supports_required_inference` runs `trusty-review --version`
before stage 1 and rejects anything below 0.15.0. DOC-67 §2 gives the sweep one
non-interactive shot, and this is the second whole-run precondition knowable up
front, alongside the credential the same run already checks there. A binary that
cannot be spawned, exits non-zero, or prints an unparseable version is allowed
through deliberately — the not-installed case has a better-worded error at the
render step, and the second guard catches the rest.

`require_rendered_report_carries_synthesis` reads the `.json` twin the renderer
printed and requires its `synthesis` object to carry a non-blank executive
summary, a top-risk row, or finding prose. That is the invariant 0.15 guarantees
(a pass with nothing left is `SynthesisError::NoVerifiableContent`, which fails
the render), so it holds against any version — including one that reports 0.15
and degrades anyway, which the version check alone cannot catch. A report that
cannot be read fails rather than passes; passing on "I could not look" would
reopen the hole.

Both messages name the remedy — that the installed renderer predates #5454 and
must be upgraded — rather than only the symptom.

fix(trusty-search): index_file honours skip_vector and skip_kg (#3048) (#5506)

* fix(trusty-search): index_file honours skip_vector and skip_kg

`CodeIndexer::index_file` is the choke point every incremental write funnels
through — the file watcher, the boot-time reconciler, and
`POST /indexes/:id/index-file`. It called `embed_chunks_in_batches`
unconditionally and ended with an unconditional `rebuild_symbol_graph`, so an
index configured BM25-only kept paying the embedder on every file save and kept
building and persisting a symbol graph, while its own `/health` reported both
stages `Skipped`. The batch reindex path has routed `skip_vector` through
`parse_files_only` since #2984 Phase 1 and has skipped KG construction since
#313; this path never caught up.

`skip_vector` now mirrors onto `CodeIndexer` itself, as `skip_kg` already did.
Reading `IndexHandle::skip_vector` at the call site does not work: the watch
loop holds only an `Arc<RwLock<CodeIndexer>>` and never sees a handle, and
`IndexHandle` is rebuilt on every `PATCH /indexes/:id/config`, so any snapshot a
long-lived task took is permanently stale. The `indexer` `Arc` is preserved
verbatim across those rebuilds, which makes it the one place all three callers
read a current value. `apply_component_transition` syncs it on every vector
turn-on and turn-off, so a `PATCH { "vector": false }` stops the watcher
embedding immediately rather than at the next daemon restart.

The skip_kg gate sits at the `index_file` call site, not inside
`rebuild_symbol_graph`, which is shared with reindex, `remove_file`, and
contributed-graph ingest — their skip_kg semantics are not this change's to
alter.

Both gates ship with a control test asserting the enabled case still embeds and
still builds a graph, so the pair proves the flag decides rather than the code
path.

Closes #3048

* fix(ci): SemVer gate must not read zero executed checks as a pass

cargo-semver-checks skips its entire lint set when the baseline -> current
delta already permits breakage, and says so at exit 0:

    Checked [   0.000s] 0 checks: 0 pass, 254 skip
    Summary no semver update required

check_semver.sh keyed `verdict_computed` on that summary line EXISTING, so it
read "254 lints declined" as "254 lints satisfied". preflight-publish.sh
CHECK 5 then passed having verified nothing. Measured on trusty-common under
rustc 1.94.1. The gate failed closed on that machine only because a newer
installed toolchain crashed rustdoc instead, producing no summary at all —
remove that toolchain and the gate silently approves every publish.

verdict_computed now parses the leading `N checks:` count and requires it to be
at least 1; a zero or unparsable count is NO VERDICT (exit 3), the same status
a rustdoc failure already gets. The two causes get different messages, because
"it never ran" and "it ran and skipped every lint" have different remedies.

The fixture that drove the self-test's "clean" case was itself this shape —
`0 checks: 0 pass, 254 skip` — so it is renamed to all-skipped.out and now
drives the two new regression cases, and clean.out is a real 196-pass capture.

* fix(trusty-memory): bound the noun-phrase walk to its own line and resolve inflections (#5399)

Review of the head-noun walk found two ways it over-collects past the true
head, and `phrase_head` takes the rightmost token it collected.

Neither was caught because every fixture in the eval set passes a SINGLE LINE,
and `examples/kg_dump.rs` read one line per extraction. Production does not:
`auto_extract_and_assert` and `kg_rebuild::rebuild_one` both hand the extractor
a whole multi-line drawer body. The corpus figure behind the parent commit is
line-scoped and characterises none of this. `kg_dump` grows a `--whole-file`
mode so the harness can measure the shape production actually uses.

The walk had no newline boundary, so `left` and `right` spanned the entire
body and the run crossed a line break: `trusty-search is a daemon\ncargo builds
it` asserted `trusty-search --is-a--> builds`. That is a correct-to-wrong
regression — the pre-#5399 one-token path read `daemon` here. Only a trailing
period saved the terminated variant. Both sides now clip to the marker's line.
The consequence is worse than a bad triple: the KG keeps one ACTIVE triple per
(subject, predicate), so a rebuild REWRITES rather than accumulates, and a
regressed walk supersedes a correct stored object with no signal.
`rebuild_does_not_supersede_a_good_object_from_a_later_line` covers that at the
persistence level.

WordNet indexes base forms, so participles read as unknown, and #5399 made
unknown mean "eligible to head a phrase" — every participle became a candidate
head and won by sitting rightmost. `Each skill is a directory containing:`
asserted `containing`. `WordNetPos::mask` now retries a regular -s/-es/-ies/
-ing/-ed inflection against its base form, so `containing` resolves to the verb
`contain` and the phrase ends before it. Refusing unknown tokens outright would
have taken `parsers` with it; the suffix retry is what separates them, and
`parsers` stays a valid head. A suffix table, not a stemmer: a wrong stem
simply misses and falls back to the unknown behaviour that already existed.

Two smaller rules follow. An unknown token may OPEN a phrase but never joins
one that already has a head, so a file path cannot displace the real noun. And
`inside`/`outside` join the closed-class preposition list — WordNet records
both as nouns, so they passed the POS check and continued a phrase they close.

Not fixed, and measured rather than assumed: a gerund WordNet lists as a noun
in its own right still takes the head (`daemon running` -> `running`,
`estimate clearing a budget` -> `clearing`). No retry fires, because the direct
probe hits. Stopping the run at any -ing word whose base is a verb would fix
those two; over this repo's 1,276 markdown files it repairs ~25 participles and
breaks ~18 legitimate heads (`mapping` -> `field`, `warning` -> `error`, plus

not lexical membership, so it needs a tagger.

fires on every minor bump of a 0.y.z crate, so the releases most likely to

`execve` is refused with ETXTBSY while any process holds a writable fd to
the target inode. A sibling test thread that forks between this process's
write and close of a freshly created executable hands its child an
inherited copy of that fd, so an otherwise valid exec fails — the race
that made `probe_alternate_screen_reads_back_off` and its `tmux`
fake-binary siblings flaky in CI.

5 ms back-off doubling each time, and only for ETXTBSY. ETXTBSY can only

third attempt. Same fix #1634 and #3570 settled on in trusty-agents and
trusty-common.

fix(ci): diff the changelog gate against the live base branch, not a pinned base.sha (#5413)

The per-PR changelog-fragment gate failed PR #5018 for trusty-analyze,
trusty-git-analytics and trusty-review — three crates that PR does not touch.

Its workflow passed CHANGELOG_GATE_BASE=github.event.pull_request.base.sha, a
snapshot frozen when the PR event fired, while actions/checkout resolves a
pull_request event to refs/pull/N/merge, whose FIRST parent is the base
branch's current tip. The stale SHA is an ancestor of that merge ref, so
git merge-base hands it straight back instead of finding a fork point, and the
diff spans every commit main took in between — 1279 paths across 16 crates for
a 9-path, 1-crate PR. A release inside that window folds a crate's fragments
into CHANGELOG.md and deletes changelog.d/*.md; the gate excludes deletions
from evidence, so release-time CONSUMPTION reads as this PR's OMISSION.

Pass the base BRANCH instead, re-fetched right before diffing, so the merge
base is the merge ref's own first parent. Same failure and same fix as #4688
(check-pr-version-bump.sh) and #4960 (detect-docs-only.sh); this gate was the
last one still pinned to base.sha.

The script also refuses a bare-SHA base that lags HEAD's base parent under a
merge ref, so a future workflow edit reintroducing base.sha fails loudly
naming the base rather than silently blaming untouched crates. Comparing
(BASE, HEAD) cannot distinguish a stale base from a correct one — both are
ancestors of HEAD — so the guard rejects the one provable shape and is scoped
by four conditions to leave every legitimate caller untouched.

scripts/check_changelog_base_selftest.sh replays the shape on a synthetic repo
and pins all five behaviours, including the true positive.

perf(ci): shard the Test job four ways with nextest, and stop PRs evicting the cargo cache (#5366)

Test was the critical path of every CI run at 16-24 minutes. Measured over
seven recent runs, step-level:

  build (cargo test --no-run)   466-472s warm / 704-827s cold
  test execution (cargo test)   416-454s, near-constant
  everything else               ~50s

Run the tests under cargo-nextest, split four ways by `--partition hash:N/4`.
`cargo test` runs the ~220 test binaries one after another and parallelises
only WITHIN a binary, so it drains a tail of idle cores ~220 times; nextest
schedules from one global queue, and the partition splits that queue across
four runners.

Partition rather than crate group. Splitting by crate (`-p a -p b` per shard)
would cut the build too, and was the first version of this change. It silently
loses coverage: cargo resolves features across the packages in ONE invocation,
so a shard building a subset resolves a subset of features. Measured — a shard
holding trusty-common plus its six nearest neighbours saw 24 of the 37
trusty-common features `--workspace` resolves, dropping embedder, memory-core,
bm25 and migrations, and listed 1340 trusty-common tests where the workspace
run executes 2099. Four green shards, 759 tests not run, nothing saying so.
`--partition` splits the test list of an unchanged `--workspace` build, so
feature resolution is byte-identical to before and every test lands in exactly
one shard by construction.

Doctests are not part of what nextest runs — it has no doctest harness — so
`cargo test --doc` runs them in shard 1 rather than letting them silently stop.

Save the cargo cache only from main. GitHub scopes a cache saved on a PR ref to
that PR alone but counts it against the repo-wide 10 GB quota; the repo was at
11.03 GB with four byte-identical 1.29 GB copies of this job's cache, one per
open PR, none readable by any other PR, which had evicted the refs/heads/main
copy every PR restores from. That eviction is the cold column above: ~half of
all Test runs recompiled the whole 864-crate dependency graph. All four shards
now share one cache key, since they run the same build.

The #4402 comment claiming nextest was blocked by a trusty-memory test-order
bug was stale in its specifics: #4413 fixed THAT coupling at its root in
2026-07. A second one remains — 17 trusty-memory tests rely on a sibling test
in the same process having called `seed_shared_embedder_with_mock()`, and under
process-per-test they fall through to a real HuggingFace download. A local
nextest run does not catch it (the download succeeds on a developer machine);
CI does, with HTTP 429. Those tests must establish their own precondition
before this lands. .github/scripts/attribute_test_failures.py is deleted: nextest
names the owning crate for every test, which is what it reconstructed from
panic source paths.

Branch protection needs no edit. The required check is the literal context
"Test"; the new aggregate job keeps that name and fails unless every shard
reports success.

Two verified defects in the harness, plus the CI wiring that would have
caught both. Neither bug was reachable by review alone; both were latent
because the harness's four test scripts and its one mechanical invariant
ran nowhere — `grep -rn "vmtest" .github/` returned zero.

#5014 — `local x=$(f)` is not exempt

`check-no-swallowed-die.sh:248` exempted both `x=$(f)` and `local x=$(f)`
from its argument-position finding. The bare form is correct: it propagates
the child status to `set -e`. The `local` form is not, and the driver
already says so at `vmtest:28-29` — `local` is itself a command, so its own
status (always 0) is the one the shell sees and the child's is lost.
Verified on the documented target, /bin/bash 3.2.57: `x=$(f)` yields rc 60,
`local x=$(f)` yields rc 0 and continues past the fatal.

That matters more than "the run continues past a die". The side channel
records the classification but does not restore control flow, and `on_exit`
(`vmtest:659`) exits with `$rc`, not `VMTEST_EXIT` — so a failed install run
exits 0 with a MEASURE line contradicting its own exit status. `vmtest:649-657`
records that a runtime exit-code override was tried, reverted, and declined
*because this static guard covers it*. The guard is a load-bearing
precondition of the exit-code contract, not a lint.

Deletes `(local[ \t]+)?` from the regex and corrects the comment, which had
claimed both forms propagate. Currently latent: every real call site already
follows declare-first/assign-second, so the narrowed guard stays green on the
clean tree with zero call sites to repair and zero new false positives.

The selftest gains a `local`-form case (10 -> 11), because the guard's green
was not evidence of coverage without one. Confirmed load-bearing: restoring
the old regex makes that case pass the mutation, exit 0.

#5015 — the tool-name invariant was red on main

`lib/vm.sh:3` declares that file the only one in the harness that may contain
the virtualisation tool's name, so a second backend can be swapped in
(DOC-1 §12.2). The check listed two files: `lib/verify.sh:1442` named the tool
inside a prose comment, 1,429 lines after that file's own warning at :13-15
that the grep "matches COMMENTS as readily as code". A regression, not an
accepted exception — `MANIFEST.md:1913-1919` records the check green at
`f181a44e`. Reworded to name the tool by description.

CI wiring

New `.github/workflows/vmtest-harness.yml`, one lightweight job modelled on
`line-cap.yml`, path-filtered to `vmtest-harness/**` and the workflow file.
It runs the guard selftest, the guard, `subshell-classification.sh`,
`test-preflight-single-run.sh`, and the invariant grep as its own failing
step. Selftest before gate, matching line-cap.yml's ordering.

Every script is host-only: no VM is created and no network is touched.
`subshell-classification.sh` sources the driver through `--source-only`;
`test-preflight-single-run.sh` puts a stub for the virtualisation CLI on PATH

test(trusty-memory): each test seeds its own mock embedder (#5378)

* test(trusty-memory): each test seeds its own mock embedder

Under `cargo test` every test in a binary shares one process, so the
`retrieval::shared_embedder()` OnceCell was set once — by whichever sibling
got there first — and satisfied every other test for free. Under nextest's
process-per-test isolation each test gets a virgin cell instead, reaches for
the real ONNX model, and fails on the HuggingFace download:

    Caused by:
        0: acquire shared embedder for remember
        1: init shared FastEmbedder
        2: failed to initialise fastembed (tried AllMiniLML6V2 and AllMiniLML6V2Q)
        4: request error: http status: 429

Not an assertion failure — HuggingFace rate-limiting a download that a unit
test should never perform. Same defect class as #4413, which fixed the
palace-enforcement env var the same way.

Every test that embeds now establishes the precondition itself, by calling
`seed_shared_embedder_with_mock()` — in the shared fixture where the tests
use one (`tools::tests::test_state` / `test_state_warming`,
`web::tests::test_state`, `messaging::tests::fresh_palace`,
`prompt_context::tests::spin_up_test_daemon_with_palace`,
`mcp_stdio_tools`'s `Fixture::new` / `seed_palace`), and inline in the eight
tests that build `AppState` directly. The call is idempotent (`OnceCell::set`,
first caller wins), so order does not matter.

CI run 31438217228 shard 1 reported 17 such failures. That is the subset that
lost the HuggingFace lottery on that run, not the population: the model is
cached on disk after the first successful download, so which tests 429 varies
run to run. The real population is 64 — measured, not assumed, by making the
embedder deterministically unavailable
(`TRUSTY_EMBEDDER_INIT_TIMEOUT_SECS=0`) so every test that reaches
`FastEmbedder::new()` fails rather than only the unlucky ones. Fixing only the
reported 17 would have left the next nextest run red on a different subset.

Measured with that probe, per-test process isolation, before and after:

    before:  719 tests run: 655 passed, 64 failed, 21 skipped
    after:   719 tests run: 719 passed (2 leaky),  21 skipped

so the suite no longer needs a model download at all. It also passes with the
embedder available, both isolated and shared-process:

    cargo nextest run -p trusty-memory   719 passed, 21 skipped
    cargo test -p trusty-memory          629 passed; 0 failed; 4 ignored (lib)

`remember_succeeds_and_defers_embedding_while_state_is_warming` documented the
coupling as a deliberate choice: it skipped the seed so as not to race
`dispatch_remember_then_recall`'s use of the real embedder. But the cell is
process-wide and first-writer-wins, so that made it depend on whichever
sibling initialised the cell, and under isolation its `shared_embedder()` call
failed outright. It now uses the mock — a deterministic hash, so the
backfilled vector and the query vector match exactly — and
`dispatch_remember_then_recall` passes on the mock as well. Its doc comment
now says that rather than the opposite.

fix(trusty-mpm): detect, disclose, and repair a corrupt session store (#5027)

* fix(trusty-mpm): detect, disclose, and repair a corrupt session store

`SessionStore::upsert` reloads before every save, so a `sessions.json` the
daemon cannot read is one it can never rewrite. On 2026-08-06 the store was a
complete JSON document followed by 1111 stale bytes from a longer earlier
version of itself; every mutation failed for an unknown period while `tm ls`
kept printing a healthy fleet from the in-memory fallback, and the only fix was
a human hand-truncating JSON.

Detect: a parse failure is now `StoreError::Corrupt`, whose message names the
file, the byte offset where the valid document ends, the size of the trailing
junk, and the repair command. A new `session_store` check in `tm doctor`
reports the same before anyone stumbles into it.

Recover: `tm repair session-store` backs the file up to a timestamped sibling
and truncates it to the longest complete document at its head, refusing when
the discarded bytes name a session the recovered document lacks.

Stop the silent mask: the last-known-in-memory fallback stays — a transient
read error must not report an empty fleet — but corruption now logs at ERROR
and rides out on the list response as `store_health`, which every `tm ls` and
picker invocation turns into a stderr warning.

Likely cause, fixed: `save()` staged through one fixed `sessions.json.tmp`
shared by every writer in every process. The rename is atomic; the staging
write is not exclusive, so two concurrent savers leave a file as long as the
longer document and as valid as the shorter one — the observed shape. Staging
is now per-store-instance.

Also: `read_file` answered every read error with an empty store, so a
permissions failure would have made the next `save()` write that emptiness over
the whole fleet. Only a genuinely absent file now means "fresh store".

fix(trusty-mpm): split binary_provenance version skew by direction, amend ADR-0021 (#4964) (#5025)

* fix(trusty-mpm): split binary_provenance version skew by direction (#4964)

`provenance_report` matched the running binary to a cargo ledger record by
path, then reported `Fail` on any version disagreement. Epic #4964 makes that
a false positive: after Phase 1 (daemon upgrades stop invoking cargo) and
Phase 3 (destination flips to `$CARGO_HOME/bin`), a downloader-placed binary
lands at the exact path a stale ledger entry describes, so the path match
succeeds, the versions disagree, and `tm doctor` fails a clean, successful,
cargo-free upgrade.

Cargo rewrites its ledger whenever it writes, so a disagreement at the same
path can only mean a non-cargo writer replaced the file. Which side is newer
decides what that means:

- running NEWER than the record -> Unknown. The ledger is stale; the binary is
  current. Same verdict the same file already gets from `~/.local/bin`, so the
  destination flip changes no severity.
- running OLDER than the record -> Fail, unchanged. An older binary on top of
  a newer install is the #4033 defect verbatim.
- versions not orderable as semver -> Fail. An unverifiable mismatch is still
  a mismatch.

`Warn` remains the correct terminal verdict for a `cargo install --path`
install per ADR-0021.

ADR-0021 is amended, not superseded: its rule (registry installs only, never
path installs) is unchanged and unreversed, and the amendment records the
third provenance class the original text could not have reasoned about.
Status stays Proposed — the blocking prerequisites are untouched.

* fix(trusty-mpm): make the shared-tree dispatch guard record while it answers

`tm hook --pm-guard` asked the daemon which agents were already writing in a
working directory and computed its verdict from the answer. Nothing claimed the
directory in between, so two `Agent`/`Task` dispatches issued in one PM turn
could both ask before either was recorded, both see an empty set, and both be
admitted — and a PM dispatching several agents in one message is the framework's
own documented pattern for parallel work, so that was the common shape.

The query is now a POST that answers and claims in one critical section. What it
claims is not new state: it hands the payload to the delegation tracker's own
`PreToolUse` observer, so the record is the one the daemon's `matcher: "*"` hook
would have written a moment later, with the same correlation key, the same
liveness, and the same staleness sweep. That observer is idempotent on
`tool_use_id`, so whichever hook arrives second is a no-op and exactly one record
exists either way.

Every fail-open branch is preserved and still covered: an unreachable daemon, a
malformed answer, an unresolvable working directory, an unknown agent, an untyped
dispatch, and a non-dispatch tool all allow the call. The claim adds none of its
own — the daemon re-derives eligibility from the payload rather than trusting the
caller, and claims nothing when it denies, when the dispatch is read-only or
isolated, when the tool is not a dispatch tool, or when the payload carries no

* feat(trusty-mpm): deny a second concurrent unisolated subagent dispatch into one working tree

An in-conversation Agent/Task subagent inherits the dispatching PM's working
directory. Two concurrent file-mutating subagents there race over a single git
HEAD, and git does not refuse the collision: `git checkout -b` refuses only when
a tracked file differs between both branches' committed versions AND carries an
uncommitted local change, so untracked files and edits the branches agree on
transfer onto the wrong branch silently. `isolation: "worktree"` was the escape
hatch, was opt-in, and nothing enforced it.

live delegation already writing unisolated in the same directory. Delegation
records carry the declared `isolation` mode, and a new read-only route serves
the question so liveness comes from real SubagentStop signals rather than a
timer.

The guard fails open at every step: only bundled engineer-tier agents are
classified as file-mutating, and a read-only dispatch, an unknown agent, an
unresolvable cwd, or an unreachable daemon all allow the call. A false deny
lands on the PM and halts every dispatch in the system; a false allow only
reproduces prior behaviour.

grandfathered over the SLOC cap at a frozen budget and could not take a new

* fix(tga): redact stage-failure text before excerpting it (#5239)

A security review of #5239's gap reporting found that a credential
straddling the excerpt boundary reached the delivered report. Stage
messages were truncated to 160 characters in `sweep_gap_lines`, then
scrubbed later in `build_dd_manifest`. `scrub_secrets` matches a
credential's whole value, so a token starting before char 160 and ending
after it survived the cut as a prefix fragment that no downstream scrub
could match — into `manifest.toml`, into `ReportModel.gaps`, and onto the
page as a Gaps & Caveats bullet. Verified: the raw manifest carried
`ghp_STRADD…`.

The fix reverses the order and makes the ordering unreachable rather
than merely correct today. `gaps::redacted_excerpt` scrubs the full
untruncated message, flattens whitespace, then truncates, so the cap
binds the redacted text and output length stays bounded. The needle set
is now a required argument of `sweep_gap_lines`, so a truncated stage
message cannot be obtained without having supplied the credentials to
remove from it first. `report::dd_manifest::configured_secrets` becomes
public so the sweep and the manifest builder redact against one derived
set instead of two.

`build_dd_manifest` still scrubs every string it emits — that stays the
manifest-wide guarantee; re-scrubbing an already-clean string is a no-op.

The pre-existing `configured_token_never_reaches_the_manifest` could not
catch this: it hands the builder short gap strings directly, so the
excerpt never runs. Three tests now drive the real
`sweep_gap_lines` -> `build_dd_manifest` path with a >200-character stage
failure: a token straddling char 160 (fails without this change), a
second token beyond the boundary that moves inside the window once the
first collapses to `[REDACTED]`, and a length-budget check. Each asserts
that no 8-character prefix survives, 8 being `scrub_secrets`' minimum
needle length and therefore the shortest fragment nothing downstream
could ever remove.

fix(trusty-mpm): make the supervisor read the persisted auto_resume setting (#5287)

* fix(trusty-mpm): make the supervisor read the persisted auto_resume setting

The console's `auto_resume_set` wrote `~/.trusty-mpm/auto_resume` and
reported success, but the only reader was the console's own status
display. `TRUSTY_MPM_AUTO_RESUME`, read once at supervisor startup, was
the sole gate on a resume — so toggling auto-resume in the console
changed nothing in the running fleet and raised no error.

`Supervisor::tick` now re-reads the file every sweep. Precedence: the
persisted file when present > the boot-time env / `--auto-resume` flag >
off. The read goes through a new tri-state `read_override_at`, which
tells "file absent" (leave the boot flag alone) apart from "file says
false" (turn a running supervisor off); the existing `read_desired_at`
flattens both to false, which would have let a never-touched toggle
disable an env-enabled supervisor. An unreadable file holds the last
known value and logs at error rather than failing open to off.

The layer above: a failed auto-resume used to be a warn line plus a
counter on an endpoint the console does not read, while the session
stayed `Stopped` and the next sweep silently retried it forever. It now
marks the session `Errored`, which lands in `FleetMetrics.errored` and
drives the console's Degraded health; `resume` still accepts `Errored`
so a manual retry works.

`supervisor_status` / `console_metrics` gained an `effective` field and
now report `pending_restart: false` — the "restart pending" hint
described the old behavior and would be a false claim now.

fix(scripts): stop the SemVer gate reporting a build error as a version-bump verdict (#5290)

check_semver.sh printed "a public API change requires a matching version bump"
over any nonzero cargo-semver-checks exit, including a rustdoc build failure. A
reader saw a SemVer verdict where nothing had been compared, and the two failure
modes were indistinguishable from the output. preflight-publish.sh CHECK 5 — the
last barrier before cargo publish — repeated it, advising a version bump on no
evidence.

The gate now concludes only from positive evidence: a verdict exists when
cargo-semver-checks printed its own `Checked ... N checks:` summary. No summary
means no comparison happened, whatever the exit status was, including exit 0.
That is reported as NO VERDICT on exit 3, distinct from exit 1 (a computed
verdict that says break). Exit-code classification alone would not do: 101 is
both a rustdoc failure and a baseline-retrieval failure. Every path that cannot
compute a verdict — unscanned diff, unreachable registry, missing tool — now
shares exit 3, and none of them can exit 0.

The gate also could not run at all under the repo MSRV. cargo-semver-checks
re-resolves in a scratch project that ignores Cargo.lock, took takecell 0.1.2
(rust-version 1.96) where the lock pins 0.1.1 via teloxide-core, and rustdoc
refused to build under rustc 1.94.1. takecell reaches every default build of
trusty-mpm through cli -> telegram. It now runs under the newest installed
rustc; pinning the dependency would fix one name until the next one raises its
floor. RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN is ineffective here because mise shims never consult
rustup, so the toolchain's bin directory is prepended to PATH instead. A machine
with no newer toolchain degrades to the NO VERDICT path, never to a silent pass.

Self-test cases 5-8 replay fixtures captured verbatim from real runs through a
stub cargo, leaving all of the gate's own logic under test. Checked by mutation:
deleting the classification fails cases 6 and 7, making the no-verdict status 0
fails five cases, and forcing the classifier to always answer "no verdict" fails

`Bm25Index::queryTopK`, `Sha256Hasher::finalizeInto`,
`OAuth2Client::refreshToken` and `Utf8Error::validUpTo` all reached the
mixed-case branch of `looks_like_secret` and blocked memory writes.

Root cause is the CamelCase rule, not the delimiter set: a segment carrying

misses per 30k at 15 input bytes and 291 -> 1973 at 20, and still does not fix
this issue.

ADR-0036 made every worktree a flat sibling under `.claude/worktrees/`. Two
passages predating it could be read as asserting the nesting it forbids:

dispatched them", and DOC-66 §5 was titled "Agent worktrees as children" with

`Inbox::list` had zero production call sites. A relayed delivery reached the
receiver's inbox, was acknowledged — which let trusty-console delete its only
copy — and stopped there. No review, no analysis, no comment, and a spool that
reported empty because the hand-off had succeeded.

bounded, and quarantined rather than deleted. Console meters quarantined
deliveries separately and reports Error, because quarantining takes an entry out
of the held count and would otherwise turn the signal green at the moment a
delivery was confirmed never to be processed.

legacy HTTP routes now share the drain's event classifier so the two transports
cannot drift on what a webhook means.

registry, and the NDJSON logs — every one of them a per-user file under

fix(trusty-agents): resolve workflow-mode config hierarchically, not from cwd (#5227)

The workflow-mode pre-flight tested one CWD-derived path while the agent
registry resolved hierarchically. A process whose CWD has no
`.trusty-agents/` — the macOS `.app` sidecar runs with `cwd = /` — logged
`agent registry loaded from hierarchical search paths count=28` and then
bailed with ``no `.trusty-agents/agents/` found in /``, so every
Implementation task launched from the GUI failed.

The pre-flight now routes through `agents::registry::agent_search_paths`,
the resolver the registry already uses, and names every path it searched
instead of naming only the CWD.

Widening the pre-flight alone would have moved the failure two steps later:
`--workflow <name>` read `<name>.json` from a single CWD-relative
`.trusty-agents/workflows`, and the bundled definitions existed only inside
a checkout of this repo — no `~/.trusty-agents/workflows/` is created on any
machine. So workflow lookup (and resume) now walks the same hierarchy, and
the bundled definitions deploy to `~/.trusty-agents/workflows/` at startup
through the agent roster's existing stamp/lock/refresh path rather than a
second copy of it.

`agent_search_paths` and the new `workflow_search_paths` are both thin
wrappers over one `config_search_paths(config_dir, leaf)`, so the tiers
cannot drift apart again.

Verified end-to-end: from an empty CWD with a populated `$HOME` agents tier
and no workflows tier anywhere, `tagent --workflow prescriptive` deploys
`prescriptive.json`, passes the pre-flight, and loads the definition.

* fix(trusty-common,trusty-agents): scrub known credentials from captured child stderr

`run_task` spawns the workflow subprocess with no `env_clear()`, so the child
holds every provider credential the parent does — OPENROUTER_API_KEY,
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN, the AWS chain. The preceding commit
started routing that child's stderr into `PmResponse.narrative`, which reaches
the task API, `.trusty-agents/state/tasks.json` unencrypted, and the GUI chat
view. A child that echoed a key into its own error message would have published
it.

trusty-common gains `credentials::scrub_secrets` — the promotion of the scrub
that was private to `inference::config::ops`. That call site now routes through
it, so redaction has one implementation rather than two.
`credentials::resolved_secret_values` supplies the needle set by walking the
provider registry through the usual env > `.env.local` > store resolver, so a
newly registered provider is covered without the caller changing. Needles are
applied longest-first, and values under 8 characters — the empty string
included — are skipped, since replacing "" would blank the whole message.

trusty-agents resolves the values once per task and scrubs each captured stderr
line before the per-line truncation, so a key straddling the length limit
cannot leave a fragment behind; `format_subprocess_failure` scrubs the
assembled narrative again as the user-facing boundary.

This catches only values the process holds. A secret it never resolved — one a
child read from its own config, one quoted inside a provider's error body —
still passes through, and the doc comment says so rather than implying the path
is now safe. The raw lines this module also `eprintln!`s to the parent's own
stderr are deliberately left unscrubbed: that sink already holds the parent's
environment and is not user-facing.

feat(vmtest-harness): propagate the host GITHUB_TOKEN into the Tart guest for pattern (b) (#4933)

* feat(vmtest-harness): propagate the host GITHUB_TOKEN into the guest for pattern (b)

`vmtest run branch` cloned the public repository anonymously inside the guest,
sharing one github.com rate-limit quota with the host and every concurrent guest
on the same egress IP. The host has a GITHUB_TOKEN; the guest had no credential
plumbing at all. It does now, for pattern (b) only.

Two findings shape the implementation and are recorded at the change site so
they are not rediscovered:

  - `credential.helper store` silently does nothing here. Git consults a helper
    only after a 401, and github.com serves a public repository with 200 — so no
    challenge, no helper call, and a deliberately invalid token still clones
    successfully. `http.https://github.com/.extraheader` is used instead: it is
    sent preemptively on every request.
  - the pinned `tahoe-base` image ships a ~/.gitconfig wired to the interactive
    Git Credential Manager. Without clearing it first, writing the header fails
    with `cannot overwrite multiple values with a single value`, and a rejected
    credential makes guest `git ls-remote` hang in the headless VM. Git's
    documented empty-value reset runs first and turns that hang into a
    sub-second failure — which matters most on the run where the token expired.

Leak discipline. The token is read straight from the host process environment,
never through conf_load/CONF_KEYS (`print_banner` prints every key's value on
every run, --dry-run included). It crosses to the guest on stdin via
`vm_exec_stdin` only — never as a `vm_exec` argument, which becomes host argv —
into a 0600 include file created under `umask 077`. It never enters `repo_url`
(logged verbatim on success, tail'd on failure) nor `$VMTEST_GUEST_ENV`
(prefixed onto every guest command for the run's duration). Only presence and
the pass/fail outcome are logged. `git config --global --add include.path` takes
the PATH, so the secret never enters a command string.

Gating. The pattern test is the first statement of `provision_github_token`, so
every branch that can `die` sits below it: an expired host token cannot fail
`vmtest run local` or `vmtest run released`, neither of which contacts
github.com. A new `propagate_github_token` boolean (default true) is the second
gate, and the fail-safe direction is withhold. An absent GITHUB_TOKEN is not an
error — the run clones anonymously and exits 0 exactly as before.

Validation runs in a new `preflight_config()` before any VM is cloned, so a
typo'd `VMTEST_PROPAGATE_GITHUB_TOKEN=0` is FAIL[10] in a second rather than
after a 30s+ boot, and `--dry-run` catches it too. It is deliberately not folded
into `conf_load()`, which `vmtest clean` shares: a typo'd override must never be
able to break cleanup.

Verification is an in-guest `git ls-remote` against repo_url — an actual network
proof, not a configuration echo.

Known gap carried forward deliberately: `--add include.path` is not idempotent.
Unreachable today because every run gets a fresh guest clone; switching to
`--replace-all` is the right change only if guest reuse is ever introduced.

Static verification: `bash -n` clean on all three modified shell files;
shellcheck 0.11.0 reports 17 findings before and 17 after, byte-identical after
line-number normalisation (zero new); the `tart`-literal invariant grep is
unchanged; `--dry-run` exits 0 for all three patterns; a malformed boolean
exits 10 at preflight with no VM created.

fix(trusty-agents): authenticate the /api/events SSE stream and stop cross-origin reads (#5052) (#5185)

* fix(trusty-agents): authenticate the /api/events SSE stream (#5052)

`GET /api/events` was exempt from bearer auth outright, because a browser
`EventSource` cannot send an `Authorization` header. A loopback bind did not
contain that: any page open in the operator's browser could call
`new EventSource("http://127.0.0.1:7654/api/events")` and read
`PmThinking.text`, `AgentMessage.text`, and `PmDelegating.task_preview`
cross-origin — no shell access, no token, no non-loopback opt-in, unlogged.
The shipped Tauri sidecar starts that port by default.

Two changes, because two different configurations were exposed:

- The stream now requires a matching `Authorization: Bearer <token>` or a
  short-lived ticket minted at the new `POST /api/events/ticket`, which a
  browser can carry in the `EventSource` URL. Minting is a write method, so
  the router-wide same-origin guard already covers it even with no operator
  token configured — that is what closes the shipped default. A ticket that
  leaks into an access log or `Referer` grants five minutes of read-only
  stream access, not the whole `/api/*` write surface.
- trusty-agents drops `allow_origin(Any)` for a policy that reflects only
  same-machine origins. Its GET surface — `/api/tasks`, `/api/task/{id}`,
  `/api/sessions/{id}/recap` — is conversation content, and the write guard
  never covered reads because it is method-gated.

`/api/health` and `/api/config` stay exempt deliberately: the sidecar polls
health before it holds any credential, and `/api/config` publishes only the
`auth_required` boolean that any 401 already reveals.

Client side: the Svelte UI mints a ticket before opening `EventSource` and
owns the reconnect loop (the browser's native retry re-uses an expired
ticket forever); the desktop shell's Rust SSE bridge mints one per attempt.

fix(trusty-common): scan exactly below 256 points instead of trusting HNSW recall (#5178)

* fix(trusty-common): scan exactly below 256 points instead of trusting HNSW recall

`HnswStore::search` returned only the points reachable from the graph's
descent pivot along pruned layer-0 neighbour lists, so a genuinely relevant
drawer could be absent from the candidate pool. `hnsw_rs` seeds its
level-assignment RNG from OS entropy and the graph is rebuilt on every palace
open, so which drawer went missing changed on every restart.

Measured against brute-force truth on 1354 real 384-dim palace embeddings:
2.1-4.4% of queries lost a true top-5 neighbour at 6-16 points, and raising
`ef_search` from 64 to 256 barely moved it (8.4% -> 7.0% at 1024 points),
confirming reachability rather than candidate budget is the binding
constraint. 93% of this machine's 94 real palaces hold 64 vectors or fewer;
99% hold 256 or fewer.

Below 256 points the scan is exact and no more expensive than the traversal it
replaces: end-to-end `search` went 34.1us -> 27.3us at 64 points and
55.6us -> 45.3us at 128, and cost 5% more at 256. Larger indexes keep the
graph path unchanged.

Also stops `search` returning one drawer twice when a re-upsert left a shadow
copy of its vector in the graph, and guards the empty index — `hnsw_rs`'s
point iterator unwraps an entry point that does not exist before the first
insert.

* fix(trusty-common): score a shadowed drawer by its current vector, gate on live count

Two review findings on #5171.

A re-upsert leaves the drawer's previous embedding in the graph under the same
vector_id, and ranking by whichever copy was nearer meant a query against text
the drawer no longer holds returned it at distance 0.0 — similarity 1.0 to
VectorStore::search, enough to clear a 0.99 near-duplicate threshold against
superseded content. palace_reembed creates that state in bulk. upsert now
records which ids have a shadow copy, and search re-scores exactly those
against their VECTORS row, which is the only authority on what a drawer
currently holds. Costs one point read per shadowed candidate and nothing in
the steady state, where no re-upsert has happened since the palace opened.

The exhaustive path was selected on Hnsw::get_nb_point(), which counts
tombstones and shadows. delete never removes a point and upsert inserts
unconditionally, so a small palace could churn past 256 graph points
mid-session and silently revert to the approximate path. The gate is now the
live drawer count.

Excluding tombstoned ids inside the scan rather than after it, because the
scan truncates to a small over-fetch: a palace that has deleted most of its
drawers filled every returned slot with dead ids and handed the caller
nothing.

* fix(trusty-common): rank re-embedded drawers before trimming, not after

Two review findings on #5171, plus a commit-hygiene fix.

Re-scoring a shadowed drawer corrected its distance but not its selection.

optimistic, and the list was cut to a 2k over-fetch on that provisional key
before resolve_shadowed could correct anything. A drawer whose SUPERSEDED
vector sat near the query therefore outranked one whose CURRENT vector was a
true neighbour, and evicted it — the same lost-neighbour defect #5171 exists to
close, reached through re-embedding rather than through graph reachability.

bounding, on the corrected scores. Cost stays bounded by the gate that selects
this path: at most one entry per live drawer.

upsert inserted the shadow point into the graph before marking the id in
shadowed, leaving a window where a concurrent search saw the shadow with no
flag and scored the drawer by whichever copy was nearer — the pre-fix
behaviour, for one query. The two steps cannot be atomic, but the asymmetry
runs one way: over-marking costs one point read against the already-committed
