* feat(trusty-console): webhook ingress with a spool that is durable before the ack (#5089 step 3)

Both existing webhook handlers return 202 and *then* do the work
(trusty-review/src/service/webhook.rs:305-309,
trusty-analyze/src/service/handlers/review.rs:210-214). GitHub never
retries an acknowledged delivery, so every post-ack failure is permanent
silent loss with health still reporting green. This builds the console
path that replaces them; the two handlers stay live until step 4.

POST /api/webhooks/{source} multiplexes review and analyze. The order of
operations is the fix: unknown source 404s before any secret handling;
the HMAC is verified once over the exact received bytes, with an unset
secret and a bad signature both 401 (ADR-0034 §2 unifies the policy to
trusty-review's fail-closed answer); the delivery is written and fsync'd
to a spool under the console data directory; and only then is a 202 sent.
A spool write that fails returns 5xx and never acks, so GitHub keeps the
delivery redeliverable.

A relay outcome other than an explicit "ack": true leaves the entry
pending with an incremented attempt count and a durable reason. Reaching
the target is deliberately not enough — treating a successful connect as
a successful delivery is the same silent loss one layer down.

GET /api/console/metrics/webhooks reports oldest-pending age, pending
count and failed-attempt total, red once the oldest entry passes the
threshold. The scan runs on the request rather than from a cache, so the
signal stays honest if the background retry sweep stops; a spool that
cannot be read is red rather than empty.

trusty-common gains the two shared entry points this needs rather than a
fourth bespoke copy of each: uds::rpc::send_framed_request (the framed
UDS transport ADR-0034 §4 names, dialling through connect_hardened) and
webhook_hmac (one GitHub signature verifier, returning a three-state
verdict so "no secret configured" cannot collapse into permission to
proceed). The existing UDS clients and the two HMAC copies migrate in a
follow-up.

Spawn-on-demand is step 4. Until then no target binds a listener, every
relay lands in Unreachable, and that is a durable pending state.

* fix(trusty-console): claim the spool path before the write, and derace the sweep test (#5089 step 3)

CI was red on `sweep_does_not_relay_an_entry_the_request_path_is_still_relaying`
while it passed locally. Diagnosing it found both a racy test AND a real code
defect; they are separate and both are fixed here.

The test was racy. It slept 150 ms and assumed `ingest` had reached its claim
by then. It does not control that window: printing the whole SweepReport at
sleeps of 0/1/5 ms shows every field zero, meaning `list_pending` returned an
EMPTY spool — the spawned task had not persisted yet. That is exactly CI's
signature (`in_flight: 0` with nothing else set). Moving the write onto the
blocking pool in aeba7970a lengthened the pre-claim phase enough to lose the
race under CI load. The test now rendezvouses with the target stub: the stub
signals once it has read the frame and waits to be released, so the sweep runs
when the relay is provably in flight. No wall clock, and it drops from 0.64 s
to 0.04 s.

The code was also wrong. The claim was taken AFTER `persist_new` returned,
leaving the entry on disk and unclaimed for the gap between the write landing
and `ingest` being re-polled. At sleep=20 ms the sweep reported `acked: 1` —
two relays for one delivery, the exact defect the claim exists to prevent.
The claim is now taken on `entry_path` before the write; the path is a pure
function of the receipt time and delivery id, both already fixed, so the window
does not exist. Backoff's first-attempt grace also covered it in production,
but two guards that each fully close it is the point.

No regression test pins the ordering. The window is one scheduler poll wide,
and a rendezvous, a select! loop and a 4-worker parallel hammer all passed
against a claim-after-write build as readily as against the correct one. A
test that cannot tell the two apart is a false assurance, so none was kept and
the code carries a comment saying so.

Evidence: the deraced test is 30/30 green under 12-way CPU saturation, and
5/5 red against a build whose sweep ignores claims.

feat(trusty-common): promote the BM25 supervisor to a generic UdsServiceSupervisor (#5089 step 2) (#5170)

* feat(trusty-common): promote the BM25 supervisor to a generic UdsServiceSupervisor

ADR-0034 §1 needs trusty-console to start trusty-review / trusty-analyze at
webhook-delivery time so neither has to be resident (milestone tm 1.3.5
criterion (c)). ADR-0032 said that spawn-on-delivery mechanism "does not yet
exist"; it did, as trusty-memory's Bm25Supervisor. This promotes it into
trusty-common behind a new `uds-supervisor` feature, so the next service
inherits the hardening from #2845, #2846, #5085 and #5119 instead of
re-earning it. Bm25Supervisor becomes a thin face over it with an unchanged
public API.

Two invariants survive the promotion intact.

Liveness stays SOCKET-BACKED. try_wait() answers "has this child been reaped",
not "is it serving" — a SIGKILLed daemon closes its listener during do_exit and
only becomes reapable once the kernel finishes tearing it down. SocketVerdict
stays three-state and only ENOENT / ECONNREFUSED mean NotServing; a timeout or
any other errno is Inconclusive and leaves the child alone. The doomed queue is
still drained UNDER the spawn gate, because the doomed child unlinks the shared
socket path as the last step of its own shutdown.

The timeouts become per-service. SPAWN_PROBE_TIMEOUT (3 s, justified by BM25
having no model to load) and SIGTERM_PATIENCE (5 s, bound to the daemon's own
SHUTDOWN_FLUSH_TIMEOUT) are now fields of a ServiceTimeouts value. The
`const _: () = assert!(...)` that tied them together could not cross into a
crate that cannot name any particular daemon's flush budget, so the check moved
into ServiceTimeouts::new — a const fn. trusty-memory declares BM25_TIMEOUTS as
a const item, so the assert still fires at compile time, now bound to the value
actually passed to the supervisor.

Adoption is verified rather than assumed: a socket that answers but fails
verify_socket_for_connect is refused with SupervisorError::UntrustedSocket. That
is the one path where the target's own bind_hardened never runs, which #5099's
dialer docs already named.

fix(security): enforce UDS socket permissions the ADRs already claim exist (#5124)

* fix(security): enforce UDS socket permissions the ADRs already claim exist

No production code in this workspace set permissions on any Unix-domain
socket — every `set_permissions` / `PermissionsExt` hit was a test fixture.
Sockets were created at the process umask (commonly 0755), and two of the
three path conventions placed them in `$TMPDIR` falling back to `/tmp`,
world-writable on a Linux host with `TMPDIR` unset.

ADR-0031 and ADR-0032 both rest their case for UDS over loopback TCP on
"a 0600 socket", and ADR-0034 (#5090) states the requirement: 0700 on the
containing directory, 0600 on the socket, peer-uid check on accept.

New `trusty_common::uds` is the single entry point all four bind sites route
through. The ordering trap — binding creates the file, so a chmod after bind
leaves a window — is closed by the DIRECTORY, not the chmod: the parent is
created at 0700 via `DirBuilder::mode()`, which passes the mode to mkdir(2)
atomically, so no other uid can name the socket at any point. The 0600 chmod
is defence in depth. Setting the process umask around the bind was rejected:
umask is process-global and racy under a multi-threaded tokio runtime.

Bind sites migrated (all four; ADR-0034 named three clients, but the binds
live on the server side and `trusty-agents`' message bus was a fourth):
  - trusty-embedderd/src/uds_server.rs
  - trusty-bm25-daemon/src/server.rs
  - trusty-agents/src/ctrl/socket.rs (bind + bind_singleton)
  - trusty-agents/src/bus/mod.rs

Path resolvers moved to a per-uid `<$TMPDIR or /tmp>/trusty-<uid>/` directory,
in lockstep so client and daemon still agree. Costs 11 bytes of the sun_path
budget; a running daemon must be restarted to be found at the new path.

Peer-uid check uses `SO_PEERCRED` on Linux and `getpeereid` on macOS/BSD via
`libc`, already in `[workspace.dependencies]` — no new dependency; its
trusty-common target gate widens from macOS-only to `cfg(unix)`.

feat(trusty-mpm): add a tmux alternate_screen config option (#5151)

* feat(trusty-mpm): opt-in tmux.alternate_screen config knob

The alternate screen buffer, not history-limit, is why tm sessions have no
scrollback. tm sets history-limit to 100,000 and verifies the readback, and
panes hold thousands of lines — but a full-screen TUI draws into the alternate
screen, which tmux discards rather than appending to the pane's history.
Measured: panes with the Claude binary rendering report alternate_on=1; plain
shells report alternate_on=0. tm never set alternate-screen at all.

Adds `tmux.alternate_screen` to ~/.trusty-tools/trusty-mpm/config.yaml
alongside history_limit and mouse, defaulting to `on` — tmux's factory value
and today's behaviour. A configured `off` is what turns it off.

alternate-screen is a pane option inheriting from the window scope, not a
server option. Against live tmux 3.6b, `set-option -pg alternate-screen off`
and `set-option -s alternate-screen off` both exit 0, a same-flag readback
reports "off", and the pane still enters the alternate screen; only `-wg`
takes effect. The new SetWindowGlobalOption / ShowWindowGlobalOption pair
keeps the set and its verification probe on the same scope, so a wrong-scope
set cannot verify green. The option rides the existing #3386 apply-and-verify
path before new-session.

The cost of turning it off is documented on TmuxConfig::alternate_screen: the
tmux server is shared, so vim, less, htop and man also stop restoring the
screen they covered, each leaving its final frame in the scrollback. It is
not retroactive.

Inline `mod tests` blocks in the three touched files are split into sibling
_tests.rs files — the basename made them count as production SLOC and all
three crossed the 500 cap.

ci: move the SemVer gate from per-PR to release-time (#5150)

The per-PR job installed a pinned cargo-semver-checks and warmed a cold
target/semver-checks cache before crate selection had even decided whether the
PR was exempt — 20+ minutes on every PR, docs-only ones included. A SemVer
break only becomes a defect when something is published.

  <pkg> immediately before `cargo publish`. This is the barrier that blocks a
  bad upload: `cargo publish` runs locally, so no CI job can stop it, and a
  crates.io publish is irreversible except by yank. No override — the remedy
  for a firing gate is to bump the breaking position, which the gate then skips
  as an already-breaking release.
- .github/workflows/semver-checks.yml retriggers on `push: tags: ['*-v*']` plus
  workflow_dispatch for on-demand runs. The pull_request trigger is removed.
  The tag lands before `cargo publish` in this project's sequence, so a red run
  is still visible in time to call the release off.
- check_semver.sh: --crate now accepts a crates/ directory name as well as a
  package name, so a release tag's prefix resolves in either accepted form
  (#1128). A missing cargo-semver-checks is a hard failure with a remedy, never
  a skip — on the release path this gate is the last barrier.

Accepted trade, documented in CLAUDE.md and docs/reference/semver-gate.md:
between releases nothing checks this, and a break surfaces at the release that
would ship it.

fix(trusty-review): scope the redb dedup lock to a transaction, not the process (#5064)

* fix(trusty-review): scope the dedup redb lock to one operation, not the process

`DedupStore` held redb's exclusive file lock for its whole lifetime, so the
second process to open `{LOG_DIR}/dedup.redb` got `DatabaseAlreadyOpen`.
`build_app_state` downgraded that to a `warn!` and continued with `dedup: None`,
leaving a server running with no claim gate and every health signal green.

Two openers already exist (`serve` and `serve --stdio`); ADR-0034 adds a third,
a console-spawned webhook worker that runs `allow_posting: true` and genuinely
needs the store, so the collision could not be resolved by skipping the open.

The store now owns a path rather than an open database: each operation opens
redb, runs one write transaction, and drops it, waiting out a concurrent holder
for up to 2s and returning the new typed `DedupError::Contended` if it never
frees. `build_app_state` takes an explicit `DedupNeed`: `serve --stdio` declares
`NotNeeded` and never touches the file, while a posting-capable mode declares
`Required` and propagates an open failure instead of swallowing it.

Closes #5064

fix: eliminate BM25 supervisor eviction race on process teardown (#5085)

* fix(trusty-memory): stop the bm25 supervisor reusing a daemon that stopped serving

`Bm25Supervisor::ensure_running`'s fast path decided liveness from
`tokio::process::Child::try_wait()` alone. That call answers "has this child
been reaped", which is not the same question as "is it serving": a SIGKILLed
daemon closes its listening socket during `do_exit` and only becomes reapable
once the kernel finishes tearing it down. For that window `try_wait()` returns
`Ok(None)` for a process that is already refusing connections, so the supervisor
handed the caller a socket path nothing was listening on and reported nothing —
a fail-open, and the cause of `a_dead_child_is_evicted_and_respawned` flaking in
CI.

Measured on an idle 16-core host: in 35 of 40 SIGKILL rounds the socket stopped
accepting before `try_wait()` reported the child exited, with a maximum gap of
32.6us. That is why 62 local runs never reproduced it and a 2-core CI runner
under `cargo test --workspace` does.

`lookup_live` now requires both that the child is un-reaped and that its socket
is not definitively unserved. The probe runs with the map lock released so a
slow connect never blocks another palace, and eviction re-acquires and fires
only when the map still holds the same child, so a concurrently-spawned
replacement is never evicted by a stale verdict.

Eviction keys off a new three-state `SocketVerdict` rather than a bare bool.
Only ENOENT and ECONNREFUSED — where the kernel proves no listener is bound —
count as `NotServing`. A timeout or a saturated accept backlog is
`Inconclusive` and leaves the child alone, so load cannot turn into a respawn
storm.

Tests: `a_live_child_that_stopped_serving_is_evicted_and_respawned` pins the
same `lookup_live` state deterministically by unlinking the socket while the
daemon runs, so the child is alive by `try_wait()` forever. It fails 20/20 runs
against the pre-fix supervisor and passes after. That state is also a real
production one: a `$TMPDIR` reaper leaves a daemon alive and permanently
unreachable.

Closes #5085

* fix(trusty-memory): flush an evicted live bm25 daemon before replacing it

Review follow-up on the #5085 fix. The unserved-socket eviction added there is
the first in this module that removes a child which is still ALIVE — every
other arm evicts a corpse, so dropping the handle costs nothing. Here it cost
data: BM25 acks a write on the in-memory apply and only writes it out at the
end of the batch window, and `trusty-bm25-daemon`'s shutdown flush (which
exists for this supervisor) runs only on SIGTERM. The `kill_on_drop` SIGKILL
therefore discarded acked documents with nothing left to recover them — the
supervisor cannot reach `mark_dirty`, so no repair sweep revisits the palace.

Evicted-but-live children now go to a `doomed` queue that `reap_doomed` drains
with the same `terminate_child` + `remove_socket_file` sequence `enforce_limits`
and `shutdown` use. `lookup_live` only pushes (a lock, no wait), so the fast
path never blocks on a kill.

The drain runs under the spawn gate rather than in a detached task, which the
review suggested. Detaching is unsafe here: the doomed daemon unlinks the shared
socket path as the last step of its own shutdown, so a concurrent termination
can land that unlink AFTER the replacement bound the same path — leaving the
replacement alive and unreachable, which is this very bug reintroduced by its
own fix. Draining before the respawn orders the two so it cannot happen.

  spurious eviction is the daemon's shape (1024 backlog, per-connection tasks),
  not the classification. Recorded as a constraint for the #5089 promotion.

fix: apply a relevance floor to prompt-context injection (#5037)

The UserPromptSubmit hook asked for top_k drawers and rendered whatever
came back. `truncate(top_k)` was the only length control anywhere in the
retrieval chain and no layer applied a minimum score, so a prompt with no
good answer still injected a full K. A probe of "what is the capital of
France" against the live 1,332-drawer palace returned five drawers all
scoring exactly 0.15 — `importance * L1_NO_SIMILARITY_PENALTY`, the score
`rescore_l1_by_similarity` gives an essential drawer the vector search
never returned — formatted identically to a genuine 0.56 hit.

Four changes, the owner's contract for #5037:

1. Relevance floor. New `memory_core::retrieval::relevance` in
   trusty-common owns the one implementation; `RecalledDrawer` parses the
   `score` the recall endpoint has always sent and drops what falls below.
   Default 0.35, `TRUSTY_MEMORY_PROMPT_MIN_SCORE` overrides, 0 disables.
2. Larger budget: DEFAULT_TOP_K 5 -> 12 (ceiling 20 -> 30),
   INJECTION_BYTE_CAP 4 KB -> 8 KB.
3. Whole-input query, now pinned by a test against the truncating
   `hook_prompt_excerpt` helper next to it.
4. A withheld notice, so a floor that returns nothing is visible rather
   than indistinguishable from an empty palace.

The threshold comes from measured distributions, not a guess. Against the
live palace: 150 candidates from 15 off-topic prompts span 0.1500-0.3439
(75 at exactly 0.1500); 57 self-retrieval correct-drawer hits span
0.4844-0.9743; 1,200 candidates from real logged hook prompts span
0.4042-0.7527. 0.35 is the smallest swept value at which no off-topic
candidate survives.

`recall`/`recall_scoped` keep their contract — gating inside `truncate`
would change every MCP and CLI caller, which the ruling does not ask for.

fix(trusty-common): persist the HNSW vector-id allocator so two live stores cannot alias drawers (#5005)

* fix(trusty-common): persist the HNSW vector-id allocator so two live stores cannot alias drawers (#5005)

`HnswStore` allocated vector ids from a process-local `AtomicU64` seeded at
open from `max(VECTORS, VECTOR_KEYS) + 1`, and `upsert` inserted at the
allocated id with no uniqueness check. Two live stores over one palace file —
a configuration the in-process vector-db cache deliberately supports, since it
hands the same `Arc<Database>` to every `UsearchStore` opened for a palace —
each seeded a private counter from the same high-water mark and then issued the
same ids. `VECTOR_KEYS` aliased several drawers onto one `vector_id` and
`VECTORS` overwrote in place, silently: on the live `trusty-tools` palace,
`vector_id` 988 is shared by 5 uuids and 4 of them are embedded nowhere.

The counter now lives in redb (`vector_id_seq`) and is reserved inside the same
write transaction that writes the row claiming it, so every writer on the file
serialises against it. `upsert` additionally refuses an id that already has a
`VECTORS` row — it allocates past it, or fails with `IdAllocationFailed`, but
never overwrites.

Existing palaces have no counter row. Every read-write open raises it to
`max(VECTORS, VECTOR_KEYS) + 1`, as a max rather than a set-if-missing, so the
seed is idempotent and a rolling upgrade that interleaves a pre-fix binary
cannot leave the counter behind the tables.

Detection, which #5000 also needs: `embed_health` and `palace_reembed` now
report `vector_key_rows`, `distinct_vector_ids`, and the aliased drawer ids.
Key presence — the only thing they checked before — reported a false all-clear

fix(trusty-search): answer INDEX_NOT_READY, not 404, for a never-indexed worktree (#5057)

* fix(trusty-search): answer INDEX_NOT_READY, not 404, for a never-indexed worktree

A search against a worktree the daemon has never indexed returned the
daemon's `404 unknown index` verbatim. "Unknown" reads as permanent, so a
caller gives up or silently falls back to grep and the gap stays invisible.
The state is transient: the index will exist, it just does not yet.

The MCP tool surface now distinguishes the two. When the daemon 404s on the
index this session ADVERTISED as its default (`tools/list` annotates the pin,
#1373), `search`, the four per-lane search tools, `grep`, and `index_status`
return `INDEX_NOT_READY` — JSON-RPC code -32011 on the bare-method form, or
`_meta.error_code` under `tools/call`, mirroring the existing STAGE_NOT_READY
contract (#138). The payload carries `state`, `reason`, `retryable: true`,
and `suggested_fallback: ["grep", "find"]`, so an agent branches on data
instead of pattern-matching an English string. A 404 on any other id stays a
genuine unknown index.

One state, `not_indexed`. "Indexing in progress" already has its own signals
(`503 index_loading`, per-lane STAGE_NOT_READY) and a stale index still
answers, so neither gives a caller a different action.

This does not decide when indexes get created — the auto-provision question
on #4715 stays open.

feat(bm25): lossless backfill + bounded daemon process model + stats op (#5048)

* feat(bm25): lossless backfill + bounded daemon process model + stats op

The BM25 lexical lane has never run: `bm25_search_optional` returns on its
first line unless `TRUSTY_BM25_DAEMON=1` was set at daemon startup, which no
plist, installer, or shipped path sets. There are zero BM25 index directories
across ~99 palaces, so the fusion code in `handle_memory_recall` has never
executed. This makes enabling it mean something. It does NOT enable it.

Three defects stood between "the lane is on" and "the lane works":

The write path drops silently under load. `tools/bm25.rs` enqueues into a
256-slot channel with `try_send` and drops on full. That is defensible for the
write path — the drawer is durable in redb and `memory_remember` must not wait
on daemon RTT — so it is left exactly as it is. It is not defensible for a
backfill: the largest palace holds 1311 drawers, five times the queue, so a
backfill routed through it would drop roughly 80% of the corpus and leave the
palace answering from a fifth of its content. Backfill gets its own feeder
that awaits each document's ack, so nothing is ever offered to a full queue.

`Bm25Supervisor` never evicted. Only `shutdown` removed a map entry, so one
cross-palace `recall_all` over ~99 palaces left 99 resident subprocesses for
the daemon's lifetime — each one's memory scaling with its palace's drawer
text. A cap with LRU reaping and an enforced per-daemon RSS ceiling now apply
on every `ensure_running`, and spawns are serialised so a burst fan-out cannot
satisfy the cap per-caller and violate it in aggregate (#2845, #2846).

Nothing could ask whether a palace was fully indexed. The protocol had `index`
and `search` only, so an empty hit list was ambiguous between "no match" and
"nothing indexed". A `stats` op reports `doc_count` and `total_text_bytes`;
backfill reads coverage back from the daemon rather than trusting its own
submission count.

Also fixes a durability defect the cap surfaced: the daemon exited on SIGTERM
without flushing, losing up to one write window. Latent while daemons only
died at shutdown; routine once the supervisor reaps them.

Fail-open throughout: daemon absent, spawn refused, socket wedged, index
empty, index partial, and queue saturation each degrade to a reported status
with a bounded wait, never an error into a caller's path and never a hang.

Scope: piece 1 of 3. The default-on flip, hook routing to /rpc, and
`handle_memory_recall_deep`'s missing fusion are pieces 2 and 3.

fix(trusty-analyze): persist SCIP graph overlays and make absent-vs-empty explicit (#5054)

* fix(trusty-analyze): persist SCIP graph overlays and make absent-vs-empty explicit

`POST /indexes/{id}/scip` wrote into an in-process
`HashMap<String, KgGraph>` and answered HTTP 200. A daemon restart
discarded the ingest, and `GET /indexes/{id}/graph` then served a
tree-sitter-only graph that no caller could tell apart from one where the
overlay had been applied. A SCIP index is uploaded by the operator and is
not re-derivable from the corpus, so the ingest is real work lost.

The overlay now lives in a redb store (`scip_overlays.redb`, a sibling of
the facts store, so `--facts-path` still governs the whole data
directory). An unreadable overlay database fails the daemon's startup
rather than being recreated empty the way `FactStore` is — facts are
re-derivable, an uploaded SCIP index is not, and a silent empty
replacement is the same data loss by another route.

Persistence stops the loss but not the silence: an index nobody ingested
and an index whose SCIP payload carried no symbols both contribute zero
nodes to `/graph`. `GET /indexes/{id}/scip` now answers 404 for the first
and 200 with `{index_id, nodes, edges, ingested_at}` for the second, and
`/graph` carries the same fact as an `x-scip-overlay: present|absent`
header while its body stays a bare `KgGraph`. A store read failure is a
500, not a silent fall-through to the tree-sitter-only graph.

Breaking (library API): `AnalyzerAppState::scip_overlays` is now
`core::ScipOverlayStore`, and `new` / `with_registry` take it as a
required argument rather than a `with_*` override — omission was the bug.

Closes #5049

* fix(trusty-analyze): quarantine an unreadable overlay redb instead of refusing to boot

Review found the justification for the startup refusal was factually
wrong. `FactStore::open` does not recreate an unreadable database empty —
it renames the file to `facts.redb.v2-incompatible`, logs an ERROR, and
boots. It quarantines; nothing is discarded.

The trade the wrong claim supported was also wrong. redb's on-disk format
has already gone obsolete once here (#702), so the next bump would have
taken facts, smells, review, clusters, NER and the whole MCP surface down
over one optional feature's sidecar file — and the only remedy, deleting
it, destroys the overlays anyway.

Both stores now share one policy in `core::redb_open`. It classifies the
redb error first: an obsolete on-disk format is renamed aside and the
store starts empty, while a transient failure to open — permissions,
disk, a held lock — stays fatal, because recreating on top of a file that
is merely unavailable would destroy data that is still good. A shared
implementation is the point: two copies would drift into giving opposite
answers to the same byte-level cause.

Quarantining is safe here because of the other half of #5049 — after one,
`GET /indexes/{id}/scip` answers 404, which honestly reports that no
overlay is available rather than serving a graph that silently lost one.

- The redb calls in the graph handlers now run on `spawn_blocking`, the
  convention `handlers/facts.rs` established after #67. The `put` is the
  expensive one: it serializes a whole-repository `KgGraph` and fsyncs it.
- `ScipOverlayStore::put` returns `()`. Its doc claimed the caller used
  the returned record; no caller did.
- Documented that `x-scip-overlay` describes the overlay's existence, so a
  `?language=` filter that removes every SCIP node still reports `present`.

perf(trusty-search): measure per-stage reindex cost instead of one residual (#5029)

Refs #5024.

## Defect

The reindex reported `walk_ms`, four subsystem accumulators summed inside the
batch loop (`parse_ms`/`embed_ms`/`bm25_ms`/`vector_upsert_ms`), and `kg_ms`.
Everything else — the hash-cache load, the incremental carryover copy of the
live corpus into staging, the prune pass, both staged-swap commits, and RSS
poller teardown — was folded into `model_load_approx_ms`, a residual computed by
subtraction in `finish.rs`. #5024 asks how much of a cold index is embedding, and
a separate proposal wants to seed a worktree's index by copying an indexed
clone's corpus and delta-reindexing. Neither could be sized against that residual.

## Resolution

Each of those stages now carries a coarse `Instant` delta — one pair per stage
per run, not per file — in a new `StageTimings` accumulator threaded
`runner` → `finish`. `other_ms` is the genuine unattributed remainder, and
`walk + stages + kg + other` partitions `elapsed_ms`. The breakdown goes to the
`reindex phase timings` log line and the `complete` SSE event's `timings` object.

`tests/reindex_stage_profile.rs` is an `#[ignore]`d harness that prints cold and
warm breakdowns against a throwaway `tempfile::TempDir` corpus with colocated
`.trusty-search/` storage, so every redb/HNSW artifact including staging stays
inside the temp dir. It never touches a live index or the running daemon (#402).

## Measurements

Release build, this workspace's own `crates/trusty-search/src/`, in-process ONNX
embedder, `defer_embed=false` so embedding is inline.

### Cold full reindex — 371 files, 5518 chunks, 330 142 ms

| stage | ms | % |
|---|---:|---:|
| walk | 34 | 0.0% |
| hash-cache load | 4 | 0.0% |
| corpus carryover copy | 49 | 0.0% |
| batch pipeline | 328 872 | 99.6% |
| prune deleted | 0 | 0.0% |
| HNSW commit | 18 | 0.0% |
| corpus commit | 71 | 0.0% |
| KG / symbol graph | 203 | 0.1% |
| RSS poller teardown | 836 | 0.3% |
| other | 55 | 0.0% |

Within the pipeline: parse 422 (0.1%), **embed 318 977 (96.6%)**, bm25 1642
(0.5%), HNSW upsert 4685 (1.4%).

### Warm incremental — 5 of 371 changed, 81 chunks, 12 639 ms

| stage | ms | % |
|---|---:|---:|
| walk | 9 | 0.1% |
| corpus carryover copy | 600 | 4.7% |
| batch pipeline | 10 717 | 84.8% |
| prune deleted | 222 | 1.8% |
| HNSW commit | 13 | 0.1% |
| corpus commit | 49 | 0.4% |
| KG / symbol graph | 416 | 3.3% |
| RSS poller teardown | 584 | 4.6% |
| other | 29 | 0.2% |

Within the pipeline: **embed 10 134 (80.2%)**, HNSW upsert 353 (2.8%).

A 119-file/1615-chunk corpus reproduces the shape: embed 96.5% cold, 86.2% warm.

### What the numbers say

**Ceiling A — global content-addressed embed cache.** Embed is 96.6% of a cold
index, so a cache with a 100% hit rate removes at most that. The 3.4% floor is
parse (still needed to compute content hashes), bm25, HNSW upsert, KG, corpus
write, and poller teardown — 11 165 ms against 330 142 ms, a ~29× ceiling.

**Ceiling B — corpus copy + delta reindex.** The warm pass is the delta path:
12 639 ms against a 330 142 ms cold index, so copy-plus-delta removes 96.2%. The
part that is fixed regardless of how many files changed is carryover 600 + prune
222 + KG 416 + poller 584 + commits 62 + walk 9 ≈ 1893 ms, i.e. **0.57% of a cold
index**. Everything above that floor is re-embedding the changed chunks, which is
ceiling A's problem, not B's.

**This contradicts the assumption the design was built on.** The KG/symbol-graph
rebuild that `meta_ops.rs:317-320` runs unconditionally — the thing expected to
cap a copy-based scheme — is 203 ms cold and 416 ms warm: 0.1% and 3.3%. It is
not the limiter. Neither is the corpus copy itself, at 49–600 ms for a
5518-chunk corpus. Both proposals bottom out on the same thing: embedding.

**Incidental finding, not fixed here.** RSS poller teardown is 584–952 ms of pure
tick-wait on every reindex — `stop_pollers` awaits join handles whose loops check
the stop flag only after a `tokio::time::interval` fires (1 s daemon poller,
500 ms embedderd). It is invisible on a cold index and 4.6–8.5% of a warm delta
pass. Naming the stage is all this PR does; a `select!` on a notify would remove
it, as its own outcome.

**Caveat on absolute numbers.** These use the in-process ONNX embedder, not the
Apple-Silicon python/MPS default (~2.4× faster). At that rate embed would still
be ~92% of a cold run — the share moves, the conclusion does not.

## Gates — rung 3

Localized behavior inside one crate: `service::reindex` internals plus one new
private module. No public API and no cross-crate surface changes — the only
externally visible change is additive keys on an existing SSE event.

docs: ADR-0031 transport by purpose — UDS inter-crate, one shared HTTP server external (#5046)

Records the transport architecture as it actually stands, plus the owner's
stated direction, and gives a reader a test that places a new endpoint without
asking.

The record corrects three things people currently believe:

- The STDIO/HTTP split does not describe today's topology. `trusty-memory
  serve --stdio` is a pure proxy to `POST /rpc` and never opens redb (#1078);
  trusty-search's and trusty-analyze's MCP servers are HTTP clients of their
  own daemons. Choosing STDIO today does not avoid HTTP, it adds a spawn in
  front of it.
- The recall divergence was a routing defect, not a transport one — two
  handlers over one store — compounded by a BM25 lane that was never enabled
  anywhere (zero index dirs across 102 palaces).
- Performance does not justify a transport change. Loopback floor is 0.26-0.6ms
  warm against 1.22ms recall and 7.72ms hybrid search; the prompt-context hook
  spends under 2% of its ~30ms on HTTP. The case rests on access control, port
  lifecycle, and failure surface instead.

The daemon is not negotiable either way: redb takes a cross-process exclusive
flock and its MVCC concurrent-reader property is in-process only, so
single-process store ownership is a correctness requirement (#1078, #59,
#3992). Per-session STDIO processes doing real work is the architecture #1078
abandoned. The daemon is also the shared-state host (1775MB RSS / 28 indexes).

Consistent with / Extends ADR-0018 rather than amending it — different axis
(bind-address reachability vs. which local transport one caller class uses),
and ADRs are immutable (DOC-46 4). Both of ADR-0018's costed objections to UDS
dissolve under this scope rather than being overridden.

Status is Proposed: UDS adoption is an open owner evaluation ("let's
consider"), all-or-nothing across inter-crate transport if taken, with
trusty-console as the single translation boundary.

Retention: `SessionRecord::terminal_at` records when a record entered

daemon's existing GC tick, ahead of the tmux probe so a machine without tmux
still sweeps. Two guards keep it safe: a record whose workspace directory still

`prune_orphaned_worktrees`'s protected set — dropping the record would collapse
both of that sweep's independent reads at once), and a record with no

evict the whole legacy backlog with no retention at all.

* fix(trusty-mpm): close the fail-open existence check in the retention sweep

HIGH: `Path::exists()` maps every stat error to `false`, so a permission error
on an ancestor, a stale NFS handle, or `EIO` from a departed volume read as "not
there" — and "not there" evicts. The `workspace_path` that leaves with the
record is what keeps `prune_orphaned_worktrees` from deleting the worktree, so

answers both mean KEEP; the doc that claimed the check "can only evict fewer
records" now describes what the code does. The probe is injected, so the error
branch is tested deterministically rather than provoked with real permissions.

Retention also now debounces like the two sibling destructive sweeps in the same

observation was not enough because "the workspace is gone" is a live filesystem
reading, and an external volume that unmounts between ticks answers Ok(false)

* fix(trusty-mpm): backfill legacy terminal records from their own history

Stamping `terminal_at = now` on records that predate the field grandfathered
the entire pre-existing backlog for a further seven days — 76 of 116 records on
the reporting machine, holding 76 of the slot numbers that put NUM in three
digits. The owner would install the fix and still see NUM 116.

`inferred_terminal_at` dates such a record from its latest evidence of life:
`last_activity_at` when set, else `created_at`, never earlier than `created_at`.
A timestamp in the future is not evidence — clock skew or corruption — and falls
back to `now`, so such a record gets a full window rather than being deleted on
the strength of a value that cannot be true. `RetentionVerdict::Stamp` now
carries the inferred time so the one call site that acts on it cannot silently
substitute its own.

The earlier reasoning against inference was right about the mechanism and wrong
about the goal: the auto-prune does decommission long-idle records, so this can
date a record earlier than it truly died — but only for records that predate the
field, and only toward clearing a backlog already weeks old. Ordering is
unchanged: the inferred date is written to disk first and only a LATER sweep can
evict, so the value is auditable before anything acts on it and the record still
passes the debounce and phase-3 re-validation.

Every safety property is untouched. `retention_verdict` still returns Keep on
`!is_terminal() || workspace_on_disk` BEFORE reading `terminal_at`, so the
workspace guard runs ahead of the backfill; `workspace_present` still resolves an
undetermined `try_exists` to present; the two-observation debounce and the phase-3
re-read are unchanged.

Measured against the live store (116 records, 40 shown): 27 evicted, 8 spared by
the workspace guard, 41 spared as genuinely recent — 36 of those created AND
decommissioned inside the last week. Max NUM 116 -> 89 on the first sweep cycle,
falling toward the shown-row count as the recent tombstones age out.

feat(trusty-mpm): `tm reinstall` — redeploy assets to every destination (#4991)

* feat(trusty-mpm): `tm reinstall` — redeploy assets to every destination

Asset deployment is two hops, and no command covered both across all the
destinations. Hop 1 materializes the compiled-in bundle into
`~/.trusty-mpm/framework/{agents,skills}`; hop 2 copies it into a deploy
target — and the targets are owned by different commands. `tm install`
writes the tm-managed `claude-config/agents` plus `~/.claude/skills`, a
daemon-managed session additionally writes `<project>/.claude/skills`, and
the standalone driver (`tm run`/`load`/`login`) writes
`~/.trusty-mpm/claude-config/` and never runs hop 1 at all. So an operator
who redeploys through one command still runs stale assets under another,
with nothing saying so.

`tm reinstall` runs hop 1 once and hop 2 into every destination, reporting
deployed / repaired / preserved / unchanged / failed per destination. A
destination that cannot be written is reported and the rest are still
served.

Ownership is the deployers' existing model, unchanged: a framework-owned
file that drifted or was corrupted is repaired (#4408), a file the operator
owns or edited is preserved. `--force` clobbers, backing every file up
first — agents through `agent_reset::reset_agents`, skills through the new
`skills::reconcile::force_adopt_bundled_skills`, whose roster match stays
the only admission test so an operator's own skill is never touched.

Assets always; the binary only with `--binary`, routed by install
provenance (#4033): a crates.io install upgrades through
`trusty_common::update`, a `cargo install --path` install rebuilds from its
recorded source directory, and an unclassifiable install refuses rather
than guessing.

feat(trusty-mpm): add `tm shell-init <zsh|bash|fish>` (#4986)

* feat(trusty-mpm): add `tm shell-init <zsh|bash|fish>`

`tm run <alias>` launches a session in the alias's repo directory, but a
process cannot change its parent shell's cwd — so when the session exits the
shell is still where it started and a later bare `tm` re-detects the wrong
project. Only a function sourced into the shell can fix that, so `tm` now
prints one.

`tm shell-init <shell>` writes a `tm` wrapper to stdout; the user installs it
themselves with `eval "$(tm shell-init zsh)"` (or `tm shell-init fish | source`).
PRINT-ONLY: nothing here or anywhere else in trusty-mpm writes to a shell rc
file.

The wrapper resolves the repo through the existing `tm path <alias>`, which
derives the path from `(alias, root)` and never persists it — so it resolves
identically after `tm run` exits. No state file, temp-file signal, or env-var
channel.

Correctness properties, each pinned by a test that runs the emitted snippet
under a real shell against a stub `tm`:

- the real exit status passes through unchanged
- `cd` happens only for `tm run`, never for any other subcommand
- a failing, empty, or stale `tm path` result produces no `cd` and no output —
  in particular `cd ""` (which jumps to $HOME) is impossible
- a `--task` value is never mistaken for the alias, and `--root` is forwarded
  to `tm path` so a non-default root resolves against the root the session used
- `command tm` inside the function, so it cannot recurse

zsh and bash share one POSIX body; fish gets real fish (`set -l`, `switch`,
`$status`, `end`). All three verified with `zsh -n`, `bash -n` (5.3 and 3.2),
`sh -n`, and `fish --no-execute`, and behaviorally under `set -eu`.

  `backfill_missing_vectors()` re-embeds them — idempotent, and a no-op on a

  to repair). Exposed through the new `palace_reembed` MCP tool, which runs

The write path is still asynchronous. Storing a drawer must not fail or hang
because the embedder is slow or down (#1970); the fix is to stop LOSING the

* fix(trusty-common): close two races in the #4906 durability path

Both found by adversarial review of PR #4975. Neither can make a drawer
undetectable — `embed_health()`'s set difference against the vector index is
the authoritative surface and needs no ledger — but both destroy the ledger
annotation in exactly the mass-failure scenario it was built for.

HIGH-1 — ledger lost update. `record` was load → retain → push → save with
nothing serialising it. Two tasks that both load before either saves each
publish their own single-row result and the later rename wins. That is the
design load, not a corner case: `spawn_deferred_embed` spawns one detached task
per drawer, all sharing a backoff schedule, so a burst against a broken
embedder lands every one of them in `record_loss` within milliseconds. Measured
with the new test: 1 of 16 rows survived.

The fix routes both `record` and `clear` through `json_rmw::update`, this
workspace's existing entry point for a locked load → mutate → publish cycle. It
is strictly stronger than the per-directory mutex first written here: an
advisory `flock` serialises separate PROCESSES as well as threads, it re-reads
under the lock rather than trusting a stale copy, and it fsyncs. It also
deletes the bespoke atomic-write helper this module carried.

One deliberate semantics change follows: `json_rmw` never fails open, so a
write over an unparseable ledger now returns `Err` and leaves the bytes alone
instead of replacing them. `load` keeps the opposite position and degrades to
empty — a read must never stop a palace opening. Losing an annotation costs
less than refusing access to the memories; destroying one costs more than
declining to write.

The module doc claimed the per-invocation tmp name made concurrent writers
safe. It never did — that stops a torn FILE, not a lost UPDATE. Corrected, with
the two hazards named separately.

HIGH-2 — spawn before push. `remember_with_options` fired the deferred task
before the drawer reached `self.drawers`, and `record_loss` refuses to write a
row for a drawer absent from that table. A task that failed before the push
therefore recorded nothing for a drawer about to become durable and
vector-less — the exact combination this lane exists to eliminate. The spawn
now happens after the redb commit and the in-memory push.

Tests: `concurrent_ledger_records_keep_every_row` (16 threads released by a
barrier; fails 1/16 without serialisation),
`concurrent_clear_and_record_do_not_lose_each_other`, and
`embed_ledger_load_degrades_to_empty_on_malformed_json` pinning both sides of
the read/write divergence.

fix(trusty-common): rank memory recall by relevance, not importance (#4904) (#4970)

L2/L3 scored a candidate `eff_importance * similarity`. The two factors are
not comparable in scale: inside one candidate pool, similarity spans 0.067
on average while `eff_importance` spans 0.436. Multiplying by it did not
weight the ranking, it replaced it — over 200 real hook queries the final
top-5 matched the similarity top-5 once.

Importance now tilts the score by at most 5% (`IMPORTANCE_TILT`), the
tiebreaker role its own docs described. Measured on the 1,272-drawer
trusty-tools palace with a 400-drawer self-retrieval probe (each drawer
queried with its own leading text, so the right answer is known):
recall@5 295/400 -> 351/400, recall@1 102/400 -> 291/400. 351 matches what
similarity alone scores, so the tilt costs nothing it used to buy.

L2 and L3 now share one `rank_score` instead of repeating the expression,
so deep recall cannot be left on an older formula.

Every L2 candidate is also traced with its score components before the
`top_k` truncation, on the `memory_recall_rank` target. Without it, a fact
absent from an injection looks identical whether it never entered the
candidate set, entered but ranked below the cutoff, or was never queried
for — and that is what made this issue undiagnosable until now.

fix(trusty-mpm): stop startup hygiene destroying gitignored content in the managed checkout (#4962)

`run_hygiene_for_base` ran `git reset --hard origin/<default>` on every
daemon start, gated on `git status --porcelain`. Porcelain never reports
gitignored paths, so gitignored working-tree content read as clean and was
silently overwritten whenever it collided with a path tracked by the target
commit. `write_recovery_ref` records only a commit SHA, so never-committed
content had no recovery path.

The update is now `git merge --ff-only`, which refuses rather than
overwrites, plus an explicit collision gate: refuse when any path the update
would write already exists untracked on disk. The gate is required because
`merge --ff-only` clobbers ignored files identically to `reset --hard` —
`--overwrite-ignore` is git's default and merge cannot disable it. Adding
`--ignored` to the dirty check was rejected: `target/` is gitignored and
present in any built checkout, so hygiene would become a permanent no-op.

Also refuses off the default branch, where the ahead-count validated
`origin/<checked-out>` while the operation moved the branch to
`origin/<default>`, and adds a `.trusty-mpm-no-hygiene` per-repo opt-out.

fix(trusty-mpm): branch session worktrees from fetched origin, not stale local main (#4958)

`create_session_worktree` ran `git worktree add -b session/<name> <path>`
with no start-point and no preceding fetch, so every session branch was cut
from the base checkout's local `HEAD`. On a machine whose local `main` had
not moved in three weeks, every session started 667 commits behind
`origin/main` and eight `session/*` branches all pointed at the same July
commit.

Resolve the repo's actual default branch (never hardcoded to `main`), fetch
`+refs/heads/<branch>:refs/remotes/origin/<branch>`, and pass
`origin/<branch>` as the start-point. A failed fetch degrades to the
last-known remote-tracking ref (or `HEAD`) and is `warn!`-logged with the
stale tip's sha and date, so an offline spawn cannot read as a clean
success. A repo with no remote still branches from `HEAD` without a warning.

Closes #4957

fix(trusty-common): stop a poisoned ENV_LOCK cascading 1 embedder failure into 7 (#4939)

Two independent defects made a single fastembed initialisation failure
present as a seven-test flake blocking the merge queue.

1. Cascade. Every env-touching embedder test acquired the shared
   `ENV_LOCK` with `.lock().unwrap()`. When
   `default_model_matches_sentence_transformers_reference` panicked, the
   `Mutex<()>` was poisoned and the six `resolve_*` tests — pure
   model/provider/cache-dir resolution that never touches fastembed —
   died on `PoisonError` instead of passing. Call sites now use
   `test_env::env_lock()`, which recovers via `PoisonError::into_inner`.
   The lock guards no data, and `EnvVarGuard::drop` restores the
   environment during the panicking test's unwind, so recovery is
   correct rather than a suppressed failure.

2. CI root cause. The Test job's fastembed model cache was keyed on
   `hashFiles('Cargo.lock')` — the whole lockfile — while its comment
   claimed the fastembed version, so any dependency bump rotated the key
   and left the cache cold. It was also saved by `actions/cache`'s post
   step, which is `post-if: success()` and therefore never fires on a
   failing job. Together those ratcheted: HuggingFace rate-limits the
   pre-seed, the model is missing, the accuracy gate fails, the job
   fails, the cache is never saved, the next run is cold again. The key
   now uses the fastembed version, the save is an explicit
   `actions/cache/save` that runs before any test, and the retry budget
   grows from 75s to ~250s. The pre-seed's warning no longer claims the
   model-dependent tests are `#[ignore]`-gated — that sentence was false
   and is what got this misdiagnosed.

Closes #4940

feat(memory): ADR-0028 Tier C write path — fact_key, default TTL, atomic retire-on-write (#4909)

* feat(memory): ADR-0028 Tier C write path — fact_key, default TTL, atomic retire-on-write

A point-in-time fact fails by the opposite mechanism from a standing rule
(ADR-0028 §C7): it stays ranked high long after it stopped being true,
because nothing retires it. The estate's most-injected drawer is a 19-day-old
session checkpoint reaching 44.8% of turns, pinning an origin/main SHA that
has been wrong for four weeks. #4884 built the slot index; this makes it a
write path.

Naming a fact_key is what makes a write Tier C. `RememberOptions` carries
`fact_key` and `expires_at`, and `remember_with_options` is the single
admission point — it is the only surface that can name a slot, so the gate is
unbypassable rather than conventional. Paths that build a Drawer by hand and
call `kg.upsert_drawer` directly (kuzu migration, git narrative, semantic
consolidation) never set the field and cannot claim a slot at all.

Admission fails CLOSED (D4). A key that breaks the `<domain>:<id>/<aspect>`
grammar, or an `expires_at` already elapsed, is refused Tier C and the drawer
is written exactly as the pre-ADR code would have written it — never
admitted-and-warned, because a privileged fact that goes stale is worse than
an ordinary stale drawer. A slot with no explicit expiry takes the 24-hour
default, so an admitted Tier C fact always declares how it ends. `live_while`
is out of scope per the ADR's own Implementation-scope section.

Retire-on-write is atomic in two senses. The read-decide-write sequence runs
inside the per-palace write mutex (#154), so no concurrent writer on the
palace interleaves; and both drawer rows commit in ONE redb transaction
(`upsert_drawers_atomic`), so a crash cannot land between retiring the
incumbent and landing the replacement. The mutex orders writers; the
transaction makes each write indivisible.

Two decisions the #4899 review left open, resolved here:

- The displaced drawer's own `fact_key` is cleared, not merely un-indexed.
  Leaving it would let `load_drawers()` show two drawers claiming one slot,
  and any consumer trusting the field over the index would read the retired
  fact as live. `expires_at` is cleared with it: on a Tier C drawer that field
  IS the retirement condition, supersession has discharged it, and leaving it
  set would make the demoted record self-destruct at the next sweep —
  contradicting D6 and orphaning the pointer #4887 will hang off it.

- The expiry sweeps skip drawers holding a slot. Read-time expiry (#4885)
  already stops an expired current fact being served, which is the demotion
  D6 asks for; deleting the row on top of that destroys the corrected record
  D6 preserves on evidence (109 hand-written amendment edges).

MCP: `memory_remember` and `memory_note` take both arguments and report the
tier they actually landed in — `tier: "C"|"E"`, plus `tier_c_refused` naming
the reason. Fail-closed that nobody can observe teaches a writer nothing. A
malformed `expires_at` string is a hard error (caller typo); semantic
refusals degrade.

Red-first proof. With the retirement disabled and only #4884's index
maintenance in place, 16 concurrent writers left 16 drawers all claiming
`pr:4818/state` and the displaced-field test failed with
`Some("pr:4818/state")` where `None` was required — the index-only version
looks correct until you read the rows. With the retirement restored but the
write guard released before the persist step, the same test failed with 3
claimants. Both pass with the change; a sequential test passes either way,
which is why the concurrent one exists.

Closes #4886

* feat(trusty-mpm): tm register takes the URL first with an optional alias (#4912)

`tm register <ALIAS> <URL>` becomes `tm register <URL> [ALIAS]`. With no
alias, one is derived from the URL as hyphen-joined `owner-repo`.

Both positional orders are accepted. Whichever positional is URL-shaped
(`://`, leading `git@`, or a `/`) is taken as the URL, so the legacy
`tm register <alias> <url>` keeps working. A valid alias matches
`^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9._-]*$`, which admits no `/`, `:`, or `@`, so the two
shapes cannot overlap.

Derivation delegates to `trusty_common::palace_id::owner_repo_from_git_remote`,
the workspace's existing git-URL parser, rather than adding a second one. It
already handles the `.git` suffix, trailing slashes, scp-syntax SSH,
non-GitHub hosts, and explicit ports, and it collapses the separator to a
hyphen because an alias becomes a path segment wherever it is consumed.

No discernible owner falls back to the bare repo slug; a host-only URL errors
with the explicit-alias escape hatch. A derived alias already bound to a
different URL refuses before `save()` is reached, so the registry file is
untouched.

* fix(trusty-agents-common): serialise the skill manifest's read-modify-write (#4881)

`SkillManifest::load`/`save` took no lock, so overlapping deploys raced on
load-modify-save. One process wrote a skill and saved its manifest; a slower
one then saved a snapshot taken before that write, dropping the entry. The
recorded checksum for that key then named an older revision than the bytes on
disk, and `deploy_one_file` read the mismatch as "the user hand-edited this"

future updates, silently. Three such skills were measured frozen on
2026-08-05, each byte-identical to an official historical main commit.

The agent ledger closed the identical race in #4409 with an fd_lock sidecar;
the skill ledger never got it. This ports it:

- `with_skill_manifest_lock` wraps the WHOLE cycle in `deploy_skills_filtered`
  and in the unmanaged-skill adoption, plus the two trusty-mpm writers
  (`tm doctor --fix-skills` repair, `tm catalog apply --prune`).
- `SkillManifest::save_if_current` refuses a save whose base snapshot has gone
  stale, so a writer that bypasses the advisory lock cannot clobber a newer
  record. The ledger is now the durable record of the user's customizations,
  so a stale write corrupts more than bookkeeping.
- The flock critical section is one implementation (`with_ledger_lock`) shared
  by both ledgers rather than two copies that can drift.

`memory_recall` and `memory_recall_deep` returned the same drawers for
every query. 19 distinct queries against a 1,066-drawer palace — including
a nonsense control — came back as one identical 5-drawer list, all at
score 1.0.

The store and the vector search were fine. The HTTP `/recall` route
discriminated correctly against the same palace at the same moment; only
the MCP tool path was broken, and the difference is the readiness gate at
tools/memory_ops.rs:417. When it reads `Warming` the handler takes
`recall_without_embedder`, which returns L0/L1 by raw importance and never
reads the query beyond an optional BM25 lane.

That gate was reading a flag with exactly one writer: the startup warm-up
task at main.rs:919. A single failed attempt left it `Warming` for the
daemon's whole life — observed live at 24,680 s uptime still reporting
`warming` while serving correct vector results over HTTP. The flag could
never recover, because a recall that degrades never calls `embedder()`,
so the path that reads the flag could never produce the event that
clears it.

Two things kept the flag from describing reality, and both are fixed:

- `AppState` carried its own embedder `OnceCell`, separate from
  `retrieval::shared_embedder()`. Startup latched readiness off one cell
  while every recall consumed the other, so the flag described an embedder
  the request path never touched — and the daemon loaded two ~90 MB ONNX
  sessions. `AppState::embedder` now delegates to the shared cell, and
  resolving it marks the daemon ready.
- The recall handlers now ask whether the embedder is actually live rather
  than trusting the latch alone, which breaks the deadlock above. This
  never triggers a cold init, so issue #1970's "never block a recall on
  embedder warm-up" guarantee is unchanged.

* feat(trusty-memory): enforce the Tier S cap of 20 facts and the 80-char form constraint

Tier S — the four hot predicates `is_alias_for`, `has_convention`, `is_fact`,
`is_shorthand_for` — is unranked, unfiltered, and placed first in the prompt
block, so every fact on it is paid for on every turn of every session. Its size
is a hard budget, not a preference (ADR-0028 D2/D8).

Adds `check_tier_s_admission` in `prompt_facts.rs`, next to `HOT_PREDICATES` and
the injection budget it governs:

- Cap of 20 (`TIER_S_MAX_FACTS`). The 21st write is refused, and the refusal
  names all 20 occupying facts with their subject/predicate plus
  `remove_prompt_fact` as the tool that retires one — a bare "cap exceeded"
  gives the caller nothing to act on.
- 80-character object limit (`TIER_S_MAX_OBJECT_CHARS`), reported with the
  actual length. A rule that does not fit is a document and belongs in
  `CLAUDE.md` behind a pointer.

Both refusals are fail-closed: the write never reaches storage.

Enforced on every path that can create a hot triple, not only the two obvious
ones. `POST /api/v1/palaces/{id}/kg` accepts an arbitrary predicate and is the
path trusty-mpm's provisioner seeds its identity `is_fact` through, so it was a
live bypass rather than a hypothetical one:

- `kg_assert` and `add_alias` MCP tools
- `discover_aliases` auto-discovery loop
- `MemoryService::kg_assert` (HTTP `POST /api/v1/palaces/{id}/kg`)
- `add_alias_handler` (HTTP `POST /api/v1/kg/aliases`)

Two counting rules the tests pin down. The cap is on ACTIVE facts, so a
retracted fact frees its slot immediately — retraction closes the interval
rather than deleting the row, and `gather_hot_triples` reads through
`list_active`. And re-asserting an already-active `(subject, predicate)` in the
same palace supersedes rather than adds, so it stays admitted at the cap;
without that an author who filled the surface could never fix a typo.

`discover_aliases` is the one bulk writer and stops at the cap instead of
aborting: aliases that fit are written, the rest come back in a new `rejected`
array with a single `rejected_reason`. A workspace with more crates than Tier S
has slots is ordinary — this one has — so aborting would make the tool unusable
here and strand the aliases written before the refusal.

Cold predicates are untouched: neither limit applies to ordinary KG writes,
which never reach the injected surface.

feat(trusty-common): fact_key slot index and read-time expiry enforcement (#4899)

ADR-0028 storage groundwork plus the retirement invariant it depends on.

#4884 — Drawer.fact_key + DRAWERS_BY_FACT_KEY

ADR-0028 D5 gives a Tier C fact a writer-chosen namespaced slot
(`pr:4818/state`); writing that slot retires its prior occupant, which is
what keeps the store self-limiting. The write path therefore has to ask
"who holds this slot?" once per write, and answering it from DRAWERS means
decoding every drawer row in the palace.

Adds `fact_key` to `Drawer` and `DrawerRecord`, and a `DRAWERS_BY_FACT_KEY`
secondary table modelled on TRIPLES_BY_OBJECT / TRIPLES_BY_PREDICATE:
maintained inside the same write transaction as the row it describes, so
no reader can observe the two disagreeing. `drawer_id_for_fact_key()` is
the point lookup. Nothing consumes it yet — the Tier C write path is a
later ticket — and nothing writes a non-None value.

Index maintenance is a diff, not an overwrite: the prior slot is read
before the row is replaced, and released only when the departing drawer
still owns it. Without that guard, deleting a drawer that had already lost
its slot to a newer writer would evict the live owner's entry and report a
taken slot as free. The single-op, batch, and import paths now all route
through the same two helpers rather than each open-coding an insert.

Purely additive on disk: no DRAWERS row is rewritten. A new
`PreFactKeyDrawerRecord` extends the positional-postcard fallback chain;
without that link the reader would skip to `PreTaskDrawerRecord` and
silently drop `completed_at`, marking finished tasks open again. The chain
itself moved into `decode_drawer_record` so the index path reads a row's
prior fact_key through the same walk instead of a second copy.

#4885 — enforce expires_at at read time

ADR-0028 §C8 says expires_at "is enforced nowhere". That is wrong: the
open-time sweep in `open_with_intent` prunes expired drawers at every
palace open (issue #61), `purge_expired` exists, and SessionEvent already
gets a 7-day default TTL.

The real gap is that expiry was consulted ONLY at open. Production opens
the palace once as OpenIntent::Writer and holds that handle for the
daemon's lifetime, so a drawer expiring mid-session kept being injected
until a restart. `retrieve_l0_l1`, `retrieve_l2_scoped`, and
`retrieve_l3_scoped` now drop expired drawers on every read, which is the
enforcement point ADR-0028 D4 asks for. It also closes a second gap:
`l1_drawers` is filled from the L1 cache snapshot, which the open-time
sweep never pruned — so an expired L1 drawer survived even a reopen.

The read paths filter without deleting. Deleting would need the write lock
on `handle.drawers` plus async I/O while retrieval holds a read guard over
the same RwLock, and it would let a failed cleanup fail a read. Filtering
cannot fail open; reclamation stays with purge_expired and the sweep. The
cost is that an expired drawer keeps its row and vector slot until a sweep
runs — storage, not correctness.

The sweep, purge_expired, and all three read paths now share one predicate,
`Drawer::is_expired_at`, instead of hand-copying the comparison. The sweep
still cannot simply call purge_expired: it runs inside `open_with_intent`
before any PalaceHandle exists, it is sync where purge_expired is async,
and the two delete through different mechanisms (delete_drawer_sync vs
forget, which also clears the vector index). Only the predicate was
duplicated, and that duplication is now gone.

Tests: the three read-time expiry tests were confirmed to fail against the

fix(trusty-search): a write-quarantined index performs no durable write (#4866)

* fix(trusty-search): a write-quarantined index performs no durable write

The #4122 write quarantine gated the ingest family only. `CodeIndexer` has a
second write family — the snapshot writers — whose enabling condition is
`self.corpus.is_none()`, which is exactly what quarantine guarantees. So the
shutdown flush of a quarantined index fell through `flush_corpus_to_disk` to
`save_chunks_to_disk` and wrote its deliberately-EMPTY in-memory corpus over
the legacy `chunks.json` snapshot, while the refusal diagnostic told the
operator "the on-disk corpus is untouched and still recoverable".

That snapshot is not inert: `JsonCorpusToRedbMigration` reads it at warm boot
to seed an empty redb, `service::server::status` reads its mtime for
`last_indexed`, and `commands::migrate_storage` relocates it. Emptying it
destroys a recovery source.

Gate the family rather than the `chunks.json` call: `refuse_durable_write`
covers `save_chunks_to_disk`, `flush_corpus_to_disk`, `save_vector_store`, and
`spawn_incremental_persist`. That also closes the HNSW graph, which the same
shutdown flush wrote — `build_store_for_entry` runs before the corpus open, so
the store is wired even on a quarantined index, and `UsearchStore::save`'s own
guards are inert below 1 000 on-disk vectors.

The gate keys on `corpus_open_failed`, never on `corpus.is_none()`, so
legitimate BM25-only / legacy indexers keep persisting their snapshots.

* fix(trusty-mpm): make the agent-cost persistence allowlist judge flags, not just subcommand names

The escape hatch resolved a git subcommand through git's global options and
then asked only "is the subcommand allowlisted?". Four shapes therefore passed
as persistence while executing an arbitrary program:

  git -c diff.external='cargo test' diff
  git -c protocol.ext.allow=always push ext::sh -c 'cargo test' HEAD
  git push --receive-pack='cargo test' /tmp/repo HEAD
  git diff <(cargo test)

Each is the same mistake — an unrecognised construct was allowed through — so
the classifier moves to its own module and is rebuilt structurally rather than
against those four strings. Three default-deny rules plus one enumerated set:

- the program must be `git` itself: no env-assignment prefix
  (GIT_SSH_COMMAND, GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF), no sudo, no env;
- global options are default-denied, allowing only -C/--git-dir/--work-tree/
  --no-pager/--no-optional-locks/--literal-pathspecs, so `-c` is rejected
  outright rather than having its values judged, and so are --config-env and
  --exec-path;
- any live shell metacharacter disqualifies: `$`/backtick outside single
  quotes, and `(`/`)`/`<`/`>` outside quotes entirely, which covers process
  substitution and redirection in both directions without recognising any
  spelling. Quoted occurrences stay legal so commit messages survive;
- arguments may not name a program: any `::` token is a remote-helper
  transport, and the --exec/--*-pack/--ext-diff/--textconv/--output families
  are rejected wherever they appear.

The post-subcommand rule is the one enumerated set, deliberately: a false
reject there strands the work this hatch exists to save, so ordinary flags
stay permissive.

`shell_lex::git_subcommand` is untouched. It exists for the deny side, where
skipping an unrecognised global option is the safe direction; here it is the
unsafe one, and reusing it is how `-c` got through.

- the key fell back agent_id -> session_id, and in the resolution case where
  transcript_path already points under subagents/ there is no agent_id — so

* fix(trusty-mpm): close the git option-abbreviation bypass in the persistence hatch

git's parse-options resolves any unambiguous PREFIX of a long option, so `--exe`
IS `--exec` and `--rece` IS `--receive-pack`. EXEC_OPTION_DENY matched names
exactly, so three abbreviated spellings classified as "persistence only" past the
agent-cost ceiling and executed the program they named. `--receive-pack` was not
even on the deny list — it rode the `-pack` SUFFIX rule, which an abbreviation
strips off entirely, so no suffix rule could ever have covered it. Reproduced on
git 2.54.0 against a real bare remote; all three ran the planted program.

Adding `--exe` and `--rece` would have been the third round of the same mistake,
so the post-subcommand long-option surface inverts to default-deny against
SAFE_LONG_OPTS, matching what rule 3 already did for globals. The abbreviation
question then stops needing an answer: an abbreviation of a dangerous option is
absent from the safe list and denied, and an abbreviation of a safe option is
denied too — a false reject in the harmless direction. The false-reject cost is
smaller than the original reasoning assumed: the hatch is not a general git CLI,
and `git add` / `git commit -m` / `git push` in their plain spellings still work.

Also in this change:

- The program check compared the BASENAME, so `./git`, `/tmp/evil/git`, and
  `../../tmp/evil/git` all answered "git" and a planted script by that name ran.
  It now requires the literal token `git`. Resolving the path instead would mean
  stat-ing from inside a PreToolUse hook and still could not tell a planted `git`
  on PATH from the real one, so the check matches what it can prove; PATH is a
  documented residual.
- The residual note claimed the on-disk exec route was confined to "the
  repository's own config". `-C` and `--git-dir` are allowed globals, so the repo
  is attacker-choosable in the same command — `git -C /tmp/evil diff` runs a
  `diff.external` from an attacker-chosen path. Note corrected, and a test pins
  the residual so it cannot be silently claimed closed.
- stop_reason now names the metacharacter rule and the single-quote fix, so
  `git commit -m "fix $ISSUE"` no longer denies without a hint — the retry burn
  that function exists to prevent.

ADR-0027 ticket T9. A Wing is the scope/ownership axis ("who") over rooms;
a Room stays the topic axis ("what"). This is what lets engineer/Planning
and pm/Planning coexist as distinct rooms without name mangling.

The ADR gated T9 on a #3064 consumer existing, because "a level nobody
reads is the defect" — Wing had zero construction sites since the day it
was written. The owner lifted the wait on #3064, so the reasoning is
honoured instead by shipping Wing WITH its own consumer: wing_list /
wing_create / wing_rename, an optional wing on memory_remember /
memory_recall / memory_list, and wing-scoped recall. No dark table.

Storage
- WINGS / WING_KEYS redb tables in the palace's kg.db, initialised in the
  same transaction as DRAWERS and ROOMS so the schema is never half-present.
- wing_identity.rs: canonical keys and UUIDv5 minting, mirroring
  room_identity. No I/O.
- store/wings.rs: record shape, default-wing seeding, create/rename/list,
  and the rooms-in-wing join.
- kg_redb/wing_ops.rs: insert-only accessors, except the put/remove pair
  that serves wing_rename — an explicit human act, unlike seeding.

Migration safety — naming, never reclassification
Every RoomRecord has carried DEFAULT_WING_ID since T1, so placing existing
rooms in the default wing needs no write to ROOMS at all: the migration
inserts ONE row describing a wing every room already points at. Zero
drawer rows change and zero room ids are rewritten, proven byte-for-byte
on both tables rather than by a decoded compare. Seeding probes by id, so
it is idempotent and a wing renamed between opens keeps its new name.

Wing is never required of a caller
No existing call site gains an argument. retrieve_l2 and recall keep their
signatures and delegate to the scoped implementations with RecallScope::All
or ::Room, reaching exactly the code that ran before. A wing-less write
resolves in the default wing, byte-identically to the previous line.

Scope boundaries fail closed
A wing that cannot be resolved admits NOTHING, not everything — a topic
filter that fails open shows extra rows, but a scope that fails open is a
leak, which is the #3064 criterion this anchors. At the MCP boundary the
posture flips to fail-loud: an unknown wing errors and names wing_list,
because a typo'd wing returning zero results reads as "no memories".

Deferred deliberately: wing_count on PalaceInfo. T8 owns the semantics of
that field (it had to choose between 1, absent/Option, or deprecated while
wings did not exist) and feat-rooms-surface is not on origin yet. Reporting
real wings there is a follow-up that must agree with T8's choice rather
than guess at it.

The test suite registered fixture roots in the operator's

Two paths reached production state, and neither was closed by the

fix(trusty-agents): persist slack pairing and make it completable headlessly (#4856)

Closes #4853. Closes #4854. Cutover epic #3852; Telegram precedent #467.

The Slack gateway went live but the pairing gate is unpassable: the owner DMs it, gets `:lock: Not paired. Send /slack-start to begin.`, runs `/slack-start`, and is told to run `/slack pair` in a REPL that does not exist under launchd. Separately, nothing persisted pairings, so even a successful pair died at the next restart.

## What changed

**#4853 — persistence.** `run_slack_bot` built `PairedChannels` fresh on every call and nothing wrote it to disk. Adds `paired_channels_state_path` / `load_paired_channels` / `save_paired_channels` over `~/.trusty-agents/state/slack-paired.json`, loaded on boot and saved on pair. Mirrors `telegram::pairing` (#467) closely: same user-level state dir, same atomic tmp+rename write, same fail-open load (missing or corrupt file degrades to empty and logs, never blocks boot).

**#4854 — headless completion.** Adds the pure predicate `should_auto_pair(channel, sender_is_known_to_rbac)`: a **DM** from a user **already in the Slack RBAC table** pairs itself. Both inbound paths go through one `ensure_paired` wrapper so they cannot drift.

**`/slack-start`** now branches on real state — already paired, unauthorized DM, or shared channel — instead of unconditionally describing the impossible REPL flow.

`record_listener_event` and its helpers moved to a new `slack/events.rs` because `handlers.rs` crossed the 500-SLOC cap. It is re-exported from `handlers`, so the #3852 call site and its tests are untouched.

## Trust model after this change

Unchanged where it matters, and stated plainly:

- **Persona access is gated per-USER by RBAC, not by pairing, and that is untouched.** `handle_message` already returns the static `VIRTUAL_CTO_MESSAGE` — no LLM call, no tool dispatch — for any user absent from `SlackRbacConfig`. RBAC is strictly stronger than pairing and remains the real boundary.
- **Pairing is a per-CHANNEL gate whose remaining job is controlling *where* an authorized user's output can land.** That job is fully preserved: every non-DM channel still requires an explicit code, so `cto-assistant` output cannot be steered into a room with arbitrary readers.
- **Auto-pair grants no new capability.** A DM channel is readable only by that one user and the bot. Auto-pairing it for a user who already holds an RBAC tier gives them exactly the persona they were already entitled to, in a room nobody else can read. An unauthorized user still cannot pair themselves — they are not in the table, so the predicate is false, and even if a channel were paired for them RBAC would still refuse them.
- DM detection uses the Slack channel-id kind prefix (`D` = IM, `C` = public, `G` = private/group), which Slack assigns and delivers over the authenticated Socket Mode socket — not attacker-controlled content. The prefix is used rather than the message event's `channel_type` because slash-command payloads do not carry `channel_type`, and both inbound paths must reach the same answer.

## Alternatives rejected

- **`tagent slack pair` CLI writing the persisted store.** The most general option, and the trust model would have been clean (shell access on the host, exactly what the REPL path assumes). Rejected because the running daemon holds the map in memory and must not be restarted — the CLI would not take effect without either a restart or adding a disk-re-read on every unpaired message. That is extra machinery on the hot rejection path to serve a case nobody is blocked on. The persistence added here is the foundation if we later want it.
- **Env allowlist of pre-approved channel/user ids.** Duplicates `SLACK_RBAC_USERS`, which already carries the authorization data, and would create a second source of truth for "who may talk to the bot" that can silently disagree with the first.
- **Dual-REPL / second Socket Mode connection.** Slack fans events across all open connections for an app, so routing becomes nondeterministic. Not attempted.

## Tests — and proof they bite

Seven new tests. Each was proven to catch the defect by reverting the fix and observing red, then restoring.

**Revert A — `load_paired_channels` forced to always return empty (the pre-fix behavior):**
```
test slack::tests::slack_paired_state_round_trip ... FAILED
assertion `left == right` failed: both pairings should survive the restart
  left: 0
 right: 2
```

**Revert B — `should_auto_pair` forced to `false` (pre-fix: no headless path):**
```
test slack::tests::auto_pair_allows_known_user_dm ... FAILED
assertion failed: should_auto_pair("D0A6V2W1M2R", true)
test result: FAILED. 3 passed; 1 failed
```

**Revert C — `should_auto_pair` forced to `true` (the naive "just drop the gate" shortcut this PR must not ship):**
```
test slack::tests::auto_pair_rejects_unknown_user_dm  ... FAILED
  an unknown user must not be able to pair themselves
test slack::tests::auto_pair_rejects_public_channel   ... FAILED
  a public channel must still require an explicit pairing code
test slack::tests::auto_pair_rejects_private_group    ... FAILED
  a private group must still require an explicit pairing code
test result: FAILED. 1 passed; 3 failed
```

The restart test is a genuine simulated restart: pair two channels, save, **drop the in-memory map entirely**, reload from disk, assert both survive.

## Gates — rung 5 (persistence + security boundary), crate-scoped, exit codes checked

```
GATE cargo test -p trusty-agents                          = 0
GATE cargo clippy -p trusty-agents --all-targets -Dwarnings= 0
GATE cargo fmt --check                                    = 0
GATE bash scripts/check_line_cap.sh                       = 0

fix(trusty-search): preserve --no-auto-discover across service install (#4823) (#4835)

* fix(trusty-search): preserve --no-auto-discover across service install (#4823)

`trusty-search service install` regenerated the launchd unit from a fixed
template, so an operator who deliberately disabled the auto-discovery scan
lost that setting the moment the unit was reinstalled — and hand-editing the
generated plist was itself undone by the next install. The setting could not
be made durable by any supported means.

The obvious remedy — adding TRUSTY_NO_AUTO_DISCOVER to PERSISTED_ENV_VARS —
would have crashed the daemon. The arg is declared as a clap `bool` with
`env = "TRUSTY_NO_AUTO_DISCOVER"`, which makes the CLI flag a presence flag
but routes the env var through strict FromStr<bool>. Copying the `=1` value
that already sits in many daemon.env files into the plist produces:

    error: invalid value '1' for '--no-auto-discover': [possible values: true, false]

and launchd then throttle-loops a daemon that never boots.

Three changes:

- `service install --no-auto-discover` writes the flag into the generated
  unit's ProgramArguments. A later `service install` preserves it and says so;
  re-enabling the scan requires an explicit `--auto-discover`, so a capability
  change is never a silent side effect of reinstalling. The suppression never
  travels as an EnvironmentVariables entry, so a generated unit cannot carry a
  value the daemon would refuse to parse.
- Operator tunables from PERSISTED_ENV_VARS that the installed unit already
  carried now survive regeneration instead of being blanked whenever
  `service install` runs from a shell exporting none of them. An exported
  value still wins.
- `--no-auto-discover` / TRUSTY_NO_AUTO_DISCOVER accepts 1/true/yes/on and
  0/false/no/off, fixing the footgun at its source so the spelling the README,
  the #314 changelog, and existing daemon.env files all use finally works.
  An unrecognised spelling stays an error rather than a silent false.

Closes #4823
