fix(trusty-agents): install the rustls CryptoProvider and let TAGENT_PROJECT_DIR beat exe inference (#4831)

Closes #4825
Closes #4826

Two defects that together made the Slack gateway unusable for the CTO Assistant cutover: it could not start, and had it started it would have answered against the wrong project.

## #4825 — startup panic on the first WSS handshake

A single `rustls 0.23.40` instance in the graph carries BOTH provider features — `ring` (reqwest's `rustls-tls` → `__rustls-ring`, `tokio-rustls`, `ureq`) and `aws-lc-rs` (the `aws-smithy-http-client` stack) — so rustls cannot auto-select and panics the moment `tokio-tungstenite` builds a `ClientConfig` from the process default. Nothing in the workspace called `install_default()`.

**Chosen fix: install the provider explicitly, not deduplicate the graph.** The two providers arrive from independent subtrees (HTTP client vs. AWS SDK), so dropping either means changing reqwest's TLS backend workspace-wide or dropping the Bedrock SDK — a far larger blast radius, and one a future dependency bump could silently undo. An explicit install is one call, immune to that, and auditable.

**Placement:** `runtime::run()`, not `main.rs` — `trusty-agents-local` also calls `run()`, and `main.rs` would have covered only the `tagent` binary. It sits ahead of the `config` / `mcp-serve` early dispatches because those make HTTPS calls too.

**Error handling: not `.ok()`.** `install_default` returns `Err` for exactly one reason — a provider was already installed — which is benign, so that value is discarded. What makes the discard safe is the postcondition check that follows: if the process still has no default provider, `install_crypto_provider` returns a startup error rather than letting the process reach a handshake and abort. A silently swallowed failure would have re-hidden this exact bug.

## #4826 — gateway resolved $HOME as the project

`detect_self_project_with_hint` honoured its env hint only if the hinted directory itself carried `.trusty-agents/agents/pm.toml`; otherwise it dropped the hint silently and walked up from `current_exe()`. Under launchd that walk reached `~/.trusty-agents/agents/pm.toml` and returned `/Users/masa`, beating both `TAGENT_PROJECT_DIR` and `WorkingDirectory`. An explicit hint is now honoured whenever it resolves to a real directory; marker-based inference remains the fallback for when no hint is given. An unresolvable hint still falls through to inference, with a warning.

## Tests

Both were confirmed to fail against the unfixed code before the fix landed.

`tests/slack_wss_crypto_provider.rs` drives the real Socket Mode connector against a local throwaway listener, captures the client's first flight, and asserts it is a well-formed TLS ClientHello — an invariant that only holds if the provider was resolved and used. Against the unfixed tree the same test panicked at `rustls-0.23.40/src/crypto/mod.rs:249:14` with the identical message from the production log, and no bytes reached the listener.

`detect_self_project_hint_beats_exe_inference` asserts the returned path equals the hint, not merely `is_some`. Against the unfixed tree:

```
assertion `left == right` failed: an explicitly-set project-dir hint must win over exe-path inference
  left: Some("/Users/masa")
 right: Some("/private/var/folders/…/cto")
```

## Live verification

**A green build proves nothing here, so the handshake was exercised for real.** A completed TLS + WebSocket handshake through the exact `tokio-tungstenite` connector the gateway uses:

```
LIVE WSS HANDSHAKE OK  url=wss://echo.websocket.org/  upgrade_status=101 Switching Protocols
```

The built binary was then run as `tagent --slack` with deliberately invalid tokens, under `env -i HOME=/Users/masa` so the `~/.trusty-agents/agents/pm.toml` marker that caused #4826 was present:

```
INFO trusty_agents::runtime::startup: trusty-agents v0.38.6 build #1
INFO trusty_agents::slack: Starting Slack bot in Socket Mode project=/private/tmp/…/fakecto
ERROR trusty_agents::slack: Slack socket error; reconnecting in 5s error=apps.connections.open failed: invalid_auth (status 200 OK)
```

No panic; startup completed; `project=` is the directory `TAGENT_PROJECT_DIR` named, not `$HOME` — #4826 reproduced-and-fixed live under the production condition.

**What is NOT verified, and what the owner must do.** The production Slack app A0AMPRM4W0J was deliberately not touched, so no real Socket Mode session was established. The invalid-token run reaches `apps.connections.open` (plain HTTPS via reqwest, which carries its own provider) and stops there — it never opens the `wss-primary.slack.com` socket. The Slack-specific leg therefore rests on the public-endpoint handshake above, which uses identical TLS mechanics and differs only in endpoint and auth.

The owner should confirm on the real deployment: install the binary, `launchctl kickstart -k gui/$UID/com.trusty.agents.slack`, and check `~/Library/Logs/trusty-agents/slack-stderr.log` shows `Slack Socket Mode connected` followed by a held connection with no panic, and a `project=` line naming the CTO directory rather than `/Users/masa`.

fix(trusty-common): stop dir_size_bytes aborting the daemon on a double panic (#4764) (#4818)

* fix(trusty-common): stop dir_size_bytes aborting the daemon on a double panic

`sys_metrics::dir_size_bytes` self-aborted the trusty-search daemon 40 times
in one week, roughly every 7 minutes under load.

Root cause: `std`'s `impl Drop for DirStream` (`sys/fs/unix.rs:1031`) asserts
that `closedir(3)` returned 0. The walk was recursive, so descending N levels
held N `ReadDir` handles alive at once. When the innermost `closedir` failed,
the panic originated inside a destructor; the resulting unwind ran the
enclosing handles' destructors, a second `closedir` failed identically, and a
panic raised while unwinding is a non-unwinding panic Rust aborts on
unconditionally (`core::panicking::panic_in_cleanup`).

Fix, in dependency order:

1. `walk_bounded` is iterative and holds at most ONE `ReadDir` alive at a
   time, dropping each directory handle before descending into its children.
   That removes the second destructor from the unwind path, demoting the
   abort to an ordinary recoverable panic. This is the load-bearing change.
2. `catch_unwind` then contains that panic and returns the partial byte total.
   On its own this would NOT have fixed anything — `catch_unwind` cannot
   intercept a double panic, because the abort happens before any catch frame
   is reached.
3. The walk is bounded: 64 levels deep, 30 s wall clock, partial total on
   either. The ticker cadence drops 10 s -> 60 s in both daemons, cutting
   exposure to the concurrent reindex/prune race sixfold at no visible cost.

Also adds `panic_hook::install_panic_logger`, wired into every
`init_tracing*` entry point: macOS `.ips` crash reports carry mangled Rust
symbols but not the panic payload, which is why the literal `closedir` errno
behind these aborts is still unknown. Any future abort now arrives with its
message, location, thread, and backtrace in the log stream.

trusty-memory runs the identical ticker against the identical function and is
covered by the same fix.

Closes #4764

* feat(trusty-mpm): declare the always-deploy agent set in framework-manifest.toml (#4760)

Deployment used to COMPUTE which agents always deploy, as the complement of
the `LANGUAGE_ENGINEERS` table: `language_agent_scope` emitted an exclude list
of the language engineers a project did not match, and everything else deployed
by virtue of not being in that one table. Nothing could be retired, because
there was no list to remove it from — `ops` has been marked DEPRECATED in
`agent-delegation.md` prose with zero code-level effect and still reached every
roster.

`framework-manifest.toml` makes that a declaration. It is the FRAMEWORK TIER of
the existing `manifest.toml` format, not a second format: a `HarnessManifest`
document parsed by the same `HarnessManifest::from_toml`, differing only in
that it is compiled into the binary and describes the framework's own catalog.

The one additive schema field is `[agent_categories]`, carrying five disjoint
stem lists. `AgentSet` could not carry this: `include` is a single flat,
un-categorised selection list with no dimension for a per-name gating rule, and
`[agents]` merges by whole-section replacement, so a project manifest that set
it at all would erase the framework declaration.

Composition:

    exclude = deprecated
            u ((language u framework) \ detected stacks)
            u (platform \ detected platforms)

A `universal` stem appears in no term, so nothing can exclude it. An unknown
project type (no stack marker at all) still keeps every language and framework
engineer, unchanged. Platform has no such fallback — that is the intended
behavior change.

* feat(trusty-mpm): gate framework engineers on framework markers, add elixir-engineer (#4760)

Owner ruling 2026-08-04. `language` and `framework` were two DECLARED
categories resolving through one gate, because four of the five framework
stems had markers that did not actually distinguish a framework:

  react-engineer    package.json                    (no framework marker at all)
  nextjs-engineer   next.config.* OR package.json   (fallback fires for any JS)
  svelte-engineer   svelte.config.* OR package.json (same fallback)
  phoenix-engineer  mix.exs                         (the ELIXIR marker)
  tauri-engineer    tauri.conf.json                 (genuinely framework-gated)

React ships no config file, and Phoenix ships nothing plain Elixir lacks, so
neither can be gated on a fixed path. Rather than invent a heuristic, this
adds a third marker form to `marker_present`: a CONTENT PROBE, written

the needle literally. Needles carry their surrounding syntax so a substring
match is an exact declaration match — `"react"` does not match `"react-dom"`,
and `{:phoenix,` does not match `{:phoenix_live_view,`. This reads a
declaration the project wrote about itself; it does not infer.

`elixir-engineer` is added in the `language` category, gated on `mix.exs` —

narrows to the web layer accordingly; a Phoenix project selects both.

* ci(release): build linux arm64 natively and stop reporting partial releases as success

The `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` leg was cross-compiled from the x86_64 runner
via zig. openssl-sys (reached through fastembed -> hf-hub -> native-tls, and
through git2/libgit2-sys) aborts under that setup — a host pkg-config cannot
answer questions about arm64 target libraries and no arm64 sysroot exists on
the runner — so no arm64 Linux binary of trusty-search has ever shipped.

Build the leg on GitHub's native `ubuntu-24.04-arm` runner instead. HOST ==
TARGET, so every `-sys` build script resolves against the runner's own arm64
libssl-dev exactly as the x86_64 leg does; cross-compilation, the actual root
difficulty, is removed rather than worked around. zig stays on the leg purely
to pin the glibc 2.17 floor.

The second half of the bug is that nobody noticed for four releases: the leg
was `best_effort`, so its failure never reached the run conclusion and the
workflow reported `success` while dropping an asset. Two changes:

- the arm64 Linux leg is no longer `best_effort` — it is a supported target
  (Graviton, arm64 containers) and now turns the run red when it fails;
- a new `release-completeness-audit` job compares produced assets against the
  requested build matrix, failing on a missing required leg and emitting a
  `::warning` plus a run-summary table for the one remaining best-effort leg
  (AL2023). A partial release can no longer look clean.

Also assert each built binary's machine type matches its target triple before
packaging, so a mislabelled asset can never ship under an arm64 name.

Refs #4087, #4125 (same real-failure-reported-as-success shape).

The native arm64 runner cleared the openssl-sys failure, and the leg then died
in `numkong` (usearch's SIMD backend): under zig's clang the baseline NEON
probe reports NK_TARGET_NEON=0 — clang rejects GCC's

`arm_neon.h` that only the NEON path includes (~20 `call to undeclared
function 'vdupq_n_s32'` errors; run 30941401868, job 92100578898).

with its SIMD paths off. Instead, ORT-bundling crates now build their arm64
leg with the runner's GCC — exactly the toolchain choice their x86_64 leg
already makes for the analogous AL2023/GCC-11 probe desync. Crates without
numkong keep the glibc-2.17 zigbuild leg, now native rather than cross.

fix(trusty-agents): gate ctrl_turn local-failure recovery on the failure, not a preference (#4788) (#4793)

## The defect

`run_ctrl_turn_via_rest` in `crates/trusty-agents/src/ctrl/ctrl_turn/dispatch.rs` — the standalone / no-PM-attached ctrl REPL's conversational surface — carried the error arm

```rust
Err(e) if local_qualifies && local_cfg.fallback_on_error => { … }
Err(e) => return Err(e),
```

byte-identical to the arm #4779 replaced on `run_pm_task_with_history`. That PR's changelog fragment explicitly scoped its guarantee to the one path and named this one as still unfixed.

`local_qualifies` ANDs in `local_inference.enabled`, so a user who sets that to `false` gets **no retry ever** — the setting meaning *avoid Ollama* was exactly what guaranteed an Ollama transport error was unrecoverable. Combined with any on-disk ctrl config still carrying an `ollama/` model slug, a raw

```
error sending request for url (http://localhost:11434/v1/chat/completions): Connection refused (os error 61)
```

reached the user as their assistant's reply. The owner hit exactly this on the sibling path.

## The fix

Both conversational surfaces now share **one** decision function — `local_fallback::local_failure_action`, introduced by #4779 — reached from ctrl_turn via a `pub(crate)` re-export rather than a copy. Its contract is unchanged: `Propagate` when the failure is not a local-adapter transport failure, `RetryRemote(model)` when a genuinely distinct remote model is configured, `Explain` otherwise. **No preference flag is an input to whether recovery happens.**

Genuine API errors (429/401/500) from either a local or a remote model, and remote transport failures, still propagate unchanged.

Two deliberate deviations from a blind copy of #4779, both about *this* route's specifics:

- **The retry keeps `registry_arc`** rather than calling `local_fallback::retry_remote`. That helper deliberately retries with an empty registry (the PM route's conversational fast path needs no tools), but this route's tools drive the end-of-turn side-effect drain — `start_pm` / `initiate_self_task` / `stop_task`. Dropping them on the retry would be a silent regression.
- **`effective_ctrl_turn_model` is extracted** so the tests exercise the actual routing instead of restating it. It pins the mechanism the old flag-gated arm missed: with the gate OFF the route does **not** stop attempting local models — it falls through to the agent's OWN configured model, which for any `ollama/` slug is itself local.

`fallback_on_error` is now consulted by no dispatch path at all; it survives only as a `/local` REPL readout, and `local_fallback.rs`'s doc comment (which named this route as a remaining consumer) is corrected to say so.

## Tests

Mirrors #4779's test approach for this path — four tests in `ctrl::ctrl_turn::dispatch::tests`, driving the same two inputs the production arm computes:

| Test | Covers |
|---|---|
| `ctrl_turn_recovers_in_both_local_gate_states` | **both `local_inference.enabled` states** crossed with a local transport failure; recovery asserted in both, and the message must not leak `Connection refused` / `os error` |
| `ctrl_turn_gate_on_falls_back_to_a_distinct_remote_model` | the retry target is genuinely remote, never the slug that just failed |
| `ctrl_turn_gate_off_still_attempts_the_agents_own_local_model` | the gate-off fall-through that produced the unrecoverable local call |
| `ctrl_turn_propagates_real_errors` | a remote transport failure and a local server that *answered* with an error both propagate |

## Changelog

New fragment `crates/trusty-agents/changelog.d/4788-ctrl-turn-local-fallback.md`. #4779's fragment (`3766-ctrl-local-model-fallback.md`) is still in `changelog.d` and unreleased, so its "the `ctrl_turn::dispatch` path carries the same defect and is NOT fixed here" scoping is updated — the guarantee now covers both surfaces.

docs(instructions): retire the blocking CI wait — agents push, report, stop (#4795)

Closes #4792

## The contradiction

Two shipped rules pointed opposite ways. The bundled instructions told agents to block on `gh pr checks <pr> --watch --fail-fast` in the foreground and never end their turn until CI settled. The standing rule for this repo forbids `--watch` outright, because it streams check output into the agent context — one engineer burned 546k tokens over 54 minutes on PR #4759.

(`--watch` runs fine; an explicit bash `timeout` raises the 120s default toward the 600000ms ceiling. The defect is context cost, not runnability. That distinction is stated inline in the new text so nobody "restores" the old advice on runnability grounds.)

## The ruling, as implemented

**Push, report, stop.** An agent finishing work pushes, takes a ONE-SHOT status read (`gh pr view` / `gh pr checks`, no `--watch`), reports, and ends its turn. It does not block on CI. The PM re-engages when CI settles.

The #2833 parked-subagent concern is still real — the remedy moved to the PM side. The PM instructions section is renamed **"Parked-Subagent Re-Engagement"** and now says plainly that a hand-back naming pending CI is correct behavior, not a park, and must not be nudged back into a blocking wait. A genuine park (goal unmet + a backgrounded wait the agent expects to wake it) is still detected and still nudged.

Own-gate commands are unchanged: builds, test suites, and release cuts still block in the FOREGROUND and hold the turn until they exit.

## Two operational facts folded into the one-shot read

- **`bucket` can report a false DONE.** Under GitHub API eventual-consistency lag a check surfaces as bucketed-complete before it has settled — cross-check `state`.
- **Repeated `gh pr update-branch` is a treadmill.** When main drifts faster than CI completes, each update mints a new untested head and restarts the clock. Merge the head that is actually green; BEHIND is not a correctness gate.

## The sweep

An inconsistent set is what produced the contradiction, so every mirrored copy moved together:

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `crates/trusty-mpm/src/assets/agents/BASE-AGENT.md` | "Foreground Execution — NEVER End Your Turn To Wait" + "chunked-repoll" replaced by "Finishing Work — Push, Report, Stop" |
| `crates/trusty-mpm/src/assets/agents/BASE-ENGINEER.md` | gate paragraph now points at the new section name and states the CI exception |
| `crates/trusty-mpm/src/assets/agents/version-control.md` | "CI Waits — Push, Report, Stop; NEVER Block" |
| `crates/trusty-mpm/src/assets/agents/local-ops.md` | "Long Waits — Block On Your Own Gates, Never On CI" |
| `crates/trusty-mpm/src/assets/instructions/sections/core.md` | "Parked-Subagent Re-Engagement (issues #2833, #4792)" |
| `crates/trusty-mpm/src/assets/skills/tm-delegation-patterns.md` | "Long-Wait Delegation" rewritten to brief both halves |
| `crates/trusty-code/src/assets/agents/{BASE-AGENT,BASE-ENGINEER,local-ops}.md` | asset mirror, kept byte-identical (verified with `diff`) |
| `crates/trusty-mpm/src/core/testdata/pm-prompt-*.md` | 3 golden snapshots regenerated via `UPDATE_GOLDEN=1` |
| `crates/trusty-mpm/src/core/bundle_tests.rs` | literal-string assertions updated to the new text, plus a new negative assertion that `--watch --fail-fast` cannot come back through any layer |
| `crates/trusty-mpm/src/core/idle_nudge.rs` | `DEFAULT_NUDGE_MESSAGE` no longer tells a stalled pane to run `gh pr checks --watch` |

Not touched, deliberately: `core::idle_parking` phrase detection. It matches parking *idioms* ("standing by", "will report back") which remain wrong under the new doctrine — a push-report-stop hand-back does not trip it.

fix(trusty-agents): never surface a raw Connection refused as ctrl's reply (refs #3766) (#4779)

## The live defect

The owner asked the Concierge for a status report and got this back as the assistant's reply:

```
conversational handler failed: raw chat completion POST failed: error sending request
for url (http://localhost:11434/v1/chat/completions): client error (Connect):
tcp connect error: Connection refused (os error 61)
```

Three defects on the same path produced it.

**1 — ctrl's bundled templates pinned a LOCAL model.** `ctrl.toml:12` and `ctrl/agent.toml:14` both declared `model = "ollama/qwen3:30b"`, and `adapter_for_model()` routes any `ollama/` slug to `OllamaAdapter` at `localhost:11434`. Re-provisioning from the repo restored that every time.

**2 — recovery was gated on a preference, not on the failure.** The error arm was `Err(e) if local_qualifies && local_cfg.fallback_on_error`. `local_qualifies` conflates two unrelated questions: "should I *prefer* a local model" and "am I *allowed* to recover from an error". The owner's `local_inference.enabled = false` (Bob's 2026-07-24 "we should not be using ollama for anything right now") forces `local_qualifies = false` on every turn — so the setting meaning **avoid Ollama** was precisely what guaranteed an Ollama transport error was **unrecoverable**. The arm never fired and `return Err(e)` leaked the transport error verbatim.

**3 — the fallback could not succeed by construction.** Even when it did fire, it retried `pm_cfg.agent.model` — which for a locally-configured agent is the *same* unreachable slug.

## The fix

- Both ctrl templates now carry the bare `claude-sonnet-4-6` that every other bundled agent uses. Which provider actually serves it is decided at runtime — see the routing note below.
- Recovery now gates on the **failure**: a transport-level failure (`reqwest::Error` carrying no HTTP status — nothing was received) of a model that resolved to a **local** adapter. No preference flag participates, so no setting can switch error recovery off.
- The retry target is a **proven-remote** model. When no distinct remote model is configured, the user gets an actionable message naming the unreachable host and the config key to change — never the transport error.

Genuine API errors (429, 401, 500, malformed request) from either a local or a remote model still propagate unchanged; only transport failures are recovered.

The recovery policy is split into `dispatch/local_fallback.rs` so `history.rs` stays under the 500-SLOC production cap (it was 486 SLOC at base and the cap is mechanically enforced).

### Correction — provider routing is NOT pinned by the TOML

An earlier revision of this PR (and the message of the first commit, `b66ff753`) claimed that ctrl's `[llm] use_anthropic_direct = false` makes the bare Sonnet slug resolve to `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6` on OpenRouter *deterministically*. **That was wrong**, and code-critic caught it. The truth:

- `pick_credentials()` (`llm/credentials.rs:105-109`) resolves in the order **ClaudeCode > AnthropicDirect > OpenRouter** — AnthropicDirect wins whenever `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` resolves via env, `.env.local`, or the secure store.
- `apply_credential_routing()` (`ctrl/config.rs:481`) then sets `cfg.llm.use_anthropic_direct = true` **unconditionally** for that branch, overwriting the TOML value before the conversational fast path ever reads it (call site: `history.rs:92`).

So the TOML value is a **default, not a routing guarantee**. Commit `7d63c319` corrects the template comments to say this. The model-slug fix stands on its own merits — it removes a local slug — but it does not, by itself, pin the provider.

## Scope notes — please read before closing #3766

**This is `Refs #3766`, not `Closes`.** It fixes ctrl's instance only. Two parts of the issue's premise turned out to be wrong, and the issue should be re-scoped rather than left as-is:

- **The bare `claude-sonnet-4-6` slugs #3766 lists as defective are NOT defective.** It names `assistant/agent.toml`, `izzie/agent.toml`, `izzie.toml`, and `personal-assistant.toml` as hardcoded sites needing replacement. `qualify_openrouter_model` (`llm/credentials.rs:188`) already converts a bare `claude-sonnet-4-6` to `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6` — the genuine OpenRouter Sonnet id — whenever credentials resolve to OpenRouter (asserted by `qualifies_bare_claude_id_for_openrouter`). Those 20+ agents carry the crate's supported spelling; changing them would be a no-op at best.
- **An `openrouter/`-prefixed slug would BREAK trusty-agents.** The crate has no `openrouter/` prefix handling at all — `adapter_for_model()` handles `bedrock/`, `ollama/`, and `fireworks/` only, and nothing strips an `openrouter/` prefix. Such a slug would fall through to the `contains("anthropic")` heuristic and be sent as a literal model id. (The `openrouter/<id>` convention is real but lives in **trusty-review**, a different crate.)
- **#3766's actual ask is untouched** — deferring model/provider to a single policy file that provisioning respects. That is a design change, not a bug fix, and was explicitly not authorized here. So is adding `openrouter/` prefix support.

## Follow-up found, deliberately not fixed here

`crates/trusty-agents/src/ctrl/ctrl_turn/dispatch.rs:210` carries the **byte-identical** buggy gate — `Err(e) if local_qualifies && local_cfg.fallback_on_error` — on the other ctrl dispatch path, which drives the standalone / no-PM-attached ctrl REPL. That is a live, user-reachable conversational surface with the same failure mode. Left alone to keep this PR reviewable; **it needs its own ticket.** The changelog fragment scopes its claim accordingly — this PR does not assert a system-wide guarantee.

`local_inference.fallback_on_error` no longer influences the fixed path. It is **not** dead: `ctrl_turn::dispatch` still honours it and the `/local` REPL command reports it, so the field stays.

Phase 1 of the Tart VM testing harness: the one unverified mechanism in the whole
design — host `git ls-files` -> `tar` -> `tart exec -i` -> guest unpack -> build —
now has a real measurement behind it instead of an argument.

## Transport verified end-to-end

`vmtest-harness/spike/spike-transport.sh` exits 0 and its three checkpoint lines
report a streamed byte count over the 80,000,000 threshold, the guest's own
`trusty-search --version`, and zero surviving VMs:

    STREAMED_BYTES 96788480 FILES 5337
    trusty-search 0.40.0
    TART_LIST vmtest-spike-* entries after teardown: 0

96,788,480 bytes / 5,337 files streamed host->guest, unpacked with an exact
file-count match, `trusty-search 0.40.0` built and installed in the guest from the
unpacked tree, and torn down with zero survivors. The host repo is never mounted in
either direction; source reaches the guest only as a tar stream. Teardown is
`vm_request_stop` (guest `sync; sync`, then `tart stop` with its status DISCARDED)
-> `vm_wait_for_stopped` -> `vm_delete`, from a trap, on every exit path. DOC-1
§14's headline gap and devil's-advocate critique #9 are retired; DOC-1 D4's fallback
re-ordering to (b) -> (c) -> (a) is NOT triggered.

## Pattern (c)'s uncommitted-work property — validated, and it HOLDS

That first run streamed a CLEAN worktree, so `-o` contributed zero files and
`git ls-files -co --exclude-standard`'s defining property — that it includes
UNCOMMITTED work — was never exercised. That property is the entire reason pattern
(c) exists rather than the slower, already-measured pattern (b). A second run
against a deliberately dirtied worktree closes it. Observed, not claimed:

  sentinel 1  tracked file + appended sentinel  -> PRESENT. Last line matches AND
              whole-file cksum equals the host's (4176744393 641), so `-c` is
              reading working-tree content, not HEAD content. An implementation
              built on `git archive HEAD` passes every file-count check in this
              phase and fails this assertion.
  sentinel 2  untracked, non-ignored file       -> PRESENT with exact content.
              This is the `-o` half, which contributed 0 files to the clean run.
  sentinel 3  gitignored file                   -> ABSENT. Path absent, ignored
              parent directory absent, and `grep -rl` over the entire 92 MB
              delivered tree finds 0 occurrences. `--exclude-standard` is what
              makes `-o` safe; without it `-o` enumerates target/ and the payload
              goes from ~92 MB to tens of GB. The pre-existing `test -d …/target`
              check passes vacuously on a host that has never built. This one
              cannot, because the file is created by the run.

96,819,200 bytes / 5,339 files, against the clean run's 96,788,480 / 5,337. Both
deltas fully decomposed: +2 files = +1 tracked fixture (committed so `-c` lists it)
+1 untracked fixture, the ignored fixture contributing 0; +30,720 B = 30 tar blocks.

`--dirty-check` is an opt-in mode. Default behaviour is unchanged and still never
mutates the host worktree. Fixture restore runs from the same trap chain as the VM
teardown and runs before it, so a VM that refuses to stop cannot also cost the host
its worktree; a non-empty `git status --porcelain` after restore is fatal (exit 70),
not a warning. Verified after the run: worktree clean, no fixture committed.

**Scope helpers** — `tsv_scope_crate_dirs`, `tsv_scope_packages`, `tsv_expect`. `tsv_scope_crate_dirs` carries the **§F-3 dedupe tripwire**: it asserts its own postcondition before emitting, dying **60** and *naming the duplicated values* if it ever emits a `crate_dir` twice. **Two integrity pre-checks**, ahead of §9.6's six steps, each enforcing something §9 already states and each dying **60**: every data row has **nine fields** (§9.1, P4-T1's acceptance made permanent instead of one-shot), and **no duplicate `(package, binary)` key** (§9.2 makes it the composite primary key). * fix(vmtest-harness): probe daemon liveness on the body, not the status code

## A real coverage gap closed

`trusty-analyze` was never proven able to serve. `verify_stack_doctor`'s health term accepts `down` for any plist-less launchd member, and `down` is what every daemon reports pre-start, so that term was vacuous for analyze. The other four daemons were separately proven live by the liveness probe; analyze was not. It is now probed — five of five.

## The 200-only rule replaced with body-based classification

This matches what the product settled in #4246: `trusty-analyze` answers 503 + `status:"degraded"` where `trusty-review` answers 200 + the same body, so the status code is not the signal.

The new predicate newly accepts only a non-2xx code carrying a well-formed body. It still fails on:

- no address
- no HTTP response at all
- unparseable JSON
- absent, empty, or non-string `.status`
- `.status` in {`down`, `error`, `unhealthy`}

## `tctl stack health --json` was evaluated as a delegate and declined

`trusty-mpm` is deliberately unprobed by the product (`OwnVerb` → `unknown`, #4246), though it does answer `/health` on 7880 — which the oracle's own probe reaches and proves. Delegating would have lost an assertion. The product's classification rule was adopted; its command was not. `stack health` is now logged in the input snapshot, never asserted on.

## RC-1 unchanged, now on evidence

The substitute recovers uniform body-based classification but cannot give the envelope — no `version`, no per-daemon body, no `service` discriminator — so the #3364 squatter-collision class stays open and is closable only by the product change.

## An ordering hazard recorded

Adds an opt-in `--degraded-check` fault-injection mode to the vmtest harness. Default behaviour is unchanged: without the flag, nothing about the existing run path differs.

## Both directions, one run, one predicate

**Positive direction.** With `trusty-search` stopped and its unreachability confirmed by polling first, `trusty-analyze` returned HTTP 503 with `{"status":"degraded","version":"0.8.0","search_reachable":false}`. The predicate accepted it and the run continued to exit 0.

**Negative direction.** `trusty-review` SIGKILLed produced `curl 000`, and the run failed with exit 60 — from the *same* verdict run that accepted the 503. Both directions hold in one run of one predicate.

## Why SIGKILL is load-bearing

Every daemon removes its own `http_addr` on graceful shutdown. A `tctl stop`-ed daemon can therefore never reach `curl 000` — its address is gone before the probe runs, so the harness reports "no address recorded" instead. The obvious implementation would have silently tested the wrong branch.

`verify_daemon_liveness` re-runs `tctl start --json`, which would have resurrected the daemon the fault had just killed. It is split at exactly that call into `_verify_daemon_set` / `_verify_liveness_verdict` / `_verify_probe_liveness`. Predicate logic is unchanged — the check exercises shipped code, which is why the result transfers to the default path.

- unparseable body

* fix(trusty-search): close four review findings on the reindex resume checkpoint (#4721)

PR #4721 (`4cc249fb`, shipped in trusty-search 0.42.0) landed
resume-from-checkpoint with four advisory findings against it. All four are on
the live reindex data path, so they are production defects rather than cleanup.

1. Separator-free config fingerprint. `name=value;` framing with `,`-joined
   lists is not injective: `exclude_globs = ["a","b"]` and `["a,b"]` hashed
   identically, and a value containing `;name=` forged a field boundary
   outright. A collision means a checkpoint is accepted as valid for a
   configuration it was not built under. Every field and list element is now
   length-prefixed (no separator byte is safe — all of them are legal inside a
   glob or a path), and paths are absorbed as raw `OsStr` bytes rather than a
   lossy UTF-8 rendering. `CHECKPOINT_SCHEMA_VERSION` bumped 1 → 2 so records
   written by 0.42.0 invalidate on the version gate and fall back to a full
   reindex.

2. Env-mutating test. `resume_kill_switch_disables_adoption` set
   `TRUSTY_REINDEX_RESUME` in-process under `#[serial]`, which does not exclude
   the binary's non-serial tests. It now runs alone in a child process with the
   variable supplied via `Command::env` at spawn — the #4213 technique, factored
   out of `root_hijack_tests` into a shared `test_isolation` helper. The two
   unit-level env tests are replaced by pure parse functions plus one isolated
   test that pins the variable NAMES.

3. Staging-corpus double-open. Sequential in practice (the probe's handle was
   dropped inside its blocking task before the adoption re-opened the file), so
   never two live handles — but redb locks the file exclusively, so the two
   opens were mutually exclusive by construction, and a failure of the second
   was swallowed into `Ok(None)`, silently abandoning the resume. The probe now
   hands its open handle to the adoption; the file is opened once.

4. Checkpoint-exclusion enforced by call order. Clearing the record needed the
   installed store and releasing the handle had to precede the rename — two
   statements whose order was load-bearing and unguarded. They are now one
   operation yielding the `PromotionRelease` token the rename requires, with a
   fallback clear on the released file when the in-store clear cannot be
   confirmed (the #4718 `BoundedRestoreOutcome` pattern).

Three independent defects turned a healthy Python/MPS embedding backend into a
permanent, unreported CPU/ort fallback on nearly every daemon start.

1. A timeout was treated as proof the venv is broken.
   `verify_full_import_smoke` ran `import sentence_transformers` under a flat
   10s budget while the daemon warm-booted hundreds of indexes, so torch's
   import routinely exceeded it under purely self-inflicted contention.
   `ensure_venv_checked` read that `false` as "corrupted" and rebuilt an intact
   venv. Rechecks now return a three-state `RecheckOutcome`: a timeout is
   `Indeterminate` (retried once with a much larger budget, then reused), never
   `Failed`. Same "slow is not broken" classification #4333 applied to a corpus
   open timeout.

2. `uv` was looked up on PATH only, and the daemon's PATH lacks Homebrew.
   `locate_uv` used a bare `which::which("uv")`; `uv` lives in
   /opt/homebrew/bin, which launchd's minimal PATH omits. Every needless
   rebuild from defect 1 hard-failed and pinned the daemon on ort for its
   lifetime. Now resolved through `trusty_common::bin_resolve::resolve_binary`,
   the shared resolver #1298 added for exactly this bug class — it was simply
   never wired up here.

   `embedder_bootstrap` was reported and aggregated nowhere, so `Failed` and

   existing degraded condition, following #1870/#3408/#3706. `embedder:
   "ready"` is unchanged — it describes the active backend, which really is
   ready; what was missing was "we did not get the backend we asked for".

`core::claude_md_sections` is explicitly reader-only, so every write to a
project's `CLAUDE.md` has been performed by hand against a grammar only the
reader knows. Prose cannot be idempotent: the same hand-merged pattern stacked

  writer asks `CustomizationTier::permits` rather than carrying its own list,
  matching the reader's "the package, and only the package" doctrine.
- Every refusal (protected section, empty body, a marker line inside the body,
  an unpaired marker in the host, an unreadable host) leaves the file
  byte-identical and the bundled section in force.
- `ensure_compiled_pointer` records where the composed prompt lands, using
  delimiters deliberately outside the `TRUSTY-MPM:` grammar so the reader sees
  no override and raises no diagnostic.

The grammar is not duplicated. The writer borrows the reader's recogniser via
three new `pub(crate)` accessors (`SUPPORTED_VERSION`, `contains_marker_line`,
`locate_blocks`), so a writer/reader divergence cannot be expressed.

fix(ci): blame the right diff, and re-check main on the registry's clock (#4736)

The `PR version bump vs crates.io` gate diffed from
`github.event.pull_request.base.sha` — the base tip frozen when the PR was
last opened or synchronized. `actions/checkout` resolves a pull_request to
`refs/pull/N/merge`, whose first parent is CURRENT main, so the two drift
apart the moment anything else merges and the diff spans every commit main
took in between. Run 30839255128 failed PR #4666 — two files under
docs/specs/ — with `[FAIL] trusty-common 0.27.0`, ~20 commits of someone
else's work swept into its diff. Rebasing "fixed" it only by moving the base
past the innocent commits.

Diff from the base BRANCH as it is now instead. The merge base is then the
merge ref's own first parent, so the range is exactly what the PR
contributes to the merged result. HEAD stays the merge ref on purpose: it
evaluates the post-merge tree, so a PR touching `crates/X/src/**` while main
independently bumps X reads the bumped version and passes.

On a real failure the gate now names the commits that touched the crate's
src. #4666's author had no way to tell "my change" from "main's change"
without bisecting by hand.

Separately, the post-merge authority compares two moving parts — main's tree
and crates.io — but only ever fired when the repo moved. `cargo publish`
happens out of band, so a green main can go drifted with no commit to
trigger anything: parity passed at 1ec38321 17:13Z, trusty-common 0.27.0
went live at 17:21:48Z, and nothing re-asked until an unrelated push hours
later. Add a 3-hourly schedule so the question is re-asked on the registry's
clock, and a notify job that files a tracking issue when the main-side check
does not come out green — a red square on a scheduled run nobody opened is
not loud.

No version bump accompanies this: the published trusty-common 0.27.0 tarball
is byte-identical to main's src at 745abaea, so the drift the gate reported
never existed. trusty-common is now 0.28.1, unpublished, and

* fix(trusty-agents-common): close the two #4448 review defects — gate 3 failed open, gate 4 accepted hand-authored files

Both were EXECUTED by the critic, not reasoned about, and both are reproduced
as regression tests here.

## CRITICAL — gate 3 read the exit code, not the reason

`VcsIndex::probe` mapped ANY non-zero `git rev-parse --is-inside-work-tree`
exit to `NoRepo` → `Unclaimed` → sweepable. Git exits 128 for every fatal
condition, not only "not a repository", so a live work tree git merely
declined to read reached the PERMISSIVE state and its committed agent files
were movable. The triggers are ordinary: `detected dubious ownership` on a
checkout owned by another uid, a `.git` file whose worktree gitdir is gone
(the state ~70 worktrees were left in by the 2026-07-21 incident), a broken
`repositoryformatversion`, or any failing `git` shim on PATH.

The fix branches on stderr. It is deliberately STRICTER than the review
suggested: matching the short phrase `not a git repository` would still fail
open, because a stale worktree pointer emits `fatal: not a git repository:
(null)` — that phrase, opposite meaning. Only the parenthesised "searched the
parents and found nothing" form is genuine absence; everything else, including
any future wording drift, falls through to `Unavailable`, which refuses.
Success is not enough either: a bare repo exits 0 printing `false`, so stdout
must read exactly `true`.

`agent_schema` accepted any document whose keys were a subset of a nine-key
list plus `name:`+`role:`. `role:` was the only discriminator and nothing makes
it tm's, so a minimal hand-authored agent — exactly
`name`/`role`/`description`/`model` — classified as composer output. The
review found a real one on this machine; it escaped only because a folded
description happened to contain a colon that parsed as a spurious key.

A key set can rule a file OUT (a foreign key proves the composer did not write
it). Only something PRESENT can rule it IN. That is now the composer's own base
preamble in the body: `compose_agent` concatenates the `extends:` chain

composed body carries it — byte-identical across every revision of
BASE-AGENT.md back to 2026-05-19, which matters because the files this sweep
targets were written by OLD binaries. That history is also why a compose-time
provenance key was rejected: it would mark only files written by NEW binaries,
making the sweep a no-op against its own target.

* fix(trusty-agents-common): corroborate git's "no repository" message before trusting it (#4448)

#4448 review round 2 CRITICAL. Git's absence message is not proof of absence.

`classify_failure` trusted `NO_REPO_STDERR` on its own. Git emits that exact
parenthesised text whenever discovery never got far enough to conclude
otherwise — an unreadable `.git` (mode 000), an unreadable `.git/HEAD`, or
`GIT_CEILING_DIRECTORIES` stopping the upward walk. In each the repository is
real and its agent files are committed, so the message routed a live work tree
into the sweepable state. The critic executed it and moved a tracked file.

The message is now a NECESSARY condition, never a sufficient one. It is
corroborated by a witness git does not use: `symlink_metadata` on a `.git`
entry needs only the parent's search bit, which is necessarily present because
the sweep already listed the tier below it. If any ancestor carries a `.git`
and git still reports no repository, the two disagree — and a disagreement is
exactly the "cannot be asked" state.

Three things measured rather than assumed, each now a test:

  - `symlink_metadata`, not `metadata`. A DANGLING `.git` symlink lstats
    successfully and stats as absent; following the link would conclude
    "nothing there" and hand back the permissive answer for a project whose
    `.git` is merely broken.
  - The parenthesised form still matters even with the witness in place. A
    bogus `GIT_DIR` in a directory with NO ancestor `.git` emits
    `fatal: not a git repository: '/nonexistent/x'` — it matches the short
    phrase and the witness finds nothing to contradict it, so the two defences
    do not overlap there.
  - The path is canonicalised first, and a canonicalisation failure is itself
    `Unavailable`. A RELATIVE `dir` would walk a truncated ancestor chain,
    miss the project's `.git`, and land back on the permissive answer. Not
    reachable from today's call sites, but one caller away, and it fails in
    the dangerous direction.

Two deliberate over-refusals, both fail-closed and both surfaced in the receipt
as `VcsUnknown` rather than silently: a stray empty `.git` directory, and a
project under `GIT_CEILING_DIRECTORIES`.

The trusty-mpm fragment claimed the sweep "never moves a file in a repository
git cannot read" while an executable test disproved it. It now states the real
bound — a file moves only on a POSITIVE answer from every gate, and anything

fix(trusty-search): re-drive never-walked indexes instead of recording them as up-to-date (#4680) (#4717)

Boot reconcile only ever asked "has the source drifted?", never "does this
index hold any data at all?". Both of its staleness markers answer "no drift"
for an index that was never populated:

- git path: restore re-derives `indexed_head_sha` from live git (#4391), so
  `stored == current` holds unconditionally -> counted `up_to_date`.
- mtime path: `last_indexed_unix` has no production writer (#4391), so it is
  always `None` -> counted `skipped_no_data`.

Neither branch re-drove the walk, on that boot or any later one. A production
deployment sat with 221 of 222 indexes at `chunk_count = 0` for 44 days.

`reconcile_one_index` now checks, before consulting either marker, whether an
index claims lexical work is underway (`lexical: in_progress`, what the
warm-boot classifier stamps for every restored empty corpus) while no walk has
ever been driven for it in this daemon's lifetime. Such an index is stuck, not
current, and gets a full NON-FORCE background reindex — the incremental hash
cache and staged-corpus carryover both apply, so recovery re-walks and re-adds
and never clears or rebuilds a corpus. The retry keys off
`last_walk_started_at`, bounding it to one walk per index per daemon lifetime
so a walk that legitimately finds zero indexable files is never looped.

Separately, `GET /health` reported `status: "ok"` throughout. Every existing
signal was structurally blind: `indexes` / `warmboot_summary.indexes_loaded`
count registered slots, not populated ones, and `indexes_corpus_failed` keys
off `stages.any_failed()`, which a stuck index never trips — it reports no
failed lane, only an indefinite false "walking". New `indexes_stuck_empty`
counts them and forces `status` to `"degraded"`, derived from the same
predicate reconcile uses so the count and the recovery cannot disagree.

Also adds `boot_reconcile.stuck_retried` so recovery is not hidden inside
`up_to_date` / `skipped_no_data`.

Five existing reconcile tests built their handles with `chunk_count: 0` — i.e.
they asserted that an index holding no data is "up to date". Their premise was
the bug; they now model a populated index and keep their original assertions.

feat(trusty-search): resume an interrupted reindex from its staging corpus (#4721)

A SIGKILL / OOM-kill / power loss partway through a reindex discarded every
batch the run had already committed. The batches were durable — they live in
the staging corpus `index.redb.tmp` (#603) — but the next reindex opened that
exact path with `CorpusStore::open_fresh`, which deletes the file first. On a
200k-chunk index that threw away hours of embedding on every interruption.

Every non-force reindex now stamps a versioned checkpoint record into the
staging corpus's own `_meta` table (index id, canonical walk root, crate
version, config fingerprint, timestamp). The next reindex reads it back and
adopts the staging corpus only when every field matches; otherwise it discards
the file and rebuilds exactly as before.

Two properties make adoption safe. The resume unit is the file, and the skip
stays content-verified: the adopted done-set is the staged `file_hashes` table,
but `prepare_batch_payload` still re-reads and re-hashes each file's current
bytes before skipping it, so a file edited during the interruption cannot be
skipped, a deleted one is pruned, and a new one is caught by the full re-walk.
And a staged hash implies its staged chunks — hashes are persisted only after
`commit_parsed_batch` returns Ok — so the done-set can only ever under-claim.

Adoption also drops the in-memory chunk/BM25/entity caches, which warm boot had
rehydrated from the LIVE corpus and which therefore hold the OLD chunks for any
file the interrupted run already re-indexed; they lazily rehydrate from the
adopted corpus through the existing `ensure_corpus_rehydrated` guards. A resumed
run additionally always runs the vector catch-up pass, because its inherited
chunks were only ever embedded into the never-promoted staged HNSW snapshot.

Guard interactions, both preserved:
- #2178 (root-hijack): the existing untrusted-root-move gate still runs first,
  and adoption additionally requires the checkpoint's canonical root to equal
  the current one — staged chunk paths are root-relative, so a root mismatch
  discards.
- #4122 (write quarantine): the probe is gated on `has_corpus_store()`, which by
  that module's load-bearing invariant means a quarantined index never reaches
  it, and adoption installs the store via `swap_corpus_store` — never
  `set_corpus_store` — so the quarantine is neither lifted nor bypassed.

The live `index.redb` is never read, written, or deleted by any branch of the
resume path; only `index.redb.tmp` is touched.

Knobs: `TRUSTY_REINDEX_RESUME` (set to 0 to restore the previous behaviour) and
`TRUSTY_REINDEX_CHECKPOINT_MAX_AGE_SECS` (default 86400, 0 disables).

Force reindexes deliberately neither write nor consume a checkpoint: they stage
an empty corpus and skip the prune pass, so a resumed force run could keep
chunks for files deleted since the crash — drift a clean force run would not
have.

Closes #3979

fix(trusty-search): restart the daemon after a clean exit (#4709)

The generated LaunchAgent set `KeepAlive = { SuccessfulExit: false }`, so
launchd restarted trusty-search only after a NON-zero exit. Any clean exit —
a plain SIGTERM, an orderly drain, `trusty-search stop` — left the daemon down
indefinitely with no automatic recovery and no alarm. On 2026-07-27 search was
down from 13:27:22Z until an operator hand-ran `launchctl kickstart`; every
search-backed consumer degraded silently rather than erroring.

`build_launchd_config` now emits `KeepAlive::Always` (`<key>KeepAlive</key>
<true/>`). That is a strict superset of the old policy — the non-zero-exit
restarts it already performed still happen — so the only behavioural delta is
that a clean exit comes back too. Deliberate "stop it and leave it stopped"
stays expressible through launchd's own unload path (`launchctl bootout
gui/$(id -u)/com.trusty.trusty-search`, or `trusty-search service uninstall`),
which removes the job and therefore outranks any `KeepAlive` setting.

`trusty-search stop` now says so on a host where the agent is loaded: it prints
that launchd will bring the daemon back and names the `bootout` command that
keeps it stopped, so the new policy never reads as "stop is broken".

An already-installed plist keeps the old policy until regenerated — pick the
change up with `trusty-search service install`.

fix(trusty-memory): render UNKNOWN palace counts as `—`, not `0` (#4684)

* fix(trusty-memory): render UNKNOWN palace counts as `—`, not `0`

The /ui Palaces view showed `0 wings / 0 drawers / 0 vectors / 0 triples /
0 nodes / 0 edges` directly above a section headed "Drawers (1)" listing a
real drawer — one screen contradicting itself.

Root cause is entirely caller-side. Since #4640/#4637, `list_palaces()`
builds rows from `PalaceRegistry::peek` (zero I/O, no LRU promotion) and
documents that an unresident palace comes back `cached: false` with every
count zeroed; those zeros mean UNKNOWN, not empty. On a live daemon 2,180
of 2,183 rows are in that state. That design is correct and is unchanged
here — three callers were printing its placeholders as measurements:

1. UI — header badges came from the peek-based `api.listPalaces()` while
   the drawer list right below them came from `api.listDrawers()`, which
   opens the palace. Two sources, one screen, one of them cold.
2. UI — `api.getPalace()` (the route that opens one palace, ~0.1s) existed,
   was exported, and was never called anywhere.
3. CLI — `monitor palaces <id>` filtered the row out of the bulk list even
   in single-id mode, so its answer depended on LRU residency.

Changes:

- UI: expanding a palace now also fetches `GET /api/v1/palaces/{id}` and
  merges the live counts into that row; an in-flight badge shows `…` so it
  never flickers stale → real.
- CLI: `MemoryClient::fetch_palace()` hits the single-palace route and the
  single-id path uses it.
- Schema-level guard: `PalaceRow` carries `counts_unknown`, and the new
  `vectors()` / `drawers()` / `kg_triples()` / `nodes()` / `edges()`
  accessors return `Option<u64>` — a type that can express "unknown". Every
  count renderer (UI, CLI, TUI, dashboard) goes through one formatter that
  prints `—` (JSON `null`) for `None`. A daemon that omits `cached`
  entirely predates #4640 and is still trusted, so counts do not regress to
  `—` against an older daemon.

Wire shape is deliberately unchanged: emitting `null` counts would fail
`PalaceWire`'s strict `u64` deserialization in every already-installed
client and drop the rows entirely — a worse defect than the one fixed.

Closes #4682

feat(trusty-agents): unattended detection via last-human-turn timeout (#4652) (#4683)

* feat(trusty-agents): unattended detection via last-human-turn timeout

Nothing could answer "is a human currently attending this assistant?".
`SessionRecord.last_activity_at` advances on the assistant's own tool and
hook activity exactly as it does on a human typing, focus tracking is a
routing map with no lease, and SSE counts no connections — so this is a
new signal, built to owner decision D3: a last-human-turn timeout with one
tunable threshold, not SSE counting and not a manual do-not-disturb toggle.

`TurnOrigin` makes the distinction structural: only `Human` advances the
clock, and `Assistant` is a documented no-op that writes nothing, so an
unsure call site has a correct default and cannot manufacture attendance.
`AttendanceTracker::is_unattended` takes `now` as a parameter so the
threshold boundary is tested exactly rather than slept through.

Threshold defaults to 15 minutes (`TAGENT_UNATTENDED_AFTER_MINS`). State is
one JSON record per instance under `~/.trusty-agents/attendance/`, written
through `state_writer`'s lock+tmp+rename — durable because an in-memory
tracker would report a fresh process as never-attended, letting a restart
mid-conversation license a notification to a human who is right there.

Recorded at the four human-facing surfaces: `POST /api/task`, the REPL,
Telegram and Slack. Signal only — no notification path, no queueing, and
no `trusty-mpm` dependency.

fix(trusty-memory): bound the chat-session store cache to stop an unbounded fd leak (#4639) (#4669)

* fix(trusty-memory): bound the chat-session store cache to stop an fd leak

`AppState::session_stores` was an unbounded `DashMap<String,
Arc<ChatSessionStore>>` with no `remove`, no TTL, and no cap. Every palace
the daemon ever touched leaked one `chat_sessions.redb` file descriptor for
the lifetime of the process. A live daemon (PID 29856, v0.21.2, up 8 days)
was measured holding 844 such handles — all 844 pointing at files already
unlinked from disk — growing ~250-300/day against an 8192 fd ceiling, i.e.
a hard EMFILE in ~3-4 weeks.

`PalaceRegistry`'s LRU (issue #463) already bounds kg/usearch/recall handles
at 64 and those sat correctly at 66-71 in the same measurement;
`chat_sessions.redb` was simply never tracked by it.

Replace the DashMap with `SessionStoreCache`: an LRU capped at 32 resident
handles (`TRUSTY_MEMORY_MAX_OPEN_SESSION_STORES`), and drop the cached
handle in `delete_palace` so deleting a palace actually releases its fd.

Two invariants keep eviction safe, both enforced under the cache mutex:

1. Eviction skips any entry a caller still holds (`Arc::strong_count > 1`).
   redb takes an exclusive flock and `ChatSessionStore::open` has no
   snapshot fallback, so reopening a file still open in this same process
   fails hard with "Database already open. Cannot acquire lock." The chat
   streaming handler holds an `Arc` across an entire SSE response, so a
   naive LRU would have traded a slow leak for an immediate outage — the
   `in_use_store_is_never_evicted` test reproduces exactly that failure when
   the guard is removed.
2. The open runs while the cache mutex is held, so two concurrent callers
   for one palace can never both open the file.

Tests assert the real symptom, not a proxy: `open_fd_count_is_bounded_by_cap`
reads the process fd table via `fd_metrics::count_open_fds` and pins growth
across 120 distinct palaces (unbounded: +120; bounded: +8).

Closes #4639

* fix(trusty-code): stop the turn recorder minting one palace per session (#4638)

`SessionRegistry::memory_sink_for` derives the turn recorder's palace id from
the session's project root, so a session bound to a `tempfile::TempDir`
produced a per-RUN-unique id (`t-tmp<random>` on macOS) and the drain task's
`ensure_palace` step (#2424) auto-created that palace on the live daemon at
the first turn. Nothing could ever read it back — the root it is keyed to is
swept when the run ends — so orphans accumulated at ~250-300/day: 5,667 in
three weeks, 97.8% of every palace on the machine, which turned
trusty-memory's O(n) full-registry handlers (#4637) into a ~90-minute
`GET /api/v1/status`.

The sink now carries an explicit `PalaceCreation` entitlement — `Allowed`
only for a durable project root, `Forbidden` for one under a system temp root
— making `palace_create` structurally unreachable from an ephemeral root
rather than merely unlikely. N sessions therefore mint at most ONE palace
(the project's), reused by every session on that project and shared with the
PM catch-up digest, with sessions distinguished inside it by

feat(trusty-common): CredentialRef, Secret, and resolve-at-use-time (#4565) (#4629)

`credential_ref` had zero hits under `crates/*/src/**` despite being an
acceptance bullet of #2808, which is closed COMPLETED. Without a reference
type, anything that needs to *refer* to a credential has to *hold* one — which
is why `McpService.env` is a `HashMap<String, String>` of literal API keys in a
hand-editable TOML, and why "no secrets in the assistant home" is a rule people
remember rather than a property of the types.

This adds the three pieces DOC-45 §4, §7 and §10 specify:

- `CredentialRef` — an opaque, durable, non-secret handle. Its grammar
  (lowercase-kebab segments, at most one `/`, 64 bytes) is restrictive enough
  that no realistic API key, JWT, OAuth token, or PEM body can satisfy it, so a
  value cannot be laundered into a ref — and thence into the audit stream —
  by accident. `C-2.4`.

- `Secret<T>` — renders a constant that is independent of the value (the
  Debug/Display impls carry no `T: Debug` bound, so they cannot read it), and
  implements neither Serialize, Deserialize, Clone, Deref, nor PartialEq. Three
  compile-time assertions fail the build if any of the three traits is added.
  `C-8.2`, `C-8.3`.

- `resolve(&CredentialRef, &Principal, &Scope)` — one entry point, called where
  the credential is consumed. `resolve_client` is the same entry point with the
  value consumed in place, so a caller that never sees the string cannot leak
  it. `C-3.3`, `C-3.4`, `C-8.4`.

Plus `CredentialError`'s five variants and the `Principal`/`Scope` vocabulary
the final signature is written in. `Principal` ships `Operator` and `Service`
only and is `#[non_exhaustive]`: `C-1.3` is PROVISIONAL pending owner Q-B and
says in terms not to implement the `Assistant` variant yet.

This adds no authorization. `resolve` accepts a `Principal` and checks no grant
against it — that is #4566. The signature is final so no consumer is migrated
twice.

Four workflow-layer holes, one change set.

1. Cancelled runs read as green (#4179). Every workflow used
   `cancel-in-progress: true` on a group keyed to `github.ref`, which on a
   push is `refs/heads/main` for every merge — so each merge killed the

   concluded `cancelled`). The notifier then asked
   `contains(needs.*.result, 'failure')`, and `cancelled` is not `failure`,
   so it reported success. Push runs now use a per-COMMIT concurrency group,
   so nothing cancels them; the notifier's verdict moves to
   scripts/classify-ci-results.sh, which folds every conclusion into
   green/red/inconclusive and fails the run on anything but green.

2. Stacked PRs got zero checks (#4179). No workflow declared `types:`, so
   `pull_request` used the default opened/synchronize/reopened set and a
   base-branch retarget — delivered as `edited` — fired nothing. PR #3838
   merged with an empty statusCheckRollup this way. Every `pull_request`
   trigger now declares `types: [opened, synchronize, reopened,
   ready_for_review, edited]`.

   continue-on-error (#4179). Resolved in favour of required: the flag is
   gone, the header rewritten, and the job joins the notifier's `needs`.

   classifies the diff via scripts/detect-docs-only.sh; the heavy jobs still

* perf(trusty-mpm): stop re-reading assets for stopped sessions in tm ls (#4322)

Bundled agents deploy into ONE machine-global directory — #4409 deliberately
exempted `FrameworkPaths::agent_deploy_dir()` from `for_managed_project`'s
per-workspace rewrite — so every session in a `tm ls` listing resolved the
same 42 agent files and read them independently. On the 32-session fleet the
issue measured, that is 1344 opens and 30.2 MiB of the 41.9 MiB the listing
moved, producing 32 byte-identical answers.

The listing now reads that tree ONCE per request and shares it across the
per-session fan-out, mirroring exactly what #2444's review already did for
the catalog half: compute the shared part once, fan out only what genuinely
differs per session. Skills are untouched — they still deploy per workspace,
so two sessions can genuinely disagree and there is nothing to share.

This is deduplication WITHIN one request, not a cache across requests.
Nothing is retained after the listing returns, so the next `tm ls` re-reads
from disk and sees any change immediately — there is no invalidation window.
The shared read supplies input BYTES only; each session still applies its own
manifest selection and ignore predicates afterwards, so per-session verdicts
stay independent.

Measured on a 32-session synthetic fleet, timing the old and new fan-outs
ALTERNATELY in one process (this laptop's load swung between 2 and 58 during
development; the identical baseline measured 213 ms and 1301 ms at the two
extremes, so two git checkouts timed minutes apart would have been noise):

  deployed-side reads  3008 -> 1706   (-43%, deterministic)
  bytes read           41.9 -> 12.7 MiB (-70%)
  warm median          230-236 ms -> 147-152 ms  (1.53-1.57x, 3 runs, 21 reps)

Steps 1 and 2 of the issue's plan (skip Stopped, parallelize) already landed
in #4326. Step 4 (precompute in the 60s loop) is deliberately NOT implemented:
it would serve an answer up to 60 s old, so a `sync-assets` run would leave a
stale `[stale-assets]` marker on screen, and it would burn the I/O forever on
an idle machine. Step 3's literal mtime-keyed memo is also skipped — directory
mtime does not change on an in-place file rewrite, so it can report a drifted
asset as fresh, and a faster wrong answer is strictly worse than a slow right
one.

Tests: the read-count invariant is mutation-verified (reverting the hoist makes
it observe 8 reads instead of 5 and fail); the shared and unshared paths are
pinned to identical `stale` flags AND identical change lists; a mid-process
asset change is asserted visible on the very next call; and a mixed

A gate that iterates a file set and exits 0 when that set is EMPTY reports
success identically to one that scanned everything and found nothing wrong. A
required check that cannot fail is not a check. Nine gates were in that state;
each already computed the number that would expose it and none asserted a floor
on it.

Every affected gate now counts what it examined, fails loudly below a declared
minimum, and prints the count on success so a future regression shows up in the
CI log instead of silently. Floors sit far below current reality and far above
zero, so a partially-broken enumeration trips them too. Nothing was made to pass
by weakening it — no exclusions, no `|| true`, no narrowed globs; every gate's
true positive was re-verified.

the tool actively failed and the gate still passed:

    a git exiting 128 arrived as an empty stream and the gate printed "0

    enumeration is now materialised into a file whose exit status is checked;

docs: DOC-63 OKG Sources specification

## Summary

Adds **DOC-63 — OKG Sources**, specifying how an agent's canonical OKG is built and kept current from external stores, plus the catalog row and the bumped `next free DOC-N` hint in `docs/specs/README.md`.

Spec document only. No crate source changed, so no CHANGELOG entry.

**Renumbered DOC-62 → DOC-63.** Two concurrent spec passes both claimed DOC-62 — this one and PR #4529 (Style Modes for Coding Delegation). Neither erred: both correctly ran scan-before-claim against `origin/main`, both found DOC-61 as the highest claimed number, and neither could see the other's unmerged branch. `check_doc_numbers.sh` cannot catch this class either — it scans the tree, and its own header records that unmerged/prose reservations are out of scope by design. **#4529 keeps DOC-62** as the earlier, further-advanced PR; mechanical tie-break.

**DOC-63 verified free three ways**: `origin/main`, every remote branch, and **every open PR** — the last being exactly the check that was missing the first time. (Also worth noting for future authors: DOC-55 is claimed by `okg-universal-importer.md` via self-label only, its filename carrying no number, so a filename scan alone is insufficient in either direction.)

⚠️ **Expect a `docs/specs/README.md` conflict when #4529 lands** — it adds its own DOC-62 catalog row and next-free hint. Resolution on rebase: keep **both** rows and the DOC-64 hint. Do not drop #4529's row.

## The canonical model (§2.1) — the spine of the document

Owner, 2026-08-01:

> *"Each agent has one canonical OKG which is an OKF store, internal, built, indexed by trusty-search. These are POPULATED by one or more document STORES, either a pointer to a local directory, or an extract from a connected system."*

```
agent → exactly ONE canonical OKG (OKF · internal · BUILT · indexed)
          ▲ populated by one or more
        STORES ─ kind 1: pointer to a local directory (materializes nothing)
               └ kind 2: extract from a connected system (target + state)
```

**"Built" is drawn out explicitly** (`SPEC-OKGSRC-12~draft`) as the property most likely to be lost in implementation. The OKG is a *derived* artifact, which makes three things normative rather than nice-to-have: it is **rebuildable** from its stores (which is what ADR-0022 already assumes when it decides a new machine re-ingests); **idempotency is a property of the build** — the ledger, fingerprints and watermarks are what make "built" mean anything, not defensive plumbing bolted onto a fetcher; and **the store set is the source of truth**. A corollary keeps this compatible with #4325's user-editable home: hand edits are tolerated and never clobbered — what is forbidden is the *system* depending on hand-authored content.

**Terminology reconciled.** "OKG Source" and "document store" are the same concept named twice. **`store` is the single canonical noun** (matching the owner's latest framing and the `stores/` path segment); "OKG Source" is recorded as an earlier synonym so readers of older tickets aren't confused. They are deliberately **not** modelled as two entities.

## The build path (§2.1a)

Owner requirement: *"the concierge will offer to build an assistant, or the user can do it manually."* Both paths produce the same thing — a per-agent home holding the canonical OKG and the `stores/` that populate it. A concierge-built assistant and a hand-built one are the same object.

**The concierge flow is deliberately NOT designed here** — that is **#4590**. This document's only claim is that the OKG and its stores come into existence through that path.

**Creation precedes provisioning**, an ordering easy to invert: the concierge (or user) *creates* the assistant; PR #4523's startup provisioning then *finds* it and ensures its layout — even though provisioning is what runs first at boot. A design that let provisioning invent instances would create homes and OKGs for agents nobody asked for.

**Two agents that must never be provisioned an OKG**, both verified against the tree:
- **`ctrl` IS the concierge persona.** It declares `role = "assistant"` (a deliberate 2026-07-24 change so Concierge appears in role-filtered pickers) plus `kind = "system-tool"`, but neither is nor extends the base. **The GUI's null `activeAgentId` means `ctrl`.**
- **`personal-assistant` is a TEMPLATE, not an instance.** Its config declares `role = "assistant"` and `hidden = true` with **no `extends` field at all**, so PR #4523's `is_instance()` excludes it only *incidentally* — because it happens to extend nothing, not because anything marks it a template. Making that explicit is **#4591**.

## Three mechanisms, kept distinct

| | Trigger | Section |
|---|---|---|
| **Stores, kind 1** — local-directory pointer | Automatic (trusty-search watcher) | §3 |
| **Stores, kind 2** — connected-system extract | Automatic (user-managed schedule) | §3, §9 |
| **Bound-store extraction** — pull entities out of any bound index | **Explicit command only** | §4 |

The local/remote asymmetry is the **primary type distinction**, not an implementation detail: kind 1 materializes nothing because the bytes are already on disk; kind 2 gets an extraction target at `<home>/<agent>/stores/<store-identifier>/` holding state (last extraction, per-item manifest, coverage interval, credential *reference*) — which is where the watermark lives.

**The contamination guard belongs to bound-store extraction alone**, and the spec says why, verified against `origin/main`: `feed_bound_index` (`crates/trusty-agents/src/tools/okg/index_feed.rs:32-50`) resolves the agent's **bound** index via `bound_index_for_tree` (`:53-77`) and pushes ingest output into it — the binding is bidirectional in effect. Automatic extraction from a bound *populated* corpus would mix generated entities into a store the user bound only to read.

**The overlap case is specified** (§3.3): a directory is both a kind-1 store and a bindable index, so its index is recorded **store-owned** and bound-store extraction over it is **declined with a reason** rather than silently re-deriving from chunks what the ledger already ingested from files.

## The untrusted-content boundary (§6) — the core of the spec

Not imported from general LLM-security literature; **this repo's own recorded, enforced, test-pinned position**. `assistant/agent.toml:84-87` states verbatim that *"`izzie` ingests UNTRUSTED content (Gmail/Drive/Calendar), so that put untrusted input one hop from a cross-project read primitive: a prompt-injection exfiltration shape"*, pinned by `bundled_personas_pin_git_reach`; `l0_exec.rs:8-18` states *"L0 must never ingest untrusted content"*; `okg/policy.rs:11-15` calls the read path *"an exfiltration primitive"*.

**The specific gap identified.** Two of three necessary mechanisms exist — capability reduction (built, pinned) and prompt-level fencing (built: `UNTRUSTED_PREAMBLE`, `persona_memory.rs:420-533`, which already says drawer content arrives from Gmail/Drive ingestion). The third does not: **no trust label on the content itself.** Per-entity `source_id`/`source_kind` provenance exists but is descriptive metadata nothing reads as a trust signal. So an assistant's **memory drawers are fenced while its OKG is not** — a chunk retrieved via `vector_search` arrives with no provenance and no fence.

Required: labels at ingest, **carried into the search chunk** (a label that stops at the file is worthless — the model sees chunks), fenced on retrieval by **lifting the existing seam** rather than writing a second one, failing closed on unlabelled chunks.

**SENT-only is analysed, not credited as sufficient.** A real partial mitigation and a genuine signal-quality choice — but sent mail quotes and forwards inbound content verbatim, so one reply lands an attacker's text in the "trusted" corpus. Drive, Slack channels, Notion and Granola have no author constraint at all and cannot have one. All stores carry the same `untrusted-external` label. **Residual risk is stated plainly** (§6.5) and put to the owner as Q3.

## Search: tiering and a verified-absent provenance gap (§10.5–§10.6)

Owner: *"the internal OKG has priority for search, then attached stores for fan out."*

**"Priority" is resolved as RANK-ABOVE, not short-circuit**, on the owner's own rationale — *"not all useful content in a store will be entity-extractable"*, so a query the OKG appears to satisfy may still have better material in an attached store. Short-circuiting would **invisibly** suppress exactly what search-only attachment exists to make reachable. Latency is bounded instead by concurrent tiers plus per-tier budget/timeout; an unreachable tier is reported, not dropped; tier is a tie-break, not an override of the ranker.

**Result provenance verified absent, not assumed.** `VectorSearchTool` resolves **one index per call** — `effective_index_id` (`vector_search.rs:221`) returns `Option<String>`, `daemon_query` (`:453`) queries that single index. There is no fan-out and therefore no tier/origin on a result today. Fan-out and provenance must ship **together**, or #4007's *"every result identifies its tier and origin"* gets closed rather than satisfied.

**Attachment and extraction are decoupled** (§3.4): a store's **searchable-corpus** and **OKG-contributor** capacities are orthogonal. Search-only is a **complete, legitimate end state** — never pending, never an error, and no surface may nag or emit a coverage metric framing it as a shortfall. Extraction coverage is partial by nature: the OKG holds entities, a store holds documents.

## Other substantive positions

- **Credentials (§7)** — a **consumer of epic #4040**, designing none of it. Names exactly what would otherwise be duplicated (gworkspace two-tier `TokenStorage`; the `trusty_common` three-tier resolver; Slack's env-var posture; **Notion's total absence of first-party handling**, the most likely to grow a bespoke path; **Granola's API-key-not-OAuth shape**). Carries forward the honesty note that today's Google ingest grants are write-capable and not scope-gated at all.
- **Watermarks (§8)** — the correctness trap: a **scalar cursor supports only forward extension**, silently making "reach further back" a no-op or a full refetch. An **interval** is required. The watermark is an optimisation; the ledger stays authoritative.
- **Scheduling (§9)** — no scheduler, cron parser, or job registry exists anywhere in the workspace (verified: zero hits across every `Cargo.toml`). Coarse intervals, not cron. Its own runner reusing `listeners::poll`'s *pattern* but not DOC-47's `EventSource` *semantics* — a refresh wakes no agent and creates no goal. Overlap: **skip, don't queue**. Fixes the hardcoded `match cfg.connector.as_str()` anti-pattern via the registry.
- **trusty-search (§10)** — the daemon **does** auto-watch every registered index root (`watcher_manager.rs`; opt-out env-only; **no `watch` flag on `create_index`**), but the OKG path **pushes** via `IndexFeed`. Both retained with separated roles. One index per agent. Cites real hazards: root-containment post-filtering (#64/#541), the **reindex root-hijack incident** (so the runner never calls `reindex`), orphan-index leakage, and the opt-in allowlist prerequisite (#767).
- **Extension point (§11)** — adopts DOC-55's open `Locator::Connector`; tabulates what a store type must provide (auth *declaration*, enumerate, fetch delta, normalize, watermark, schedule defaults, trust posture) and what it must **not** (dedup, tombstoning, entity writing, extraction, credential storage, scheduling). Fireflies and Notion-transcripts walked through as drop-ins.
- **`${TRUSTY_AGENTS_HOME}` (§2.6)** — recorded as **one system-level value** whose relocation requires a **migration**, with the migration design **explicitly out of scope and deferred**; noted, not specified, not ticketed. Verified: today the only lever is `KB_KNOWLEDGE_DIR`, a process-global env var relocating every agent's tree at once, and on `origin/main` `AgentStoreBinding` (`stores/config.rs:49-62`) has **no root or path field at all** — so per-store relocation is currently *unexpressible*, not merely unmigrated. PR #4523 adds it.
- **Settled and recorded (§2.7)** so they are not re-litigated: **`config.toml`, not `config.yaml`** (no format migration); the **dotless** home spelling; and **app-generated, NOT access-controlled** — access control is out of scope and this document specifies no enforcement.

## Open questions for the owner

Genuine forks only; each states what stays blocked.

- **Q1 — What is trusty-memory's KG's relationship to the canonical OKG?** *Which* store is canonical is now **answered** (the OKF store). What is not: naming it canonical does **not** retire trusty-memory's KG — the two are separate and unbridged, and a prior decision gives every assistant a memory palace **and** a default OKG. No recommendation; likely warrants an ADR. *Blocks #4406's closure and any bridging work.*
- **Q2 — Do you accept the residual prompt-injection risk (§6.5)?** Fencing is a mitigation, not a guarantee. *Blocks every capability grant in the epic.*
- **Q3 — Scheduled refresh as a listener, or its own runner?** Recommends its own runner; recorded because a reviewer could reasonably reverse it.

## Tickets

Epic **#4531** with 17 children on M2, split into **plumbing** (scheduled) and **capability grants** (#4546–#4549, deliberately unscheduled, `blocked` label, no milestone — gated on #4040, the §6 boundary, and Q3). Sequenced against #3904, #4283, #4289, #4007, #4325 and #4363 rather than duplicating them. Re-scope recommendation left as a comment on #4406; not closed.
