fix(ci): pin the instruction floor byte-exactly instead of grepping three needles (#4581)

* fix(ci): pin the instruction floor byte-exactly instead of grepping three needles

The floor guard was theatre. `check_instruction_floor.sh` verified the
non-overridable instruction floor with three `grep -qF` substring checks, so it
reported PASS on a floor whose every rule had been INVERTED ("always emit
`Co-Authored-By: Claude`"), on a floor reduced to the three bare needles and
nothing else, and on a floor wrapped entirely in an HTML comment. All three
mutations were run against the old guard and all three passed it.

The floor is now pinned byte-exactly. The guard recomputes a sha256 for every
artifact that makes up the floor and diffs the result against the committed
`scripts/instruction_floor.sha256`; any byte difference fails. Pinned:

  1. every `sections/*.md` sourced by a `customization_tier: "fixed"` section
     of the PM instruction package manifest;
  2. a canonical projection of the manifest's fixed sections and their blocks,
     so retiering a floor section to "project", repointing it at another file,
     or deleting its block fails even though no section file changed;
  3. the guard's own workflow file.

A deliberate floor change is a two-part commit: edit the floor, run
`bash scripts/check_instruction_floor.sh --update`, commit the regenerated
digests alongside. The failure message states that path.

The guard also runs inside ci.yml's required `Format check` job, which has no
path filter, so deleting `.github/workflows/instruction-floor-guard.yml` turns
a REQUIRED check red rather than silently disarming the gate.

Adding the standalone `Instruction floor guard` job to the repo's required
status checks remains a branch-protection change, made separately.

docs: style-mode specification (#4346)

Adds **DOC-62 — Style Modes for Coding Delegation: `hack` / `vibe` / `engineer`**
(`docs/specs/DOC-62-style-modes-coding-delegation.md`, `SPEC-STYLE-01~draft` …
`-10~draft`), the foundational spec for epic #4345's pillar-(a) chain. Spec
document + catalog row only — **no code**.

`DOC-62` claimed scan-before-claim per DOC-38 §4.1, verified against
`origin/main` **and every remote branch** (highest claimed number anywhere is
`DOC-61`). No fifth grandfathered collision added.

## What it specifies

1. **The ceremony/gate boundary (§3)** — stated first because it conditions
   everything else. Defines *ceremony* (process tcode chooses to run) vs
   *gate* (a check the target repository enforces, verdict rendered outside
   the delegated task), and eleven normative rules SM-1 … SM-11.
2. **Per-axis style definitions (§4)** — spec artifacts, ticketing,
   branch/worktree, testing, verification, review, commit discipline, PR
   expectations, docs, for each of the three tiers.
3. **Where style lives and how it resolves (§5)** — closed three-variant enum;
   `caller > config > built-in (engineer)`; escalation permitted,
   de-escalation not.
4. **Cross-boundary carriage (§6)** — text preamble, with the constraint that
   makes it safe.
5. **Acceptance criteria (§8)** mapped to #4348 / #4349 / #4350 / #4353.

The load-bearing sentence the spec exists to protect: *a style that runs
**fewer** gates is legitimate; a style that makes a **failing** gate report
success is not.* SM-3 makes that mechanical (no deleting/ignoring/weakening a
test to go green; no adding a ratchet row to silence a new violation; no
rendering "skipped" as "passed"), and SM-4 forces an honest three-state gate
ledger — `passed` / `failed` / `not-run(style)`.

## Q5 — can a style mode disable a repo-enforced gate? **No. Firm recommendation, with evidence.**

The spec takes the hard line: a style mode selects tcode's own internal
ceremony and can never disable a gate the target repository enforces. An audit
of `crates/trusty-code`, `crates/trusty-agents`, `crates/trusty-mpm`,
`scripts/`, and `.github/workflows/` found **no path by which any
caller-supplied parameter suppresses any repository-enforced gate**. Four
structural reasons, cited in §3.3:

- **The gates are server-side.** Line cap, changelog fragment, sld-lint,
  doc-numbers, fmt/clippy/test all run in GitHub Actions from a fresh
  `actions/checkout@v5`. The design is explicitly anti-bypass:
  `changelog-fragment.yml` deliberately carries no `paths:` filter ("a
  required check that is skipped by a path filter never reports on the PRs it
  skips"), and `scripts/check_changelog_fragment.sh` states there is
  "deliberately NO 'trivial change' escape hatch".
- **The ratchets can only shrink** — grandfathering a fresh violation is
  itself a red build, so "add an allowlist row" is not a shortcut for any
  style.
- **The delegation is propose-only, structurally.** `ProposalEnvelope`'s only
  constructor `for_cross_product` hardcodes `Disposition::Proposal`
  (`cross_product.rs:270`); its doc comment says making this the sole
  constructor "is what makes DOC-41 §5.5's absolute rule **structural rather
  than a convention** a future edit could forget". **The spec recommends
  modelling the style field on exactly this pattern** (recorded,
  non-authorizing, enforced by construction).
- **tcode never reaches the merge surface.** No Rust code in the workspace
  constructs an argv containing `--admin`, `--no-verify`, `gh pr merge`, or
  `git push` — the only `--admin` occurrences are agent prompt text
  *forbidding* it. `gh_tools` is read-only by construction with a test
  asserting no tool name contains `merge`/`create`/`comment`/`close`/`edit`.
  tcode terminates at a diff (`run_task/mod.rs:820-829`).

### Finding the epic did not anticipate — flagged prominently, not as a footnote

**The trusty-review gate is process-enforced, not CI-enforced.** It has no
workflow file; it is invoked by the PM via
`mcp__trusty-review__review_diff`/`review_pr`
(`crates/trusty-mpm/src/assets/skills/tm-pr-workflow.md:100-108`). It is the
one gate on #4345's list that does **not** inherit the structural protection
the GitHub Actions gates have. No parameter can reach it — but a
lower-ceremony *convention* plausibly could erode it. §3.2 **SM-10** closes
this with a rule: a style value is not admissible as justification for
skipping the review gate and must not appear in any waiver rationale.

Two further audit results are recorded because they change the shape of
#2596's questions (§7.1):

- **trusty-code has no circuit breaker at all** — they live only in trusty-mpm
  (`core/circuit.rs`, enforced unconditionally at `daemon/mcp_backend.rs:232-238`
  from a hardcoded `CircuitConfig::default()`). #4345's Q2 presumes a construct
  that does not exist in the product it targets.
- **The verify gate is attached unconditionally at all three production sites**
  (`runner/in_process.rs:420`, `run_task/mod.rs:428`, `task/executor.rs:491`),
  its only inertness condition content-derived (`verify_gate.rs:187`).
  `TaskRunParams` has no field any `with_finish_gate` call consults. Making
  `vibe` verify less is new plumbing, not a flag flip.

Also stated rather than assumed away: the bash tool is an unrestricted `sh -c`
with no denylist (`tools/bash/mod.rs:155`). A *model* can author any shell
string. Not parameter-reachable, and SM-11 makes explicit that a style value
never touches the tool surface — but "no parameter can reach it" and "nothing
can reach it" are different claims and only the first is true.

## Q4 — preamble or system-prompt composition? **Text preamble. Firm recommendation, with evidence.**

The epic called a preamble "the cheap, already-precedented path". The code says
something stronger: **it is the only path that exists** (§6.2).

- The boundary is **one argv slot**: `run_tcode` spawns
  `tcode run-task <agent> <task> --project <dir> --json`
  (`pm_bridge_backend.rs:134-148`); the backend trait is
  `run(route, target: Option<&str>, task: &str)`. No slot for a system prompt,
  persona, or structured context.
- Flattening to text is the **existing documented design**:
  `render_preamble()` (`cross_product.rs:144-174`), whose doc comment says
  *"the external CLI leg accepts one task string and nothing else, so a
  structured handoff must be flattened… Plain text (not JSON) because the
  receiving side is an LLM persona, not a parser."*
- The join is a string prepend: `format!("{preamble}\n{task}")`
  (`pm_bridge.rs:254-257`), after cap validation and fail-closed target
  resolution.
- The 4 KiB cap already exists and is fail-closed (`HANDOFF_MAX_BYTES`,
  `cross_product.rs:50`, validated at `:108-114`).
- **System-prompt composition across products does not exist.** DOC-61 §4
  concedes the compose chain is *"not yet universally shared: today, only
  trusty-mpm's own builder actually resolves `extends:`"* (`:272-275`) and that
  the versioning work is *"new work, not already built"* (`:298-302`).
- `run-task` has no style parameter today on either side (`main.rs:144-188`,
  `cli/run_task.rs:69-75`, `task/protocol.rs:98-126`).

**The constraint that makes this ruling safe (§6.3, SM-7/SM-8):** a preamble is
text a model reads, advisory by construction. It may carry a ceremony level and
a statement of policy. It must **never** be the sole enforcement of a security
control — `NON_CODING_TARGETS` (`cross_product.rs:69`) stays a code-enforced
closed literal applied "regardless of caller configuration". A payload derived
from untrusted content (live Gmail/Drive, #4126) is exactly where advisory text
is worth least.

## Q1–Q3 — ownership call: **#2596 owns them; this spec consumes them**

They are inherited verbatim from #2596 and are VIBE-**tier** pipeline decisions,
not style-**mode** interface decisions. §7 draws the line: DOC-62 owns what
`vibe` is called, how it is requested, how it resolves, how it travels, and what
it may never do; #2596 owns what `vibe` does inside `crates/trusty-code/src/intent/`
dispatch. Absorbing them here would relocate a ratification decision (vision spec
§10 D3) away from the issue that tracks it.

Q1 is split: **(a)** how a style is selected at the interface is answered here
(§5); **(b)** how tcode routes an unstyled task and what triggers automatic
escalation remains #2596's.

**The chain is NOT blocked on #2596.** §7.3 **SM-9**: until #2596 lands, a
resolved `vibe` executes the `engineer` pipeline and **reports** effective style
`engineer` with reason `tier-unimplemented`. Degrading upward is the only safe
direction; reporting it is what stops it being a silent no-op. #4349, #4350, and
#4353 can therefore ship the full vocabulary, plumbing, and UI now, and #2596
later changes behavior only — no interface change, no re-plumbing.

### A tension worth the owner's eye (§5.4)

#4345 decision 3 lets the caller specify style. This repo's own captured
research says the opposite about risk classification:

> "Classification must be **automatic**, derived from the semantic diff plus the
> blast radius/dependency graph — **not** from author tags, since an agent has no
> self-awareness of how risky its own change is."
> — `docs/research/quality-gates-agent-prs-article-2026-04.md:122`

A caller-supplied style *is* an author tag. §5.4 resolves this: a style is a
**ceiling request the callee may raise but never lower**. Decision 3's ergonomics
survive; the research finding is honored. Same source, on the goal: "the fix is
smarter routing, not a weaker mesh" (`:120`).

## Genuine open questions remaining for the owner (§9)

#4345's Q4 and Q5 are **not** in this list — they are decided in the body with
evidence. Q1–Q3 are not either — they belong to #2596.

- **OQ-1** Config-default scope: per-assistant, global, or both? *Rec: both,
  per-assistant wins.*
- **OQ-2** Does `hack` belong on the delegation surface at all, or is it a
  category error to reject at the boundary? *Rec: accept + escalate per §4.1.*
- **OQ-3** The `engineer` style value collides with the tcode `engineer`
  sub-agent role; once the PM is addressable a user may read `style=engineer` as
  "delegate to the engineer agent", which decision 2 forbids. *Rec: keep the wire
  value, disambiguate in GUI label and preamble wording.*
- **OQ-4** Gate ledger structured or prose? *Rec: structured — SM-4 is the rule
  most likely to erode silently.*
- **OQ-5** Which product's circuit breakers does #2596's Q2 mean? trusty-code has
  none. *No rec — #2596's call; flagged because the question presumes a
  nonexistent construct.*
- **OQ-6** Expose a per-delegation style override in the GUI given §5.4? *Rec:
  expose it, but render the effective style and resolution path so the override
  is honest rather than decorative.*

chore: dissolve crates/cto-assistant (#3732)

## What

Owner directive: *"crates/cto-assistant should not be a crate. It is an assistant."*

Deletes the `cto-assistant` workspace crate — `Cargo.toml`, `src/lib.rs`,
`README.md`, `LICENSE` — plus its `default-members` entry, its `Cargo.lock`
entry, and every stale reference to it. **The assistant itself is untouched.**

Net: **121 insertions, 613 deletions** across 17 files.

## Why it is safe to delete

| Concern | Finding |
|---|---|
| Workspace dependents | **None.** PR #3310 severed the last edge (`trusty-agents-local -> cto-assistant`). `cargo check --workspace` passes and drops the crate from `Cargo.lock`. |
| crates.io | `publish = false`. **Never published** — no yank, no deprecation, no version-bump step. |
| Git tag prefix | None. The repo's per-crate tag convention has no `cto-assistant-v*` prefix. |
| `.test-pointer-allowlist.tsv` | No `crates/cto-assistant` row. (One row *citing into* it is handled below.) |
| CI path assumption | None. `release.yml`'s only mention was an **echo help-string inside the default-skip `else` branch**, not a config branch — verified before editing. Removing the word changes no control flow. |
| Reachable behaviour | **Zero.** Its `AgentPlugin` had no `install_plugins(...)` call site after #3310, so no binary ever registered its tools (#3700). |

## The assistant is untouched

`cto-assistant` continues to live exactly where every other assistant does — as
a bundled agent package at
`crates/trusty-agents/.trusty-agents/agents/cto-assistant/`
(`agent.toml` + `persona.md` + `events/slack.md`, plus the flat
`cto-assistant.toml` extends-shadow), alongside `izzie`, `assistant`, and
`ctrl`. Not one byte of that directory is modified by this PR.

## No capability is lost

The four CTO DB tools — `query_headcount`, `query_budget`, `query_risks`,
`query_work_classification` — remain invokable through the declarative `cto-db`
Python skill (`crates/trusty-agents/.trusty-agents/skills/cto-db/`) landed in
#4476. The agent's `agent.toml` references them **by name** in `[tools].allow`;
`crate::tools::python_skill` discovers the skill generically at startup and
installs it via the same `AgentPlugin` seam the deleted crate used.

## The hallucinated README

`crates/cto-assistant/README.md` (314 lines) documented a CLI binary with
command groups, a config file, and an env var. **None of it existed** — the
package had a `lib` target only and did not depend on `clap`. It is deleted
outright; no content was migrated anywhere, deliberately.

## Does this close #3656?

**Yes — `Closes #3656`.** Reasoning, having read the issue rather than assuming:

#3656 objects that `crates/cto-assistant/src/lib.rs` implements four bespoke DB
tools via `cto_db_tools()` and registers them under the literal persona name
`"cto-assistant"`, making them *reachable only by writing Rust* — the one live
counterexample to DOC-41 §2.0's declarative-only constraint. Its suggested
direction was to *"expose the four DB queries as a platform-hosted primitive
that the manifest can reference by name, so cto-assistant becomes pure
instructions + YAML."*

That is now the actual state, and I verified each leg:

1. **The cited artifact no longer exists.** `crates/cto-assistant/src/lib.rs`,
   with `cto_db_tools()` at line 102, is deleted by this PR.
2. **The suggested direction is implemented.** #4476's `cto-db` skill is the
   platform-hosted primitive; `agent.toml` references the four tools by name.
3. **The bridge is genuinely generic.** Every `cto` occurrence in
   `crates/trusty-agents/src/tools/python_skill.rs` is inside `#[cfg(test)]`
   (the bundled skill is used as a test fixture). The production dispatch path
   names no agent and no tool.
4. **No persona-gated Rust tool registration survives.** The only
   `persona_name ==` in the tree is `agent_plugin.rs`'s generic filter, which
   is now fed exclusively by discovered *declarative* skills.

So the agent is instructions + manifest, the implementation is skill-hosted
Python, and the platform hosts no agent-specific Rust. #3656's objection has no
remaining referent.

**Attribution note:** #4476 did the substantive work; this PR removes the last
artifact. I am closing #3656 here because it is the PR that makes its claim
false, but credit belongs upstream.

## Scope discipline

`crates/tc-services::cto_db` and `crates/trusty-cto-db` are **explicitly scoped
out of #3732** and are **not touched**. They may now be orphaned — filed as
**#4598** for their own assessment (they are not zero-touch: `trusty-cto-db` has
a `.test-pointer-allowlist.tsv` row, both are in `default-members`, and the
`cto-db` skill's README cites `trusty-cto-db` as its schema-of-record).

## One thing that contradicted the brief

The brief listed four cosmetic cleanups. There was a fifth class it did not
mention: **six doc comments in `trusty-agents` / `trusty-agents-common` citing
the deleted crate**, two of which were `Test:` pointers naming
`cto_assistant::execute_outcome_maps_to_tool_result` — a test that this PR
deletes. That is issue-checklist item 4 ("remove stale references in
trusty-agents comments/docs"), so I fixed them rather than leaving them.

The two pointers were on `ToolResult::is_error` / `is_fatal` and were suppressed
by a grandfathered allowlist row. Rather than leave a row that could *never*
become resolvable, I restored the deleted assertions as two unit tests beside
the predicates they actually cover (`tool_result_is_error_distinguishes_variants`,
`tool_result_is_fatal_only_for_non_recoverable`), repointed the docs at them, and
**retired the allowlist row** — a ratchet step in the right direction. `+20`
lines of test is the entire net addition to `src/**` in this PR.

## Raw gate output

`cargo check --workspace` (bare) fails on a **pre-existing, unrelated**
`trusty-code-gui` proc-macro panic (`frontendDist` "ui/dist" doesn't exist — the
crate needs the pnpm/Svelte toolchain). This reproduces on unmodified `main`,
which is exactly why CI excludes the three GUI crates. Gates below use CI's own
exclusion form from `.github/workflows/ci.yml`.

test tests::tool_result_is_error_distinguishes_variants ... ok

test result: ok. 2 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 367 filtered out; finished in 0.00s

All gates re-run green after rebasing onto current `main` (`1630db0e`).

## A CI gate that could not be satisfied

`Per-PR changelog fragment` failed on the first push, and **not because a
fragment was missing** — because `scripts/check_changelog_fragment.sh` can never
go green on a crate *deletion*:

```
FAIL cto-assistant: crates/cto-assistant/src/** changed with no changelog record
```

Removing a crate deletes every `crates/<crate>/src/**` path, which the gate
reads as a source change requiring a fragment. But that fragment would have to
live inside `crates/cto-assistant/changelog.d/` — the directory being removed —
and the gate validates by running `assemble-changelog.sh cto-assistant`, which
cannot run for a crate that is not there. Unsatisfiable, with no escape hatch
(the script documents, correctly, that it has "deliberately NO 'trivial change'
escape hatch" — but a dissolution is not a trivial change, it is an impossible
one).

Fixed by exempting a crate that no longer exists at HEAD, probed via
`git cat-file -e HEAD:crates/<crate>/Cargo.toml` so a **dissolution** is
distinguished from a merely large deletion inside a surviving crate. Every
surviving crate is still checked exactly as before, so the removal is still
recorded — here in `crates/trusty-agents/changelog.d/`.

Verified in both directions locally:

```

GATE_EXIT=0

# negative test — temporarily drop one surviving crate's fragment:
OK   trusty-agents: changelog.d fragment present and valid
FAIL trusty-agents-common: crates/trusty-agents-common/src/** changed with no changelog record
OK   trusty-agents-local: changelog.d fragment present and valid
```

The exemption fires only for the deleted crate; a surviving crate still fails
without its fragment.

The same run also correctly demanded fragments for `trusty-agents-common` and
`trusty-agents-local` (both had non-test `src/**` edits — doc comments, plus the
restored `ToolResult` unit tests). Both added, as `Documentation`.

feat(trusty-agents): document-type gating — markdown editable, others view-only (#4360)

## What

Replaces the single `isMarkdownPath` predicate with an explicit **document-type table**: the enumeration #4360 asks for, plus the three-way gating it drives.

## The type table

`crates/trusty-agents/ui/src/lib/projectFiles.ts` — `DOCUMENT_TYPES`, a flat `readonly DocumentType[]` of `{ extension, kind, label }`:

| Extension | Kind | Label |
|---|---|---|
| `.md`, `.markdown` | `editable` | Markdown |
| `.pdf` | `view-only` | PDF |
| `.docx` | `view-only` | Word document |
| `.xlsx`, `.xls` | `view-only` | Excel workbook |
| `.txt` | `view-only` | Plain text |
| `.csv` | `view-only` | CSV |
| *anything else* | `unsupported` | — refused |

`DocumentKind = 'editable' | 'view-only' | 'unsupported'`. Enumerated rows are only ever `editable` or `view-only`; `unsupported` is what the *absence* of a row means, so the default is refusal.

**Only markdown is editable**, per the parent requirement — which is why `.txt` and `.csv` sit under `view-only` despite being trivially writable text. The view-only set is exactly what `trusty-search`'s extractor already understands (`core/extract/mod.rs`, #2923) plus the two plain-text formats, so a future viewer builds on extraction that exists rather than on a type nobody can read.

## Single source of truth

Three lookups resolve through the one table — `documentTypeFor` → `documentKindFor` → `isEditablePath`, plus `editRefusalReason` for shared wording:

- **Write guard.** `writeProjectFile` refuses via `editRefusalReason(path)` before the request leaves the client, replacing its own `isMarkdownPath` check.
- **UI.** `ProjectFilesPanel` derives each row's `disabled`, `title` and badge from `documentKindFor`, and the editor's `readonly` prop from `isEditablePath`.

Neither carries its own extension list, so what the UI offers and what the client will send cannot drift. `projectFiles.test.ts` pins this directly: it walks every row of `DOCUMENT_TYPES` and asserts the guard attempts exactly the editable ones and refuses the rest.

## Behaviour

- Refused rows now say **why**, and say it differently: a view-only row is badged with its type name (`PDF · view-only`), an unsupported one reads `unsupported`. Previously both shared one `Only markdown files can be opened yet` tooltip. The badge is visible text, not just `title`, because a tooltip is invisible on touch and to a keyboard user tabbing a disabled row.
- `readonly` is **derived, not hardcoded**. Only editable documents open from this list today, so it resolves to `false` — it is wired so #4401 can mount a view-only document in this pane and get a read-only editor with no save affordance, without re-deriving editability.
- `save()` checks `viewOnly` too. CodeMirror's `Mod-S` binding fires regardless of `EditorState.readOnly`, so without that guard the keyboard path would surface the write guard's refusal as an error banner for a document the user was never offered a way to save.
- Extension matching reads the base name (`docs/v1.md/NOTES` is not markdown) and treats a leading dot as a dotfile, not an extension.

## Left open for #4401

No preview rendering, no Mermaid, no canvas. Displaying a view-only document is the canvas viewer's job, and its three owner questions (Mermaid render path, live-vs-toggle preview UX, canvas-surface reuse with #4368) are all untouched. View-only rows remain listed-but-unopenable — that row is the seam, deliberately labelled and left empty.

Also deliberately absent from the table pending the owner call the issue asks for: `.pptx`, images (`.png`/`.jpg`/`.gif`), `.rst`/`.org`. nothing answers:

- Stale/absent file  -> spawn `tcode serve --http`, forwarding

- Explicit but dead

* fix(trusty-code): the TUI never stops the daemon, and never attaches to the wrong project

Two amendments to PR #4514, both against `tcode tui`'s new attach-or-spawn
path. They share the same rewritten files, so they land together.

1. The TUI no longer stops the daemon on exit — ever.

PR #4514 shipped "if the TUI spawned the daemon, the TUI SIGTERMs it on
exit". Per the owner directive of 2026-08-01 that is wrong: the tcode
daemon owns PM lifecycle, agent dispatch, and agent communication, and
CLIs/TUIs merely ATTACH to it — so quitting one client must never destroy
live PM or agent work.

Removed, not disabled: `Ownership`/`Ownership::Spawned(Child)`, the whole
`DaemonSession` wrapper and its `shutdown`, `terminate()` and its
`SHUTDOWN_GRACE`, and `kill_on_drop(true)` on the spawned `Command`.
`ensure_daemon` now returns the daemon URL, and `cli::tui::run` has no
teardown step at all. A daemon the TUI spawned simply keeps running,
exactly like one started by hand.

Quiescence-gated idle exit (a daemon that stops itself once it has no
attached clients and no active PM/agent sessions) is follow-up work and is
deliberately NOT implemented here — no leases, refcounts, or idle timers.

The auto-spawn half is unchanged: discovery order, the `Lookup`/`Source`
split, `ensure_daemon`'s attach-or-spawn shape, `cli::tcode_exe::resolve`,
racing `spin_until_ready` against `Child::wait`, the spawned-daemon log
file, the explicit-URL refusal, and `--project` forwarding all stay.

`shutdown_stops_a_daemon_we_spawned` and
`terminate_handles_an_already_exited_child` asserted behaviour that is now
forbidden and are deleted. `shutdown_leaves_a_pre_existing_daemon_running`
becomes `the_tui_never_signals_the_daemon_on_exit` and asserts the
universal rule for BOTH cases — a daemon we spawned and a pre-existing one
— against real processes, after everything `ensure_daemon_with` returned
has been dropped.

2. Report and verify the daemon's project binding.

A daemon binds exactly one `ProjectBinding` for its whole life
(`build_router`), and `/health` published nothing about it. That was
harmless while the TUI refused to run without a hand-started daemon; with
auto-attach, a TUI launched in project B silently drives project A's
daemon and every session lands in the wrong repository.

`health_payload` now carries `pid` and `binding` (additive — `server`,
`version`, `status` unchanged), threaded from `build_router`/`run_http`
rather than resolved per request. `lookup_daemon` parses it into a
`ReportedBinding`, and `ensure_daemon` refuses any daemon whose binding
differs from the client's: no attach, and no competing daemon spawned on a
port already in use. The error names both projects and the ways forward.

Projectless and bound are a mismatch in either direction — attaching a
projectless TUI to a bound daemon would grant it a project nobody named
(the implicit-binding bug `ProjectBinding` exists to prevent), and
attaching a bound TUI to a projectless daemon would withdraw indexing and
git affordances the operator explicitly asked for. A daemon too old to
report a binding is refused too: it fails CLOSED, because "old build" is
no evidence its project is the right one.

feat(trusty-agents): per-assistant home dir + OKG store model (#4325)

## What changed

Adds `crate::assistants` — the per-instance container that models **instance isolation for the Assistant TYPE**, plus the `[[stores]] root` field #4325 lists as requirement 1.

| File | What |
|---|---|
| `crates/trusty-agents/src/assistants/instance.rs` | `ASSISTANT_ROLE` / `is_assistant_role` (the TYPE discriminator) and `AssistantInstanceId` (a validated INSTANCE name) |
| `crates/trusty-agents/src/assistants/home.rs` | `AssistantHome` — layout, resolution, app-generated `ensure()`, and `store_root()` |
| `crates/trusty-agents/src/assistants/health.rs` | `inspect()` / `HomeHealth` / `HomeIssue` — the detection half of the resilience requirement |
| `crates/trusty-agents/src/assistants/error.rs` | `AssistantError` (`thiserror`) |
| `crates/trusty-agents/src/stores/config.rs` | new `AgentStoreBinding.root` + its `validate()` rule |

Added: 1584 / Removed: 3 / Net: +1581 (of which 546 lines are the four test modules).

## The instance-isolation model

Per the owner's 2026-07-30 wording: **"Assistant" is a TYPE. `izzie` and `cto-assistant` are INSTANCES of that type — they are NOT distinct agent types.** The repo already encoded the type half (`assistant/agent.toml` declares `role = "assistant"`; both named personas carry `extends = "assistant"`). Nothing encoded the instance half — an instance's three belongings were spread across shared pools with no per-instance container:

- persona → the shared agents directory
- OKG tree → the flat `<knowledge_dir>/<slug(agent)>` pool, addressed by naming convention
- store root → did not exist as a field at all (#3890's data-model gap)

That is precisely why adding an instance reads as adding a *type*. This PR adds the container, and nothing else:

```
~/trusty-agents/<instance>/                # DOTLESS, visible, browsable
├── instructions.md
├── config.toml                            # TOML — confirmed, not assumed
├── agents/
├── okg/                                   # indexed by trusty-search
├── attachments/
└── stores/                                # parent only; <store-identifier>/ is a later spec
```

`TAGENT_ASSISTANTS_DIR` overrides the root. Two instances of the same type get two homes, two `okg/` trees, two `agents/` dirs — verified by `two_instances_get_separate_homes`.

**Resilience.** #4325 makes external modification EXPECTED. So:
- `ensure()` is additive and idempotent — it creates only what is missing and never rewrites a file the user edited (`ensure_never_overwrites_user_edits`, `ensure_restores_only_what_is_missing`). Restoring its own seed over a user's work would be exactly the intolerance the ticket rules out.
- `inspect()` never fails and never repairs. It returns structured findings — kind, path, detail, and a **remedy** — and `HomeHealth::narration()` is the seam #4320's concierge renders from. A missing home is one finding, not five.
- No auto-migration and no auto-relocation, per the ticket.

**`[[stores]] root`.** Optional, relative, traversal-free; resolved by `AssistantHome::store_root()` and defaulting to the home's `okg/`. Absolute or `..`-bearing values are refused at resolution AND reported by `AgentStoreBinding::validate()` (fail-soft, matching the module's existing posture — a bad store degrades, it never blocks boot). Bindings that omit `root` parse and validate byte-identically to before.

## Startup wiring (owner answer, 2026-08-01)

`ensure()` now runs on the boot path. **This is user-visible:** the first launch after this lands creates `~/trusty-agents/<instance>/` trees that did not exist before, logged at `info` (`created assistant home directory`) — not silent. A home that cannot be created logs at `warn` with its reason and remedy.

**Call site: `runtime::startup::run_startup_init`**, immediately after `ensure_bundled_agents_deployed()`. Two reasons it is that line and not another:

- It is the single per-launch choke point, and it runs **before** the `--api`/`--serve` early dispatch further down. One call therefore covers the API server, the Tauri GUI, the `start` daemon, the REPL/TUI and every one-shot subcommand.
- The GUI needs no second hook: `ui/src-tauri` spawns `tagent --api` as a sidecar (`sidecar.rs::ensure_api_server`) rather than provisioning anything itself; its `setup()` only builds the tray. Same for the daemon — `service::start_service` is a detached `tagent --serve`, so it re-enters this path.

**Not covered, deliberately:** `config` and `mcp-serve` return before `run_startup_init` runs. Both are intentionally daemon-less and stdout-protocol-sensitive, and neither touches an assistant home. That is the honest full answer to "does more than one entry point need this" — one site covers every launch mode, and the two it misses should miss it.

**It cannot fail startup.** Nothing in the new `provision` module returns `Result`. A read-only `$HOME`, a denied permission, a full disk, or a file left where a directory belongs becomes a `HomeIssueKind::NotCreatable` finding carrying the reason and a remedy, surfaced through the `health::narration()` seam built earlier in this PR. No panic, no `unwrap()`, no propagated error. It also cannot repeat the sidecar's historical `cwd=/` EROFS crash: the root resolves from `$HOME`/`$USERPROFILE`, never the cwd.

**Creation only.** No migration, no relocation, no cleanup; the dotted `~/.trusty-agents` tree is untouched. Relocating a home needs a migration process that stays future work.

### A judgment call worth your eye: which agents get a home

`role = "assistant"` alone is the **wrong** rule. `ctrl` declares it too — and the GUI's null `activeAgentId` *means* ctrl (Concierge), so provisioning it a selectable instance home would model the one agent that is not an instance as if it were. Selecting on role alone would have silently created it.

`roster::discover_instances()` uses role **plus lineage**: be the base `assistant`, or declare `extends = "assistant"`. Mechanical, no name special-casing. On the shipped roster that yields `assistant`, `izzie`, `cto-assistant` and excludes `ctrl`.

**It also excludes `personal-assistant.toml`**, which declares `role = "assistant"` but extends nothing. I judged that correct — it is a standalone persona, not an instance of the base — but it is a genuine call, so flag it if you disagree; it is a one-line rule change.

Note this introduces the **first boot-time agent enumeration** in the codebase (`agent_roster()` is per-request today). It is a partial, forgiving TOML read of `[agent]` only — the same shape `stores::binding::load_stores` already uses — so a malformed file is skipped, never fatal.

### Still no persisted selection

Confirmed by inspection: `activeAgentId` is in-memory only (`ui/src/stores/app.ts:145`), `user.toml` carries no agent field, and the backend documents the null default as deliberate. So "provision the selected assistant" has nothing to select yet — every discovered instance is provisioned, which is what makes #4281's selection land on homes that already exist.

## Owner decisions since the first push

**The store path is the owner's, verbatim (2026-08-01): `trusty-agents/<agent>/okg/`.** My original spelling carried an extra `assistants/` segment — flagged at the time as my own choice, not the ticket's — and has been dropped. Home is now `~/trusty-agents/<instance>/`, `okg/` sits directly under it, and `okg_store_path_matches_the_owners_spelling` pins the full absolute path rather than only the accessors (an accessor-only test would not have caught the extra segment, and the OKG Sources spec is being written against this path).

**`stores/` joins the layout (2026-08-01).** `<trusty-agents home>/<agent>/stores/<store-identifier>/` — one subdirectory per remote store, holding that store's extraction target and extraction state. **This PR creates the parent directory and nothing else.** It gets the same additive/idempotent/never-overwrite `ensure()` semantics and the same health findings as every other layout directory; store-identifier derivation, the extraction-state record, per-store subdirectories and extraction logic are all absent by design, because a separate spec defines them. `ignores_whatever_lives_under_stores` pins that boundary — inspection looks at the directory, never at its contents, so whatever the spec later puts inside cannot make a home report unhealthy. Creating the parent now means that slice needs no PR just to add a `mkdir`.

**TOML is confirmed, not assumed.** The `config.yaml` vs `config.toml` question is closed per the owner's 2026-07-29 correction: TOML stays, no format migration. Same correction confirms the dotless spelling, and narrows "protected"/"app-generated" to **ownership of origin with access control explicitly out of scope** — no write-enforcement, no floor, no narrow-only semantics. The doc comments have been softened accordingly (`assistants/mod.rs`, `AssistantHome::ensure`); nothing in the code ever enforced anything, but two comments read as if it might.

**#4406 is settled for this layout, by the owner rather than by me.** The owner specified `okg/` as a filesystem store indexed by trusty-search — the trusty-kb tree shape — which confirms the minimal read I flagged in the first push. The binding's separate `palace` field correctly stays untouched, so the trusty-memory leg remains addressable without changing this layout. I did not decide this; it was decided for me and matches.

1. **`attachments/` is created but its lifecycle is undefined.** The owner's comment scopes it to binary chat attachments and records the blocker: no binary→text extraction exists anywhere (`read_text` rejects NUL-bearing files; zero hits for `docx|pptx|xlsx|pdf_extract|lopdf|calamine|zip::`). New capability, not this ticket.
2. **`config.toml` is deliberately minimal** (`id`, optional `display_name`, unknown keys tolerated). Agent behaviour still comes from `agent.toml`; this file exists so instance-scoped settings have a landing place without a second format decision.

## Notes for the OKG Sources spec

Nothing here blocks a pluggable extractor writing into `okg/` on a schedule, but four things in the current shape are worth the spec accounting for:

1. **`StoresConfig::validate()` warns above ONE binding per agent** (`crates/trusty-agents/src/stores/config.rs`, pre-existing since #3816). If each OKG Source became its own `[[stores]]` binding, every multi-source assistant would emit a config warning. Sources should sit *under* the single store — e.g. `[[sources]]` in the home's `config.toml`, which already tolerates unknown keys — not as sibling bindings.
2. **`store_root()` confines the DESTINATION, not the source.** An extractor cannot repoint `okg/` outside the home (deliberate — it is what stops one instance writing into another's store). Reading from an arbitrary directory, Gmail, Drive, Slack, Notion or Granola is entirely unaffected. If a source type ever needs to write outside the home, that is a new decision, not a tweak.
3. **There is no place for per-source refresh state yet.** `health::inspect()` checks that `okg/` exists and is a directory; it knows nothing about last-run time, cursors, or a failing credential. A scheduled refresh needs that state, and `HomeIssue`/`HomeIssueKind` is the natural place to surface a stale or broken source through the same concierge narration seam — but the kinds are filesystem-shaped today and would need extending.
4. **Secrets must not land in the home.** The home is deliberately human-browsable and user-editable; a Granola API key or Slack token in `config.toml` would be sitting in a directory the product invites users to open. The spec should name a separate credential store.

Both halves of the same plumbing, built against **DOC-62 §5/§6** (PR #4529, read from that branch). Milestone 22 (M2), pillar (a) coding delegation.

Closes #4349
Closes #4350

## #4349 — `HandoffContext` style field + TA-PM-policy preamble

- `HandoffContext` gains `style: Option<ExecutionStyle>` — a **typed** field, per DOC-62 §6.4's shaping note ("do not have callers hand-write style prose into `summary` or `constraints`"). `ExecutionStyle` is a closed three-variant enum (`hack`/`vibe`/`engineer`, lowercase wire form). An unrecognized value is a `serde` error the bridge returns before anything is dispatched — never a silent default (§5.1).
- `render_preamble` gains the TA-PM-policy block. It carries exactly what SM-7 permits: the effective style, the ceremony/gate boundary (SM-1/SM-5), the honest-reporting rule (SM-4), the no-capability rule (SM-11), and decision 2's PM-only statement **as information**. Per SM-8 the block ends by saying that last boundary is *"enforced in code, not by this text"*, so no future reader mistakes the paragraph for the mechanism.
- Ordering follows §6.4: the policy block renders **after** the caller's `- Constraint:` lines and under its own heading (`Delegation policy (system-supplied, not from the caller):`), so caller text is not confusable with policy text. Pinned by `policy_block_follows_caller_supplied_constraints`.
- **Backward compatibility is literal.** `style` is `skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none"`, so an unstyled `HandoffContext` serializes to the same bytes as before and the 4 KiB cap measures the same payload. `ResolvedStyle::is_explicit()` gates the block, so a dispatch with no style anywhere renders no block at all — `an_unstyled_dispatch_carries_no_policy_block` asserts the task body is byte-identical.
- The block is **bounded and task-independent** (`policy_block_is_bounded_and_task_independent`, < 1 KiB across the full request×floor cross-product), so the cap can never become a function of task size.

## #4350 — addressable coding PM, `NON_CODING_TARGETS` preserved

- `CODING_PM_TARGET = "coding-pm"` names the external coding project manager the coding lane has always run (`DEFAULT_TCODE_AGENT`). Naming it makes the existing route **selectable and stylable** instead of reachable only by accident of task phrasing.
- Style resolves **caller > `[subagents] default_style` > built-in `engineer`** (§5.3). The config key is new and additive; absent falls through to `engineer`, i.e. today's behaviour, and an unrecognized value is a config parse error.
- The resolution path travels back to the caller on the `ProposalEnvelope` (§3.4 / AC-4), so a `vibe` request that actually ran `engineer` says so in the result, not only in the outbound preamble.

### `NON_CODING_TARGETS` is unchanged and still code-enforced

```rust
pub const NON_CODING_TARGETS: &[&str] = &["research", "ticketing"];
```

Byte-identical on this branch. Three tests pin it:

- `non_coding_targets_floor_membership_is_pinned` asserts exact membership (AC-5), so a future widening is a red build rather than a review miss.
- `coding_pm_is_not_reachable_through_the_non_coding_floor` asserts that a *permissive config* listing `coding-pm` still gets `Err` from `SubagentAllowSet::resolve` — the coding name cannot be smuggled onto the non-coding floor.
- `the_coding_pm_name_does_not_open_the_non_coding_lane` asserts `research` / `ticketing` / `engineer` / `pm` are all still denied with no allow-set configured, and that a denial dispatches nothing.

The reserved name resolves on a **separate path** that never consults the allow-set, precisely so the floor stays a single-vocabulary closed literal. Nothing became data-driven; nothing is enforced by preamble text.

## DOC-62 conformance — §5/§6

| Rule | How |
|---|---|
| §5.1 closed enum, error on unknown | `ExecutionStyle` + `an_unknown_style_is_a_caller_error_not_a_silent_default` |
| §5.2 built-in default `engineer` | `ExecutionStyle::BUILT_IN_DEFAULT` |
| §5.3 caller > config > built-in | `precedence_is_caller_then_config_then_built_in` |
| §5.4 raise, never lower | structural — see below |
| §6.1 preamble, not prompt composition | extends `render_preamble()`; no new mechanism invented |
| §6.3 SM-7 / SM-8 | policy text names its own advisory status |
| §6.4 typed field, block after caller lines, bounded, `None` renders nothing | four tests, listed above |
| §7.3 SM-9 | see below |
| SM-11 style never touches the tool surface | see below |
| AC-10 disposition unchanged | `a_styled_envelope_is_still_only_a_proposal` |

## SM-9 fallback behaviour

`vibe` is unimplemented (#2596), so a resolved `vibe` runs the `engineer` pipeline and **reports** effective style `engineer` with reason `tier-unimplemented`. Implemented as `ExecutionStyle::implemented()` — one function that changes when #2596 lands, with no interface change and no re-plumbing.

The caller sees it in both directions: `Effective execution style: engineer` plus `Requested style was vibe; raised to engineer (tier-unimplemented)` in the outbound preamble, and `"escalations": ["tier-unimplemented"]` in the returned envelope. Asserted end-to-end through the bridge by `a_styled_coding_delegation_carries_the_policy_preamble`, and in isolation by `vibe_degrades_upward_to_engineer_and_says_why`.

## How the style invariant is made structural

Modelled on `ProposalEnvelope::for_cross_product`, whose doc comment calls hardcoding `Disposition::Proposal` in the sole constructor *"structural rather than a convention a future edit could forget"*. Four properties compose:

1. **`ExecutionStyle` variants are declared in ascending ceremony order**, so the derived `Ord` makes `a.max(b)` mean *"the higher ceremony of the two"*. Every escalation in the module is a `max`.
2. **`ResolvedStyle::resolve` is the only constructor.** No `Default`, no `From`, no public field, no mutator. There is no way to obtain a `ResolvedStyle` except by resolving one.
3. **Every input is combined with `max`**, and the tier fail-safe `implemented()` is itself monotonically non-decreasing (`implemented_never_lowers_ceremony`). The composition is therefore monotone: no code path yields an effective style below the floor.
4. A `debug_assert!` postcondition at the single construction site, backed by an unconditional test.

The one thing convention still guards, stated in the type docs: reordering the enum variants would silently invert `Ord` and therefore the whole property. `ceremony_order_is_ascending` fails if anyone does.

## The ceiling test

Asserted over the **full request × floor cross-product**, not one happy path:

```rust
#[test]
fn a_caller_can_never_lower_ceremony_below_the_callee_floor() {
    for requested in ALL {
        for floor in ALL {
            let resolved = ResolvedStyle::resolve(Some(requested), None, floor);
            assert!(resolved.effective() >= floor);
            assert!(resolved.effective() >= requested);
        }
    }
}
```

Plus `a_config_default_can_never_lower_ceremony_below_the_callee_floor` (a config default is an author tag too) and, at the delegation surface, `a_hack_request_to_the_coding_pm_does_not_lower_ceremony` — a caller asking the coding PM for `hack` gets `engineer` and is told both reasons.

## Style never touches the tool surface (SM-11) — structural, with the honest boundary

**Structurally impossible within this diff.** `ResolvedStyle` exposes no accessor that reaches a tool list, a permission, or a command line; the only consumers of the resolved value are `render_policy_block()` (a `String`) and the envelope field. `route`, `target`, the argv, the allow-set, and `restricted_tiers()` are all computed *before* `ResolvedStyle::resolve` is called, from inputs that do not include a style. Asserted by `style_does_not_change_the_route_target_or_rbac_surface`: for the same task, all three styles produce the same route, the same target, and the same RBAC tier list.

**What remains only conventional, stated plainly:** the policy block is *text a model reads*. A model on the far side could disregard it, or be persuaded by it — which is exactly SM-8's point, and why the `NON_CODING_TARGETS` boundary is enforced in code and the preamble says so about itself. This PR does not, and cannot, make a preamble tamper-proof.

## On reach — naming the PM adds none

`DispatchTarget::CodingPm::backend_agent()` returns `None`, so the coding leg falls through to the backend's own hardcoded `DEFAULT_TCODE_AGENT` and **no caller-supplied string can become the coding leg's `<AGENT>` argv slot**. `naming_the_coding_pm_matches_the_unnamed_coding_dispatch` asserts the `(route, target, task)` tuple crossing the boundary is identical to the unnamed coding dispatch the router already produces for the same task.

One behavioural delta, stated rather than glossed: a caller can now *force* the coding lane for text `route_task` would have sent to `Tm`. That is not new reach — `route_task` is a pure function of caller-authored text, so the caller already fully controlled that choice and only had to phrase around it — but it is now explicit instead of implicit, which is the point of the issue. No shell capability is granted, widened, or assumed here.

## Where DOC-62 / the issues did not survive contact with the code

Reported plainly rather than worked around quietly.

1. **#4350's "LLM is told tcode PM exists … (opposite of `scrub_branding`)" is only half-implemented, deliberately.** The black-box contract is owner-locked (#3052 PR B): the schema must not name a backend, and `scrub_branding` strips backend identity from every transcript. DOC-62 never rules on de-branding. I made the target addressable under an **unbranded capability name** (`coding-pm`) and described what it does, so the LLM now knows a coding PM exists and can name it — but it still does not learn the backend is `tcode`. `schema_advertises_the_coding_pm_and_the_closed_style_vocabulary` pins that no branded token leaked. **If the owner intends the branding rule itself to be relaxed, that is a separate decision and this PR did not make it.**
2. **DOC-62 never says what the coding lane's ceremony floor IS.** §5.4 only says the callee MAY raise. To make the ceiling testable at the delegation surface I had to pick one, and derived `vibe` from §4.1 (*"`hack` is not coding with no gates … a delegation that asks for `hack` and then turns out to require a code change MUST escalate"*). That is an **inference from §4.1, not a spec statement.** If the owner wants a coding delegation to be able to resolve to `hack`, one constant changes.
3. **§3.4's gate ledger (`passed`/`failed`/`not-run(style)`) and AC-7 are not in this PR and are not satisfiable from it.** That data does not exist on this side of the boundary — the tcode return payload is a `Session` snapshot with no per-check detail (§6.2 point 6; OQ-4 is still open on structured-vs-prose). This PR delivers the §3.4 half that *does* live here: effective style, resolution path, and escalation reasons.
4. **AC-4's "resolution path present in the returned result" holds only on the named-target path.** An unnamed dispatch returns a bare scrubbed transcript with no envelope — byte-identity that is a pre-#4026 requirement I did not want to break. A styled *unnamed* dispatch therefore carries the policy block outbound but gets no structured resolution back. The remedy is to name the target, which is what #4350 adds.
5. **§6.4 asks for a "fixed-length" policy block; mine is bounded and task-independent but not literally fixed-length** — it grows one line when an escalation occurred. Literal fixed length would mean not reporting the escalation, which SM-4 / §3.4 require. I chose honest reporting over the literal word.
6. **OQ-1 (per-assistant vs global config default) is still unanswered.** I implemented **per-assistant only** (`[subagents] default_style`), matching OQ-1's own recommendation but not ratified. A global level can be added later as a fourth precedence step without touching the resolution shape.
7. **AC-6's recommended repo-wide "no style value reaches a merge/push/gate-skip flag" check is not included.** It was outside the stated scope and its natural home is a workspace-level gate, not a `trusty-agents` unit test. The narrower structural property *is* asserted, and no code in this diff constructs an argv from a style value.

feat(trusty-agents): persist selected assistant across launches (#4281)

## What changed

`activeAgentId` (`crates/trusty-agents/ui/src/stores/app.ts:145`) was the last
significant piece of desktop-client state that did not survive a reload — a
plain in-memory `writable<string | null>(null)` that reset to Concierge on
every launch, while the API token and the theme already round-tripped through
`localStorage`. Per the product model, "Assistant" is a TYPE and `izzie` /
`cto-assistant` are INSTANCES of it, each with its own home/OKG/persona — so
which instance is selected is user-meaningful state, not an incidental UI
toggle.

- **New** `crates/trusty-agents/ui/src/lib/selectedAssistant.ts` (169 lines) —
  the codec, as pure functions over an injectable `SelectionStorage`:
  `readSelectedAssistant`, `persistSelectedAssistant`,
  `reconcileSelectedAssistant`, plus `SELECTED_ASSISTANT_KEY` and
  `defaultSelectionStorage`.
- **Modified** `crates/trusty-agents/ui/src/stores/app.ts` (+35 lines) — seeds
  `activeAgentId` from storage at import time, writes back through a
  subscription, and reconciles against `agentRoster`.
- **New** two test files (23 tests).

Per the owner decision of 2026-07-28, stickiness is **per-app-launch**
(last-used, persisted client-side), **not per-workstream** — a per-workstream
binding would cut against DOC-54 §9.2's "workstreams are filters, not
containers". The second acceptance criterion ("filtering to a workstream must
not change `activeAgentId`") is pinned by a test rather than assumed.

## The persistence surface, and how #4404's picker consumes it

**The store IS the surface.** `activeAgentId` is seeded from `localStorage` at
module-import time and written back by a subscription on the store itself, so
persistence is not a separate call any site can forget:

```ts
export const activeAgentId = writable<string | null>(readSelectedAssistant());
activeAgentId.subscribe((id) => persistSelectedAssistant(id));
```

For the picker in #4404 this means one line — `activeAgentId.set(entry.id)` —
and the selection sticks. No `saveSelection()`, no picker-owned storage key,
and the three existing selection sites (`ChatHeader.svelte`,
`AgentSwitcher.svelte`, `Sidebar.svelte`'s workstream resume) inherit the
behaviour without being touched. Subscribing rather than wrapping every `.set`
was deliberate: it makes the store the single choke point, so a future
selection surface cannot regress persistence by construction.

Two details that matter for a card-based picker:

- **Concierge encodes as the `ctrl` sentinel**, not as a cleared key. The
  persisted vocabulary is therefore identical to the one the config surface
  already addresses agents by (`configAgentName` in `lib/roster.ts`), so a card
  list containing Concierge + instances can persist a card's id verbatim with
  no second mapping table. Reading `'ctrl'` back as `null` is also a
  correctness guard: `ctrl` legitimately appears in `$agentRoster`, and
  dispatching it *by name* routes through the tools-OFF persona path
  (`handlers.rs::resolve_agent_for_chat`), silently stripping Concierge's
  delegation capability.
- **Storage key** is `tagent.selectedAssistant`, matching the existing
  `tagent.apiToken` namespace.

Scope held to persistence: no picker UI, no OKG/store work, no boot-path
directory creation. `crates/trusty-agents/src/assistants/` and
`stores/config.rs` (#4325 / PR #4523) were read for the instance-identity shape
and **not modified** — the persisted value is the instance id (a
`[a-zA-Z0-9_-]` slug, the same charset the Rust `is_valid_agent_slug` enforces
and `slugify` produces), so it refers to instances the same way that model does.

## Degradation behaviour, with test evidence

Persisted state is a hand-editable file, so every failure axis resolves to the
pre-existing Concierge default — never a throw, never a blocked startup.

| Failure | Behaviour | Test |
|---|---|---|
| Key absent (first launch) | Concierge | `readSelectedAssistant_absent_key_is_concierge`; store: `defaults to Concierge on a first launch…` |
| Corrupt value (JSON blob, spaces, path traversal, >64 chars, empty) | Concierge, **and the value is evicted** so it is never re-parsed | `readSelectedAssistant_corrupt_value_is_concierge_and_evicted`; store: `falls back to Concierge when the persisted selection is corrupt` |
| `localStorage` absent | Concierge, no throw | `defaultSelectionStorage_returns_null_when_unavailable` |
| `localStorage` throws (`SecurityError` / `QuotaExceededError`) on get/set/remove | Concierge, no throw | `readSelectedAssistant_survives_throwing_storage`, `persistSelectedAssistant_survives_throwing_storage` |
| **Stale** — names an assistant that no longer exists | Demoted to Concierge once a **populated** roster contradicts it | `reconcileSelectedAssistant_drops_a_stale_selection_to_concierge`; store: `demotes a stale selection to Concierge once a populated roster contradicts it` |

That last row is the one deliberate asymmetry. `App.svelte`'s
`refetchPickerCatalogsOnReady` exists because the first `/api/agents` call
races the cold-start sidecar and fails outright; an empty roster therefore
means "not loaded", never "your assistant is gone". Treating it as stale would
discard a valid selection on every cold start — exactly the bug this issue
exists to fix. The cost is a stale label until the roster arrives.

touches the global now forces the branch it means with `vi.stubGlobal`, so both
runtimes assert the same thing. A side benefit on the newer runtime: every

feat(trusty-agents): markdown editor component integration (#4359) (#4518)

Writing tools are an M2 pillar and the trusty-agents UI had no editing
surface at all — `ui/package.json` carried zero markdown or editor
dependencies. This adds one.

`MarkdownEditor.svelte` is a controlled CodeMirror 6 surface: `value` in,
`change`/`save` out, `readonly` to make it view-only. It owns editing and
nothing else — no fetching, no persistence, no knowledge of projects — so
every markdown workflow in the app can mount it.

`ProjectFilesPanel.svelte` owns the other half: browsing a registered
project root, deciding what may be opened, and writing edits back through
the per-project file routes (#4357). Non-markdown entries are listed but
not openable, which is the seam #4360 replaces with a document-type table
and a view-only preview.

CodeMirror was chosen over Monaco (IDE-weight), ProseMirror/Milkdown/Tiptap
(they own the document model and round-trip markdown through an AST, so
byte-fidelity of a tracked file is not guaranteed) and TinyMCE (HTML-first,
licence-encumbered). It edits source text, bundles with no CDN fetch, and
its decoration model is what #4401 needs to render ```mermaid blocks as
live diagrams inside the document — none of #4401's three open questions is
answered here. It loads through a dynamic import() on first open, so its
~176 kB gzipped never reaches the startup path of a user who opens no
document.

fix(trusty-installer): refuse a launchd bootstrap when a foreign process holds the daemon port (#4470) (#4517)

* fix(trusty-installer): refuse a launchd bootstrap when a foreign process holds the daemon port

`launchctl bootstrap` exits 0 whether or not the job it loads can actually
bind. When an unsupervised orphan — typically an older binary — already holds
the daemon's port, the documented `bootout -> install -> bootstrap` restart
convention completes cleanly while the orphan keeps serving that port, so a
signed install plus behavioural verification can all pass while shipping
nothing (#4230 records the near-miss on the 1.2.3 deploy).

#4466 detected the state after the fact via `tm doctor`'s `daemon_orphan`
check and documented an operator pre-check, but nothing intercepted the
bootstrap itself. This adds that interception on the installer side, where the
bootstrap is actually issued.

New `commands::port_guard` refuses whenever the member's port is held by a PID
launchd does not report running for that label. The refusal names the offending
PID, the port, and the `lsof` / `kill -TERM` recipe to clear it.

Fails closed: an unreadable port probe, or a `launchctl` query that cannot be
answered, is a refusal — never a pass. `TCTL_ALLOW_FOREIGN_PORT=1` is the
single documented operator override, named in every refusal message.

All bootstrap-issuing paths route through the one shared check, so no branch
can drift (the #3841 lesson):

  - `service_bootstrap::bootstrap_one`, on BOTH the fresh-install branch and
    the #3841 already-present-plist repair branch, reported as the new
    `BootstrapAction::RefusedForeignPort`
  - `verify_tail::attempt_verify_fallback`, the second-layer repair
  - `lifecycle::launchd_control` for `tctl start` / `tctl restart`

For `restart` the gate runs BEFORE the `bootout`, so a refusal never stops a
running daemon and then declines to bring it back — the fail-open shape where
the failure branch has already advanced state.

The port checked is the member's recorded `http_addr` when present, falling
back to the documented table, so a daemon that legitimately port-walked
(trusty-memory walks 7070..=7079) is not falsely accused.

`verify_launchd_state`'s single `launchctl list` primitive now carries the
running PID and distinguishes "launchd says no such label" from "launchd could
not be asked" — the conflation #4466 identified as a HIGH on the trusty-mpm
side. No new parser was added; `service_bootstrap.rs`'s inline tests moved to a
sibling `_tests.rs` to stay under the 500-SLOC production cap.

* fix(trusty-installer): report a port-guard refusal as a failure, and gate the supervisor bootstrap too

Review of PR #4517 found the guard was correct but its consequences were not
wired through. Two HIGH, three MEDIUM.

HIGH-1 — a refusal was reported to automation as SUCCESS, inverting the fix.
`install.rs` classified failure with an inline `matches!(action, Failed(_))`
that never learned about `RefusedForeignPort`, so a refused member set
`service_ok: true`, `all_ok` stayed true, and `tctl install` exited 0. An
orphan holding the port became a silent green install — worse than no guard.
Classification moves onto `BootstrapAction::is_failure()` as one exhaustive
match beside the definition, so the next variant cannot repeat it.

HIGH-2 — the enumeration was wrong and nothing failed when it was wrong.
`plist_bootstrap::install_mpm_supervisor` is a fifth bootstrap site and was
ungated. It matters more than a member's: the supervisor binds
`TRUSTY_MPM_SUPERVISOR_ADDR` before its supervision loop and fails fast, and
the plist sets `KeepAlive=true`, so a foreign holder makes launchd restart it
into the same collision indefinitely. Now gated through the injected
`LaunchctlPort` seam (preserving #3551 test isolation), placed before both the
bootout and the plist write. `bootstrap_sites_tests` adopts the #4475
fail-loud allowlist pattern: it enumerates the bootstrap sites actually in the
source and fails on any unaccounted for, so a sixth site is a build failure
rather than a silent bypass.

MEDIUM-1 — a fail-open branch inside the fail-closed function. Without root,
`lsof` reports only the caller's own processes, so another user's listener
produced the same empty output as a free port and classified as `Free`. An
empty `lsof` result is now cross-checked with a real bind; only a successful
bind yields `Free`. The observation is injected into `probe_port_holder_from`
because a fixture listener the test owns is one `lsof` CAN see — the first
version of this test passed against the fail-open code, and mutation testing
caught it.

the bypass while every refusal message says to set it to `1`. Now parses the

* fix(trusty-agents): wait on the api server's readiness signal, not a 5s budget

ApiServer::spawn already polled /api/health rather than sleeping, but under a
5s ceiling — small enough to be a bet on the machine being idle. It held on
CI's single-tenant runner and lost locally at load 22-38, where api_e2e.rs went
red 3/3. Reproduced here: at load 277 the 5s arm failed all 4 tests in 5.19s,
i.e. it hit exactly the ceiling, while the same binary with a real bound passed
in 1.10s.

The ceiling is now sized as a "something is wrong" bound rather than an
expected-latency one, and three things make overshooting it free:

- a child that exits fails immediately via try_wait, with its status, instead
  of sitting out the ceiling and reporting an anonymous timeout;
- each probe is individually bounded, so one stalled request cannot consume
  the whole wait and turn a retry loop back into a single fixed wait;
- the child's stdout/stderr are drained continuously. Nothing read those pipes
  before, so a chatty startup could fill the buffer and block the child before
  it ever bound the port. Draining removes that hang and puts the child's own
  output in every readiness failure message — which already paid off: the
  reproduction above reports "child still running", proving a slow start
  rather than a crash.

wait_for_task likewise retries a failed poll instead of treating one transport
hiccup as terminal. The condition is "the task left running"; a failed GET says
nothing about it, and the poll is most likely to fail exactly when the server
is busiest.

`provider_for` CONSUMES a slug's `<prefix>/` marker to pick a provider, but the
slug then travelled into the request body unchanged. With an `OPENAI_API_KEY`

`api.openai.com` receives `"model": "openai/gpt-4o-mini"` — not a model id it
publishes — and answers 400. `DEFAULT_MANAGER_MODEL` and `DEFAULT_CLASSIFIER_MODEL`
both carry that exact slug, so an operator with an unrelated OpenAI key silently
lost the manager digest and activity classifier with no config change of theirs.

`ProviderId::wire_model_id` removes exactly one leading marker, and only when it
names that provider, so a slash inside a genuine model id survives
(`accounts/fireworks/models/…`, `meta-llama/…`) and so does a nested vendor
segment (`atlascloud/openai/gpt-5.6-sol` -> `openai/gpt-5.6-sol`). The shared
`OpenAiCompatAdapter::prepare_body` applies it, which covers every OpenAI-dialect
provider on both the buffered and streaming paths.

OpenRouter is exempt and still transmits the full `vendor/model` slug verbatim:
it routes BY that slug and serves first-party models under a real `openrouter/`
vendor (`openrouter/auto`), so a global strip would break the primary provider.
Two tests pin that byte.

Bedrock and Anthropic-direct had each hand-rolled this strip for their own
provider — that duplication is why the OpenAI-dialect family had none. Both now

fix(trusty-mpm): scrub inherited CLAUDE_CODE_CHILD_SESSION so managed sessions keep transcripts (#4475)

* fix(trusty-mpm): scrub inherited CLAUDE_CODE_CHILD_SESSION so managed sessions keep transcripts

When `tm` is invoked from inside a Claude Code session it inherits the
process-local markers Claude Code injects into its child processes, and
passed them straight through to the `claude` it spawns. An inherited
`CLAUDE_CODE_CHILD_SESSION` makes Claude Code turn session persistence
off, so the managed session had no native --resume/--continue/rewind
recovery and never appeared in `--resume`. Since tm's own pause/resume
writes only a condensed summary, a session that died lost everything
since its last snapshot.

The marker set is read from the `claude` 2.1.220 bundle's own child-env
injector, not guessed. Scrubbed: CLAUDE_CODE_CHILD_SESSION (the sole
transcript-saving trigger), CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID, CLAUDECODE,
CLAUDE_PID, CLAUDE_EFFORT, CLAUDE_CODE_EXECPATH. Deliberately kept:
CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR (#4455 relies on the relocation to reach the bundled
roster via the `user` settings tier), CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN,
CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS and CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT.

Applied to every spawn path, not just the default one: `spawn_command`
and `resume_command` share the `env -u` prefix, while the in-place
relaunch and the headless stream-JSON backend exec through a `Command`
and use `env_remove`.

Adds a `transcript_saving` doctor check (24 checks, was 23) that fails in
both directions — under-scrub loses transcripts, over-scrub loses the
agent roster. It parses the scrub set out of the real spawn prefix rather
than restating the constant, so removing the flags from the builder makes
it fail.

fix: make five non-hermetic test fixtures deterministic (#4306, #4413, #4414, #4415, refs #4407) (#4482)

* fix(trusty-mpm): replace the racy bind-and-drop dead-address fixture

Three copies of a `dead_loopback_url()` helper — in `tui::project_ctl::poll::
tests`, `tui::coordinator::tests` and `tui::project_ctl::tests`, feeding 13
call sites — obtained a "known dead" address by binding an ephemeral port and
then dropping the listener. That releases the port back to the OS pool, so the
premise the fixture exists to provide ("nothing can be listening here") held
only until another binder was handed the same port. Then the connect succeeds:
`classify_connect_error_is_transport`'s `expect_err` panics, or the request
fails at the HTTP layer and misclassifies as `NonTransport`.

Measured, rather than assumed: a bind-and-drop port was reassigned to a
competing binder — and accepted a connection — after 16,103 ephemeral binds,
one wrap of macOS's 49152-65535 range, which a full suite's port churn reaches.

All three copies now share one fixture in `test_support`, on `127.0.0.1:1`:
privileged (so `bind` needs root — measured `PermissionDenied`) and outside
every ephemeral range, so no binder can be handed it. This is already the
workspace convention — trusty-review and trusty-analyze use the same address
for the same reason.

Two rejected alternatives are recorded in the fixture's docs. Binding a port
and deliberately not calling `listen(2)` reserves it, but macOS silently drops
the SYN rather than resetting it, so connects TIME OUT instead of being refused
(measured: `TimedOut` after a full 10s) — which would have gone green while
making 13 tests slow and handing the classification tests the wrong error kind.
Serialising the tests was rejected because it masks the invalid premise instead
of removing it.

The fixture verifies its own premise once per test process, so a machine that
does have a listener on port 1 fails immediately and by name instead of
several frames downstream. Two new tests pin both properties (refusal, and
non-bindability) so the guarantee is checked rather than documented, and a
compile-time assertion stops a future edit moving the port above 1024.

* fix(trusty-mpm): assert telegram backoff reset on a paused clock

`healthy_run_resets_transient_backoff` asserted `backoff_component < 20ms`
against a policy `base` of 2ms. The 18ms of headroom was there purely to
absorb scheduler jitter, which means what the assertion actually measured on a
loaded machine was wakeup latency, not backoff state. It reddened the shared
gate three times in one working session at 34.4ms and 21.79ms observed, in PRs
touching zero files under `telegram/`.

The test now runs on tokio's paused clock. `supervise` takes every timing
decision through `tokio::time` — `Instant::now()`/`elapsed()` for the run
duration, `sleep` for the backoff — so under `start_paused` the runtime
advances virtual time to each deadline while idle and every gap is exact.
Widening the bound was rejected: a wider wall-clock bound is the same defect
with a longer fuse.

Exactness let the assertions get stricter rather than looser. The two bounds
became equalities (`== delay_for(3)`, `== base`), and two new assertions pin
the earlier steps of the escalation schedule, which the old `>= 25ms` could
not distinguish from the 400ms cap. Also fixes the isolation arithmetic: it
subtracted `policy.healthy_run` where the run actually lasted
`healthy_run + 5ms`, a 5ms error the loose bound hid.

Verified the test still has teeth by mutating the production reset. Removing
it entirely is caught (128ms vs 2ms). A PARTIAL reset — to 1 instead of 0,
giving `delay_for(2)` = 8ms — is also caught, and is exactly what the old
`< 20ms` bound would have accepted, so this is a strengthening and not
merely a translation.

* fix(trusty-mpm): join banner tests to the crate-wide $HOME serial group

The plain-mode banner tests serialised themselves with a FILE-LOCAL

describes — unrelated plain-mode tests reddening together and clearing on the
next run with no code change.

mutex is gone, so they participate in the group that actually excludes the
other writers.

`banner_source_missing_falls_back` exercises `load_banner_art()`'s NotFound
arm, which calls `write_default_if_absent()` — a WRITE to
`$HOME/.trusty-mpm/banner.txt`. With the ambient $HOME that seeded a real file
in the developer's own home (confirmed present locally), and under the old lock
it could land inside a concurrent test's $HOME tempdir and corrupt that test's
fixture. It now points $HOME at its own tempdir and asserts the seeded content,

on PR #4482 against a fragment that PR did not write.

Why: `InferenceAdapter::chat_stream` had no Bedrock override, so every
`bedrock/*` turn fell back to the trait's buffered default — the whole
answer arrived as ONE delta after the model had already finished. Bedrock
streaming is not new work in this workspace: `chat::bedrock_impl` has
driven ConverseStream in production (trusty-agents' chat path) since
#3767. This moves that capability onto `inference::InferenceAdapter`, the
surface epic #4429 is converging on, so the winning adapter is the one
that can stream.

What:
- New `inference/bedrock/stream.rs`: `ConverseStreamDecoder` folds
  `ConverseStreamOutput` framing into the neutral event model, plus
  `drive()` which turns an event source into a `ChatStream`.
    * `ContentBlockDelta::Text` -> `ChatStreamEvent::Delta` (empty
      fragments dropped)
    * tool-use block starts -> introducing `ToolCall` (id + name);
      partial-JSON argument fragments -> continuation `ToolCall`s.
      This EXTENDS the reference impl, which ignores tool use entirely —
      without it the shared adapter could not stream an agent turn.
    * tool slots are re-indexed dense from 0, because Converse's
      `contentBlockIndex` counts every content block (leading text makes
      the first tool block index 1) while `ToolCallDelta::index` is the
      OpenAI-dialect call ordinal consumers accumulate by.

      `Done` (Bedrock splits the summary across two non-final events,
      and reports usage exactly once — dropping it would silently zero

feat(trusty-code): consume the shared streaming chat adapter, delete the local one (#4436)

* feat(trusty-code): consume the shared streaming chat adapter, delete the local one

trusty-code owned a parallel LLM abstraction: `llm::LlmClientTrait` plus
duplicate `ChatRequest`/`ChatResponse`/`ChatMessage`/`UsageBlock`/`LlmError`
types and an `llm::convert` bridge whose only job was translating between that
copy and `trusty_common::inference`'s. The duplication had a concrete cost, not
an aesthetic one: the shared adapter gained native SSE streaming
(`InferenceAdapter::chat_stream`, epic #3696 Gap B) and trusty-code could not
reach it, because its own trait had no streaming method — so every `tcode tui`
turn could only ever arrive as one paste.

Delete the local abstraction. Every trusty-code call site now depends on
`trusty_common::inference::InferenceAdapter`, and `crate::llm` re-exports the
shared wire types so existing import paths keep resolving.
`OpenAiCompatClient`, `DispatchingLlmClient`, `BedrockChatClient`, the
transcript recorder, and the debug-capture decorator are now IMPLEMENTATIONS of
that trait, each overriding `chat_stream` — the trait's buffered default would
have silently disabled streaming on exactly the production paths that wrap the
transport in a decorator.

`AgentLoop` streams when a sink is attached: `agent_message` is called per
content chunk with `done: false` and once with `done: true` and an empty delta.
With no sink (the run-task CLI path, every scripted test) it takes the blocking
`chat` call, byte-identical to before. A `chat_stream` handshake failure is
propagated, never silently retried as a blocking call — a degraded-but-working
tcode would make "is streaming working?" unanswerable from outside.

trusty-common gains two things the migration exposed as genuine gaps:
`StreamAssembly` (the inverse of `buffered_stream` — rebuild a `ChatResponse`
from streamed events, so a consumer can stream for display without forking its
non-streaming pipeline) and `InferenceError::MissingConfig(String)`, which
`MissingCredential { provider }` cannot express.

Bedrock streaming is the buffered fallback for now — the pre-existing behaviour,
no regression. Its real `ConverseStream` transport is #4426 and lands entirely
inside `trusty_common::inference::bedrock`, with no edit to trusty-code.

Net −478 lines across the two crates.

concurrent_open::backoff_sleep_ms with a memory_remember hung ~1800s, and both
`tm doctor` and `trusty-memory doctor` reported HEALTHY throughout. They checked
HTTP liveness, fastembed cache state, and lock-file staleness — every one of

127.0.0.1:7070" while MCP memory_recall/memory_remember succeeded against that

behind a mutex and enumerates open file descriptors — work the MCP path never
does — so under load it exceeded a 2s single-shot budget that real traffic
never approached. The probe was measuring its own impatience.

The signal chosen for the wedge is the AGE OF THE OLDEST IN-FLIGHT OPERATION,
registered at open_palace_handle — the single choke point every recall/remember
passes through, and where the #3992 wedge actually occurred. It is the cheapest
signal that observes worker liveness rather than process liveness: a plain
in-flight COUNT cannot distinguish healthy concurrency from a wedge, and only
age can. Implemented as a fixed-size lock-free slot table — one CAS in, one
store out, no allocation and no syscall on the hot path — so the gauge cannot
become the load problem it exists to detect. Registration is RAII, because the
operations being tracked are exactly the ones that fail and unwind; an explicit
release would leak slots on the error path and read as a permanent phantom
wedge.

Rejected as too expensive or too invasive: thread-state sampling (platform
debugging APIs), mutex wait-time histograms (needs parking_lot internals).

The third state is the part worth keeping if nothing else survives review.
Both doctors gained an Unknown/indeterminate status that renders ❔, never ✅,
and in trusty-mpm ranks above Warn so one indeterminate check can never leave
the aggregate report reading healthy. A timeout now yields Unknown instead of a
false Fail; a 2xx carrying no worker observation (an older daemon, an
unreadable body) is Unknown rather than a pass doctor cannot support.
