fix(trusty-common): exempt slash-separated PR-number lists from the secret scanner (#4216)

A PM session checkpoint enumerating tickets as `#2763/#2774/#2780/#2782/#2790`
was rejected by `remember_with_options` as a "likely secret/credential token".
The token contains no letters at all, but the `/` separators set `has_b64_sym`
and the digits set `has_digit`, so the base64-blob branch of `looks_like_secret`
fired. The slash-path branch of `is_structural_token` does not rescue it,
because `#` is deliberately excluded from `is_word_segment`.

Observed live twice. Agents worked around the rejection by rewording or
dropping detail, silently degrading checkpoint fidelity.

Fix: allowlist `[#/0-9]`-only tokens in `looks_like_secret`, alongside the
existing git-SHA carve-out and using the same early-return pattern. Widening
`is_word_segment` to admit `#` was rejected as the alternative: it would have
loosened the structural bypass for every path and `key=value` token, a far
larger blast radius than this false positive warrants.

The exemption is a keyhole, not a hole. The `{#, /, 0-9}` charset has no
character-class spread, so no base64, hex, or base32 alphabet can be expressed
in it, and no known credential format contains `#`. It is strictly narrower
than the git-SHA carve-out, which admits the full hex alphabet.

Tests: `slash_separated_pr_number_list_not_flagged` uses the exact string from
the issue and fails before this change. `real_secrets_still_blocked_after_2800_exemption`
is the guard and passes both before and after — its load-bearing cases are a
`#`/digit/slash token with one alphabetic segment smuggled in, and a
digit/slash token carrying a `+`; both must stay flagged, proving the exemption
is charset-scoped.

Closes #2800

* test(installer): make dead_addr deterministic instead of TOCTOU-racy (#4246)

dead_addr bound an ephemeral port, recorded the address, dropped the
listener and returned it. Between that drop and the caller's connect the
OS may hand the same port to any ephemeral request — including a sibling
stub in the same concurrently-running test binary — so the expected
ECONNREFUSED could become a successful connection. That made the two
#4246 regression guards (probe_distinguishes_failure_causes,
verify_one_kickstarts_a_genuinely_down_launchd_daemon) latently flaky for
a reason unrelated to the code under test.

Use a fixed privileged loopback port (1/tcpmux) that an unprivileged
`cargo test` cannot bind, and have the helper VERIFY the refusal before
returning so the documented guarantee is asserted rather than assumed.

Two seemingly-obvious repairs were measured and rejected: holding the
listener open without accept() still completes the handshake from the
backlog (yielding Timeout, not Refused), and holding a socket bound
without listen() drops the SYN on macOS (also Timeout).

No ProbeOutcome expectations change — the affected tests still assert
Refused.

* test(installer): un-invert the probe timeout bounds so the read path is unambiguous (#4246)

probe_distinguishes_failure_causes built its client with
connect_timeout(500ms) and timeout(400ms) — a total-request budget SHORTER
than the connect budget. That made the connect bound unreachable dead
config, and left the `silent` case unable to show WHICH deadline it
proved: the case exists to demonstrate that a peer which completes the
handshake and then goes quiet yields Timeout on the READ path, but with
those bounds a connect-phase timeout was equally consistent with the
assertion.

Reordered to connect 250ms / request 2s, so a loopback handshake has ~1000x
headroom and the read path an 8x margin over the connect bound. The
assertion is unchanged and still requires Timeout specifically.

NOTE on the reported cause: the review described this as a race that could
yield `Refused` under load. That specific inversion is not reachable.
hyper-util reports a connect timeout as io::ErrorKind::TimedOut
(client/legacy/connect/http.rs), reqwest's is_timeout() matches that kind,
and classify_transport_error tests is_timeout() BEFORE is_connect() — so a
connect timeout also lands on Timeout, never Refused. The inverted bounds
were still worth fixing for the reason above.

* docs(installer): pin the health_string / is_confirmed_down asymmetry (#4246)

health_string() maps NoAddress, HttpError, BadEnvelope and ProbeFailed to
"down" while is_confirmed_down() returns false for all four. That gap is
deliberate — the kickstart gates on the variant, not the string — but it is
a trap: a future caller who reads `health_string() == "down"` as
"safe to restart" reintroduces #4246 in one line, hard-restarting a member
whose address merely failed to resolve or whose port hosts a squatter.

Document the invariant on BOTH methods, from each side: health_string()
now states it is display/reporting only and MUST NOT authorise a
destructive action, and is_confirmed_down() states it is strictly narrower
than the "down" string, naming NoAddress as the sharpest case.

Add down_health_string_is_not_a_kickstart_licence, which asserts the
asymmetry EXISTS rather than checking each view separately: over every
down-rendering variant, the confirmed-down set must be a strict, non-empty
subset. If someone "tidies" the two views into equivalence, that test
fails. It also asserts the mirror property — some "down" must still
authorise repair, or a genuinely dead daemon is never kickstarted (#2498).

NoAddress deliberately keeps mapping to "down" rather than "unknown":
"unknown" is tolerated by VerifyTailReport::build and status's exit code,
so it would report VERIFIED for a member whose address never resolved.

fix(trusty-review): refuse to confirm registry claims nothing looked up (#4081) (#4212)

* fix(trusty-review): refuse to confirm registry claims nothing looked up

A review of a one-line CI change (`ruff>=0.6.0` -> `ruff==0.16.0`) reported
that `0.16.0` "does not exist on PyPI", reasoning explicitly from the reviewer
model's training cutoff. It was the current latest release, and all ten checks
on that PR were green on that exact dependency. Nothing in the pipeline
performs a registry lookup, so nothing had checked the claim -- yet it carried
`code_provable: true` and `verified: "confirmed"`, the two signals a consumer
reads to decide a finding is trustworthy, and hard-clamped the verdict to
BLOCK/F. A hallucination wearing a confirmation is worse than no finding at
all: it inverts the trust signal. And it lands on dependency bumps, the one
diff shape where a reviewer's version knowledge is stale by construction.

New `pipeline::claim_grounding` pass, wired into
`finding_hygiene::sanitize_findings` so both the unified and map-reduce paths
get it. A finding whose text pairs a registry subject (PyPI, npm, crates.io,
requirements.txt, package.json, ...) with a registry-state assertion (version
absent, withdrawn, deprecated, "latest release is...", "as of my knowledge
cutoff") is demoted to the advisory tier: `code_provable` cleared, `effort`
capped at Medium, `confidence` capped at the advisory band, and `verified`
pre-stamped with a new `VerifyOutcome::Unverifiable { reason }`.
`verify::select_candidates` now skips any finding whose outcome is already
decided, so such a claim is never put to the verifier LLM -- a second model
with the same stale training knowledge would only launder the recollection
into a "confirmed".

Refuse-to-confirm, not look-up. Querying the registries was considered and
rejected: it buys nothing the reported harm needs, and adds a live network
dependency, rate limits, and a new way for the review path itself to hang. The
principle encoded is stronger than any lookup -- a claim may be marked
`verified: "confirmed"` only when something actually verified it.

The finding is never dropped. It still surfaces verbatim with an advisory note
telling the author nothing checked it; only its grading weight is removed. A
genuine, diff-provable finding alongside it keeps full weight and still drives
BLOCK.

Closes #4081.

The bundled PM instruction package was a Rust literal, not an authored
artifact: sections, tiers, block order, joins and generators were a `vec![]`
in `bundled_pm_package.rs`, `InstructionPackage::from_json` had zero non-test
call sites, and the shipped JSON Schema had no instance under it. Other
tickets already recorded "the composed instructions payload is generated from
the instruction package JSON" as settled fact. It now is.

Schema v2 adds a `{"kind":"file","path":"..."}` body variant. Prose keeps
living in reviewable markdown under `sections/`; the manifest references it by
path and resolves through a compile-time `include_str!` table
(`instruction_pipeline::SECTION_SOURCES`), so the build stays hermetic and a
renamed section is a compile error rather than an empty block. Inlining the
prose instead would have turned `core.md` into one 23 KB JSON line and moved
the floor text out of the files `check_instruction_floor.sh` greps. The
version bump is required by the format's own evolution policy: a v1 build
reading a v2 manifest rejects it loudly rather than composing a prompt missing
the new field's effect.

The mechanism half moves nothing. All three composed-prompt goldens passed
byte-unchanged with the manifest in place and the content below absent.

Three owner language rules ride along, authored as inline `text` blocks in the
manifest rather than in markdown (owner order, 2026-07-29: the 1.3 rules
belong in JSON). Same family as the plain-prose rule from #4316.

  * Clickable References (core) - issue/PR/ticket/commit references always
    render as clickable markdown links, never bare numbers.
  * Banned Word "honest" (core) - banned from PM responses, delegation briefs
    and review instructions; a report states facts, and labelling them honest
    implies the alternative was considered.
  * Opportunistic Fixes (workflow) - an easy fix found while working on a file
    is noted on the CURRENT issue and made in the same work, never a new
    issue; new issues are for genuinely separable schedulable work.

Once a rule may be authored in the manifest, rebuilding the legacy
multi-section strings from the `include_str!` constants would deliver it to
the packaged composer and silently withhold it from the `.trusty-mpm/`
override assembly and from `assemble_system_prompt()` - the roster-free prompt
`tm install` writes and `tm launch` passes to `--append-system-prompt-file`.
So `pm_instructions()`, `base_pm()` and the new `workflow_section()` /
`delegation_doctrine()` project the same manifest through

feat(trusty-mpm): read named-section PM instruction overrides from CLAUDE.md (#4324)

Project customization of the PM prompt lives in five separate files under
`<project>/.trusty-mpm/`, which forces every project to maintain a second
instruction surface next to the `CLAUDE.md` it already has and gives each
override whole-document granularity. This adds the READER for the replacement:
a named section marked out inside `CLAUDE.md` overrides exactly the matching
section of the bundled instruction package, and nothing else.

New module `core::claude_md_sections`. Grammar, matched whole-line:

    <!-- TRUSTY-MPM: WORKFLOW START v=1 -->
    …override content…
    <!-- TRUSTY-MPM: WORKFLOW END -->

The token is the section id kebab-case uppercased (CORE, MEMORY, SEARCH,
WORKFLOW, AGENT-DELEGATION), matched case-insensitively; content is what lies
strictly between the marker lines, trimmed; text outside markers is ignored.
Hosts are scanned in precedence order — `<project>/CLAUDE.md`, then
`<project>/.trusty-mpm/INSTRUCTIONS.md` — with `CLAUDE.md` winning a
same-section collision. A marked block in `INSTRUCTIONS.md` is removed from the
additive addendum so it is delivered once; a marker-free `INSTRUCTIONS.md` is
passed through byte-for-byte and keeps feeding `project-addendum` as before.

THE PACKAGE IS THE SOLE AUTHORITY on what may be overridden. The new
`InstructionPackage::with_overrides` asks each section's declared
`customization_tier` rather than consulting any list held by the reader, so the
three floor sections refuse every `CLAUDE.md` override and compose
byte-identically to no `CLAUDE.md` at all. An override replaces only its
section's authored text blocks; generated blocks survive, so an
AGENT-DELEGATION override rewrites the routing doctrine but cannot suppress the
live agent roster.

NEVER FAIL CLOSED. A missing or unreadable host, an unclosed or nested marker
pair, an unknown token, an unknown `v=`, an override aimed at the floor, an
empty body, and a package that stops validating all degrade to the bundled
section, each with a `warn!` naming the file, line and reason. A missing `v=`
is accepted as `v=1` for this release, with a warning.

This ships the reader BEFORE the floor text that advertises the mechanism.
Advertising an override no code reads is what left the `.trusty-mpm/` override
table a silent no-op for two years. The five legacy override files are
untouched and keep working; a project still carrying one composes through the
sectionless legacy assembly, and its named sections are reported unapplied
rather than dropped in silence.

Tests: 39 in the new module, covering the grammar and its refusals, every
fail-open path, the per-floor-section byte-identity gate, roster survival, and
that resolving a prompt never writes a project's `CLAUDE.md`. A third committed
prompt snapshot, `testdata/pm-prompt-claude-md-override.md`, makes the
delivered shape of an override reviewable; both existing goldens are
byte-unchanged.

feat(trusty-agents): register agent's declared [[plugins.python]] tools (#4313)

The `PythonToolPlugin` subprocess primitive (spawn `python3 <script>`, one
NDJSON `tool_call` in / one `tool_result` out, per-call timeout, fail-closed
RBAC tier guard) has shipped fully unit-tested since it was written, and
`AgentConfig` has parsed `[plugins]` into `AgentPluginsConfig` for just as
long -- but `PythonToolPlugin::from_config` had ZERO production call sites
anywhere in the workspace. An agent or skill package declaring a
`[[plugins.python]]` tool therefore had its declaration parsed and then
silently dropped: never registered, never advertised, never callable, and no
warning emitted. This adds the missing seam.

`run_pm_task_with_persona` now reads `persona_cfg.plugins.python` and
registers each entry via a new `persona_plugins::register_python_plugins`,
resolving a package-relative `script` / `schema_file` against the agent/skill
package dir (the same `config_dir` the delegation runner is handed), so
`script = "../skills/foo/foo.py"` reaches a co-located skill package. The
helper lives in its own module for the same reason `persona_gate` does --
`persona.rs` sits just under the 500-SLOC production cap -- and mutates the
EXACT registry the dispatch path arms, so the tests drive the production
construction rather than a re-derived copy.

Registration is not a grant: the `[tools].allow` glob filter, the RBAC tier
filter and the scope gate all still decide whether the tool reaches the model.
Two non-fatal skip paths keep one bad line in one agent TOML from taking down
a chat turn:

- an entry `from_config` rejects (e.g. an unknown `restricted_tiers` string,
  fail-closed since #3236) is logged and skipped;
- an entry whose name is already taken by a native or MCP tool is refused
  rather than registered. `ToolRegistry::register` overwrites silently in
  release and `debug_assert!`s in debug, so an unguarded registration here
  would have made a debug-build panic reachable straight from user-authored
  config, and a production tool hijack reachable the same way.

Tests: four unit tests on the helper (registered AND dispatchable through the
real `ToolRegistry` with a package-relative script; malformed-config skip;
name-collision refusal; empty-list no-op) plus
`tests/persona_python_plugin_wiring.rs`, which drives the REAL
`run_pm_task_with_persona` against a sandboxed throwaway agent package and
asserts on the tracing output that the plugin was both registered and survived
the allow/RBAC/scope gate into the advertised set. That last one is the only
test that goes red if the CALL SITE is deleted while the helper survives --
verified by removing it and watching the assertion fail with `tools=[]`.

fix(tga): gate Tier-3/4 identity fuzzy fallback on alias-table presence (#4291)

`IdentityResolver::resolve` runs four tiers. Tiers 1/2 are exact alias lookups;
Tiers 3/4 are Jaro-Winkler fuzzy guesses. The fuzzy tiers exist to catch
identities a project never declared, but they ran unconditionally, including
when the project had already supplied an exhaustive `aliases_file`. Once
cto-reports moved its ~130-entry roster into a 177-entry alias file, every
additional entry enlarged the fuzzy haystack and the guesser began collapsing
distinct people onto similarly-spelled colleagues (Crispian Alvarenga ->
Crisandra Fonseca, Nico Vanderbergheim -> Nico Mercer, Marci Dalton -> Marcel
Sutton, Josh Dorsey -> Joshua Kepler, Joseph Wu -> Joshua Kepler).

Presence of an `aliases_file` now disables Tiers 3/4 by default, via a new
top-level `fuzzy_identity_fallback` config key:

- unset (default): Tiers 3/4 run unless a declared `aliases_file` successfully
  loaded a non-empty alias table
- true: force Tiers 3/4 on even with an alias file (pre-2.11.0 behaviour)
- false: force Tiers 3/4 off even without an alias file

The gate gives way to the documented pre-2.11.0 behaviour whenever the alias
table is not actually loaded: a declared-but-broken or empty alias file logs at
`error!` and leaves fuzzy enabled rather than silently disabling it. A
deliberately rejected alternative was a "comprehensiveness score" coverage
threshold, which would stack a second guessing layer on the first and turn a
reproducible bug into a tuning problem.

fix(trusty-mpm): serialise projects.json writes across processes (#4258)

`ProjectStore::upsert` performed an unsynchronised read-modify-write of the
whole registry file: `reload_if_changed()` -> mutate the in-memory map ->
write `projects.json` back. `ProjectRegistry`'s `tokio::sync::RwLock` only
serialises tasks within ONE process, but `projects.json` is written by the
daemon, `tm project ...` CLI invocations and MCP tool calls concurrently. Two
processes interleaving read/read/write/write dropped one registration entirely
while BOTH callers saw `Ok`.

A cross-process test exposed a second, worse failure from the same window:
every writer used one fixed `projects.json.tmp` scratch path, so overlapping
writes interleaved into that single temp file and the rename published a
document that no longer parsed:

    child: upsert: Serialize("trailing characters at line 19 column 2")

Fix: add `trusty_common::json_rmw` — the one implementation of the locked
read-modify-write cycle that trusty-mpm's `projects.json`, trusty-gworkspace's
`tokens.json` (#3502) and the epic #4207 worktree registry all need. It takes
an exclusive advisory lock on a `<path>.lock` sidecar, re-reads the document
under that lock (never trusting a caller's stale copy), applies the mutation,
and publishes it atomically via a per-writer-unique temp file + fsync + rename
+ directory fsync. `fd-lock` was already the workspace's advisory-locking
choice for exactly this problem shape.

`ProjectStore` now funnels every mutation through a single `mutate` entry
point built on it, run via `spawn_blocking` so the blocking lock syscall never
parks a runtime worker. `PATCH /api/v1/projects/{name}` gains the same
guarantee: `ProjectRegistry::update_with` delegates to `ProjectStore::
update_with`, so its fetch->mutate->persist happens inside ONE held lock
rather than a `get` and a later `upsert`. The lock-bypassing `save()` is
removed so no second write path can reintroduce the race.

Does not fail open: a lock that cannot be acquired returns the new
`ProjectStoreError::Lock` rather than falling through to an unsynchronised
write, an unreadable-but-present file is never silently replaced by an empty
one, and a closure returning `Err` aborts the write with the file unchanged.
Readers deliberately take no lock — atomic rename means they always observe a
complete document, so a reader can never deadlock against a writer.

Tests: `crates/trusty-mpm/tests/projects_json_concurrency.rs` spawns REAL
child processes (re-exec of the test binary, released from a shared barrier)
rather than threads, so it observes the shipping failure mode. It fails
against the pre-fix store and passes after. Also covers a SIGKILLed writer
leaving `projects.json` parseable with its prior entries intact, lock
contention completing rather than deadlocking, the fail-open path, and stale
temp-file debris. Store unit tests moved to `store_tests.rs` (pure code
motion) to stay under the 500-SLOC production cap.

fix(trusty-channels): clamp search.messages count to Slack's documented 100 (#4242)

`slack_search_messages` clamped `count` against `MAX_PAGE_SIZE = 1000`,
documented as "the widest window Slack's `search.messages` accepts". That
claim was false. Slack documents a maximum `count` of 100 for this method:

  "Pass the number of results you want per 'page'. Maximum of 100."
  "the max `count` value is 100 and the max `page` value is 100"
  https://docs.slack.dev/reference/methods/search.messages

Any `count` in 101..=1000 therefore passed local validation, was forwarded
verbatim, and was rejected live with `{"ok": false, "error":
"invalid_arguments"}` — a slug `interpret_envelope` surfaces unchanged, so
the caller saw only an opaque error with no hint at the cause.

`MAX_PAGE_SIZE` had exactly one production consumer (`search.rs`); the
`conversations.*` family already uses `MAX_CONVERSATION_PAGE_SIZE = 999`.
It is renamed to `MAX_SEARCH_COUNT = 100` rather than duplicated, so no
mis-documented constant survives. An over-large `count` is reduced to 100
rather than rejected: Slack caps the page either way, so the caller gets
the most results available instead of a failure, and the response's `count`
still reports how many matches actually came back. The tool schema now
states the cap so callers see it before they call.

The defect survived review because the only coverage mounted a mock that
answered `ok:true` regardless of `count`. The new tests assert on the
outgoing request body, so a regressed ceiling produces no matching route
and fails.

fix(trusty-mpm): derive worktrees from git instead of walking five shapes (#4207) (#4224)

* fix(trusty-mpm): derive worktrees from git instead of walking five shapes (#4207)

Worktree discovery and ownership were both inferences, not facts.

Discovery walked five hard-coded location shapes (`.worktrees/`,
`.base/.worktrees/`, `.claude/worktrees/`, `.base/.claude/worktrees/`, and
`.base/.worktrees/<id>/.claude/worktrees/`). Every one of those was added by a
bug report about a location the previous list had missed (#3649, #3971, and
its follow-up), and the list could never be complete.

Ownership — "which checkout owns this worktree?" — was the candidate's
GRANDPARENT directory. That guess is wrong for `<repo>/.claude/worktrees/<n>`
(it names `.claude`, not a repository) and, worse, for the fourteen worktrees
observed on 2026-07-27 living under `<repo>/.base/.worktrees/` but registered
to the parent repo `<repo>`: the guess asked `.base`, `.base` correctly said
"not mine", and the reclaim path skipped them conservatively — forever. They
were not merely un-reclaimed, they were STRUCTURALLY unreclaimable.

Both questions have exact answers. `git worktree list --porcelain` is the
registry; `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` names the checkout that owns it.

- New `session_manager::worktree_registry`: the porcelain parser,
  `registry_root_for` (replaces grandparent inference), and
  `enumerate_registered_worktrees`.
- `prune::find_orphaned_worktrees` delegates discovery to it; the five-shape
  walk, `scan_worktree_shape`, and `list_immediate_dirs` are deleted.
- `worktree_safety::git_worktree_list_agrees` asks the CANDIDATE'S OWN
  repository instead of its grandparent.
- `decommission::remove_session_worktree` aims git at the registry root.

Every probe returns `Option`, never `bool` — a missing `git`, a permissions
error, or a stalled mount can never be read as a fact about a worktree. A
candidate that will not canonicalize is skipped, so a failed observation may
only ever shrink what is proposed for deletion, never enlarge it.

Every worktree in the affected tests is now a real `git worktree add`; a
`mkdir` is no longer a candidate, and the previous fixtures would have passed
vacuously.

hard-coded path shapes to every worktree git registers anywhere under the

walk never produced, FIVE of them the operator's own long-lived checkouts

repository has already lost a bare clone to an over-broad removal (2026-07-21).

A candidate must now additionally be a STRICT DESCENDANT of the managed project
directory whose registry named it. That is a positive assertion the path is
inside a tree trusty-mpm provisions — an invariant of the write side, since the
provisioner only ever creates worktrees beneath <repos_root>/<owner>/<repo>/.

the project qualifies, so the "we forgot a location" bug class #4207 deletes
stays deleted. And it is not a denylist of known operator paths — an operator
checkout is excluded by its POSITION relative to the repository that owns it,
so a new one is excluded the day it is created, under any name.

retains all 54 .base-resident worktrees (the class that was structurally
unreclaimable before this PR), and leaves the count of sentinel-bearing — i.e.

* fix(trusty-mpm): stop the liveness guard's own first stat swallowing io errors

Review HIGH on PR #4209. `workspace_liveness` opened with
`if !path.is_dir() { return Absent }`, and `Absent.is_dead()` is `true`.
`Path::is_dir()` folds EVERY io error into `false`, so a genuinely LIVE linked
worktree — `.git` pointer file intact — behind a parent directory the process
cannot traverse classified as dead. The module asserted "a failed observation
is never death" in absolute terms while its first branch violated it; this is
the same swallow-the-error defect as the predecessor's `canonicalize().ok()`,
moved one call earlier rather than eliminated.

The first stat now goes through `fs::metadata` and matches on `ErrorKind`,
exactly as the `.git` stat already did. Only a DEFINITE observation yields
`Absent` — a successful stat finding a non-directory, or `NotFound`. Every
other error kind yields `Indeterminate`, which `is_dead()` reports as not
dead. `metadata` follows symlinks just as `is_dir()` did, so a symlinked
workspace keeps its previous verdict.

This matters beyond its current blast radius: both call sites only gate a
refusal to write, so today the bug is over-refusal rather than data loss. But
`is_dead()` ships as a reusable absolute contract and epic #4207's git-native
work is DESTRUCTIVE and will inherit it. The contract has to be true before
anything deletes on it.

Docs corrected rather than left claiming a property the code lacked: the module
doc now states the invariant holds of EVERY stat including the first, and names
`is_dir`/`exists`/`is_file` as predicates that must not be reintroduced into
this decision; the `Absent` docstring now says an unreadable path is never
`Absent`.

Also, per the same finding, the sweep's `Absent` arm was a bare `continue` —
no outcome, no log. It now warns and records a skip outcome, so a live session
record pointing at a vanished workspace is visible to the operator instead of
disappearing. Note the primary fix already removes the io-error case from this
arm, so it is now reached only by a definite observation. WARN, not ERROR, is
deliberate: a stale record is routine, and only ERROR persists to
errors.jsonl / tm doctor, where a benign recurring condition would be noise —
the returned `WorkspaceResetOutcome` is the operator-facing surface here.

fix(trusty-search): quarantine incremental writes when the corpus open failed (#4122) (#4220)

* fix(trusty-search): quarantine incremental writes when the corpus open failed (#4122)

An index whose durable redb corpus failed to open at load time was left
fully live, watcher included. Ordinary, unrelated file saves in the
worktree kept flowing into the handle, so a FRESH, PARTIAL corpus was
built and persisted over the never-opened original — turning a
recoverable outage into permanent data loss. In production
`duettoresearch-hackathon-tm-hackathon-01` climbed 0 -> 68 -> 1334 chunks
this way and came back "healthy" on the next restart holding the wrong
content; the sibling `cto-duetto` hit the identical open failure in the
same boot, took no watcher writes, and recovered all 200,090 chunks.

A `corpus_open_failed` index is now write-quarantined:

* `CodeIndexer::index_file` — the single choke point for every
  incremental write (watcher, boot-time reconciler, and
  `POST /indexes/{id}/index-file`) — refuses with an `Err` so the HTTP
  endpoint reports 500 rather than falsely answering `"indexed": true`.
* `watch_loop::handle_modified` carries the same guard so a quarantined
  index does not read and chunk every saved file just to discard it.
* Bulk `index_files_batch*` (full reindex) is deliberately NOT gated —
  a reindex is the documented way out of this state.

The refusal is observable: it logs at ERROR (the only level
`trusty_common::error_capture`'s BugCaptureLayer persists to
errors.jsonl / list_recent_errors / tm doctor), throttled to the 1st and
every 100th refusal, and is counted on
`CodeIndexer::refused_incremental_writes`.

The quarantine is not terminal. `set_corpus_store` — the sink every
successful `CorpusStore::open` funnels through — lifts it and resets the
counter, so the clean-restart recovery path is unaffected.

Reads are unchanged; corpus-failed indexes still serve empty results
(that is #4087, not fixed here).

* test(trusty-search): make the #4122 watcher test survive a loaded Linux runner

CI's `Test` leg went red on my own test — and on its POSITIVE CONTROL, which
is the control doing exactly its job: it refused to report a pass from an
environment where the healthy sibling index never indexed at all, so a
refusal could not be distinguished from a stalled watcher. Product code is
unaffected; this commit is test-only.

Two real defects in the test, both mine:

1. It ran on the DEFAULT current-thread runtime. The watcher bridges its OS
   notification thread into the async loop, and that pipeline can starve with
   a single worker. Every passing watcher test in this crate already opts into
   `#[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)]`
   (`watch_loop::tests::modified_file_triggers_indexing`); mine did not. This
   is why it passed on macOS/FSEvents and failed on Linux/inotify.

2. It saved each probe file exactly ONCE, immediately after spawning the watch
   loop. A one-shot event that lands before the OS watch is armed is lost
   permanently, and nothing ever regenerates it — so a startup race became a
   full 30 s budget burn and a red build (CI: `finished in 30.02s`).

Fix: multi-thread runtime, plus `await_condition_resaving`, which rewrites the
probe file with CHANGING content once per 500 ms debounce window while polling
the same observable every 25 ms. The wait now ends as soon as the watcher is
genuinely live instead of depending on a startup sleep being long enough.

This STRENGTHENS the test rather than weakening it — the broken index gets
more chances to wrongly accept a write, and the control must still
demonstrably index before the test proceeds. Re-verified by neutralizing
`refuse_incremental_write` to always return `false` (pre-fix behaviour, API
intact): all three tests still fail, and test 1 still fails on the CORRUPTION
assertion rather than on the control or a missing counter:

  assertion `left == right` failed: #4122: a write-quarantined index must not

fix(trusty-git-analytics): stop JIRA changelog pagination silently truncating oldest transitions (#4155)

JIRA's search-embedded changelog (`expand=changelog`) is itself paged.
`search_with_changelog` read only `changelog.histories` and never consulted
`changelog.total`, so any ticket with more history than fits one embedded page
silently lost its OLDEST transitions — no error, no warning. Those are exactly
the transitions a historical backfill exists to capture.

`search_with_changelog` now compares `changelog.total` against the embedded
entry count and flags the shortfall on `ChangelogIssue::truncated_history_total`;
`tga jira sync` then walks `GET /issue/{key}/changelog` to exhaustion and
replaces (never merges) the truncated history. A complete embedded changelog
issues zero extra requests. A repair that cannot retrieve every entry the
server reported fails with `CollectError::IncompleteChangelog`, naming the
ticket and the expected-vs-retrieved counts, rather than returning a partial
history that reads as complete.

The repair runs in `run_sync`'s per-ticket loop, not inside the search walk, so
one bad ticket no longer costs every other ticket its data: the bad ticket is
recorded failed and holds the cursor, the rest still land, and the run exits
non-zero naming it. Both per-ticket paged walks are bounded at 200 pages
(`CollectError::PagingBudgetExceeded`) against a server that ignores `startAt`.

Also fixed, same fail-open shape:

- `fetch_comments` no longer silently ingests a partial comment set.
  Termination was `start_at >= total` with `total` defaulting to `0` when
  absent, so a response omitting the field ended the walk after one page —
  100 of 150 comments ingested, `Ok`, cursor advanced past the ticket
  permanently. The walk now terminates on a short page measured against the
  server's own echoed `maxResults`, which Atlassian may set below the value
  requested.
- `ChangelogPageResponse::total` is `Option<u64>` rather than
  `#[serde(default)] u64`. An absent `total` read as `0`, ending the walk after
  page 1 and making the `retrieved < total` completeness check pass vacuously,
  so the repair could return less than the truncated data it was invoked to fix.
  The count the search itself reported is now carried in as a standing lower
  bound.
- `jql_time`'s DST step-back no longer emits an unvalidated bound when it
  exhausts its ceiling. The 180-minute ceiling rested on "historic DST shifts
  never exceed two hours" — false: `Antarctica/Casey` folds exactly three hours
  (UTC+11 to UTC+08), saturating the loop with zero margin. Saturation is now an
  explicit error, and the ceiling derives from the -12:00..+14:00 UTC-offset
  span.

`CollectError` and `ChangelogIssue` are now `#[non_exhaustive]`. `tga` is a
published crate, so adding the two new variants and the new public field would
otherwise each be a SemVer-major break for downstreams — the same defect
currently forcing `trusty-common` to a minor instead of a patch. Cost in-tree
is zero: every existing `match` already carries a wildcard arm, and
`ChangelogIssue`'s sole constructor is the `pub(crate)` `from_api`, so external
callers only ever receive one and read its fields.

Tests are wiremock-backed, no live network. Each round-2 regression test was
mutation-verified to fail against the pre-fix semantics.

Closes #4084
Closes #3966

fix: refuse cross-branch git push from managed worktrees (#2867) (#4090)

* fix: refuse cross-branch git push from managed worktrees

Two independent guards against the PR #2863 clobber shape, where a worktree
whose branch tracked a foreign PR branch ran a bare `git push` and destroyed
that PR's reviewed lineage.

Part A — never leave a worktree armed with a foreign upstream.
`configure_session_branch_tracking` wrote `branch.<session>.merge =
refs/heads/<default>` FIRST and pinned `push.default = current` afterwards,
both best-effort. Any failure of the pin (old git, unwritable base config,
sandboxed `git config`) therefore left the worktree tracking a branch it does
not own with nothing keeping a bare push off it. The pin is now established
first and READ BACK from the effective config stack; if it cannot be
confirmed, no upstream is written at all. Audited the other two upstream
writers: `RealGitBackend::worktree_add` never writes one (now locked in by a
test that enumerates every `branch.*.merge`), and `worktree_sync`'s fixture is
test-only and now mirrors the pinned production shape.

Part B — a `pre-push` hook that refuses a cross-branch push. The incident
worktree was created by an agent's own `git worktree add`, not by the
provisioner, and no live process owner was ever identified — so only a guard
that fires on the push itself can cover the real case. Verified empirically
(git 2.54.0) that `$GIT_COMMON_DIR/hooks` is shared by the base checkout,
linked worktrees, AND ad-hoc worktrees alike, and stays shared under
`extensions.worktreeConfig`, so one file installed at clone time covers every
worktree that base will ever host. A relative `core.hooksPath` was verified NOT
to work for this (it resolves per-worktree and silently never fires).
Installation refuses rather than overwrites when a foreign `pre-push` hook or a
`core.hooksPath` redirect is present, and is scoped to FRESH clones only —
retrofitting an already-provisioned base is an operator decision, not a session
side effect. `TM_ALLOW_CROSS_BRANCH_PUSH=1` permits a deliberate cross-ref push.

Closes #2867

locally before changing anything.

HIGH — the round-2 exemption rested on a FALSE empirical claim. It exempted
every anonymous-source push from a detached HEAD, reasoning that git refuses a
bare `git push` while detached so all such pushes must be explicit refspecs.
That `fatal: You are not currently on a branch` comes from `push.default`
resolution ONLY, and git never consults `push.default` when

    git checkout --detach HEAD && git commit -m "unrelated work"
    git push          ->  43a4c2b..ae8f65e  HEAD -> victim   (CLOBBERED)

`<remote sha>` field (all zeros on create), and never on HEAD state or on how
the push was spelled. A create cannot destroy a lineage that does not exist
yet; an update must come from a branch of the same name. Applied before the
name comparison, so it lands identically for named and anonymous sources and
for attached and detached HEAD — which also removes the round-2 asymmetry

fix(trusty-mpm): refuse to reclaim a worktree holding unsaved work (#4091)

## What

Adds the dirty-tree safety check the worktree reclaim path never had, and makes
destroying unsaved work require an explicit, separate opt-in.

Closes #4091.

## The defect, confirmed against the code

The issue's analysis holds exactly. Verified before changing anything:

- **The #3649 owner/sentinel guard works as described and is untouched by this
  PR.** `SentinelOwner::Unknown` → `owner_unknown`, reported but never fed to
  the deletion loop (`prune.rs:889-897` pre-change). `find_orphaned_worktrees`
  does walk all five shapes including `.base/.claude/worktrees/`. Owner-unknown
  ad-hoc worktrees were, and remain, never auto-deleted.
- **The gap was exactly the known-owner + dirty case.** Nothing in the reclaim
  path inspected `git status`, the index, or untracked files.
  `session_context_pause` prunes by default (`session_dispatch.rs:181-184` →
  `mcp_context.rs:172-197`, trailing `false` = not a dry run), so this fired on
  an ordinary `/tm-session-pause`.
- **One thing the issue did not say, which raises the stakes on the unpushed
  leg:** `decommission::remove_session_worktree` runs
  `git branch -D session/<leaf>` after a successful removal
  (`decommission.rs:100-120`). Committed-but-unpushed work is therefore not
  merely "left detached in the object store" — it loses its last reachable ref
  and becomes garbage-collectable. The unpushed check is load-bearing, not
  defence in depth.

## How "dirty" is defined

`session_manager::worktree_safety::inspect_dirt` returns `None` **only** when a
candidate is provably free of unsaved work. Dirty means any of:

1. **Working tree** — `git status --porcelain` reports an entry: modified or
   staged tracked files, and untracked-but-not-ignored files. Gitignored files
   are excluded (build artefacts are not work).
2. **Unpushed commits** — `<upstream>..HEAD` when the branch has an upstream;
   with no upstream, commits reachable from `HEAD` but from no remote-tracking
   ref (`rev-list --count HEAD --not --remotes`). In a repo with no remotes at
   all, `--remotes` expands to nothing and every commit counts as unpushed.
3. **Not a git worktree root, and not empty** — git cannot speak to it, so only
   an empty leftover shell (nothing but the ownership sentinel) is treated as
   clean. This preserves the #1838 case the sweep exists for.
4. **Any error** — see below.

A deliberate deviation from the issue's wording: for the no-upstream case the
check asks "is this commit on *any* remote-tracking ref", not specifically "is
it on `origin/main`". That subsumes the `origin/main` rule (a commit on neither
`origin/main` nor anything else is counted) while not flagging a branch that
genuinely *was* pushed under its own name without upstream tracking configured.

**Fail-safe direction.** Every error resolves to DIRTY: git that cannot spawn,
exits non-zero, or returns an unparsable count; a directory that cannot be read.
An error on the check never becomes a green light to delete.

**One carve-out, and it was found the hard way.** trusty-mpm writes two
artefacts into every managed worktree it creates — the `.trusty-mpm-worktree`
sentinel and the `.trusty-mpm/` scrollback directory — and host projects
typically do not gitignore them. The first draft counted them, which marked
*every* managed worktree permanently dirty; that would have shipped a guard that
silently disabled all reclamation and buried genuinely-dirty worktrees in noise.
Untracked entries at those two paths are excluded. A **tracked** edit under
`.trusty-mpm/` still counts as work
(`inspect_dirt_counts_tracked_trusty_mpm_edit`).

## Never silent, and hard to trigger by accident

A skip is surfaced as `OrphanSweepOutcome::skipped_dirty` (path, reason,
`dirty_files`, `unpushed_commits`) and propagated to every surface:
`skipped_dirty_worktrees` from the `session_context_pause` MCP tool, the
`prune-worktrees` HTTP response, stderr from `tm session prune-worktrees`, and a
per-path `warn!` from the daemon orphan-GC loop. The `/tm-session-pause` skill
is updated to require reporting them to the user.

The override is `DirtyWorktreePolicy::{Skip, ForceDiscard}` — an enum rather
than a `force: bool`, so it cannot be positionally confused with the
`dry_run: bool` beside it. `Skip` is the `Default`. `ForceDiscard` is reachable
only from `discard_dirty: true` on the HTTP route / `tm session prune-worktrees
--discard-dirty`. `--force` alone does **not** imply it. The pause path passes
`Skip` unconditionally and the pause tool's schema is closed with no
force/discard/dirty property at all — pinned by
`session_context_pause_schema_has_no_dirty_override`.

## Tests

All against throwaway `tempfile::tempdir()` git repos built by
`worktree_git_fixture`. No live worktree is touched.

Reclaim-path behaviour (`prune_orphan_tests`), each with an aged sentinel so the
#3649 gate *passes* and the new gate is the only thing that can spare it:

- `prune_orphaned_worktrees_skips_modified_tracked_file`
- `prune_orphaned_worktrees_skips_untracked_file`
- `prune_orphaned_worktrees_skips_unpushed_commit`
- `prune_orphaned_worktrees_reclaims_clean_pushed_worktree` — the control case;
  without it the guard could "pass" everything by never deleting anything
- `prune_orphaned_worktrees_skips_when_dirty_check_errors` — `git status` made
  to exit 128 while the worktree registration stays intact, so the candidate
  genuinely reaches the gate
- `prune_orphaned_worktrees_force_discards_dirty`
- `prune_orphaned_worktrees_default_policy_cannot_delete_dirty_work` — the
  regression test, asserting on `DirtyWorktreePolicy::default()` so it fails if
  anyone flips the default
- `prune_orphaned_worktrees_dry_run_reports_dirty_skip`

Checker in isolation (`worktree_safety_tests`), 12 tests including the
gitignored-files carve-out, the two bookkeeping exclusions and their
tracked-file counterweight, and the missing-path fail-safe. Plus
`prune_worktrees_request_defaults_to_skip_dirty` and
`cli_prune_worktrees_discard_dirty_is_opt_in`.

No test was `#[ignore]`d, cfg-gated, excluded, or deleted.

## Quality gate

```
cargo test -p trusty-mpm    -> 3635 passed; 0 failed (lib)
                               1240 passed; 0 failed (bin tm)
                               1240 passed; 0 failed (bin trusty-mpm)
                               + all integration targets, 0 failed
cargo clippy -p trusty-mpm --all-targets -- -D warnings -> clean
cargo fmt --all --check        -> clean
scripts/check_line_cap.sh      -> 7 allowlisted, 0 violations - OK
scripts/check_test_pointers.sh -> 0 dangling pointers - OK
cargo check --workspace --all-targets \
  --exclude trusty-mpm-gui --exclude trusty-code-gui -> clean
```

`cargo check --workspace` without those two exclusions fails on
`trusty-mpm-gui` / `trusty-code-gui` with `frontendDist ... "ui/dist" ...
doesn't exist`. That is pre-existing and environmental: `ui/dist` is a build
artefact with zero tracked files (`git ls-files .../ui/dist` -> 0), so it is
absent in any fresh checkout, and this branch touches no GUI code.

`prune.rs` lands at 494 SLOC against the 500 cap — `git_worktree_list_agrees`
was moved verbatim into the new module to make room. Worth knowing before the
next change to that file.

## Residual risk — what this does NOT protect

- **`git stash` entries are not checked.** The stash is repo-level, not
  per-worktree, and stashed work survives worktree removal, but a stash created
  *in* a worktree that is then deleted is easy to lose track of.
- **Untracked files under `.trusty-mpm/`** are excluded by design. Anything an
  agent wrote there is not protected.
- **Gitignored files are excluded by design.** If real work lives in a
  gitignored path (a local `.env`, a scratch dir named in `.gitignore`), it is
  not seen.
- **The non-git empty-shell carve-out.** A directory that is not a git worktree
  root and contains nothing but the sentinel is still removed without further
  inspection.
- **TOCTOU.** The check runs before removal; work written between the check and
  the `git worktree remove` is not seen. The pre-existing residual window
  documented on `prune_orphaned_worktrees` is unchanged.
- **`--discard-dirty` still destroys work**, by design. Nothing stops an
  operator from passing it.
- **Nothing here protects against removal by any path other than this sweep** —
  a manual `rm -rf`, or the out-of-band deleter behind #3715, is untouched.

* fix(trusty-search): reap stale cold-store record on create/relocate/reindex

Round-2's write-side collision guard (find_root_path_collision now scanning
state.cold_store) fixed the theft direction but never reclaimed the
now-dead cold record left behind when an id is re-created at a new root:
create_index(foo, root_new) over a cold foo->root_old left root_old
permanently claimed, falsely 409-rejecting any later unrelated
create_index(bar, root_old).

Fix: create_index_handler, relocate_index_handler, and the reindex
root_path override all call cold_store.mark_loaded(&id) after a
successful (re)registration, reaping only the record for the exact id
just registered (mark_loaded is keyed by IndexId, never by root_path, so
an unrelated id's legitimate claim on its own root is untouched).
relocate/reindex cannot themselves create the hole (both require the id
to already be live to reach the write), so their calls are
defense-in-depth against residual corruption predating this fix.

Leaves the reindex override's narrower pre-existing TOCTOU window
(two concurrent overrides racing onto one unclaimed root) as a follow-up:
unlike create/relocate, reindex has no synchronous fresh-corpus open to
hang a corpus_open_failed backstop on, so closing it needs a
registration-wide lock -- a larger change than this fix's scope.

* fix(trusty-search): close mark_loaded/cold_park_index orphan race (#3993 round 4)

PR #3995 round 4 (HIGH): the round-3 `ColdIndexStore::mark_loaded` reap,
called by create/relocate/reindex-override right after each registers a
fresh handle, is an uncoordinated second writer of `cold_store.entries`,
racing the residency-sweep's `cold_park_index`. Since both mutate the map
with no `.await` between their DashMap ops, a relocate (or reindex-override)
racing a residency-park of the same id could leave it in neither the live
registry nor the cold store.

`cold_park_index` now snapshots the handle it intends to park before
inserting the cold entry, and compares that snapshot against whatever
`remove_and_get` actually removes via `Arc::ptr_eq`. On a mismatch, the
swapped-in handle is restored (new `IndexRegistry::restore`, identity-
preserving) and the park's own cold-store insertion is undone, so the id is
never left in neither store.

(cold_park_index_restores_concurrently_swapped_handle_instead_of_orphaning)
using a test-only hook seam that lands the concurrent write's exact sequence
inside the race window — RED at pre-fix head, GREEN after.

fix(trusty-mpm): serialize concurrent ~/.claude.json trust seeds (#4075)

`core::home_trust_seed::preseed_home_trust` and
`core::session_launch::settings::preseed_workspace_trust` both perform an
unsynchronised load -> mutate -> store cycle over the SAME `~/.claude.json`,
and the daemon runs them concurrently: `provisioner::workspace` calls the
former and then, via `prepare_session`, the latter, once per provisioned
session, from independent tokio tasks.

Two defects fall out of that:

1. Lost update. The slower writer serialised the snapshot it read BEFORE the
   faster writer's store, silently deleting that session's whole
   `projects.<workspace>` entry -- trust acceptance AND its
   `enabledMcpjsonServers` approval. Nothing was logged; both writes
   "succeeded". The operator then hit the exact "Do you trust the files in
   this folder?" / "new MCP servers found" dialog the seed exists to dismiss.

2. Torn write. `preseed_workspace_trust` used a truncating `std::fs::write`
   (unlike `preseed_home_trust`, already atomic), so a concurrent reader could
   observe a half-written file. Every reader in this crate treats malformed
   JSON as "skip, leave it alone", so the seed was silently lost.

Fix: both seeders hold one process-wide lock (`core::claude_json_guard`)
across the whole read -> mutate -> store cycle, and `preseed_workspace_trust`
writes through `trusty_common::claude_config::write_json_atomic`.

This also removes the recurring CI flake in
`core::session_launch::tests_manifest_toggle_trust_3934::prepare_session_excludes_spoofed_trusty_search_when_injector_disabled`,
red on the full-workspace Test job for PRs #4057 and #4067 (neither touching
`session_launch`) and green in isolation. The lib test binary runs `#[serial]`
tests that redirect the process-global `$HOME` to a temp dir alongside
non-serial tests that resolve `$HOME` at call time and drive the real
provisioner, so a foreign test's seed landed in -- and clobbered -- the serial
test's temp `.claude.json`, leaving the panic
`enabledMcpjsonServers is an array`.

Regression coverage (`tests_claude_json_concurrency_4072.rs`) drives the real
seeders from 8 threads against one file, with a distinct workspace key per
cycle so a clobber cannot self-heal. Against the unmodified pre-fix code both
tests fail with the two defects above:

    a seeded .claude.json must always be valid JSON: Error("trailing characters", line: 94, column: 2)
    the two seeders clobbered 29 of 80 entries when run concurrently against one ~/.claude.json

Closes #4072

* feat(trusty-agents): report dead [tools].scopes grants instead of silently denying everything

Refs #3987 (option C).

`ScopePattern` matching fails closed AND silent. An agent that declares a
scope pattern no tool can ever advertise gets no error, no log line — just a
persona whose entire scoped tool surface is dropped before the model sees
the registry. That is indistinguishable from "this agent has no tools",
which is exactly how #3938 and #3987 both stayed invisible.

The motivating case is the bundled base `assistant`'s `google.read`: every
gworkspace tool's dotted scope is `google.<family>.<access>`
(`registry::google_scope`), and `google.read` is a no-wildcard pattern
requiring string equality, so it matches nothing at all.

This adds `tools::registry::dead_scope`, a pure detector, and wires it into
two surfaces:

- `ctrl::pm_task::dispatch::persona` — the #3208 enforcement site and the
  only place holding BOTH the agent's post-`extends` scope patterns and the
  vocabulary the registry actually built. A dead pattern now emits a
  prominent WARN naming the agent, the pattern, and the nearest reachable
  scopes, so the log line is actionable rather than merely alarming.
- `GET /api/agents/{name}/skills` — a `dead_scope_patterns` array, the
  scope-side analogue of the existing `unmatched_patterns`, so the GUI/CLI
  can show "this agent has dead scope grants" instead of rendering
  `granted: true` cards for tools dispatch will drop.

No false positives by construction: reachability is the union of the live
registry's discovered scopes and the closed compile-time Google vocabulary
derived from `FAMILY_TABLE`, and a pattern is only judged when its namespace
appears in that set. A `gworkspace` or `trusty-memory` daemon being down can
therefore never make a working grant look broken.

Deliberately a WARN and not a load error: the shipped base `assistant` still
carries the dead `google.read`, and every `extends = "assistant"` overlay
inherits it by union, so failing closed here would break every assistant
load on this very commit. Escalation to a hard error is the intended
follow-up once #3987's option B removes the pattern from the shipped base —
stated in `dead_scope`'s module doc, at the `persona.rs` call site, and in

feat(trusty-agents): function skills — grant a capability bundle with one line (#4052)

* feat(trusty-agents): function skills — grant a capability bundle with one line

Adds a *bundling* tier above the one-skill-per-tool base shipped in #3964. A
`SkillKind::Function` row names a fixed, compile-time set of member skill ids
instead of wrapping a tool, and naming it in `[skills].allow` grants every
member — epic #4021's OQ-1, resolved *grant-the-bundle* by the owner on
2026-07-26. The first exemplar is **Ticketing**, bundling the ten existing
`ticket-*` leaf skills.

The 1:1 model is untouched. Every tool still maps to exactly one leaf skill,
every leaf stays independently grantable, and a bundle **compiles down** to
those leaves inside `SkillCatalog::expand` — *before* the three permission
layers run. The 1:1 layer and the allow-glob/RBAC/scope gates therefore never
see a bundle id, only exact leaf tool names, so #3964's defence in depth (exact
ids, no glob dialect, the glob-laundering fix) applies to a bundle unchanged
rather than by a parallel implementation that can drift. That is pinned twice:
`function_skill_never_leaks_its_bundle_id_into_the_tool_patterns` at the
manifest layer and `skills_route_bundle_grant_never_shows_the_bundle_id_as_a_tool`
at the audit surface.

Bundles are built-in `const` data only. The authored `.md` frontmatter dialect
has no `members:` key and its parser requires a `tools:` list, so no file
dropped into a skill source can widen one grant into N — a bundle is the one
skill shape that turns one config line into N capabilities, which is exactly
the shape a privilege-escalation bug wants, so the set stays closed, reviewable
in a diff, and test-checked. Membership is an explicit list rather than a
`ticket-*` prefix scan for the same reason: a prefix scan is a glob dialect
reintroduced through the back door (DOC-57 S-8's "no prefix grouping"), and it
would silently absorb any future `ticket-`-prefixed skill into an existing
grant.

A bundle naming a member no manifest resolves is a MANIFEST VALIDATION ERROR
caught at build/test time — `SkillCatalog::unknown_function_members`, a
`debug_assert!` in `SkillCatalog::builtin`, and
`builtin_function_skills_declare_only_known_members` in CI — rather than a
runtime surprise. If one reaches production anyway, expansion still narrows:
the member contributes zero tools and is reported in `unresolved`, never "all
tools". Partial resolution is reported rather than dropping the whole bundle,
since revoking nine working capabilities over one typo is the worse failure.
Member recursion carries a cycle guard so a catalog bug is a bounded, logged
no-op instead of a stack overflow.

`GET /api/agents/:name/skills` surfaces bundles ADDITIVELY (the discipline
DOC-58 §5.3 set for `/stores`): every field a pre-#4022 consumer reads keeps
its name, type and meaning. Function skills appear as ordinary `skills[]` cards
with `kind: "function"`, and every card — leaf or bundle — now carries
`members`, `granted_members` and a tri-state `granted_state`
(`"all"`/`"some"`/`"none"` of the members), so a consumer needs no kind check
before reading a field. A new top-level `groups[]` index gives the Skills pane
(#4024) group headers without re-deriving membership, built from the SAME
single computation as the cards so the two can never disagree. The boolean
`granted` keeps its old meaning — for a bundle it is `granted_state == "all"`,
the conservative answer — and `granted_count` still counts capabilities,
excluding bundles. A bundle is also excluded from the tool-less "granted by
being named" clause: its state is derived from its members, the only answer
that stays true when a member fails to resolve.

Per the domain authority (epic #4021 section D), the ticketing DOMAIN routes to
the subagent modality when one is available; the Ticketing function skill is
the direct-skill fallback, and its description says so.

fix(trusty-common): bound the palace open-queue wait under sustained writer contention (#3996)

Closes #3992.

PalaceRegistry::open_palace serialises concurrent opens of the same
palace id behind a per-palace open_lock, previously acquired with an
unbounded Mutex::lock(). Each individual try_open_or_snapshot retry
under OpenIntent::Writer is already bounded (~1.55s), but a failed
Writer open is never cached, so every caller queued behind the lock
repeated that bounded dance from scratch -- the Nth queued caller
waited for N-1 earlier callers' own attempts to finish first, with no
ceiling on the total wait.

Reproduced live against a real held redb lock (not mocked): 5
concurrent openers made the 5th caller wait 9.86s; this exact
linear-with-queue-depth growth is how a single memory_remember call
was observed to hang for 1800s under sustained multi-process
contention.

open_palace now acquires the lock via try_lock_for, bounded by a new,
independently-tunable memory_core::timeouts::open_queue_timeout()
(default 60s, TRUSTY_OPEN_QUEUE_TIMEOUT_SECS) -- kept separate from
the existing write_lock_timeout (issue #906) since the two guard
different pipelines. A caller stuck behind persistent contention now
gets a clear, actionable ERROR instead of hanging indefinitely.

* fix(trusty-search): staged-write-then-swap for periodic HNSW snapshot (#3970)

The periodic HNSW incremental persister used to checkpoint straight to
the live snapshot path every HNSW_SNAPSHOT_BATCH_INTERVAL batches during
every reindex. Reindex progress is monotonic, so any reasonably large
reindex crossed UsearchStore::save's shrink guard threshold as ordinary
healthy progress, silently replacing the complete pre-reindex snapshot
with a partial one — an ungraceful crash after that point permanently
stranded the index. PR #3968 closed the equivalent race for the graceful
shutdown path only; this closes it for the periodic persister itself.

The periodic persister now redirects its checkpoints to a staging path
while a reindex is Running (CodeIndexer::begin/end_reindex_staging,
PersistState::reindexing) and publishes to the live path in one atomic
rename only when the reindex reaches Ready, reusing the exact same
StagingResolution the redb corpus swap already computes. Any other
outcome discards the staged snapshot and leaves the live one untouched.
Mirrors the redb corpus's existing atomic staged-swap (#603/#839) via
the new service::reindex::hnsw_swap module. Incremental checkpointing
during the reindex is fully preserved — the persister is never skipped,
only its destination changes.

* fix(trusty-search): close two round-2 CRITICALs in the HNSW staged swap

Round-2 adversarial review of #3970's staged-write-then-swap found two
CRITICALs in the swap logic itself, traced to concrete mechanics:

1. The staging->live swap renamed the binary before the sidecar. A crash
   strictly between the two renames left NEW binary + OLD sidecar, whose
   restored next_key sits BEHIND actual usage in the binary -- letting a
   later upsert allocate an already-occupied key and silently overwrite
   an unrelated vector. Fixed by renaming the sidecar FIRST: the only
   possible torn state is then OLD binary + NEW sidecar, whose next_key
   is always ahead of (never behind) actual usage, structurally
   preventing the collision. UsearchStore::load_from also now refuses to
   load a binary reporting MORE vectors than its sidecar describes, as
   defense-in-depth against a torn pairing from any other source.

2. commit_staged_hnsw_swap / abort_staged_hnsw_swap cleared the
   `reindexing` flag as their first action. spawn_incremental_persist is
   a bare detached tokio::spawn with no tracked JoinHandle, so a
   periodic checkpoint task that outlived the reindex's batch loop could
   still be mid-coalescing-loop when the flag was cleared; its next
   iteration would then observe `reindexing == false` and write the
   (for an aborted reindex, partial) in-memory store straight to the
   live path -- reproducing #3970 through a race. Fixed by adding
   CodeIndexer::wait_for_incremental_persist_drain and calling it before
   touching anything else, only clearing the flag once the swap (or
   abort cleanup) has fully resolved.

Also corrects a citation: the CHANGELOG now attributes the "next reindex
redoes the whole walk from scratch" gap to #3979 (its own tracked issue)
instead of #3969 (a different problem -- a reindex never automatically
retrying at all for non-HEAD-driven runs), and states plainly that this
fix buys bounded memory and a safe complete crash-recovery baseline, not
resume-from-partial-progress.

deletion (single-file removal, prune passes, bulk corpus reduction) is
never blocked no matter how large the reduction — only vectors that are
simply missing with no recorded reason trip the guard, which is exactly

An `okg_ingest_*` call wrote markdown into the KB tree and stopped there, while
`vector_search` queried an index built over an unrelated root — so an ingest
could report "N entities ingested" truthfully and the assistant would still
find nothing, with no error on either side. `okg://<agent>` was an opaque label
nothing ever resolved to a path.

Remediation (a), owner-approved: ingestion now also feeds the store's bound
index. The operator's index-root configuration is untouched.

- trusty-kb `okg::index_journal`: a second append-only journal per source
  recording what reached the index and at what content hash, plus
  `okg_index_backlog`, the pure reconcile against the item ledger. The ledger
  stays KB-tree truth — gating a ledger line on a reachable daemon would make
  ingestion non-convergent, and the ledger's own unchanged-skip would hide an
  unindexed entity forever.
- trusty-agents `stores::index_feed`: the `IndexFeed` seam, `HttpIndexFeed`
  over the daemon's index-file/remove-file routes, and the drive loop.
  Push-then-record ordering, whole-backlog reconcile every run,
  withdraw-before-replace, withdraw-on-tombstone. Fail-open, never silent:
  every run reports indexed/removed/pending plus a reason.
- trusty-agents `stores::binding`: `okg://<agent>` resolves through the SAME
  slugify as `Roots::resolve`, and a push into an index bound to a different
  tree is refused.
- Preflight found by live verification: trusty-search post-filters results
  whose path escapes the index root, so a foreign-rooted index is refused with
  the remediation instead of storing pushes nothing can return.

  index; the stores endpoint adds tree_path + pending_index/synced_index.

An agent's `[[stores]]` binding (#3878) was inert on the chat path. `persona.rs`
read `stores.default_search_index()` to route `vector_search` and nothing else,
so `binding.palace` never reached inference and the runtime handed the model no
memory at all. Izzie consequently told the owner "I don't have memories that
persist across conversations — each time we talk, I start fresh" while her
`owner-profile` palace held her `identity` drawer plus ~10 profile drawers and
her `bob-kb` index (552 chunks) was live and connected.

Each persona turn now:
- unconditionally injects the agent's `identity`-tagged drawers and semantically
  recalls the turn's query against the bound palace;
- prepends an introspected memory-architecture section built from live probe
  data (palace id + whether it answered, index id, real chunk count) rather than
  a hardcoded "you have infinite memory" literal — introspection over injection;
- persists the turn to the bound palace's chat-session store as one continuous,
  resumable session per agent, off the response path.

Fails open throughout: an unreachable palace renders "temporarily unreachable —
your stored memories still exist", never an absence of memory, and an agent with
no binding sees a byte-identical prompt. The block is appended last so the whole
preceding prompt prefix stays cache-stable (DOC-54 §9.6.3).

Recalled drawer content is UNTRUSTED — it arrives from Gmail/Drive ingestion and
the agent's own memory.write scope, and lands in the system message of a persona
holding compose_email, manage_drive_file, and delegate_to_agent. It is fenced in

preamble, and every line is neutralized: envelope tag escaped, fence runs
collapsed, leading ATX `#` escaped, mandatory indent, and CRLF/bare-CR line
endings normalized first so no segment can dodge the pass and reach column 0 as
forged prompt structure. The block's factual precedence is explicitly FACTS ONLY
and subordinate to the never-follow-embedded-instructions rule.

persona via `extends` prose concatenation — forbidding the false stateless
self-description, barring overclaiming, and bounding trust in recalled content.

describes its memory truthfully in both directions; turns persist to the bound

fix(trusty-code): durable backstop alarm for a cadence floor breach (#3941)

* fix(trusty-code): durable backstop alarm for a cadence floor breach (#3911)

The load-realistic compression soak (epic #3866, PR #3909) proved the
reactive/fallback compactor never engages even when cadence's own 60%
working-context floor is breached under heavy load (48% floor in the
exploratory run, 21 of 73 samples below target) — the safety net does
not exist for the one condition where it matters most.

Root cause: cadence::enforce_budget's own "documented floor" case
(active zone shrunk to zero, still over the overhead cap) only ever
logged tracing::warn! from deep inside that function -- no durable
record, no counter, and not the same alarm the #2308 threshold
compactor's own breach uses. That alarm cannot help either: it is keyed
to a mechanically INDEPENDENT trigger -- threshold fires once the raw
transcript crosses 75% of the context window
(CompactionConfig::for_context_window), a laxer bound than cadence's
own 40%-overhead enforcement cap. By the time cadence has already
compacted as hard as it structurally can (enforce_budget shrinks the
active zone to zero, re-compacting at every step) and still exceeds its
OWN cap, the transcript is nowhere near threshold's separate, higher
bound -- so threshold's trigger condition cannot observe a cadence-level
breach at all. The two mechanisms share no signal path, exactly as the
issue suspected.

Design decision: this adds an ALARM backstop, not additional
compaction. enforce_budget already exhausted every eligible entry
before returning within_budget: false -- the remaining content is
exactly the pinned/system/user-exempt active zone (typically a single
turn's own oversized tool-call argument), which by design can never be
evicted while still being sent to the model. No eviction-based
compaction strategy -- cadence's or threshold's, both share the same
mark_compacted exemptions -- can shrink that further without violating
the "preserve pinned skill output / user requests forever" invariant.
An aggressive backstop that tried to compact harder here would either
be a no-op (nothing left to evict) or would have to break that
invariant; instead, this makes the breach durable and countable:
agent_loop::telemetry::record_cadence_floor_breach writes a
tcode-cadence-floor-breach JSONL row plus a durable alarm line
(mirroring the existing compaction_alarm.log design), the prior warn!
is elevated to error! at the maybe_cadence_compress call site, and a
new lifetime_cadence_floor_breach_count field surfaces the count on
session.get_context_budget (stacked on #3912's low-water-mark fields).
compression_report.py gains a dedicated section reporting whether the
backstop engaged on any observed floor breach.

Validated against both compression_load_soak.py profiles: the backstop
now fires on every observed breach -- 2 fires in the primary
(160/230/300KB) run (matching its 2 samples at the 60% floor) and 21
fires in the exploratory (220/300/400KB) run (matching its 21
below-target samples exactly). Session fidelity held in both runs.

Residual limit: this closes the observability/alarm gap, not the
compaction-capacity gap. The measured floor itself is unchanged (still
60%/48% in these two profiles) -- a session whose single turn's own
tool-call argument exceeds the overhead cap will still breach the
floor; the backstop's job is to make that breach visible and countable
in production, not to prevent it. A genuinely harder profile could
still show a breach; it will now be alarmed rather than silent.

unconditionally (whenever outcome.rounds > 0, which every breach
satisfies) BEFORE record_cadence_floor_breach, for the SAME turn, with
identical tokens_before/outcome.overhead_tokens/context_window -- so
both rows carried the same working_context_pct_after. Neither
compression_report.py's compute_context_floor nor this crate's own

session_working_context_floor, and anything built on top of either --
inherits the fix for free. The paired tcode-cadence row remains the one
authoritative percentage sample for that turn; this row's only job is
to durably flag THAT a breach happened (tokens_before/tokens_after/

* fix(trusty-mpm): sessions/project list shows daemon-managed sessions (#3822)

`ProjectRegistry::auto_register_from_sessions` only ever ran ONCE per
daemon process -- inside `DaemonState::project_registry()`'s
`OnceCell::get_or_init`, seeded from whatever session snapshot existed
the moment ANY of its 15+ call sites (a status poll, an MCP tool,
`resolve_gh_env`, ...) first touched the registry, frequently before
any session existed. Nothing else called that pass again, so a
project implied by a session spawned afterward was registered
nowhere -- even though the daemon plainly knew about the session

registered" for a live, daemon-managed session forever.

counterpart to the one-shot boot pass, called at spawn time from all
three managed-session creation paths (`spawn_managed_cloned`,
`spawn_managed_inproject`, `spawn_managed_local` in
`daemon::managed_routes::lifecycle`) right after the session record
is persisted -- registration no longer depends on which caller
happened to touch the registry first.

DIFFERENT, intentionally-scoped commands (`list` = this project's
local pre-session-manager sessions; `ls` = daemon-managed sessions
from anywhere, already correctly global with no scoping bug) -- not

* fix(trusty-agents): protect the live-turn recency window in trim_to_budget

Code-critic MEDIUM on PR #3777: the water-fill truncation had no recency
weighting. In a uniformly-sized long conversation (no megabyte outlier), it
shrank the NEWEST message too — losing the guarantee that oldest-first eviction
implicitly gave (the newest turn survived at full fidelity). Empirically: 1
system + 10 × 12,000-byte messages under gpt-4's ~12.8k budget returned
truncated=10 and shrank the newest 12,000→5,055 bytes.

trim_to_budget now splits the history into three regions — protected header,
OLD history, and a RECENCY window (the live turn: from the last user message to
the end) — and applies strategies in increasing order of damage:
  1. water-fill-truncate only the OLD region, keeping header + newest turn full;
  2. evict oldest OLD messages (never header, never recency);
  3. last resort — truncate within the recency window ONLY when the oversized
     message is itself in the live turn (the #3776 MCP shape), so the question
     and every tool pairing survive rather than being evicted.

The recency window is defined by the last user message rather than a fixed K,
because the MCP live turn spans three messages (question, tool-call, result) —
a fixed K=2 would leave the question in the OLD region and re-break #3776 by
evicting it. Adds trim_preserves_newest_turn_in_uniform_history (the critic's
repro: newest turn byte-for-byte intact, old history shrinks) and
trim_truncates_oversized_result_inside_live_turn (pins the original MCP shape:
in-turn oversized result truncates, question survives). CHANGELOG updated to
state the recency guarantee explicitly.

fix(trusty-search): size-order deferred-embed catch-up queue + recompute warm_boot_degraded (#3770)

* fix: size-order deferred-embed catch-up queue + recompute warm_boot_degraded

Deferred-embed (C2) catch-up was strictly serial and size-blind: one
oversized repo (e.g. 94k chunks) that finished its fast pass before
smaller repos would head-of-line-block every other index's semantic
readiness for hours, and the boot-time warm_boot_degraded flag never
re-evaluated once catch-up finished.

- New service::reindex::defer_embed_queue module: each index's C2 job
  cooperatively polls a shared min-heap ordered ascending by chunk
  count (FIFO tiebreak for equal sizes), with a wall-clock
  anti-starvation gate (MAX_WAIT = 750ms) so a large job can never be
  starved indefinitely by a steady trickle of newer, smaller arrivals.
  Per-index tasks (not a single shared dispatcher) so no job's fate is
  coupled to an unrelated caller's task lifetime.
- GET /health now recomputes warmboot_summary.warm_boot_degraded when
  the catch-up queue fully drains, folding in a live scan for any
  index with a Failed stage so a genuinely failed embed pass still
  counts as degraded, instead of leaving the flag frozen at its
  boot-time value until a daemon restart.
- No embedder-concurrency or worker-pool changes (slice B).

* fix: correct anti-starvation semantics + key on pending embed delta

Code-critic BLOCK follow-up on #3770 (issue #3748 slice A):

1. CRITICAL: the anti-starvation gate promoted the oldest pending job
   purely because it had waited MAX_WAIT, full stop. Since an entire
   warm-boot burst enqueues within milliseconds, once the whole burst
   collectively aged past MAX_WAIT — guaranteed for any burst that
   legitimately takes a while to drain by size — best_pending_seq
   would select min-by-seq among all of them, i.e. raw arrival
   (directory-walk) order, with the giant back near the front.
   Corrected semantics: only promote the oldest pending job when some
   OTHER pending job's enqueued_at is a full MAX_WAIT LATER than the
   oldest job's own arrival — a genuinely later wave overtaking it,
   not merely a job that's been sitting in the same burst a while.
   Every job in a single burst shares near-identical enqueued_at
   timestamps, so no same-burst job can ever trigger a promotion
   against another, regardless of total drain time. MAX_WAIT also
   moves from 750ms to 5 minutes now that it measures inter-wave gap
   rather than raw age. New tests:
   same_burst_never_reverts_to_arrival_order_even_once_max_wait_has_elapsed

* fix(trusty-agents): render chat stream inside one stable bubble — no flicker

The GUI chat reply bubble visibly flickered as `task-delta` tokens arrived.
Two root causes, both re-rendering the bubble mid-stream instead of filling
one stable node in place:

1. Each delta fired TWO separate `messages` store writes — `updateMessageByTask`
   (content) then `setMessageSpeakerByTask` (speaker) — so the keyed `{#each}`
   reconciled and the `afterUpdate` scroll reflow ran twice per token.
2. `task-delta` events carry the REAL backend id, but the placeholder bubble
   still held its client-side `pending-<ts>` id until the poll loop reconciled
   it. So the first tokens matched no message and were dropped, and the poll
   loop's interim "Running…" progress text flashed into the bubble before the
   streamed text replaced it.

Fix: a single `streamDeltaIntoTask` store write funnels content + speaker
through ONE update and, via the pure `fillDeltaIntoList`, adopts the in-flight
`pending-` assistant bubble on the FIRST delta so token #1 onward render inside
the one existing bubble — its `id` is preserved, so the keyed `{#each}` never
re-mounts it. Identical/empty frames no-op (same array reference) so they
trigger no render or scroll reflow. `StreamAccumulator` is now a shared module
singleton (`streamAccumulator`) that both `ChatView` (grows the bubble) and
`InputArea` (gates its progress reconcile) consult, so neither ever overwrites
live streamed text; the authoritative `task-complete` narrative still replaces
the accumulation on completion, matching the non-streaming path.

* fix(trusty-channels): translator delimiter-collision bugs flagged by code-critic on PR #3755

Root cause across all four correctness bugs: the AST->text renderer had no
delimiter-collision awareness, so caller content could silently corrupt or
truncate on reparse -- exactly what the translator promises never to do.

1. table.rs render_table: escape a rendered cell's `|` before pipe-joining,
   or a literal `|` splits the cell (and drops the following cell) on
   reparse. Escapes ONLY the pipe, not backslash -- inline::escape_text
   already backslash-escapes every real `\` at the Text-node level, so
   re-escaping it in escape_cell would double-escape (`\\` -> `\\\\`),
   itself corrupting content; caught by the new round-trip test.

2. inline.rs Code arm: size the code-span delimiter to
   (longest backtick run in literal)+1 backticks (min 1), with a single
   space of padding on both sides when the literal starts/ends with a
   backtick or is empty, per CommonMark's own code-span rule.

3. blocks.rs render_code_block: fence length = max(3, longest backtick run
   in literal + 1) for both the opening and closing fence, so a code block
   documenting a fenced-code-block example doesn't close early.

4. lists.rs render_item: continuation-line indent must equal CommonMark's
   *structural* list-item content column (marker.len() + 1: the bullet or
   ordinal-plus-delimiter, plus one required space) -- verified empirically
   against comrak directly. This is NOT the same as the item's full rendered
   prefix width: a task-list checkbox ("[ ] "/"[x] ") is a pure inline-level

   and does not widen the block-level content column at all. Indenting a

   the real 2-column content column by 4, which crosses CommonMark's
